description: Strange Loop Conference talks from Strange Loop Conference 2022.

talks.title: "Birdsong as code" by Chris Ford (Strange Loop 2023)
talks.teaser: Live coding turns birdsong into executable models that contrast avian linear pitch with human equal temperament.
talks.summary:
The session opens with live Clojure in Vim driving Overtone, using a simple numeric example to show how code can express structure more clearly than a flat list of values. The speaker argues that programmable notation complements spectrograms and staff paper because it can be reshaped for the question at hand, then grounds the work in zoo musicology and Hollis Taylor’s framing of birds as artistic collaborators rather than specimens.

From shared physics of sound the talk builds oscillators, envelopes, and layered harmonics, then contrasts human equal-temperament stepping (twelfth roots of two) with a bird-oriented linear harmonic series. Octave equivalence is treated as a human listening habit birds may lack. For the pied butcherbird, a recognizable species motif and a passage from Taylor’s materials are encoded with overtone-based pitches; a rough squared-error comparison favors the linear model on that excerpt over the human scale.

The close maps butcherbird harmonics onto a keyboard, highlights missing and overcrowded notes across octaves, and rejects treating song as isolated regression targets. A final ensemble layers multiple synthesized birds with keyboard rhythm and harmony to mirror a dawn chorus where birds neither share tuning nor fill human rhythmic roles.

talks.title: "Software & The Game of Go" by David Nolen (Strange Loop 2023)
talks.teaser: Draws parallels between the game of Go's history and rules and the practice of writing and managing software.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the history of Go, a board game played for at least 2,500 years, and why its ancient commentators compared it to life. Unlike chess, where pieces are removed and positions can be reached without a visible path, Go places stones that never move, so the final board records everything that happened. The speaker walks through key moments: the Japanese Honinbo houses supported under the Tokugawa shogunate, the shift toward tournament play in the 20th century, and the rise of Korean players, before tying the 2016 match between AlphaGo and Lee Sedol to that longer story.

Next comes a rules primer. Stones sit on intersections, liberties are the open lines touching a group, and a group with no liberties is captured. The suicide rule and the ko rule prevent certain illegal moves and endless loops, scoring counts territory plus prisoners, and white receives compensation for moving second. The speaker then lists the golden rules of Go, such as greed never wins, do not rush in blindly, drop small and save big, and strong walls over weak stones, and maps each one to software and product work, including constraints that shape good design and fundamentals that outlast passing trends.

The talk closes with advice for newcomers: start with graded problem books and beginner texts, play on online servers such as KGS and Pandanet, review games with strong engine analysis, and join a local club. The takeaway is that the game's ideas about tradeoffs, balance and long-term influence transfer to engineering and management practice.

talks.title: "Cursorless: A spoken language for editing code" by Pokey Rule (Strange Loop 2023)
talks.teaser: Shows how a spoken language built on Talon lets programmers edit code by voice using targets, modifiers and scopes.
talks.summary:
Pokey Rule, who has programmed by voice for several years after a repetitive strain injury made keyboards painful, introduces Cursorless, an open source spoken language built on the Talon voice tool for editing text and code. The argument is that voice differs from typing: spoken vocabulary can be composed into rich commands, but each command carries a small delay, so commands should chain together and reuse words people already know.

The core model has five abstractions: marks, which produce targets; modifiers, which pass targets down a pipeline defined by scopes; and actions, which operate on the final target. Targets carry attributes such as content range, removal edit and insertion mode, so actions like wrap, chuck, paste, bring, move and clone can behave correctly without special cases. Scopes come in dumb forms like token, line, paint and round that work in any text, and smart forms like argument, call and function that rely on Tree-sitter parse trees. The walkthrough builds up a single command that clones the first argument of every function call in a sample document.

Rule explains that this style is tacit, or point-free, similar to Bash pipelines and jq, and suits short interactive edits rather than large maintained programs. He closes with planned work: interactive tutorials, support in more editors, a richer grammar, bookmarking targets across commands, and using language models for actions or scopes such as sentences.

talks.title: "Using data-driven metrics to anticipate and prevent security incidents" by Caitlin Buckshaw
talks.teaser: Shows how GitHub's product security team turns incident data into trends, better preventions and variant analysis.
talks.summary:
The talk explains how GitHub's product security team set up a follow-up group to study bugs after incident response and the postmortem are complete. The speaker, who took on her first incident as incident commander after a bug bounty report that led to seven CVEs, notes that responders often move straight to the next case, leaving little time to ask how a flaw was missed and how to prevent it.

The team's goals were to capture data on every incident, spot trends across product areas, share findings with the right teams, and run variant analysis. Incident details flow through a Slack bot into GitHub issues, then into databases and dashboards built with Python and pandas. A scoring calculator loosely modeled on CVSS applies multipliers for repeated bugs in an area, severity, whether a notification went out, bypassed preventions, bug class and variants found. Findings are shared in biweekly discussion posts, biweekly meetings with engineering, bug bounty and security champion participants, and quarterly and annual reports. Reviews stay blameless throughout.

Variant analysis runs automatically when an area receives more than two bugs in a short period, and for high-risk bugs or those that bypass a prevention. A rotating working group combines dynamic and manual testing, code search, CodeQL, Brakeman and custom authorization tools, and documents results even when no variants are found. After one year the speaker reports more internal findings, improved preventions and stronger collaboration, while noting that the effort is effectively a one-person team drawing on many others and that limited time means not every incident gets this deep review.

talks.title: "Oatmeal is Cheap: A Fundamental Theorem for Procedural Generators" by Younès Rabii
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for "Oatmeal is Cheap: A Fundamental Theorem for Procedural Generators" by Younès Rabii.

talks.title: "Swift as C++ Successor in FoundationDB" by Konrad Malawski (Strange Loop 2023)
talks.teaser: Shows how Swift was added incrementally beside an existing C++ database codebase, bringing memory and concurrency safety.
talks.summary:
The talk is a case study of adopting Swift inside FoundationDB, an open-source distributed key-value store written predominantly in C++. The team wanted to eliminate memory and concurrency bugs that can become security issues, and their existing flow language, a C++ source generator limited to a single thread, was showing its age. Rather than patching C++, the goal was to replace it, so Swift was introduced incrementally next to the existing code.

The build was extended with CMake so Swift files sit beside C++ files, with Clang modules supplying the C++ headers. Swift code calls C++ types directly, and because both compilers emit LLVM IR, inlined C++ bodies can be optimized together with Swift code. Calls in the other direction go through a generated Swift header. A bridging header with annotation macros tells Swift how to manage reference-counted C++ types. Futures receive a protocol extension so they can be awaited idiomatically, and actors enforce isolation so that shared mutable state is flagged at compile time. Exposing actors back to C++ requires bridging boilerplate, which a macro can generate.

For debugging, the talk showed backtraces that span Swift and C++ and follow async suspension points, instead of stopping at the crash site as chained futures do. The speaker reported no performance regressions on the migrated core actors when measured with existing benchmarks. The takeaway for practitioners is that Swift can be adopted side by side in a large C++ codebase, and that compile-time concurrency checks and clearer diagnostics can justify the migration.

talks.title: "Supporting Data Journalism through Compilers for Visual Inputs" by Parker Ziegler
talks.teaser: Compiler-based tools turn published charts and map designs into live programs data journalists can retarget to new datasets.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by framing data journalism as heavy programming work—cleaning public records, notebooks, D3, and scrollytelling—while newsroom tools were built for other roles. Fieldwork with journalists showed they often start from visual examples or Figma sketches, then spend as much time reverse-engineering DOM and JavaScript as building from scratch, and sometimes cannot reproduce a design in code at all.

The core proposal treats a graphic as a compilable source. Reviz, delivered as a browser extension, selects an SVG subtree from a live page, infers chart type via predicates over geometric attributes, builds a compact intermediate representation, and emits a partial Observable Plot program with holes for data columns. A demo retargets a New York Times scatter plot styling onto penguin measurements by filling those holes. Cardit targets cartography: uploading geospatial data spawns Mapbox GL JS that updates as the user pans, restyles strokes, or switches to a choropleth with Jenks bins and diverging colors, then exports runnable code.

Both systems share inferring semantics from visuals, mapping interaction to program edits, and targeting multiple output libraries from one IR. The closing argument is that compilers can collapse the gap between fixed published graphics and manipulable programs, letting the open web serve as a library of retargetable examples for smaller newsrooms.

talks.title: "Computational Physics, Beyond the Glass" by Sam Ritchie (Strange Loop 2023)
talks.teaser: Shows a browser-based Lisp computer algebra system and interactive physics visualizations for making math culture approachable.
talks.summary:
Sam Ritchie opens by describing his wish to share the culture of math and physics with his children, arguing that much of it is locked behind symbolic notation. He draws on Seymour Papert's Logo and Mindstorms and the idea of microworlds where learners explore by doing. He also points to the graduate physics textbooks by Gerald Sussman and Jack Wisdom, which are written in Scheme, as proof that a programmable approach can carry the full scope of classical mechanics. His stated problem is that the tools for this material tend to stay behind glass, such as static figures and closed commercial software.

The core of the talk is a computer algebra library, built on the Scheme utilities originally written by Sussman, that he has ported to Clojure and ClojureScript so it runs entirely in the browser. He shows symbolic differentiation of functions and vector functions, code that compiles symbolic expressions into fast JavaScript, and plots that update live as the code changes. The demos include a strange attractor with sliders for its parameters, vector fields in two and three dimensions, geodesics on a torus and on other curved surfaces, and a pendulum phase portrait whose parameters can be adjusted in real time.

He closes with next steps: a prequel series of essays on how models of the world begin, getting the library onto robots and into everyday environments where kids spend time, and a longer-term goal of an interactive textbook that uses a language model to guide learners through material. He notes that the work is now supported by an MIT lab and invites people interested in collaborating to get in touch.

talks.title: "Is my Large Language Model a Strange Loop?" by Zac Hatfield-Dodds (Strange Loop 2023)
talks.teaser: Traces how language models build internal features and how feedback training shapes their behavior, viewed as strange loops.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether a large language model can be seen as a strange loop, a feedback cycle that crosses layers of abstraction and ends up somewhere near where it began. The speaker frames the question using Douglas Hofstadter's idea and examines it from two directions: working upward from low-level building blocks, and looking downward at the behaviors that training loops produce.

Starting from the bottom, the talk walks through small convolutional image networks, where individual neurons map to features such as curve detectors or car detectors. It shows that some neurons respond to unrelated things, which is explained by superposition, where a network packs more features into fewer neurons. For transformers, it covers the residual stream and attention heads, and describes induction heads, which form at a point visible as a bump in the training loss curve. From the outside, it covers reinforcement learning from human feedback and preference models, along with experiments in which models judged their own answers, corrected their own bias, and were used for red teaming.

The final section describes reinforcement learning from AI feedback, where a model critiques and revises its own responses to balance helpfulness against harmlessness. The speaker concludes that these systems are beautiful and strange in places, but that the underlying question remains open, leaving the audience with more questions than answers.

talks.title: "A JVM threading model for the containerized times" by Luiz Hespanha and Flavio Brasil
talks.teaser: Explains how CPU throttling in containers destabilizes JVM services, and how adaptive thread concurrency at a large bank mitigated it.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with a payments platform at a large Brazilian digital bank, which runs more than a thousand JVM microservices on Kubernetes. During instant-payment peaks at the start of each month, services saturated their nodes and became unresponsive even though their average CPU usage looked low. The speakers explain that container CPU limits enforce a quota per period, so a burst of threads can exhaust that quota quickly and pause the whole container, including garbage collection and health checks. Averaged CPU metrics hid these bursts, so the team began sampling CPU usage much more finely.

To address the problem, the team built Navu, an adaptive threading model for the JVM. A heartbeat thread detects scheduling delays, which also reveal GC pauses and safepoints, and executors are redirected through Navu so the thread count can be lowered when throttling appears and raised when scheduling stays reliable. Work above capacity can be rejected to protect the service. The speakers say that disabling CPU limits or pinning CPUs to containers were not adequate for their fleet.

Results from three services were shown: one improved in stability month over month, one saw a large latency reduction, and one let the team remove over-provisioned resources without losing stability. Finer metrics also exposed an expensive development-only code path running in production, and fixing it sharply reduced P90 and P99 CPU usage while average usage stayed the same. Next steps include lower overhead for small containers, integration with Loom virtual threads, and preparing an open-source release.

talks.title: "An approach to computing and sustainability inspired from permaculture" by Devine Lu Linvega
talks.teaser: Shows how running on a boat with limited power shaped a sustainable, self-hosted virtual machine for software that lasts.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that computing practice should be sustainable over long periods and matched to the complexity a problem actually needs, borrowing permaculture's focus on working within limits. The speaker has lived aboard a 33-foot sailboat for about nine years, with a few batteries and roughly 200 watts of solar power. Modern software drained those batteries quickly, while older environments such as emulated HyperCard, Think Pascal and a Smalltalk image ran faster and used less power, which prompted a look back through the history of computing.

Software preservation is another thread. The speaker cites an estimate that most commercial games written before 2010 are no longer available, and notes that platforms which host content themselves let work disappear. Strategies such as migration, emulation, encapsulation and targeting a stable virtual machine are compared. The virtual machine approach is tied to projects that stayed playable because their specifications were published and others could write their own clients.

This led to a small portability layer: a 32-opcode stack virtual machine with a Forth-style language, an assembler written in itself, and a toolchain that runs on the same machine. It was used for a game and for the speaker's website. Examples included assembly optimizations, stack-depth checking to catch errors, and controlled self-modification. The closing takeaway is to favor open specifications and understandable systems over adopted solutions, and to measure a project's complexity against real needs. The speaker is candid that the implementation is imperfect and that the ideas are the main point.

talks.title: "From Geometry to Algebra and Back Again: 4000 Years of Papers" by Jack Rusher
talks.teaser: Traces mathematical notation from Mesopotamian clay tokens to geometric algebra as a unified language for space and physics.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation at Papers We Love, Jack Rusher argues that modern technical mathematics suffers from fragmented, suboptimal notations and suggests refactoring mathematics around geometric algebra (Clifford algebra). Framing mathematical thought through an evolutionary and cognitive lens, Rusher highlights how human spatial planning—shared across hundreds of millions of years of evolution—provides an intuitive foundation that symbolic algebra should directly support rather than obscure. Drawing parallels between mathematical notation and programming languages, he traces historical shifts in numerical systems and demonstrates how geometric algebra unifies disparate geometric concepts across arbitrary dimensions.

### Key Topics
- **Evolutionary Origins of Mathematics**: How spatial navigation, physical planning, animal counting, and social deliberation evolved into geometry, number sense, and symbolic logic.
- **Evolution of Number Protocols**: The historical emergence and frequent philosophical rejection of new numerical abstractions, including fractions in ancient Babylon, irrational numbers, negative numbers, and complex numbers.
- **Notational Shortcomings and Fragmentation**: How standard Vector Calculus notations (e.g., Gibbs and Heaviside) obscure geometric intuition compared to formulations like Grassman's and Clifford's geometric algebra.
- **Geometric Algebra and K-Vectors**: How the wedge product and geometric product generalize vectors into higher-dimensional oriented entities (bi-vectors, tri-vectors, or general k-vectors), clarifying concepts such as imaginary numbers and rotations.
- **Projective and Metric Extensions**: How parameterized metrics allow modeling diverse geometries, such as Minkowski spacetime, conformal geometric algebra, and projective geometric algebra for graphics and physics.

### Technical Details
Rusher examines arithmetic and algebraic systems as functional protocols with generic dispatch. In historical Babylon, scribes computed areas and approximations (such as calculating the square root of two to six decimal places) using place-value base-60 tables of reciprocals and squares. Modern representations evolved past natural numbers and negative numbers to complex numbers, initially cludged by Rafael Bombelli from Girolamo Cardano's algorithms before being understood geometrically as planar rotations.

In standard 3D vector algebra, rotations and cross products do not generalize naturally across dimensions. Geometric algebra resolves this by defining three forms of multiplication: the dot product, the wedge product (producing an oriented bi-vector), and the geometric product (the sum of the dot product and wedge product). Through this formulation, the imaginary unit $i$ is revealed as a unit bi-vector representing an oriented plane of rotation. Extending the algebra with metrics allows unified modeling across dimensions without altering mathematical equations. In a live coding demonstration using Clojure and Emacs, Rusher shows how a physics simulation accounting for gravity, Hooke's law, and damping operates identically across 2D, 3D, and 4D spaces simply by changing the dimensionality parameter.

### Takeaways
Rusher advocates for adopting geometric algebra across physics, engineering, and computer graphics, pointing to David Hestenes' research program and 2002 Oersted Medal lecture. Unifying technical mathematics under geometric algebra eliminates redundant tools (such as isolated cross products, Pauli/Dirac matrices, and quarternions), which could reduce physics education by several years while making advanced spatial and physical concepts vastly more accessible and intuitive.

talks.title: "War Time Proofs and Futuristic Programs" by Valeria de Paiva
talks.teaser: It links wartime proof theory to modern programs through revolutions in science, math, and computing.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by framing the Topos Institute’s mission and the speaker’s path from industry back to mathematical roots, then argues that shifting mental models in science, mathematics, and computation is slow and painful. Three historical arcs illustrate the pattern: Copernican heliocentrism and Galileo’s clash with authority, the early twentieth-century crystallization of modern proof-based mathematics, and the ongoing Curry–Howard correspondence tying logics, types, and categories.

The middle traces Hilbert’s formalist program, Gödel’s limits, and Gerhard Gentzen’s natural deduction and sequent calculus—the “wartime proofs” of the title—alongside Church, Curry, and Turing’s competing notions of computability. Lambda calculus and modus ponens show how proofs map to programs today, with extensions for effects, concurrency, and proof assistants such as Isabelle and Lean.

The close focuses on Gödel’s Dialectica interpretation, lenses as witness-preserving maps, linear logic models, and recent categorical generalizations. The takeaway is that Curry–Howard remains unfinished and underappreciated, with rich room for programmers to exploit connections between logic, proofs, and future language design.

talks.title: "Experimentation: putting research papers into prod" by Leemay Nassery
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of "Experimentation: putting research papers into prod" by Leemay Nassery.

talks.title: "Formal semantics for multi-language programs" by Amal Ahmed
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of "Formal semantics for multi-language programs" by Amal Ahmed.

talks.title: "Inside the Wizard Research Engine" by Ben L. Titzer
talks.teaser: A research WebAssembly engine balances deep runtime observability with baseline JIT speed for students and experimenters.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames WebAssembly as portable low-level bytecode run on software virtual machines, and positions Wizard as a deliberate alternative to production engines such as V8. The speaker argues that research VMs must be observable, approachable, competitively fast enough to transfer results, and flexible for trying language and wasm extensions, echoing the historical role of systems like Jikes RVM.

Wizard’s centerpiece is instrumentation through callbacks. Global probes swap the interpreter dispatch table so per-bytecode tracing adds no steady-state overhead when disabled; local probes patch individual sites, invoke user logic via a frame accessor, and can be removed so hot paths regain full speed. The talk walks through building analyses such as basic-block code coverage, loop and branch monitors, call profiling, and a bytecode-level debugger, plus library layers for trickier cases like function entry and exit.

A baseline single-pass JIT shares stack layout with the interpreter so execution can move between tiers when instrumentation changes, keeping probe overhead modest compared with rewriting wasm by hand. Benchmark plots place Wizard near other baseline compilers while remaining far smaller in code size than V8, supporting the goal of a hackable teaching artifact for wasm execution research.

talks.title: "Concatenative programming and stack-based languages" by Douglas Creager
talks.teaser: Compares stack-based languages with name-based ones, then shows how they reach Turing completeness and compile to assembly.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces stack-based languages as a family of programming languages that most developers have not encountered, defined by the absence of named values. The speaker starts with a Python program that computes a triangle's hypotenuse using variables and a function, and walks through how environments and call frames grow and get discarded during evaluation. The same logic is then rewritten for a stack machine, where literals push onto a stack and operators pop their operands. Extra instructions such as dup, swap and dig are needed to reorder values, and quotations with an apply instruction stand in for functions.

The middle section covers the formal meaning of these programs. Stack effect notation, which originated in Forth and was extended by Factor, describes how a program changes the stack. A more rigorous definition treats each program as a stack transformer, where sequential concatenation corresponds to function composition, and that property makes the composition associative. Turing completeness is argued by reducing the Lambda calculus through combinatory logic (S, K and I) to a stack language, and the instruction set is then reduced to a minimal basis. Associativity is shown to allow splitting a program into chunks, compiling each one to x86 assembly in parallel, and concatenating the results.

The talk closes with uxn, a real stack-based language with its own virtual machine, shown running a snake game, a clock and pong on an emulator and on a small device. The main takeaway is that stack languages are conceptually simple, which makes them well suited to implementation on constrained hardware.

talks.title: "Programming Distributed Systems" by Mae Milano
talks.teaser: Surveys research on programming languages that tackle data races, consistency and ownership in distributed systems.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the difficulty of programming distributed systems, where familiar abstractions keep leaking and new bugs and vulnerabilities keep appearing. The speaker frames three problems: destructive data races in shared memory, coordination overhead from strongly consistent replication, and consistency errors that arise when replicas diverge under weak guarantees. Each is illustrated with a simple example before any solution is offered.

To address consistency, the talk presents a transactional language that lets each transaction run at the weakest consistency it can tolerate. Its compiler applies an information flow type system to reject programs where strongly consistent results depend on weakly consistent data. An online game example, with win and loss tables and a tournament invitation, shows a ranking transaction that the compiler flags. The talk then covers monotonic data such as counters and sets that only grow, which let programs stay correct under weak consistency without coordination. A stable message delivery protocol is used to show how this works in a replicated setting.

For data races, the talk looks at type systems that enforce mutual exclusion at compile time. It contrasts Rust's restriction to tree-shaped references with a region-based approach that permits structures such as doubly linked lists, using an isolation keyword and dynamic checks where static analysis is not enough. The takeaway for practitioners is that better language design can rule out whole classes of concurrency bugs, though some shared state still needs transactions or locks.

talks.title: "Why Programming Languages Matter" by Andrew Black
talks.teaser: Seven decades of language design illustrate how programmer notation steers thought, tooling, and the slow path to adoption.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by arguing that programming language research deserves graduate attention, citing Turing Award winners and the claim that software—and thus languages—underpins modern infrastructure. He frames languages as spell systems that shape how programmers think, invoking a mild Sapir–Whorf analogy and urging serious projects in functional, object, process, and logic styles so paradigms become second nature rather than homework exercises.

The core is a personal genealogy: undergraduate Algol-H merging Hoare-style data structuring with Algol 68; Oxford’s readable 3R language for government quantity-surveying contracts; Eden’s EPL preprocessor hiding distributed messaging; Emerald’s location-independent objects, immutability for replication, and monitors; and Traits as Smalltalk classes without instance variables, with explicit conflict resolution instead of silent multiple inheritance. He stresses that consolidation is harder than innovation, that customers and prior languages constrain endings, and that thin language layers can hide messy distributed plumbing.

He closes that languages are dual-purpose tools—for machines and for people—which makes design and adoption socially slow. Audience questions touch effect systems after Fortress, balancing new language features against language servers and browsers, and teaching paradigms via constrained dialects versus one multi-paradigm language.

talks.title: "Ectype - bringing type safety (and more!) to vanilla JavaScript" by Holly Wu (Strange Loop 2023)
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in "Ectype - bringing type safety (and more!) to vanilla JavaScript" by Holly Wu (Strange Loop 2023).

talks.title: "Unmasking the Godfather - Reverse Engineering the Latest Android Banking Trojan" by Laurie Kirk
talks.teaser: Reverses the Godfather Android banking trojan, showing deobfuscation, emulator-check bypass and its accessibility abuse.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through reverse engineering a recent Android banking trojan called the Godfather, which hides behind a fake Google Protect app that asks for sensitive permissions such as making phone calls. The speaker explains that the family has appeared on official app stores many times, targets a large number of financial institutions, and was derived from the leaked Anubis source code. Running the sample in an x86 emulator caused it to crash, which pointed to an emulator check guarding the malicious logic.

Static analysis started with the manifest to locate the entry point, then moved into decompiled Java that was padded with junk methods, meaningless class and method names, and encoded strings. Those strings were decoded from Base64 and revealed prompts about phone administrator rights and enabling accessibility. The emulator check was defeated by hooking the method with Frida so it always returned false, after which the app kept showing an accessibility request. The accessibility handler was shown to read on-screen text, use regular expressions to match PIN and password fields, and display fake HTML overlays over targeted banking apps to capture credentials.

The talk closed with the other capabilities of this variant, including sending captured data to a server, screen recording uploaded as MP4 files, executing commands from a command and control server, and a native component able to connect to a VNC server. The main takeaway is to question why an app requests accessibility or phone permissions before granting them, since the same analysis approach carries over to other banking trojans.

talks.title: "Didn't Chrome Already Have a Root Store?" by David Adrian (Strange Loop 2023)
talks.teaser: Explains why Chrome built its own root store and certificate verifier, and how that shifts web PKI trust toward automation.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from why the web needs more than encryption: a browser also has to know that a certificate belongs to the site it names. It explains digital signatures, how certificates bind a name to a public key, and how browsers and platform vendors trust certificate authorities through root stores and root programs. Past incidents such as DigiNotar and the WoSign and StartCom backdating cases show why these trust decisions matter.

Chrome originally relied on platform verifiers and root stores, which behaved inconsistently in distrust and edge cases. Chrome's own root store and verifier, launched in Chrome 105, gave consistent results across platforms. The rollout surfaced platform quirks, including Windows drawing trust from many locations and macOS keychain calls that could hang the browser. Measurements showed fewer certificate errors, largely on older Windows machines that lacked updated roots, and slightly faster page loads.

The Chrome root program aims for security through agility and simplicity, mainly via automation. The speaker walks through the certificate authority lifecycle of domain validation, issuance and status. Automated ACME validation shortens how long a validation can be reused, and multi-perspective validation hardens it against DNS and BGP attacks. Because OCSP is costly and leaks browsing data, Chrome proposed making it optional, requiring CRLs, and allowing certificates of ten days or less that need no revocation tracking. The takeaway is that automation and shorter lifetimes are the levers for keeping the web PKI secure, including through future post-quantum migrations.

talks.title: "Astronaut Horse: Stable Diffusion Artist Collaborations" by Tom Betthauser (Strange Loop 2023)
talks.teaser: Follows a year of artists and engineers fine-tuning Stable Diffusion to make gallery-ready art and workshops.
talks.summary:
Tom Betthauser presents Astronaut Horse, an open-ended project that brings visual artists together with researchers and software engineers, mostly from the Recurse Center, to make art with Stable Diffusion. He explains the basics for a non-technical audience. The core method is textual inversion, where an artist picks five to 15 images and the training learns a new token that can be used in ordinary text prompts. He also describes the diffusion denoising process and why the model can imitate styles that appear in its training data.

The project moved from notebooks to a hosted Gradio app on Hugging Face Spaces, which is redeployed every 24 hours and loads the artist-trained concepts automatically. Betthauser walks through early runs, including one using an artist's own paintings, where the outputs picked up on nuanced choices such as color and line use rather than subject matter. Other trainings used magazine clippings, fossils, and open-access images from a museum collection. He covers batch prompting, seed cropping for variants, and a batch upscaler used to prepare large prints.

The work was shown in a gallery in Anchorage with five days of workshops for students and community members, and a second show was planned for October in Northern California. Betthauser closes by asking whether diffusion models can make fine art and what that would mean for collaboration, authorship and ownership. He says the project has left him wanting to make more analog work himself.

talks.title: "Without Open Data, there is no Ethical Machine Learning" by Erin Mikail Staples (Strange Loop 2023)
talks.teaser: Explores how ethical machine learning relies on open, well-maintained datasets, and how access to that data is shrinking.
talks.summary:
The speaker argues that machine learning models depend on the datasets behind them, and that open data is losing priority even as models spread. She traces machine learning from early checkers programs and neural network work through boosting methods to today's foundation models, then traces open data back to a 1940s belief in shared research and a 2013 US executive order making machine-readable government data the default.

Using her dog as a playful example, she shows how a model trained on one narrow dataset yields skewed results, such as a pet product catalog that would lose every peanut-based treat. A more serious case came from her graduate work on sentiment analysis of online comments, which relied on scraping Reddit and Twitter; those platforms have since restricted that access. She also warns about lobbying and the risk that a few companies set rules for many.

To fix this, she proposes a standard file format with rich metadata, clear time frames and API access, plus checks on data integrity: consent, clarity, consistency, control and consequences. Examples include a federated European cancer image project, New York City open data week, and a Brooklyn effort using open data to push for pedestrian safety. She closes by urging attendees to thank data maintainers, pay attention to context, and help keep open datasets maintained.

talks.title: "Risks and Opportunities of AI in Incident Management" by Emily Arnott (Strange Loop 2023)
talks.teaser: Weighs the benefits and hazards of using AI in incident response, from faster code triage to hallucinated fixes and tech debt.
talks.summary:
Emily Arnott opens by framing an incident broadly: any unplanned disruption that pulls engineers away from planned work needs a process behind it. She explains why incident response is hard, citing time pressure, the deep codebase knowledge needed to find root causes, repetitive ad hoc checks, and the coordination required across teams. Using a scenario where most users cannot log in, she shows how a language model could help locate relevant code spread across many files, generate throwaway scripts to test inputs, and draft retrospectives that engineers can query later to get up to speed.

She then turns to the risks. Code that people accept without fully understanding it becomes black-box technical debt. Models hallucinate nonexistent library functions when pressed for an answer, and their knowledge goes stale because training happens at fixed points in time. Letting a model decide which users to prioritize can also send a response off course, since its judgment rests on linguistic patterns rather than grounded facts about the business.

Her mitigations are mostly organizational. She recommends a robust and resilient process, training engineers in how to prompt and use these tools, giving people the broader context needed for strategic decisions, and recognizing the human work that incident response involves. She closes by stressing a blameless culture that looks for systemic causes rather than blaming whoever made a mistake, and by arguing that AI should be treated as an investment in people rather than a reason to cut staff.

talks.title: "Can a Programming Language Reason About Systems?" by Marianne Bellotti (Strange Loop 2023)
talks.teaser: Shows how an experimental DSL lowers the barrier to formal modeling for legacy and distributed system behavior.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with pain familiar in legacy modernization: unknown servers, single points of expertise, and skepticism that decades-old stacks could ever be “correct” in the verification sense. What matters instead is reasoning about complex behavior—how experts match incidents to mental models built through operations, not pristine docs and test suites—and how formal methods can communicate those abstractions.

The middle introduces Fault, an experimental C-flavored domain language that transpiles to SMT-LIB for solvers such as Z3 and Yices. The speaker walks through simulation, checking, and symbolic execution; stock-flow and bathtub concurrency models with phi normalization; and painful solver output reshaped into ordered logs. Live models cover a bathtub overflow scenario, federal vaccination policy static rules surfacing odd regulatory edge cases, and a ticket seat state chart with a timed hold window that exposes impossible transitions.

Practitioners should leave seeing formal methods as a collaboration tool for stating impossible behaviors and probing dependencies, not only proving greenfield correctness. Fault is positioned as highly experimental open source—breakage expected—with an invite to file specs that break the tooling.

talks.title: "Building Strong and Sustainable Open Source Projects" by Lawrence Gray (Strange Loop 2023)
talks.teaser: Uses road trip stories to explain how open source projects build governance, community, and sustainability.
talks.summary:
Lawrence Gray opens with a road trip he took with a friend after their summer internships, heading toward Vancouver on very little money. The trip was full of unplanned turns, including a family dinner, a house party, and days spent with strangers who offered food and beds. Gray uses these episodes to frame what a successful open source project needs: a clear purpose, openness to diversity, resilience after setbacks, and shared ownership of achievements.

The practical advice comes next. Projects should build a governance model, create spaces for discussion, and document things at three levels: user tutorials, contributor guides, and code documentation. To counter burnout, Gray's project runs three-month terms in which members sign up for a role and can step away without obligation. To stay engaged, projects can give conference talks, host local meetups and community hackathons, bring open source into university courses, offer mentorship, and take part in programs such as Google Summer of Code. Gray also recommends fiscal sponsorship through NumFOCUS for managing funds, and warns against ignoring user feedback, setting too many contributor rules, or neglecting the community.

A second story, a hitchhiking trip around Tasmania, illustrates how strangers can form a trusting network. The talk closes by encouraging listeners to submit a first pull request to a project they already use. The audience questions covered fundraising, settling bikeshedding disputes through trusted decision makers, handing off a project when burned out, corporate-led open source, and whether contributors can be paid.

talks.title: "Babashka: a meta-circular Clojure interpreter for the command line" by Michiel Borkent
talks.teaser: Shows how Babashka enables instant Clojure command-line scripting through GraalVM native-image and a meta-circular SCI interpreter.
talks.summary:
Babashka addresses slow JVM startup when Clojure developers want shell-style scripts without leaving the language. A single cross-platform binary evaluates a large subset of JVM Clojure in roughly tens of milliseconds, bundles common scripting libraries, reuses ecosystem jars, and supports Java interop and Windows alongside Linux.

Because GraalVM native-image cannot use Clojure’s usual runtime `load-string`, Babashka embeds SCI, a small self-hosted Clojure interpreter implemented meta-circularly and tuned for native-image and ClojureScript. The talk walks from naive eval through analyzer and evaluator separation, fixed-array locals instead of immutable hash maps, reflection-based interop configuration, binary size tradeoffs, and the pods extension RPC model. Sister projects such as nbb and Joyride, plus SCI hooks in clj-kondo, illustrate reuse beyond scripting.

Practitioners gain a clear picture of when Babashka beats bash or a full JVM, how built-in libraries affect stability promises, and where performance still depends on analysis-time work versus runtime reflection.

talks.title: "Turning GraalVM from Research to Product" by Thomas Wuerthinger (Strange Loop 2023)
talks.teaser: GraalVM's arc from Oracle Labs to production covers polyglot wins, failed bets, and native-image gains for cloud workloads.
talks.summary:
The presenter opens with his path from Sun Microsystems and Oracle Labs into compiler and virtual-machine research, including the “one VM to rule them all” vision and naming of GraalVM. He frames long-horizon corporate research—years without revenue—as necessary for VM complexity, and describes how a tight budget for a part-time master’s student pushed the team toward partial evaluation of interpreters instead of translating JavaScript into Java.

He walks through the 2018 “top ten” launch and which ideas failed in practice: casual multi-language mixing, cross-language tooling, LLVM-hosted native languages with heavy warm-up, and embedding the VM in arbitrary C++ apps. What gained traction included high-performance Java JIT, polyglot extensions on Java (including NetSuite), languages inside Oracle Database and MySQL, and especially ahead-of-time native images for fast startup and low footprint. He contrasts underspecified native APIs in Python and Ruby with Java’s specs and notes work on HPy for Python.

Closing sections benchmark Spring Pet Clinic on JIT versus native image, arguing that memory footprint, throughput-per-gigabyte, tail latency, and startup favor profile-guided AOT for many cloud and serverless workloads, with lower energy use. He stresses early adopters, framework partners, and major cloud vendor support for native image as keys to mainstream adoption.

talks.title: "The Economics of Programming Languages" by Evan Czaplicki (Strange Loop 2023)
talks.teaser: Explores how corporate, independent, and open source programming languages get funded, and how that funding shapes their design.
talks.summary:
The designer of Elm opens by describing more than ten years of maintaining a language, where the work grew from compiler engineering into package infrastructure, releases across platforms, community events, trademarks and foundation governance. He asks who pays for this work and why, and starts with the money flowing into browsers. He explains how search engines pay to be the default search in browsers, and how that payment makes the search bar work like a landlord collecting rent from storefronts. He backs this with the scale of the payments and the browser market shares involved.

He then sorts language funding into corporate models, such as a company-controlled platform, a corporate alliance that negotiates standards, and rewarding talent, and independent models, such as patronage, consulting, research grants, editor or usage licenses, hosting, and donations. For each one he weighs design incentives, such as whether a feature should be added, and career risks, such as depending on a funder whose goals can change. He shares his own experience with patronage, where a funder's priorities shifted and his work was no longer valued. He also describes a hosting idea that compiles Elm to C and SQL for Postgres, which he has prototyped but worries that larger cloud providers could copy.

He closes by asking authors, users and the wider community to consider a language's goals, its author's situation and the trade-offs before adopting it. He leaves open whether the search-based rent model is harmful and how small authors could address switching costs.

talks.title: "Designing Dope Distributed Systems for Outer Space with High-Fidelity Simulation" by Toby Bell
talks.teaser: Shows how deterministic, faster-than-real-time simulation testing validates an entire spacecraft flight software system.
talks.summary:
Toby Bell, a PhD student at Stanford, describes the flight control software for VISOR, an upcoming mission in which two 6U CubeSats fly in close formation in low Earth orbit to image the solar corona. The spacecraft must hold centimeter-level alignment and plan their own maneuvers autonomously, and the team cannot rely on ground stations for that loop. Because spacecraft software runs in an environment that is hard to reproduce on a desktop, the team built its testing around simulation.

The guidance, navigation and control library is compiled from the real C++ flight code, and the simulation replaces sensors, hardware, networking and the other spacecraft with models. Everything runs deterministically in a single process and thread, so a failure can be reproduced and stepped through. Cross-link messages are modeled with a latency range and a drop rate, and an event queue skips idle time. A 30-orbit run takes about a minute, which he gives as roughly a 2,880 times speed-up on his machine.

The main lesson he draws is to make every input and output explicit at the system boundary, including networking, scheduling and file access, so the software's behavior depends only on what it is given. He argues this makes simulation tests a faster default than unit tests and a more complete check than end-to-end tests. He also describes a processor-in-the-loop setup on a Raspberry Pi, where only a thin wrapper around the interfaces was needed.

talks.title: "Lessons from building GitHub code search" by Luke Francl (Strange Loop 2023)
talks.teaser: Explains how GitHub rebuilt its code search engine to index billions of files faster and support regex at scale.
talks.summary:
The talk traces why GitHub's original code search was slow, limited in what it could match, and unable to index forks. Indexing ran through a monolithic Ruby stack, and the tokenizer stripped out programming characters, so the team had to weigh trigram indexing against its storage and rebuild costs. The old system ran on 312 servers and took months to re-index, which discouraged experimentation.

The replacement, a Rust-based engine called Blackbird, used an event-driven crawler, a Kafka buffer, and a cache server that reused prior index work. To handle forks, the team deduplicated content by git blob ID and used a minimum spanning tree over repository similarity to order Delta compression. Estimating differences between repositories was a challenge because HyperLogLog accuracy depends on set size, so the team turned to a geometric xor filter, which estimates symmetric difference relative to the size of the change. Dynamic shard assignment moved compaction onto separate hosts, and each shard gained a second replica for redundancy.

The final system ran on about 130 servers across three redundant clusters, with the cache reaching a hit rate above 99.9 percent during full rebuilds. Because a rebuild takes days rather than months, the index format has changed 50 times in three years. The main takeaways: custom infrastructure can beat off-the-shelf tools when you exploit your data's structure, scaling problems recur at each order of magnitude, and designing for change pays off in delivered features.

talks.title: "IPVM: Seamless Services for an Open World" by Brooklyn Zelenka (Strange Loop 2023)
talks.teaser: Explores IPVM as open, standards-based compute that links WebAssembly, capabilities auth, and verifiable distributed workflows.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that decades of walled-garden infrastructure make it hard to compose services across providers, while TCP and HTTP excel at networking machines but not applications. Brooklyn Zelenka frames a standards-based “compute layer” comparable in ambition to HTTP: open, interoperable, and attractive enough to rival today’s clouds. She traces how always-on devices, serverless abstractions, data gravity, and latency limits trap computation in a few regions, and why place-oriented hosting poorly matches mobile users and edge workloads.

The proposed IPVM stack combines capability-style authorization, encrypted replicated data (including prior Web Native File System work), and WebAssembly execution. Jobs are hash-linked tasks with schedulers free to place work near data; completed steps emit receipts that others can reuse, enabling memoized, crash-tolerant dataflow across browsers, edge nodes, and communal networks. Routing can match heterogeneous runtimes while still failing back to conventional high-availability hosts.

Practitioners hear how trust is handled via deterministic replay, spot checks, and eventual zero-knowledge proofs, and how pure reads differ from exactly-once side effects at the end of a pipeline. The closing message is spec-first modularity: swap layers, participate as either consumer or provider, and aim for user agency over data and service choice.

talks.title: "Playing with Engineering" by AnnMarie Thomas (Strange Loop 2023)
talks.teaser: A professor shows how playful labs, circus rigs, conductive dough, and huge crowdsourced music projects reshape engineering education.
talks.summary:
Anne-Marie Thomas opens by asking why “play” and “engineering” rarely sit together in industry or academia, then sketches her own path from art-focused schooling through MIT and Caltech to running an undergraduate-heavy lab at the University of St. Thomas. She defines playful work as process-oriented, freely chosen, social, and joyful, using whimsy and surprise as practical design checks.

The middle of the talk walks through concrete teaching and outreach: dynamics lessons on trapezes and German wheels, Squishy Circuits born from salty and sugary conductive dough, surprise bus trips for freshman design classes, collaborations with deaf students and PBS SciGirls, open music-visualization work with an a cappella group, and the OK Go Sandbox effort that ties band videos to classroom lessons.

She closes with the pandemic-era “All Together Now” collaboration—mailing and digital animation frames worldwide, thousands of music submissions, multiple arranged versions of one song, and lab rules: be kind, play well with others, and clean up messes. Practitioners hear that ambitious interdisciplinary projects need legal and safety nets, but inviting the right partners and honoring student agency can yield learning tools used far beyond one campus.

talks.title: "Comedy Writing With Small Generative Models" by Jamie Brew (Strange Loop 2023)
talks.teaser: Shows how small language models trained on modest text sources can generate comedy and karaoke-style lyrics.
talks.summary:
Jamie Brew traces a path from phone predictive text to small generative models. Repeatedly accepting the suggested next words produced odd songs, and that habit led to a closer look at how the suggestions depend only on the last two words. The talk compares this to a Markov chain, noting that the user's own choices give the phone model a memory the formal definition does not allow. From there Brew builds minimal n-gram models in a few lines of Python and demonstrates one in a notebook trained on conference abstracts. Scraped sources such as Yelp reviews and Craigslist ads supply further text, and mashing Morrissey lyrics with exercise-DVD reviews shows how quickly two sources can be combined.

The middle section covers how tokenization shapes the output. A word-level model in a Harry Potter parody keeps character names intact, while invented band names for a festival poster needed character-level generation to produce words no source contained. Brew offers theories for why these outputs feel funny, including the idea that they echo the unreliability of real-world text, and borrows a framework from Emily Short for the flaws procedural text produces.

The closing section turns to a karaoke generator that uses the CMU pronouncing dictionary to swap each lyric line for a phonetically similar line with a matching syllable count from another source. Brew demonstrates it on a Beatles song with Craigslist vehicle ads and on a classic tune using conference talk titles. The takeaways are that small models stay close to their data, are easy to explain and combine, and make legible mistakes, while anything published publicly may later be reused.

talks.title: "Making Hard Things Easy" by Julia Evans (Strange Loop 2023)
talks.teaser: Explores why basic computing topics like bash, HTTP, SQL and DNS feel so hard to learn, and how to make them easier.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at Strange Loop 2023, Julia Evans discusses why computing concepts that seem basic—such as Bash, HTTP, SQL, and DNS—often take years to master. Drawing from her experience founding Wizard Zines to demystify complex computing systems, Evans emphasizes that technical friction is rarely a personal failing. Instead, it stems from systemic factors such as piles of obscure gotchas, massive underlying codebases, hidden internal mechanics, and unintuitive tooling outputs. She examines practical mental models, heuristics, and community roles that help make hard topics easier to learn and navigate.

### Key Topics
Evans breaks down why four foundational technologies are unexpectedly difficult and provides strategies to simplify them:
- **Bash and Hidden Gotchas**: Bash is an infrequently used language full of edge cases and trivia. A small script demonstrates how `set -e` fails to exit on errors when functions are used in compound statements like logical OR (`||`), which globally disables `set -e` inside the called function. Tools like ShellCheck offload trivia from human memory, while sharing real-world failure stories helps engineers decide when to avoid problematic patterns.
- **HTTP and Accidental Complexity**: HTTP structures appear straightforward (status code, headers, body), but understanding them requires dealing with browsers containing over 20 million lines of code and evolving security models. Rather than memorizing all 40+ HTTP request headers or entire command-line man pages (like `grep`), Evans advocates pruning large lists down to small, human-scale subsets of high-value items, paired with honest, reliable references such as MDN and official RFCs.
- **SQL and Chronological Execution**: In SQL, query syntax does not match execution order. Demystifying SQL requires asking what the computer executes first chronologically (e.g., `FROM` -> `WHERE` -> `GROUP BY` -> `HAVING` -> `SELECT` -> `ORDER BY` -> `LIMIT`). Evans notes that tracing chronological sequences also clarifies topics like CORS message exchanges, process startup (`behind hello world on Linux`), and cross-team service workflows.
- **DNS and Hidden Mechanics**: DNS is hard because intermediate library code, local and upstream caches, and communications between resolvers and authoritative name servers are invisible. To illuminate these hidden interactions, Evans and her friend Marie built "Mess with DNS," an authoritative name server that displays incoming resolver queries in real time. For confusing terminal tools like `dig +norecurse`, she recommends "eraser eyes"—filtering out visual noise to focus strictly on actionable signals (such as `SERVFAIL` indicating a cache miss).

### Technical Details
- **Shellcheck & Bash traps**: In Bash, constructs such as `my_function || echo 'failed'` disable `set -e` inside `my_function`, bypassing standard error termination behavior.
- **DNS Inspection**: Using `dig +norecurse` allows querying a recursive resolver specifically for cached data, where a `SERVFAIL` response indicates the resolver does not hold cached records for the query.
- **Interactive Visualizers**: Tools like `mess with DNS` and `float.exposed` expose hidden system mechanics (e.g., DNS resolver traffic patterns or spacing between IEEE 754 32-bit floating-point values) to build intuition.

### Takeaways
Difficulty in understanding foundational systems is normal and driven by hidden state, complex distributed architectures, and unintuitive outputs. Evans highlights the community ecosystem required to demystify technology: the "Grumpy Old Timer" sharing past failure modes, the "Loud Newbie" asking clarifying questions without fear of judgment, the "Bug Chronicler", the "Tool Builder", the "Today I Learned" sharer, people who answer questions, and the "Documentarian" who writes it all down. By identifying the exact reasons a system is hard, developers can create tools, prune information, and trace execution to make hard things easy.

talks.title: "New algorithms for collaborative text editing" by Martin Kleppmann (Strange Loop 2023)
talks.teaser: Explores CRDT research that merges real-time text editing with Git-like drafts, local-first storage, and efficient edit history.
talks.summary:
Collaborative editors must let each person change a local copy immediately while concurrent edits still converge when updates sync. The presentation contrasts optimistic real-time merging—as in a familiar dual-window demo where offline typing reconciles after the network returns—with the noise and tedium of suggestion-mode review when many small proposals stack up. It argues that text tools lack the asynchronous, branch-and-merge review rhythm that code workflows get from version control.

The Upwelling prototype models drafts like branches: isolated editing, optional change highlighting, explicit merges into mainline history, and automatic rebasing when another draft lands first. That flow rides on local-first storage and the open-source AutoMerge library, using an RGA-style text CRDT with per-character IDs, periodic compaction of edit logs into compact snapshots, and columnar compression inspired by analytics stores. A LaTeX keystroke trace benchmark packs roughly 250,000 operations into on the order of 184 KB while preserving full history and timestamps. Vector-clock-style markers reconstruct arbitrary past document states and power efficient diffs, including attribution by actor.

Rich text adds Peritext: formatting as timestamped span operations over character IDs rather than tree or marker models that duplicate words or bleed bold styling on merge. AutoMerge ships as a portable Rust core with WebAssembly, C, and mobile bindings, plus a separate I/O layer for persistence and sync. Practitioners gain a concrete picture of how change tracking for offline sync can double as version control for prose, and why representation choices matter for merge correctness.

talks.title: "How to Build a Meaningful Career" by Taylor Poindexter and Scott Hanselman (Strange Loop 2023)
talks.teaser: Veteran tech leaders outline grace, intentional choices, and personal meaning for long software careers.
talks.summary:
The session opens on belonging at a technical conference and pivots to what “meaning” can mean in a decades-long career: money, community, health, advocacy, or day-to-day work with people you trust. Scott Hanselman describes a promotion thank-you tour back to teachers and mentors, and the uneasy feeling that almost nothing he learned in school still exists—leading to the idea that everyone is an “amateur” but expert in their own journey.

Both speakers trade candid setback stories: empty rooms, harsh bosses, pandemic burnout, and public mistakes (including explaining HTTP to someone who helped write the spec). They argue against algorithm-driven comparison on social media, for rest and sabbaticals when job hunting feels impossible, and for recalibrating when an individual-contributor path stops fitting. Luck is framed as preparation meeting opportunity, while money and benefits (especially healthcare) are treated as legitimate motivators alongside passion.

They close with practical homework: avoid comparison, grant yourself grace after failures, choose motivation deliberately, prefer supportive managers, distinguish stretch growth from drowning, and hold medium-term goals loosely rather than rigid life plans. Meaning stays personal; the aim is to stay intentional while accepting long careers full of unknowns.

talks.title: "The Lemniscate" by Ann Johnson, Charles Comstock
talks.teaser: A programmable LED sculpture ties a browser IDE and WebAssembly firmware to live MIDI so attendees can author and perform light patterns.
talks.summary:
The session presents the Lemniscate, an interactive sculpture shaped like the Strange Loop logo and named after the lemniscate of Bernoulli. Charles Comstock and Ann Johnson describe how last year’s code kiosks grew into a fuller stack where conference visitors write sketches, simulate them in the browser, and optionally upload patterns that enter a timed rotation on the physical piece.

A Raspberry Pi 400 kiosk runs the ClojureScript IDE; WebMIDI carries controller events into ESP32 firmware that executes uploaded WebAssembly through Wasm3 and paints 581 addressable LEDs arranged as offset loops. The talk walks through a bespoke vector language—pixel color as a function of index, time, coordinates, and HSL modes—with proportional indexing so inner and outer loops stay matched, plus math helpers, debugging, and a miniature memory-map view of compilation. New for the year, MIDI control changes remap to four ports while note velocity drives a Gaussian-smoothed amplitude region in WASM memory; live demos cover sliders, pitch, chords, and velocity-driven effects.

Closing themes stress design constraints: strip length dictating size, WASM as a shared browser and device target, and MIDI’s open standard for tactile input beside code. The speakers invite custom sketches, home-built Arduino MIDI gadgets, and playful experimentation via the public project page.

talks.title: Katie Stolee: To search or not to search: it depends on the question
talks.teaser: Explains which developer questions suit code search, drawing on usage data and a faster code-to-code search approach.
talks.summary:
Katie Stolee frames code search as using search inside an IDE, a browser or another bespoke interface to locate code-related artifacts. A study of developers at Google found code search happening about 12 times per developer per day, with each search session usually running three to four queries. Code search queries took more time, more clicks and more reformulations than general web searches, which suggested room for better tooling.

She then surveyed developers to sort their searches into four needs. How questions made up about a third, what questions about a quarter, and where and why questions about 16 percent each. For how questions, the talk presents code-to-code search, where a function is the query and behaviourally similar code is the result, possibly in another language. The first approach combined token context, fuzzing-based behaviour and a language-agnostic abstract syntax tree. It produced precise results but was too slow. Swapping in a machine-learning embedding approach removed the behaviour dimension and kept precision, because developers tend to write code in predictable patterns.

The closing takeaway is that search is the wrong tool for many questions. Code comprehension (what) questions are better handled by asking a colleague or pair programming, and why questions are better rephrased as where questions. Roughly 40 percent of the questions studied fell into those categories, so knowing why you are searching matters.

talks.title: Brittany Johnson-Matthews: Causal testing: understanding the root causes of defects
talks.teaser: Shows how causal testing turns a failing test into minimally different passing and failing runs that expose a defect's cause.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a study of why developers adopt or avoid software tools. Its main complaints were hard-to-digest tool output, tool design problems, and workflow integration overhead. Follow-up work in testing noted that conventional tests can show that a defect exists and sometimes where it sits, but rarely why the behavior happened.

Causal testing is presented as a way to answer that why question using test cases a team already has. Starting from a failing test, the method perturbs its inputs to generate new valid tests, runs them, and sorts the results into passing and failing sets. Those are then compared with the original using both inputs and execution paths, so the most similar passing and failing tests point to the cause. In a directions example, the passing tests started and ended in the same country while the failing ones did not, which quickly suggested the cause. The talk also covers two extensions: causal fairness testing, which flips one attribute at a time, such as race in a loan decision tool, to measure how often outcomes change because of that attribute; and testing machine learning-based software with assertions that check whether outputs stay equal when an input such as a name changes.

A proof-of-concept implementation was evaluated with participants, who reported that the similar passing tests pointed to the cause and that the approach helped them find and fix root causes. The practical takeaway is that causal testing adds explanatory insight to existing code and tests without requiring much extra effort, and the speaker invites discussion on fitting it into a team's testing process.

talks.title: Shane McIntosh: The unintended consequences of mining software build systems
talks.teaser: Presents Build Medic, a tool that automatically repairs broken build scripts, and the noisy build data that complicates its evaluation.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a familiar frustration: a Maven build fails after a dependency's coordinates change, such as Log4j being referenced differently in Maven Central, and the fix has to be made by hand. The speaker asks why build systems cannot sustain themselves. A self-sustaining build would need tools that detect underspecified dependencies, anticipate necessary build changes, and automatically apply fixes to build scripts. The talk focuses on the last of these, automated repair.

The speaker presents Build Medic, which takes a build failure log, classifies the kind of failure, selects a repair strategy, applies it, and re-evaluates the build. If the build still fails, it loops back to try another fix. On 84 unseen breakage pairs mined from open source commit history, a little more than half were fixed automatically, and about three quarters of those were fixed in a single iteration. In the correct fixes, about a third matched the developers' change exactly, and 44 percent modified the same elements in a slightly different way.

The speaker then questions the evaluation, which assumes historical breakages are important and that developers rush to fix them. About 12 percent of passing builds had at least one actively ignored failing job, sometimes up to 87 percent of failing jobs. Roughly two-thirds of failing builds were stale, with fix times ranging from a day to years. The speaker offers two conclusions: either the evaluation is right and build data is noisy, which calls for measuring and tracking that noise, or the evaluation is flawed, and developers are invited to help improve it.

talks.title: Kelly Blincoe: The effects of destructive criticism in code review
talks.teaser: Shows how destructive code review feedback lowers developers' motivation to keep working and their willingness to improve code.
talks.summary:
This talk presents a study of how developers perceive destructive criticism in software code review, meaning feedback that is inconsiderate and non-specific. The researchers used an online questionnaire built on vignettes. Participants imagined submitting a code snippet and receiving either constructive or destructive feedback on it, and they answered questions about each version.

Destructive feedback was seen as less appropriate and less likely to help improve the code, even when participants found it valid. After receiving it, participants reported much lower motivation to keep working on the task, with the developer, and on the project as a whole. Women reported being less motivated to keep working with the developer and on the project after destructive feedback. Less experienced developers were more likely to apologize and agree with harsh comments, while more experienced developers were more likely to say the feedback should be more considerate. Respondents reported receiving destructive criticism far more often than giving it: 22 percent said they had received some in the past year, while about one percent said they had given it. Opinions were split on whether inconsiderate feedback was acceptable if it improved the code.

The takeaway is that how people are treated affects whether code gets improved and whether developers stay on a project. Teams need ways for reviewers to learn when their feedback lands badly, should adapt feedback to what each recipient prefers, and should think carefully before criticizing someone in a public venue rather than privately.

talks.title: Christoph Treude: Automatically enhancing error messages
talks.teaser: Shows how crowdsourced Stack Overflow answers can be turned into clearer Python compiler error messages inside the IDE.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a short Python script that tries to remove duplicates from a list using dict.fromkeys. It fails with a message claiming the list is not callable, which the speaker argues describes what the interpreter attempted rather than what the programmer was trying to achieve. He traces this complaint back to a 1976 paper on language design. A web search for a fix usually leads to a Stack Overflow thread, where the accepted answer explains that naming a variable list shadows a built-in name.

The middle of the talk presents Pycee, a prototype that enhances Python error messages. It parses the error, builds a Stack Overflow query depending on the error type, and selects an answer using signals such as acceptance, presence of code and votes. It then replaces variable names in that answer with the names the user actually used and summarizes long responses into a short hint, so the IDE can show a more actionable explanation.

To evaluate the approach, the researchers had 16 professional developers complete two practice exercises each, with one task using Pycee and the other using the official Python documentation as a baseline. Across 115 encountered errors, participants rated the enhanced messages as more helpful, while their agreement that the messages saved time was less pronounced. The takeaway is to crowdsource error explanations and use automated filtering to separate correct answers from incorrect ones.

talks.title: Neil Brown: How Your Mind Learns to Program
talks.teaser: Explains how long-term memory, working memory and domain-specific problem solving shape the way programmers learn.
talks.summary:
Neil Brown opens with the idea that learning, whether a first programming course or picking up a new framework, depends on how memory stores and connects facts. He separates long-term memory, which holds concrete facts and links related ones, from working memory, which can only juggle a handful of items at once and does not grow with training. Abstract ideas such as values and types are hard to grasp from a formal definition, so the talk argues for learning them through varied concrete examples, such as strings, integers and booleans, and for using examples when teaching others.

The middle section covers how expanding long-term knowledge frees up working memory. When related items merge into larger chunks, more fits into working memory at once, which is why accumulated knowledge raises the capacity to tackle harder problems. Brown also warns that the brain eagerly links new material to existing knowledge, which can create wrong links. His example is carrying Java inheritance assumptions into C++, where finer differences only surface later.

The final part challenges the idea of one general problem-solving skill. Brown argues that problem solving is learned separately in each domain through practice, so skill at chess or brain teasers says little about fixing a slow web service. Testing with puzzles is therefore a weak measure of programming ability, and a better approach is to examine the specific skill directly. The lessons are to learn abstractions from varied examples, grow knowledge to free working memory, and practise problem solving within the domain you need.

talks.title: Davide Fucci: The hidden costs and benefits of TDD
