talks.title: Marian Petre: How expert programmers think about errors
talks.teaser: Shows how expert developers treat errors as clues, mind gaps, and use pair debugging to surface hidden design flaws.
talks.summary:
Marian Petre argues that software development often treats errors as nuisances to swat quickly, while experts treat them as chances to question assumptions, spot miscommunication and gain insight. Drawing on about 30 years of studying experts and high-performing teams, she describes experts who watch for unexpected feedback, attend to interfaces and integration points, and notice what is missing from a design, the information or their tools.

She lists the practices these people use. Instead of fixing one bug and moving on, experts step back to look for related bugs and deeper design flaws, and they weigh a bug's impact against the cost of fixing it. Minor issues may be tolerated, with the deferral and its rationale documented. They seek contrary evidence, ask how a claim could be wrong or how an alternative could be right, and use pair debugging with people who know different parts of the code. When checking tools, they play methods against each other, plant deliberate errors to test a harness, and combine tools to cover each other's limits.

The takeaway is that these habits depend on a team culture focused on fixing the error rather than assigning blame. That culture gives individuals room to experiment, because peers catch slips. Petre closes by encouraging listeners to reflect on whether their own organizations make space for this kind of practice.

talks.title: Maurício Aniche: How code coverage can be used and abused to guide testing.
talks.teaser: Argues that code coverage helps developers decide where to add tests, and reviews research on its limits as a quality target.
talks.summary:
The talk defends code coverage against common complaints, such as that it can be gamed, pushes developers into pointless tests, or hides weak assertions. The speaker argues the metric is useful when it is used properly. A developer writes tests from the specification while building a feature, then runs a coverage tool and asks why each uncovered line was missed. Coverage informs whether more tests are worth writing, but it should not make that call, and tests should never be added just to lift the number.

Next the speaker reviews research on coverage and test effectiveness. A 1994 study by Hutchins and colleagues found that suites above about 90 percent coverage detected faults better than weaker ones, while full coverage alone did not guarantee good tests. A 2009 study found that targeting code not yet exercised found new faults more effectively than adding tests for already covered code. Another paper concluded that coverage reliably flags under-tested areas but performs poorly as a quality target.

For criteria, the speaker suggests statement coverage is enough for most teams, since any tool can measure it in any language, instead of chasing complex criteria like MC/DC or path coverage. The takeaways: use coverage to augment a suite, never set it as a fixed target, and remember that high coverage does not prove quality while low coverage is a clear warning sign.

talks.title: Marieli Wessel: How people really use GitHub Actions
talks.teaser: Presents a study of GitHub Actions usage across thousands of projects and what adopting them changes in practice.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by explaining GitHub Actions as a way to automate repository work, with workflows triggered by events such as new branches, comments and pull requests, and with actions that can be shared between repositories. Actions are written as configuration files that should be handled like code, but the speaker argues that teams often do not treat them that way.

The study examined the configuration files of about 3,000 projects and found roughly 700 distinct actions in 20 categories. The most common were continuous integration, utilities, deployment, publishing and code quality. A typical action was added and then never removed or modified, while a few specific actions had their arguments changed many times. Discussions among developers focused on how actions are maintained, how to build custom ones, and moving from other CI/CD tools to actions. The speaker also compared repositories before and after adoption and found two consistent effects: more pull requests were rejected, and merged pull requests were required to have fewer commits.

The main takeaway is that adopting an action means taking on a new dependency that needs ongoing upkeep, and that it can change how contributors work together. The speaker recommends measuring code performance and community metrics before and after introducing actions, so teams can spot unexpected effects early.

talks.title: Matthias Galster: Value and waste in software engineering
talks.teaser: Surveys research on software waste, code review smells, technical debt fixing, and turning human values into product requirements.
talks.summary:
The talk draws on a special issue on value and waste in software engineering and argues that these ideas are hard to act on without concrete definitions. It opens with a study that defined waste in software engineering and sorted it into nine categories, each with its causes, which teams can use when discussing and planning their work.

The speaker then gives three examples. First, poor code reviews create waste. The research names review smells such as approvals that skip real review, reviews handed to friends rather than used for knowledge sharing, back-and-forth ping-pong exchanges, unanswered reviews, oversized change sets and missing context. These lead to rework, waiting and high cognitive load. Second, technical debt is not fixed the same way across types. Code and defect debt are usually fixed by the developer who introduced them, while design debt tends to need dedicated time and is better assigned to more senior people. Third, human values such as dignity and inclusiveness can be turned into concrete descriptions, which then become requirements, for example about how user information is kept and shared, how users can unsubscribe, or how software supports different languages and cultures.

The takeaways are practical. Teams can use known review smells to plan reviews, set expectations and train novice reviewers. They can use the technical debt findings to decide what to fix and who should fix it, focusing dedicated effort on design debt. And they can translate human values into product requirements to build software responsibly.

talks.title: Sebastian Baltes: Challenges and opportunities for software engineering in Papua New Guinea.

talks.title: Alberto Bacchelli: How code review works (and doesn't) in the real world
talks.teaser: Empirical studies show file order in review tools strongly shapes which bugs reviewers catch in production and test code.
talks.summary:
Modern code review loops send changes to reviewers who comment until a patch can merge, yet little attention goes to how review tools present the work. The speaker frames code review as widespread developer practice and asks what makes the inspection step more effective at surfacing errors before production.

Instrumenting a corporate review tool revealed that more than half of reviewers open the first listed file and often move alphabetically through the list. Test files usually appear after the code they exercise and draw far fewer comments. In a controlled study with injected defects, presenting the test file first made participants about 250 percent more likely to spot the test bug, while production defects showed no ordering advantage in that setup.

Analysis of roughly two hundred thousand GitHub pull requests showed comments concentrate on earlier files regardless of change size. A follow-up experiment with five production files and two distinct bug types found that a subtle boundary-case defect was about 175 percent more likely to be found when its file appeared first; a simple missing-break issue did not vary by position. Reviewers should choose a deliberate starting point, authors can steer attention via descriptions or comments, and tool makers should let teams control file order instead of relying on silent defaults.

talks.title: "Crowd dynamics, RL and Unity: A Journey" by Tomas Diaz
talks.teaser: Models crowd movement with reinforcement learning in Unity, using Kalman filters and recorded pedestrian trajectories as training data.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Tomas Diaz presents a comprehensive exploration of modeling human movement through crowd dynamics, reinforcement learning (RL), and the Unity game engine. The work aims to predict how people navigate shared spaces given desired trajectories, with applications in environmental design, simulation, and behavior analysis. The presentation is divided into four key sections: the historical evolution of crowd dynamics as a field, foundational RL concepts, the Kalman filter for state estimation, and practical implementation in Unity.

## Historical Evolution of Crowd Dynamics
The field emerged from practical engineering needs. In the 1960s, Fruin's work quantified pedestrian sidewalk design using photography to analyze trajectories, introducing the concept of "level of service" (designations A–F based on density and expected flow). The 1970s brought a paradigm shift when Henderson's work demonstrated that Maxwell-Boltzmann mechanics from particle physics could model pedestrian movement, treating people like gaseous particles. The 1990s explosion of computational power enabled simulation-based validation. The social force model emerged as influential, positing that pedestrians are bombarded by attractive and repulsive forces—for instance, a burning wall repels nearby people. Recent research (the "crowd space" paper) revealed that no single algorithm captures all crowd configurations; instead, determining the specific space type and applying the appropriate algorithm yields better results.

## Reinforcement Learning and PPO
Diaz pivots from physics-based models to RL, recognizing that uncovering a hidden universal human motion equation is unlikely. In RL, an agent observes a state from its environment, takes actions, and receives rewards. The policy (π) maps states to action probabilities, parameterized by neural network weights (θ). An advantage function determines whether actions outperformed or underperformed expectations, calculated as discounted cumulative rewards minus expected future rewards. The presentation introduces vanilla policy gradient before focusing on PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization by OpenAI), which prevents destructive policy updates. PPO clamps the ratio of new-to-old policy probabilities within a small range (typically ±0.2 epsilon), ensuring updates remain conservative and preventing the agent from accessing data distributions it was not trained on.

## Kalman Filter and Coleman Gain
Diaz detours to explain Rudolf Kalman's work on optimal state estimation, motivated by Apollo program rocket control. The Kalman filter combines imperfect system equations with noisy sensor readings to estimate true state. The optimal weighting factor—the Kalman gain—minimizes error by dividing system error by the sum of system and sensor error. Matrix formulations account for observation matrices that collapse unmeasured variables (e.g., if only position is sensed, not acceleration). The demonstration with chaotic double pendulums shows how sensor readings "snap" the simulation back toward observed behavior. Ensemble Kalman filtering (running multiple models and averaging) improves tracking. This framework is applied to crowd dynamics: a statistical similarity measure paper uses Kalman filters to quantify how well simulations match real crowd data.

## Unity Implementation
Unity ML-Agents wraps OpenAI's Gym framework, running PyTorch backend with Barracuda inference engine (supporting ONNX format). Developers override methods: OnEpisodeBegin initializes agents and environments, CollectObservations maps environment to state vectors, OnActionReceived applies actions and assigns rewards, and policy configuration specifies PPO hyperparameters. A simple example trains an agent to hit a box by controlling ball forces in x and z coordinates.

## Practical Application and Results
Diaz trains agents on trajectory data from immutable crowds (20–30 trajectories, 2–3 seconds each). Agents receive no explicit reward for reaching destinations; instead, an entropy-based reward metric captures natural crowd behavior. Key insights: (1) sight information (raycasts visualizing nearby agents) is crucial but subject to diminishing returns around 40 rays; (2) reducing information to key dimensions accelerates learning; (3) data augmentation (rotation) and curriculum learning (progressively introducing trajectories) significantly improve performance. Trained agents generalize to unseen environments and different crowd densities without retraining, suggesting they capture underlying behavioral characteristics rather than memorizing trajectories.

## Takeaways
The work demonstrates that RL can extract generalizable crowd behaviors from limited datasets, with potential applications in entertainment and behavioral quantification. Future directions include larger datasets, real-time camera feeds to continuously update training data, and deploying agents for diverse spatial configurations.

talks.title: "Impacting Global Policy by Understanding Litter Data" by Sean Doherty
talks.teaser: Shows how computer vision turns community litter photos into city-level data that informs policy and cleanup decisions.
talks.summary:
The talk treats litter as a global data problem rather than only a waste problem. The speaker covers its scale, from the Great Pacific Garbage Patch to the estimated 200 billion dollars that cities in the United States spend each year on litter, and argues that cities often lack data showing where litter actually sits.

The middle of the talk explains how community photos become usable records. Uploads from an app used in 180 countries peak at about 30 images a second, and they pass through a queue and a spam filter that uses Hamming distance to catch near-duplicate pictures. A step function then runs detection models that box each item and assign its material, object and, where possible, its brand. Regional brand models and location-specific models are needed because litter looks different around the world. Research studies in 50 cities check the community data against statistically sound samples. Policy examples follow: San Francisco used the data to raise its cigarette tax, student-collected data in Philadelphia supported a citywide plastic bag ban, and one user's documentation led a brand to change its packaging.

The closing looks ahead to estimating how long litter has been on the ground from its decomposition, and to cheaper sources such as cameras on garbage trucks or drones. The aim is a platform where cities can monitor litter over time instead of guessing. The takeaway is that accurate local data helps cities spend cleanup money more deliberately.

talks.title: "Tech When the Sky is Falling: Tools for Crisis Response" by Emma Ferguson and Colin Schimmelfing
talks.teaser: Walks through how a volunteer mask donation project grew from a shared spreadsheet into a real database and tooling stack.
talks.summary:
The speakers describe Mask Match, a peer-to-peer site that ran from March to July 2020 and sent donated masks directly to healthcare workers during the early PPE shortage. It began as a weekend idea after two healthcare startup founders approached the presenters, and it went on to deliver close to a million masks. The talk frames tech-enabled crisis response as five phases: validate the idea, make it repeatable, scale, stabilize, then adapt or shut down.

Each phase came with its own tooling changes. The first version ran on Google Sheets and shared Gmail inboxes, which caused data conflicts and hit concurrency and send limits. The team added a small email app, then Retool for volunteer workflows, a free help-desk tool, Twilio text reminders and eventually Postgres on AWS, with an automatic matcher and Metabase analytics later on. They noted that cleaning data before the Postgres move took weeks, so investing in data quality early would have paid off.

In the final phase, hospital requests tapered off, and large offers of masks arrived that the matching model was not built for. The team chose to shut down gracefully, telling volunteers directly, restricting access and exporting the database before removing it. Their lessons include vetting volunteers, relying on donations and free tiers, and first identifying which phase a project is in before choosing tools.

talks.title: "How Tracing Uncovers Half-truths in Slack’s CI Infrastructure" by Frank Chen
talks.teaser: Shows how distributed tracing helped Slack find the causes of flaky CI tests and cut pull request flake rates.
talks.summary:
Frank Chen, who works on developer productivity at Slack, explains why flaky tests frustrate engineers and erode trust in continuous integration. Slack's CI workflows run for days or weeks and pass through GitHub, Jenkins, Kubernetes and QA environments, so the causes are spread across code, services and people. Conventional logs and metrics struggled to show where failures came from.

The first wins came from tracing the test runner. A prototype trace revealed slow git checkouts on some instances in an autoscaling group that were not being updated. During a multi-day incident, a cross-service trace showed git LFS failures on a third of the QA fleet, and pipelines were flowing again within two hours. A month of instrumenting the Cypress test runtime then linked certain runtime variables to higher flake rates, and roughly 90 hours of large machine time at peak went to tests whose results were discarded.

In an August 2021 incident, back-end unit and integration suites ran out of memory. Per-test-case traces exposed memory jumps across percentiles, and subject matter experts identified suspect experimental pull requests. Reverting one of them made tests appear to pass at a higher rate within minutes. Chen reports that the per-pull-request flake rate fell from about 50 percent to about 5 percent. His takeaway is that tracing with shared context, plus conversations that bring service and test owners together, helps teams find causes faster.

talks.title: "Functional distributed systems beyond request/response" by Melinda Lu
talks.teaser: Explains why event-driven services built on distributed logs can replace synchronous request/response calls between microservices.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the point that any software touching the internet is a distributed system, and that the default way services call each other, synchronous request/response, makes that hard. A network call can be slow, lost or ambiguous, so it is often unclear whether a retry is safe. As service graphs grow, availability and latency compound across dependencies, and teams pile on retries, caches, circuit breakers and service meshes to compensate.

The speaker proposes event-driven services as an alternative, drawing an analogy to functional programming. A producer writes an event to a partitioned log such as Kafka or Kinesis and does not wait for a reply, so consumers can be added or deployed without coordination, and the log buffers work when a consumer is down. A photo-sharing platform was used as a real example: a user following another user fed a feed worker, a push notification pipeline, monitoring and analytics, each as an independent consumer. Two ways of getting database writes into the log were compared, database change capture, which the speaker has used more often, and event sourcing. Machine learning inference was presented as simply another consumer.

The closing section covers the costs. Systems become eventually consistent, ordering guarantees depend on how topics are partitioned, and events need unique identities for deduplication. Schemas should be managed with typed formats such as protocol buffers so they can evolve safely, and deleting a user's data must reach every derived copy. The main takeaway is that event-driven designs need more up-front design but reduce coupling and make later changes simpler, even though tooling and examples are scarcer than for request/response.

talks.title: "Near-Realtime Monitoring of Drones at Sea" by Todd Bealmear
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of "Near-Realtime Monitoring of Drones at Sea" by Todd Bealmear.

talks.title: "Branchstack: branching infra for better development" by Patrick Flor and Alex Pearson
talks.teaser: Shows how branchable state and dependency graphs can let teams copy, change, and ship distributed cloud apps with HyperCard-like ease.
talks.summary:
The speakers open by contrasting HyperCard’s instant duplicate-and-edit workflow with today’s distributed cloud products, where long readmes, Docker stacks, and shared production state make it hard to start work quickly, isolate changes, or ship with confidence. They frame modern apps as graphs of stateful subsystems—databases, auth, payments, DNS—and argue developer tooling should branch that state, not only containerize code.

Patrick walks through failed shortcuts: everything on one laptop, then containers that still diverge in network and data. Alex introduces Branch Stack: metadata hacks for APIs without branching, live versus test buckets, local tunnels, and the preferred model of branching as a first-class service with parent branches and named copies. He covers Postgres branching inside a cluster, worker revisions, Kubernetes namespaces and virtual clusters, and multi-tenancy to control copy cost.

Demos show Platter Postgres CLI creating an isolated feature database and a recorded widget app flow where git checkout provisions database branches, Stripe webhooks, Cloudflare Workers on the edge, and metadata-tagged events. The closing takeaway is that serious work must run in the global cloud environment, but teams can wire branching into the same lifecycle as Git—schema merges instead of destructive data merges—and spin full environments for developers or business reviewers in seconds.

talks.title: "Carbon Footprint Aware Software Development" by Tejas Chopra
talks.teaser: Maps carbon costs from email to video streaming and surveys compiler, algorithm, and CI techniques developers can adopt.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens from Bitcoin’s electricity spotlight toward a broader question: what environmental impact does ordinary application code create? It defines carbon footprint as greenhouse gases expressed in CO₂ equivalents, then stacks everyday benchmarks—per-capita emissions, the share of digital life in a daily carbon budget, and how client devices compare with the server-side stack that carries most network emissions.

Midway, the talk grounds those abstractions in scale: video dominates global traffic, an independent Carbon Trust study cited with Netflix puts European streaming near 55 grams of CO₂ per hour (down from a prior 400-gram estimate), and large AI training runs can dwarf lifetime automotive footprints. It argues the developer-controlled slice of emissions is small today but poised to grow as data volumes explode, then walks through practical levers—returning CPUs to idle faster, algorithm and data-structure choices, loop and threading patterns, compiler optimization levels, language tradeoffs, and Linux profiling with Perf and flame graphs.

It closes by envisioning CI/CD pipelines that catch energy regressions like functional tests, mentions tooling such as Argos for watt-hour accounting across browser, network, and backend tiers, and uses audience Q&A to stress cloud billing as a rough carbon signal when direct measurements are missing.

talks.title: "How we used serverless to speed up our servers" by Jessica Kerr and Ian Wilkes
talks.teaser: Shows how a database team scaled query compute with AWS Lambda, and the limits and retry settings that mattered.
talks.summary:
Honeycomb's custom data store, called retriever, keeps raw event data in columns, groups it into time-based segments, and answers interactive queries across any fields. When customers wanted longer retention, the team moved older segments to S3 so 60 days of data stayed searchable. Queries then became CPU bound, so response time grew roughly with the time range searched, pushing the query timeout up to an hour.

To scale compute rather than wait on response time, each retriever hands its S3 segments to AWS Lambda functions written in Go, which aggregate the data and return results. Starting EC2 instances took minutes, and keeping idle capacity for spiky load was too costly. The speaker reported a median Lambda startup of about 50 milliseconds, around 1.5 seconds at the 90th percentile, and a cost roughly three to four times EC2 per CPU second, offset by running only a small fraction of the time.

The main lessons concern limits and tuning. Lambda's burst concurrency cap returns HTTP 429 errors under sudden load, so retries must be set deliberately, and default SDK timeouts did not suit their workload. S3 calls also fail routinely at scale, and responses are capped at six megabytes, so large results went to S3 and were shared as links. Gzip proved slower than newer compression, and an ARM trial gave slower tail latency, so most traffic stayed on AMD. Because serverless hides the server, observability and cost alerts matter.

talks.title: "Authorship Environments: In search of the “personal” in personal computing" by Eric Gade
talks.teaser: Reframes personal computing as literacy and previews Simpletalk, an inspectable web authoring world built on HyperCard.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by questioning what makes computing "personal," contrasting ownership and customization with mind augmentation, then dismantles the familiar bicycle-for-the-mind analogy as shallow productivity marketing. It proposes literacy instead: reading and writing create a distinct mental space for interrogating ideas, while early cuneiform stayed locked in a scribal class for millennia until books, print, simpler scripts, and social commitment enabled mass literacy.

The speaker argues that computing today resembles scribal culture—terminals echoing teletypes and a sharp split between programmers and users—and surveys HyperCard and Smalltalk as historical models where metaphors, inspectable objects, and Adele Goldberg’s “onion” layering let people peel from use down to implementation. From a short research effort with collaborators, Simpletalk emerged as an experimental web stack-and-cards world whose parts exchange messages, expose scripts like HyperTalk, and even implement their own editor from the same building blocks; the talk itself runs inside that world.

Closing themes stress that weak metaphors steer industry investment poorly and that authorship means systems people can change rather than systems that change people. Q&A touches creators versus consumers, Finder and browser malleability, games and Scratch for children, Excel, Emacs, why HyperCard faded, and ties to STEPS-style layered DSLs beyond the one layer they built.

talks.title: "Janus: Easy Complex UI with Declarative FRP" by Issa Tseng
talks.teaser: Shows how the Janus framework expresses interactive web UIs through declarative data bindings and view models.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Janus, a JavaScript front-end framework begun in 2013, which the speaker describes as ergonomic, thoughtful and flexible. The session opens with the framework's top-level exports, then walks through a task list where a model declares the shape of its data and a view binds to it without explicit event-handling code. A larger credit card form shows view models holding computed state that the underlying model does not need, along with a debug view that records why each value updated.

Further examples cover composition styles, a tabbed text editor where an enum selects the active document, and a draggable box workspace built from mouse-event bindings. A flyout menu demo shows how a small typo in a binding made the hover state silently fail, and how a sticky utility keeps a true value alive for a set period. The speaker explains the underscore convention that separates timeless calls from time-varying results, notes that the core is roughly 3,500 lines of CoffeeScript, and admits that its data transformations are eager and slower than many alternatives.

The closing section covers planned work: moving off jQuery, adding laziness to transformations, and a live-reloading debug environment that could save state and add assertions. The speaker argues that a friendlier interface can be the faster choice for users, and invites contributions. The practical takeaway is that Janus's primitives can be used directly in custom code, which eases moving outside the framework when needed.

talks.title: "Waterpark: Distributed Actors vs the Pandemic" by Bryan Hunter
talks.teaser: A healthcare platform built on Erlang actors pursues continuous availability while modeling each patient as a long-running process.
talks.summary:
Bryan Hunter describes how HCA’s integration research team set out to use enterprise clinical data and the Erlang virtual machine to help caregivers, improve outcomes, and stay resilient during disasters or a pandemic. That work became Waterpark: a continuously available Elixir system that ingests HL7 and other streams, transforms or generates signals, and deliberately implements only the subsets of caches, queues, and databases the organization actually needs so deployment and failure behavior stay under team control.

The architectural center is a long-lived patient actor for each person, retaining the full message history rather than treating care as disconnected snapshots. Bloom filters and an open-source HL7 library support efficient querying across events. When COVID-19 arrived, the mandate was production in three weeks with no planned or unplanned outages. Waterpark adopted Erlang-style “no masters” parallelism across availability zones, read replicas and writers coordinated via rendezvous hashing, consensus limited to topology rather than millions of processes, and a mailroom layer that routes messages transparently. Rolling upgrades reuse chaos-style node drops; hot code loading and dark launches enable change on a system that has not gone down since launch.

The pandemic payoff was a universal-server plugin that watches transfers from nursing homes and long-term care, detects positive COVID lab results, and alerts facility caseworkers once a checklist of conditions is satisfied—supporting early contact tracing in vulnerable settings. The closing message is to stock ideas from papers and talks, invest in observable fault-tolerant design, and aim engineering effort at work that materially helps people.

talks.title: "Remote Workstations for Discerning Artists" by Michelle Brenner
talks.teaser: Cloud workstations give Netflix artists one-click remote access, flexible tooling, and secure assets without shipping hardware.
talks.summary:
Netflix built cloud-based remote workstations so visual effects and animation artists can work from any region without desk-bound machines or fragile file handoffs. The old model tied artists to on-prem desks; scale, work-from-home, and inclusion goals pushed a rented-workstation model on AWS with persistent user settings and files kept in controlled cloud storage instead of email or FTP.

The platform splits into fleet management (Java Spring Boot control plane, Spinnaker pools, Go lifecycle agents), Salt-based configuration, immutable versioned packages, and Packer-driven image baking that moved through three iterations—from just-in-time installs at acquire time, through pre-configured pools, to heavier bake-stage images for faster startup. Remote access uses NICE DCV and Teradici, with RBAC and dashboards evolving toward APIs for pipeline engineers. Personas span artists, technical directors, and pipeline engineers.

Lessons emphasize matching on-prem table stakes (settings, tablets, monitors, latency), favoring paved paths where possible, hedging architectural bets, and pivoting from a single product to a customizable platform. Artists should expect deliberate trade-offs between cost, wait time, and experience; builders should iterate one change at a time and invest in observability rather than cutting it under deadline pressure.

talks.title: "Client Side Deep Learning Optimization with PyTorch" by Tyler Kirby and Shane Caldwell
talks.teaser: Shows how to shrink and speed up PyTorch models so they run on phones without a Python runtime.
talks.summary:
The speakers, who build machine learning systems for a moving company, explain why they moved deep learning models from servers onto phones. Server hosting costs money, real-time video needs fast frame rates, and drivers often lack a reliable internet connection. They describe earlier attempts, including a 2017 text classifier written in JavaScript that ran too hot on Android, and an object detector built with TensorFlow Lite that fell short on accuracy. They settled on PyTorch because its eager execution feels like ordinary Python and most published research code uses it.

The middle of the talk walks through the path from an eager module to a deployable one. Models are converted to TorchScript through tracing, scripting, or a mix of both, and the intermediate graph can be inspected before and after optimizations. The serialized model is saved as a .pt file and run from C++ without Python or its global interpreter lock. Practical tips include calling eval mode, warming up the model before timing it, and keeping it cached. The speakers then compare quantization methods: dynamic quantization suits a language-model LSTM, which dropped from 169 MB to 134 MB and from about 5 seconds to 1.6 seconds per batch. Static quantization with per-channel calibration suits a MobileNet, which shrank from 22 MB to 5.6 MB with inference falling from 0.13 to 0.03 seconds and accuracy dropping one point. Quantization-aware training is the fallback when accuracy falls too far.

The closing advice is to choose a mobile-friendly architecture first, serialize to TorchScript, and try quantization before custom optimizations. Track several accuracy metrics so uneven effects on regression and classification are not missed, and stick to operators PyTorch supports on mobile.

talks.title: "Injecting Security at the Cloud Edge" by Susan Hinrichs
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding "Injecting Security at the Cloud Edge" by Susan Hinrichs.

talks.title: "Training an Autonomous Pentester with Deep RL" by Shane Caldwell
talks.teaser: Shows how a reinforcement learning agent can learn Metasploit-driven pentest steps in a simulated environment.
talks.summary:
Shane Caldwell, a former penetration tester who became a machine learning engineer, argues that the breadth-oriented part of a network pentest, scanning many services for known flaws, is a good candidate for automation. He introduces reinforcement learning as a way for an agent to choose actions, and explains what it needs: a defined action space, a state space, and a reward signal. He also covers its weaknesses, including data hunger and reward hacking, using the boat-racing example where an agent farms power-ups instead of finishing the race.

He proposes Metasploit as the right level of abstraction, since it already tracks hosts, services, exploits, loot and credentials. His Metasploit Gym environment encodes each host as a fixed-size vector and rewards only novel findings, such as new hosts, unique exploits, loot and root privileges, so the agent cannot profit from repetitive scanning. Because running real commands against real machines is slow, he builds a simulated version based on partially observable Markov decision processes, keeping the same action and observation spaces so the agent cannot tell the two apart.

In a demo against the intentionally vulnerable Metasploitable 2 machine, a deep Q network agent beat a random agent over 100 episodes, averaging a reward of 35 against about 11 for random, and reached root in every episode. He closes by noting the limits: one machine is not a network, the action space is still partial, and alignment matters, since a reward-seeking agent might exploit fragile services or overreach in production. He invites engineers and pentesters to help build the project.

talks.title: "How to Equitably Close the CS Education Gap" by Jeffery Phipps
talks.teaser: Explains how industry volunteers partner with schools through TEALS to expand equitable high school computer science access.
talks.summary:
Many students never encounter computer science before college, while computing fields account for a large share of open roles and hiring demand stays high. The speaker frames that imbalance as a shared problem for communities and employers, especially where race, gender, and geography limit who gets early exposure.

The talk centers on TEALS (Technology Education and Literacy in Schools), a philanthropies-backed program that places industry volunteers alongside classroom teachers in schools that lack a CS track. Volunteers typically commit a few hours weekly, in person or over video, while teachers build independence over several years. The program scales across hundreds of schools, supports standard high school offerings from block-based intro courses through AP Computer Science, and pursues deliberate outreach in districts with predominantly Black student populations. A short film and panel with active volunteers illustrate co-teach and lab-support models, remote pairing, and moments when students gain confidence to present their work.

For practitioners in the room, the practical takeaway is recruitment: apply when the volunteer window opens, expect summer training and team planning, and help schools without CS discover the program. Even spreading the word or lining up corporate volunteer drives is treated as meaningful help when a full school-year commitment is not feasible.

talks.title: "Making Webapps Collaborative with Composable CRDTs" by Matthew Weidner and Heather Miller
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of "Making Webapps Collaborative with Composable CRDTs" by Matthew Weidner and Heather Miller.

talks.title: "Strange Dreams of Stranger Loops" by Will Byrd
talks.teaser: Relational programming demos synthesize Scheme quines, twines, and multi-interpreter relays as hands-on strange loops.
talks.summary:
Will Byrd frames the keynote around Douglas Hofstadter’s strange loops and self-reference, using a grant-review anecdote and a Grand Canyon story about noticing ants instead of vast vistas. He argues that big questions about consciousness are hard to grasp directly, and that constructive play with small computational artifacts builds intuition the way close observation of “ants” can matter as much as canyon-scale theory.

The core of the session is live work in miniKanren embedded in Scheme. Through relations such as appendo and a relational evaluator evalo, he runs queries forward and backward: recovering list fragments, generating programs that evaluate to chosen values, synthesizing classic quines, and finding “twines” that mutually evaluate to each other. Adding structural distinctness constraints yields richer twines than trivial quote toggles. He also demonstrates a quine relay across three variant interpreters differing in list and quasiquote support, stressing that results emerge from encoded semantics and search rather than hand-built quines.

He closes by linking layered biological metaphors (including CRISPR as defense against viral genetic intrusion) to why tiny self-reproducing programs deserve sustained study, announces modest prizes for future constructive entries, and briefly highlights John Doyle’s underexplored reflective interpreter ideas. A short Q&A touches on synthesizing competition rules and broader program synthesis with types and constraints.

talks.title: "The Future of Conferences" by Cristina (Crista) Lopes
talks.teaser: Weighs the value and carbon cost of conferences and what online and hybrid events mean for their future.
talks.summary:
This keynote reflects on where conferences came from, what they are worth, and what they cost. The speaker traces professional and scholarly societies back to the 1300s and notes how their number grew after the printing press. Drawing on decades of attending and organizing events, the speaker says the value of knowledge sharing has fallen as online content has grown, while networking and travel still matter. The costs include time away from family, harassment in crowds, and flight emissions, estimated at around 330 tons of CO2 over twenty years.

A committee within an ACM special interest group studied the carbon footprint of its conferences and found that venues far from North America and Western Europe emitted more. Before the pandemic, the group considered a voluntary carbon tax on registrations. The move online that followed was rapid, and the speaker helped build a virtual conference platform. Recorded videos widened reach and made live Q&A more thoughtful, but time zones, weak social features, and attendees working through what should have been breaks caused problems. The speaker stresses that organizer choices mattered as much as the software. A pre-pandemic virtual community conference was estimated at under a ton of CO2, far below the emissions of travel.

The speaker expects in-person events to return alongside hybrid formats, ranging from one large yearly event plus online gatherings to parallel in-person and online tracks. Technology is not the hard part; social and psychological issues, such as feeling present and being distracted at home, are. The talk closes by asking how to balance unsustainable travel with professionally valuable exchange.

talks.title: "Poems in an accidental language" by Kate Compton
talks.teaser: Explores how accidental grammars, bots, and domain sketches turn programming into poetry and a social way to know worlds.
talks.summary:
Kate Compton connects accidental language design to social making, starting with Tracery: a minimal context-free grammar in JSON created for a class assignment and later open sourced. Bots built with Cheap Bots Done Quick reportedly reached on the order of sixteen thousand Twitter automations, while projects such as Lost Tesla juxtapose sensor reports into unintended verse. Users layered Tracery into SVG generators, live visuals, and Campbellmax, which invents ephemeral country names and poems until a page refresh deletes the language entirely.

She then questions what counts as a programming language, favoring prototype theory over rigid buckets and citing cognitive limits from The Programmer’s Brain. Domain-specific and “little” languages appear through Inform 7 narrative prose, answer-set murder mysteries with absurd failure modes, contrasting musical notations for children versus experts, graphical and chant scores, and Laban dance notation—including a group exercise that encodes the conference name in movement.

The final thread treats ontology as collaborative play: spreadsheet parties listing opaque objects, tarot-and-procedure jams, and imperfect “cow tools” that still reveal structure. Building sketch languages and prototypes becomes a way to discover what matters in a domain, from coffee rituals to fan-tag folksonomies, before briefly relating neural latent spaces to missing vocabulary for interpreting machine learning internals.

talks.title: "Why security is the biggest benefit of using the Cloud" by AJ Yawn
talks.teaser: Argues that cloud-native controls like AWS Config and service control policies can reduce security risk and speed up response.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that security is the most overlooked benefit of cloud computing. The speaker, who runs a compliance automation company, notes that cloud pitches focus on cost, elasticity and scalability while rarely mentioning security. Security and speed are not opposing forces when controls start early in the pipeline. Core ideas such as protecting identities, knowing the perimeter and responding to vulnerabilities apply wherever workloads run. Simply lifting servers into the cloud keeps old habits, while re-architecting around cloud-native services opens up better options. Under the shared responsibility model, the provider secures the underlying infrastructure, while customers remain responsible for access, data placement and what users can do.

A live demo showed AWS Config checking a newly created S3 bucket for encryption and public access. The rule automatically remediated the bucket and sent a Slack notification, shortening the time between detection and response without waking an engineer. For account structure, the speaker recommended AWS Organizations to split workloads so that a compromised user account holding no resources has little to reach. Service control policies then restricted allowed regions and blocked disabling of security services. The demo showed that even an administrator was denied an EC2 call in a region outside the allowed list.

The closing argument is that teams should automate repetitive security checks so people can focus on proactive threat hunting. Security should be involved early in projects, and overlapping compliance frameworks can be handled through shared controls. The speaker also urged attendees to consider how tools affect people's quality of life and to widen hiring pools.

talks.title: "Keeping Your Open Source Project Accessible to All" by Treva Williams
talks.teaser: Shows how documentation, responsive reviews and mentorship help open source projects attract a more diverse set of contributors.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that open source projects lose potential contributors to avoidable friction, and that who takes part depends on how welcoming a project looks from the outside. The speaker cites Bureau of Labor Statistics figures on programmers, then a 2017 GitHub open source survey of 5,500 people in which 95 percent of respondents identified as male, 3 percent as female and 1 percent as non-binary. The most common reasons given for staying away were incomplete or confusing documentation, slow or dismissive replies to contributions, conflict, unexplained rejections and unwelcoming language.

The practical advice focuses on factors maintainers control. Documentation should be kept current and simple, should not assume the reader's knowledge, and can be checked by someone unfamiliar with the project. A glossary helps with terms that are hard to search for, and the README should be updated when major changes ship. Responding promptly and politely to pull requests, or stating when a response can be expected, matters too. Rather than rejecting a large, flawed pull request outright, a maintainer can leave detailed notes and offer mentorship, which the speaker described as turning a contributor into a community member. Small accessibility options, such as a dyslexia-friendly font, are presented as an inexpensive way to make a project usable for more people.

The talk closes with a warning against tokenism, meaning celebrating underrepresented people only on set occasions, and a point that seeing people like yourself represented encourages newcomers to get involved. OpenStack projects such as Heat, Glance and Swift were named as examples of strong documentation. The speaker also noted studies suggesting that companies with diverse hires tend to innovate faster and earn more, and argued that diverse contributions can pay off in the same way.

talks.title: "Streaming video analysis in Rust using Pravega" by Tom Kaitchuck
talks.teaser: Shows how to scale real-time multi-camera video analytics with GStreamer and Pravega, plus Rust lessons on FFI, types, and async design.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with a practical goal: deployable streaming video services that ingest many camera feeds and run analysis such as object detection with acceptable latency and scale. The speaker contrasts batch and micro-batch pipelines, including painful patterns like pushing JPEG frames through Kafka, with a model that treats live and historical footage as one continuous stream backed by object storage.

Pravega is positioned as the persistence layer that offers atomic writes, retention, fine-grained reads with low latency, and strong scalability under many writers compared with messaging systems tested in their benchmarks. An end-to-end path is sketched from camera capture through GStreamer, GPU-based detection, derived metadata, and downstream analytics such as Flink SQL over counts of detected vehicles. The implementation choice of Rust is justified less for raw CPU performance than for a stateful, recoverable client shared across languages via FFI.

The latter half shares engineering lessons: explicit cross-language contracts, ownership parallels in Java, replacing visitor-style dispatch with enums and match, encoding authentication and connection lifetimes in types, and a lightweight async channel pattern instead of heavyweight actor frameworks. The close emphasizes ecosystem crates, tooling, and how compile-time checks reduced thread-safety design overhead while enabling bolder structure.

talks.title: "Artisanal, machine-generated API libraries" by Richard Marmorstein
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in "Artisanal, machine-generated API libraries" by Richard Marmorstein.

talks.title: "Creating More Inclusive Tech Spaces: Paths Forward" by Amy Wallhermfechtel
talks.teaser: Examines how tech communities can rebalance openness with care, move policies into practice, and measure equity beyond headcount.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames inclusion as work on socio-technical systems, not on devices alone. Treating “technology” as the actor in sentences, the speaker argues, reifies objects and hides the human relations, bias, and power that actually shape outcomes. She proposes rebalancing along several axes at once: seeing systems rather than gadgets, pairing openness with civility and care, turning written policies into day-to-day practice, and shifting focus from representation headcounts toward equity.

Midway through, cross-disciplinary examples sharpen the critique. Studies of pinion jays illustrate how dominant paradigms can miss female-led hierarchies; mock “holy war” developer debates show how prized free expression can alienate underrepresented contributors. Codes of conduct, clear community-specific meanings for “diversity,” and the hazard that policy documents substitute for real change are developed in depth. Tiered corporate workforce charts show how aggregate diversity numbers can conceal concentration of authority higher in organizations. Against efficiency-and-profit framings of diversity, she introduces recursivity—measuring how value and support circulate locally—and recursive depth, favoring bespoke, democratic, small-scale programs over copy-pasted corporate templates.

The close offers six practices meant to foster generative interaction: a shared organizational purpose not reducible to diversity branding, intentional mixing across groups, sustained frequent contact, equal insider standing for diverse members, graduated sanctions akin to Maine lobster-fishery councils, and collaborative interdependence. Practitioners are urged to welcome ground-level critique, combine equity metrics with representation, and treat open source—with its social fabric and codes of conduct—as a strong venue for generative justice.

talks.title: "Asami: Turn your JSON into a Graph in 2 Lines" by Paula Gearon
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for "Asami: Turn your JSON into a Graph in 2 Lines" by Paula Gearon.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Paula Gearon, a Technical Leader at Cisco Systems, introduces Asami, an open-source graph database developed in Clojure and ClojureScript. Gearon details the background and motivations behind Asami's creation, the mathematical foundations of graph databases, and how Asami's storage and indexing architecture enables fast in-memory and durable querying. She highlights how Asami handles flexible, schema-less JSON imports in just two lines of code and shares real-world use cases, including integration into Cisco's SecureX security product and inspecting complex network packet capture files.

### Key Topics
- **Origins and Requirements**: Developing an open-source, Clojure-based graph database to run in both backend systems and web browsers via ClojureScript, evolving from in-memory pattern matching to a Datomic-style graph database with aggregates.
- **Graph Theory and Data Modeling**: Representing entities and relations as directed edges and nodes (statements/triples). Unlike systems that strictly distinguish attributes from edges, Asami maps attributes as edges and values as nodes.
- **Triple Indexing and Nested Maps**: Organizing graph statements across three column orderings to enable rapid lookups, pattern rewriting, and joins without full table scans, leveraging Clojure's immutable data structures.
- **Durability and Copy-on-Write Trees**: Storing statements as numeric tuples (up to 512 elements per array block) organized in tree indexes (such as AVL trees) using copy-on-write semantics and memory-mapped files.
- **Time-Travel and Immutability**: Tracking root node snapshots with timestamps and transaction IDs to support querying historic database states without altering committed data.
- **JSON Ingestion and Ad-Hoc Analysis**: Loading raw, untyped JSON directly using string attributes and querying unstructured keys and values using a GraalVM-compiled command-line interface.

### Technical Details
- **Compact In-Memory and Durable Encodings**: Values fitting within 60 bits (short strings, keywords, booleans, timestamps, and numbers) are packed into a 64-bit integer, using high-order bits for type tags and lengths. Data exceeding 8 bytes is serialized into buffers referenced by byte offsets and indexed with trees storing the first 16 bytes per node.
- **Layered Protocols**: Architecture separated cleanly via Clojure protocols, allowing the block graph to swap underlying implementations (e.g., tuple storage, AVL trees, and memory-mapped block buffers) without altering higher layers.
- **Pattern Rewriting vs. Hash Joins**: Asami evaluates query patterns through iterative pattern rewriting and indexed lookups, providing fast join execution.
- **Transitive Closures & Optimization**: Implementation of Sparkle-inspired transitive closures uses self-doubling steps (reaching 256 steps in 8 iterations), reducing linear query times from 90 seconds to roughly 80 milliseconds.
- **CLI & GraalVM**: Compiled to a native command-line tool, enabling analysts to ingest large files (such as a 7 MB packet capture JSON), index them, and query regex-matched attributes (like query keys containing spaces) within seconds.

### Takeaways
Asami offers a lightweight (~7,000 lines of Clojure vs. 100,000 lines of Java in older systems like Mulgara), schema-agnostic solution for loading arbitrary JSON directly into an indexed graph. While bulk indexing large multi-gigabyte datasets requires time, lazy loading and copy-on-write storage deliver sub-second query performance and time-travel querying. It is actively deployed at Cisco in security tooling such as SecureX.

talks.title: "Equitable Experiential Access: Audio Description" by Laurel Lawson
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in "Equitable Experiential Access: Audio Description" by Laurel Lawson.

talks.title: "How Flutter Can Change the Future of Urban Communities" by Edward Thornton
talks.teaser: Shows how the cross-platform Flutter toolkit speeds up building community safety apps and startup MVPs across devices.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a software developer, opens with a community safety app he built after the Ferguson unrest in St. Louis. Users post local incidents, which then appear as clustered markers on a map so residents can see where problems have been reported. He demonstrates adding posts live, and says the app was later used in Nigeria during protests over police brutality to coordinate and share information.

He then introduces Flutter, an open-source toolkit launched by Google in 2017 that compiles one codebase to Android, iOS, Linux, Windows and the web. It has two parts: an SDK with tools for building and compiling, and a widget-based user interface framework. He argues its main strengths are fast development, shown through hot reload as he changes a name and a color and sees the result immediately, a single codebase, customizable widgets, and easy adaptation to different screen sizes. He also covers lower development cost for startups building minimum viable products, plus a large community and learning resources.

He closes by showing FlutterFlow, a tool that speeds up mobile app creation further, and points to a map of countries where Flutter is gaining adoption, including Brazil, Puerto Rico and parts of Africa and the Middle East. His takeaway is that Flutter suits fast-moving urban communities and is a good starting point for beginners. He notes that its web support is still maturing.

talks.title: "Nim Nuggets: Systems Programming & Metaprogramming Magic" by Aditya Siram
talks.teaser: Shows Nim's compile-time introspection, destructor-based memory management, and C++ interop through live code demos.
talks.summary:
Aditya Siram introduces Nim, a statically typed imperative language that blends ideas from Ada, Modula, Oberon, Pascal and Lisp and compiles through C. He opens with a small web server that returns a capitalised URL path as JSON, then shows C-style manual allocation and freeing, and explains uniform function call syntax, which lets ordinary functions be chained with dot notation. He argues that fast compile times matter most for developer feedback, citing a full bootstrap of a few minutes on an old laptop.

The middle of the talk covers static introspection. Code runs at compile time through an interpreter, the compiler can report whether an expression compiles and what type it has, and a macro diffs two versions of a Person type to generate a migration type. A second example shows that a migration needing a real transformation, such as turning a string address into a structured one, must be supplied explicitly. Static resource management follows: destructors are injected after a value's last use, and a consumed value that is used again gets destroyed twice until a copy hook is marked as an error, at which point the compiler reports the conflict.

The final section covers C++ interop, mapping Nim types to std::vector and unique_ptr with templates and reusing them without leaks, plus a compile-time factorial built on a recursive template trick. The takeaway is that fast feedback, introspection, controllable memory management, and C++ interop make Nim practical in places where few languages fit.

talks.title: "Game Development in Eight Bits" by Kevin Zurawel
talks.teaser: Explains how the NES handled graphics, physics, random numbers and saves within its tight hardware limits.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through the Nintendo Entertainment System, a 1985 console built around a 6502 processor with 2 KB of system RAM, 2 KB of video RAM and no operating system or clock. Kevin Zurawel shows how developers worked within those limits. Backgrounds were built from 8x8 tiles stored as grid references, sprites were capped at 64 on screen, and Super Mario Bros. fit a 14-screen level into about 101 bytes by reusing repeated scenery.

Physics and collision needed similar shortcuts. Mario's weighted movement came from fixed-point numbers that track sub-pixel positions, since the processor could only add, subtract and shift. Contra treated the player as a single point tested against a rectangle that shifted with the player's pose. For random numbers, Tetris used a shift register, Final Fantasy stepped through a hard-coded table of 256 values, and Contra mixed the frame counter into a byte.

Saving was the last hurdle. Early games relied on passwords, and the Famicom Disk System offered writable disks that were easy to copy, so cartridges with battery-backed RAM followed. Holding reset while powering off protected save data from a processor that can misbehave as power fades, and Dragon Warrior kept several checksummed copies of its save. The takeaway is that a simple, shippable fix often beats a perfect one until it proves inadequate.

talks.title: "Whoops! I Rewrote it in Rust" by Brian Martin
talks.teaser: Follows a Twitter engineer's effort to rewrite a memcache-compatible cache server and its storage layer in Rust without losing speed.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a software engineer at Twitter, explains that the company's Pelican caching framework, written in C and used to maintain forks of memcache and Redis, needed TLS support. The team wanted to add it in Rust without giving up the throughput and tail latency of the C version. An earlier 2019 Rust server built on the Tokio runtime ran about 10 to 15 percent slower in throughput and 25 to 30 percent higher at p99.9, which was not acceptable for production. Tail latency matters because a large fan-out makes it likely that a user-facing request hits a slow cache response.

To isolate the problem, the speaker rebuilt a minimal ping server on mio, a thin wrapper over epoll, with TLS provided by BoringSSL, and it matched the C benchmarks. A cache server followed, using the standard hash map as a stand-in for storage. The C storage library was tied into the metrics and logging frameworks, so the speaker rewrote it in Rust as a single-threaded segment design. Segments group items by expiry time rather than by size, which allows efficient expiry, new eviction strategies, and about five bytes of metadata per item instead of 39 in the slab design. The Rust cache server beat upstream memcache at high throughput, and persistent memory storage retained about 93 percent of DRAM performance in a 4:1 read-write test.

The rewrite took about two months and duplicated earlier design work, and feature parity was still incomplete. Tools such as cargo bench, cargo fuzz, and clippy helped with micro-benchmarking, protocol fuzzing, and code quality, and an all-Rust build was easier to maintain than CMake. Remaining work includes finishing features, canary testing, multi-threaded tuning, and building a Redis replacement.

talks.title: "Software for Court Appointed Special Advocates" by Linda Goldstein
talks.teaser: Delivers lessons on building open-source SaaS for CASA volunteers, from weekly deploys to welcoming first-time contributors.
talks.summary:
Court Appointed Special Advocates are sworn volunteers who gather information about foster youth and file court reports every six months. Many excel at advocacy but not paperwork, while local chapters lack a single funding model or IT stack. Ruby for Good’s CASA Project is open-source software as a service aimed at maximum simplicity for volunteers, offered free and shaped closely with chapter administrators.

The application centers on logging case contacts, customizable per youth and chapter, with long-form notes volunteers already write by hand. Case pages surface court mandates, emancipation checklists, supervisor nudges, and Word-format court reports. Onboarding chapters means importing hundreds of volunteers, supervisors, and cases—where duplicate keys and partial failures become painful edge cases. The speaker walks through responsive web UI, a thin Android wrapper, exports, mileage reporting, and protections around sensitive data.

Maintainers treat data safety as the top priority, then volunteer ease and contributor growth. Weekly stakeholder calls, deploys, and office hours feed GitHub issues; automation handles nagging ticket hygiene; fast merges after review keep new contributors engaged. The talk closes with hard problems—issue quality, imports, Word templating, institutional memory, testing judgment—and an invitation for more CASA chapters and non-coding helpers to join.

talks.title: "Type-Driven API Design in Rust" by Will Crichton
talks.teaser: Shows how Rust traits and type-state can make a progress bar API that catches misuse at compile time.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from tqdm, a Python utility that wraps any iterable to show a progress bar with minimal code. The speaker points out its rough edges: a wrongly typed argument only fails at runtime, and some option combinations quietly show nothing, such as a custom bar format applied to an unbounded counter. Using that API as the target, the speaker builds a comparable progress bar in Rust, one step at a time.

Starting from a concrete loop, the design is generalized over the element type and then over any iterable, using generics bounded by the standard Iterator trait. A progress struct wraps an iterator so callers can use the same wrapping style as tqdm. An extension trait then adds a method to every iterator type, including types the author does not own. For bounded iterators, the ExactSizeIterator trait unlocks a method that draws a bar with a length, and calling it on an unbounded range fails at compile time. Finally, a type-state pattern encodes bounded versus unbounded in the type itself, so the delimiter-setting method exists only in the bounded state and misuse becomes a compile error.

The main takeaways are that traits are the central unit for organizing a Rust API, that they allow extending types you do not own, and that where clauses and type states can move misuse checks from documentation or runtime into the compiler. The speaker also notes the trade-off: compiler errors can be verbose and hard to read, so designers must weigh them against clearer runtime errors.

talks.title: "Incremental, zero-config Code Nav using stack graphs" by Douglas Creager
talks.teaser: Explains stack graphs, which define language name-binding rules to power incremental, zero-config code navigation at scale.
talks.summary:
Precise code navigation, such as jump to definition and find all references, is hard to offer on a hosted platform holding enormous amounts of code. Name rules differ by language: Python lets a later definition shadow an earlier one, while Rust rejects the same pattern as a compile error. Imports and re-exports can route a lookup through intermediate files, so a change in one file may alter results elsewhere.

The method uses stack graphs, a graphical notation for name binding. Each file yields its own graph, built without reference to other files, with nodes for definitions and references plus a symbol stack that records what a lookup still needs. A reference resolves when a path through the graph leaves the stack balanced. Per-file partial paths are precomputed at index time and joined at query time, so lookups stay quick. Tree-sitter parsers supply syntax trees, and a declarative graph language for each language builds the graphs without a custom build step.

A Python prototype was reported as deployed internally, with a median indexing time near five seconds per push and median query stitching around 50 milliseconds, p99 near 100 milliseconds. The lesson is to split work so per-file results are reusable, keep interactive queries to joining precomputed pieces, and describe language rules declaratively.

talks.title: "Practical Quantum Computing Today" by Alex Condello
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in "Practical Quantum Computing Today" by Alex Condello.

talks.title: "Pictures Of You, Pictures Of Me, Crypto Steganography" by Sean Marcia
talks.teaser: An entertaining narrative traces how TV stills hid Olympic curling taunts while teaching steganography basics and LSB image encoding.
talks.summary:
A speaker recounts mysterious emails from a former curling teammate: subjectless messages with stills from Buffy, Babylon 5, and Firefly. A mutual contact hints that the answer lies in the pictures themselves, not the shows.

The talk pivots to steganography from ancient wax tablets and invisible ink through microdots, and why hiding data alone is weak without cryptography. It explains how digital images store RGB pixels, bytes, and bits, and how changing the least significant bits can embed text without visible change. Ransomware and trojans are noted as real-world misuses; detection tools exist on the defense side.

Before the 2018 Winter Olympics, decoded pre-event images carried insults about Canada and the speaker’s curling; post-games repeats spelled out the U.S. men’s gold-winning score. The arc closes as comedy about rivalry and humility rather than a coding lab.

talks.title: "Program Synthesis: A Dream Realized?" by Roopsha Samanta
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in "Program Synthesis: A Dream Realized?" by Roopsha Samanta.

talks.title: "Prevent Phishing & Impersonation" by Karissa McKelvey
talks.teaser: Proposes a relationship-based identity system that replaces self-announced profiles with one-time invitation codes and local names.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with how social engineering unfolds: attackers map relationships between users and businesses, impersonate a trusted party, pull personal details, and then escalate to exploits or ransomware. Most defenses target infrastructure, key verification and phishing training, but the speaker argues the weak point is self-announced user profiles that anyone can copy and that depend on a third party to validate them. Examples include iMessage's name suggestions, which bring back spoofable lookups, and Keybase-style social proofs, where the recipient still has to check who is genuine.

The speaker presents Back Channel, a prototype built around relationships instead of global namespaces. Two people exchange a one-time numeric code that expires after about a minute; both apps derive a shared secret from it and open an end-to-end encrypted channel, with the relay treated as untrusted and swappable. Each person names the other in a local contact list that never leaves the device. Multi-device linking uses QR codes and CRDT-based syncing, and a lost device can be revoked with a tombstone message that wipes its data. Demos cover chat and document review sharing.

User tests with journalists, researchers and designers showed that most participants did not notice they never created an account. Known gaps include a single relay as an availability risk, unresolved revocation edge cases, no key rotation, and no storage peer, so messages only sync when both people are online. Group invitations and enterprise uses, such as exchanging a code with a supervisor during a video call, were left as open questions.

talks.title: "Dancing With Myself" by Mariel Pettee
talks.teaser: A performing artist applies variational autoencoders and graph neural networks to motion-capture data to break creative ruts in dance.
talks.summary:
The presenter describes falling into repetitive patterns when improvising in the studio and wondering whether machine learning from particle-physics work could suggest fresh movements that still feel like her own style. She sets goals around physical plausibility, authentic personal style, surprise, and what she calls kinetic desire—the urge to get up and move.

She contrasts earlier choreography neural networks limited by single-camera or 2D video poses with her own multi-camera motion-capture data at roughly 35 frames per second and about 50 body points. A variational autoencoder team published in 2019, enabling latent-space sampling, fringe exploration for unusual phrases, live studio feedback including latent-position visualization, and controlled noise on embeddings to vary existing phrases—work that produced a pandemic-era duet with herself. At Intel’s AI group she extended the line with a graph-based variational model inspired by neural relational inference, sparse edge types linking distant body parts, and improvisational prompts drawn from highly or poorly ranked connections.

Takeaways include uses beyond raw generation: co-creative dialogue, live performance coupling, phrase iteration, and thinking about models as partial preservation of movement practice. She closes with a framework mapping creative autonomy versus model autonomy and friend versus antagonist relationships, favoring challenging, uncomfortable models to escape ruts. Audience questions touch on codified dance styles, localized graph structure, accessibility for non-engineers, latent pose versus sequence views, and preprocessing that centers XY position like a treadmill.

talks.title: "Simple Made Easy"
talks.teaser: Argues that simplicity means unentangled parts rather than familiarity, and shows how complecting drives software complexity.
talks.summary:
Rich Hickey argues that developers often confuse "simple" with "easy" and pay too little attention to the entanglement that makes software hard to understand and change. He traces the origins of both words: simple refers to a single fold or braid, meaning unentangled, while easy is relative, tied to what is nearby or familiar to a particular person. He defines complexity as complecting, the braiding together of concerns such as state and identity, inheritance and types, or rules scattered through code.

He argues that reliability depends on being able to reason about a program, and that type checkers and test suites act as guard rails rather than direction. Chasing ease from the start, he says, is like a sprinter running flat out from the first step of a long race. He offers simpler alternatives: immutable values, plain functions, maps and sets for data, queues to decouple components, declarative rules, and protocols for polymorphism. Simple tools, he notes, can build the same sophisticated systems.

Simplicity is a choice that takes deliberate effort, and it concerns the resulting artifact rather than how code is typed. Many small separate components can be simpler than a few tangled ones. The talk closes by urging developers to build a sensitivity to entanglement so they can argue for simpler designs with colleagues.

talks.title: Strange Loop Chat with Hillel Wayne about TLA+
talks.teaser: The discussion explains how TLA+ models distributed systems to expose design flaws before teams commit to full implementation.
talks.summary:
The conversation opens by contrasting everyday implementation mistakes with rarer but more dangerous design bugs—cases where the code matches the spec yet still violates requirements, races, or catastrophic shutdown paths. Testing and types only inspect code that already exists; formal specification languages model the system abstractly so those flaws surface earlier. TLA+ is positioned as a leading option, aided by public accounts of Amazon finding serious issues in services such as S3 and DynamoDB after conventional checks missed them.

The middle walks through how TLA+ blends temporal logic with ideas from earlier formal methods, representing actions, state sequences, and the full behavior space teams must satisfy. A concrete batch-installer scenario illustrates the stakes: a third-party API that was eventually consistent and non-idempotent could leak memory or strand resources unless retries and timing were designed carefully. Modeling produced long error traces, drove redesign in days, and reportedly shortened the later build.

Practitioners hear where specification fits in the lifecycle—especially before large implementations and during refactors—and why models stay deliberately separate from production code. Keeping spec and code aligned stays a human-process problem, though trace-driven orchestration can replay modeled actions against real services. The close clarifies that TLA+ is notation checked by model checkers, not a state-machine compiler, and points newcomers toward introductory books, online material, and Lamport’s reference text.

talks.title: Strange Loop Chat with Paula Gearon about the Asami graph database
talks.teaser: Explains Asami, an open-source graph database written in Clojure for JVM and browser use, and how it handles queries and storage.
talks.summary:
Asami is an open-source graph database written in Clojure, maintained by an engineer at Cisco's Threat Grid group. In this interview, the maintainer explains that it started as an in-memory store for an internal rules engine, built so the team would not depend on a commercial system. As the storage layer grew, it became its own project. It now runs on the JVM and in the browser through ClojureScript, and durable on-disk storage is being finished ahead of a 2.0 release.

The discussion covers the data model, where nodes and labelled, directed edges represent entities and the relationships between them. The query language combines the Datomic-style EDN syntax with SPARQL semantics, so most queries written for Datomic or DataScript can be reused, though edge cases such as negation and certain unions follow SPARQL behaviour. Asami is tuned for querying and analysis over data gathered from many sources, at the cost of slower loading when writes are frequent. Because stored data is immutable, replication across a cluster is comparatively simple, and the history of earlier values is kept and can be queried.

The maintainer closes by pointing listeners to the project's GitHub repository under the threadgrid organisation, its online documentation, and the #asami channel on the Clojurians Slack. The takeaway is that Asami suits Clojure developers who need to link disparate data and run many analytical queries over it.

talks.title: Strange Loop Chat with Tejas Chopra about Carbon Footprint Aware Software Development
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Strange Loop Chat with Tejas Chopra about Carbon Footprint Aware Software Development.

talks.title: "How to Think about Parallel Programming: Not!" - Guy L. Steele Jr. (Strange Loop 2010)
talks.teaser: Parallel applications gain speed when programmers release control to runtimes via associative merges instead of accumulators.
talks.summary:
Guy Steele opens with what he calls the ugliest program he ever wrote: an 80-word IBM 1130 card utility that formatted core dumps on a Selectric console printer, using self-modifying initialization, interrupt tricks, and opcode bit patterns as constants to squeeze into severe memory limits. He walks through reverse-engineering the card decades later, then contrasts that hack with a tiny, elegant PDP-10 routine for hyperbolic sine—and notes how shaving four more bytes years later made the gem harder to understand.

The heart of the talk parallels his historical theme: programmers stopped micromanaging addresses, registers, and memory once assemblers, compilers, stacks, garbage collectors, and virtual memory took over. He distinguishes cooperative parallelism from competitive concurrency, argues that accumulator-style loops fight multi-core machines, and shows why race-prone parallel do-loops fail while tree-shaped reductions win when addition is associative.

He demonstrates a divide-and-conquer approach in the Fortress language: split strings into chunk and segment partial results, merge them with an overloaded associative operator, and let the runtime choose sequential or parallel execution.
