Algebraic properties—especially associativity—give implementations “wiggle room,” much like forbidding address-of in managed languages frees the collector. His closing plea is to treat processor allocation like memory management: express independent work and lawful combines, and let the system handle parallelism so programs stay portable across wildly different core counts.

talks.title: "Why is a Monad Like a Writing Desk?" by Carin Meier (2012)
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning "Why is a Monad Like a Writing Desk?" by Carin Meier (2012).

talks.title: "Functional Composition" by Chris Ford (2013)
talks.teaser: Live Clojure demos build sound from sine waves through scales and canons, culminating in Bach and a swing bass jam.
talks.summary:
The presenter reframes a functional programming audience as creators who need to show what their languages can build beyond language design itself. Using Clojure and the Overtone audio environment, he contrasts Western staff notation—a fixed, non-extensible notation meant for human performers—with programmatic representations where nested abstractions and pure functions can express musical ideas directly.

The session walks from sine waves and envelopes through harmonics, bell timbre, and psychoacoustic pitch illusion, then discrete pitch via octave doubling and the twelfth root of two, MIDI numbering, and concert A at 440 Hz. Notes become time–pitch data; scales and keys compose as functions. Simple tunes demonstrate the model, then domain-specific “runs” support Bach-style material. Canon forms—delay, interval shift, pitch mirror, time reversal, and their compositions—encode baroque counterpoint; Canon in D (quarter) is performed and graphed, then replayed in minor to show how small domain edits change character.

A closing live jam incrementally adds bass progression, melody, drum samples, walking bass, swing timing, tempo, arpeggios, and key changes around a Glenn Miller-style arrangement. The through-line is domain-driven design: musical concepts should map to small, composable code changes, and the same compositional habits tie development to music.

talks.title: Strange Loop Chat with Joel Holdbrooks about Meander
talks.teaser: Explains how the Clojure pattern-matching library Meander supports rewriting data, and where its next release is headed.
talks.summary:
Joel Holdbrooks, creator of the Clojure library Meander, sits down for a conversation about how the project started and where it is going. He traces his motivation to everyday programming, where code often pulls data apart one way and rebuilds it another. That asymmetry struck him as odd compared with how equations are handled in mathematics. Rewriting systems, which turn one arrangement of symbols into another, offered a model he wanted to bring into Clojure.

The discussion walks newcomers through pattern matching, starting with regular expressions and the destructuring found in mainstream languages. Placeholders bind to parts of a structure, and rewriting applies those bindings to a new shape on the right-hand side. Joel describes his goal of symmetry, where anything expressible on the left of a rule can also appear on the right. He explains that an unbound logic variable causes substitution to fail, a choice made after users reported that the earlier restriction on disjunctions was a pain point. Meander also runs in ClojureScript, where it can match on JavaScript objects and arrays, and it can be extended with new behaviour.

On performance, he says users report slow patterns, and the team has closed much of the gap with handwritten code, sometimes beating it through dead code elimination and inference. The next version aims to add an interpreter, quoted patterns, macros, explanations for why a match fails, and a unified framework, with a release targeted before the end of the year.

talks.title: Strange Loop Chat with África Periañez about predictive models and benshi.ai
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Strange Loop Chat with África Periañez about predictive models and benshi.ai.

talks.title: Strange Loop Language Panel
talks.teaser: Hickey investigates Strange Loop Language Panel.

talks.title: "Systems that run forever self-heal and scale" by Joe Armstrong (2013)
talks.teaser: Explains how isolated processes, message passing and supervision let long-running systems survive crashes and scale.
talks.summary:
Joe Armstrong opens with the goal of building systems that keep running for years, recover from crashes and grow to very large size. He argues that distributed programming is hard mainly because of data consistency and failure handling, while running many small isolated processes that exchange messages is comparatively easy. Using a hash-based placement scheme, he shows how a piece of data can be located across a cluster of machines, then explains why replicating data across just two machines leaves the system in an uncertain state after a crash. Leader election in Paxos-style protocols, he notes, is notoriously difficult to get right.

The core of the talk is a set of six rules for fault-tolerant systems: isolation, concurrency, failure detection, fault identification, live code upgrade and stable storage. Armstrong argues that isolation brings fault tolerance, scalability, testability and upgradability together, and that a failing process should be allowed to crash rather than be defended against. Linked processes and supervising workers then restart what has failed. He describes Erlang's lightweight processes, asynchronous message passing and OTP design principles, and reports that well-structured programs speed up on multi-core machines without code changes.

He points to production uses such as Ericsson telephony base station software, CouchDB, RabbitMQ and a Chef server monitoring large numbers of machines. A live profiler demo shows bottlenecks where many worker processes funnel into one central process. He closes by urging developers to reason about the collective behaviour of very large numbers of processes rather than individual ones.

talks.title: "Everything I Have Learned I Have Learned From Someone Else" by David Nolen (2013)
talks.teaser: Shows how implementing ideas from CS papers yields Clojure logic programming, optimized pattern matching, and fast ClojureScript UIs.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with how earlier ARPA-era research and interactive programming shaped the speaker’s path from BASIC through JavaScript UI work at The New York Times into Clojure. Motivated by REPL-driven development rather than purity for its own sake, the narrative follows a habit of reading papers—Bagwell-style persistent collections, miniKanren, and constraint logic programming—and turning them into engineered artifacts.

The middle covers core.logic: porting miniKanren to Clojure, speeding substitutions with persistent hash maps, polymorphic unification via protocols, and adding constraint solving while acknowledging mature solvers like Gecode and JaCoP remain far faster. A second thread implements decision-tree pattern matching from Maranget’s work in core.match, extends it to hash maps and derivable matchers, and ties the same ideas to efficient predicate dispatch.

The close argues functional programming must serve interactive clients: core.async and CSP-style code for parallel fetches with deadlines, Core Logic on ClojureScript solving the zebra puzzle in about sixteen milliseconds on V8, a functional Minecraft-like canvas demo at game frame rates, and benchmarked pattern matching on vectors versus JavaScript arrays. The closing message is that predicting the future means reading papers and engineering them into practice.

talks.title: "Evident Code, at Scale" by Stuart Halloway (2012)
talks.teaser: Shows how fine-grained abstractions and data-first APIs keep large Clojure and Datomic codebases readable as they grow.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens on project scale: not bigger data or web scale, but codebases that deliver far more value over time while changing direction, a concern raised as Clojure adoption matures. The speaker contrasts overloaded “declarative” programming with evident code—perceptible, clear, and obvious—and uses rock-paper-scissors examples to show when declarative, functional, or logic styles fit identity, performance, and team constraints.

Most of the session walks Datomic and Clojure design with concrete code. Protocols should stay tiny and split action from perception; bloated Java Map interfaces and generated AWS request types illustrate what to avoid. Queries, schema, graph navigation, and even navigation paths are treated as data, shrinking APIs toward zero methods. Datalog examples cover multi-database inputs, predicates, shipping-cost joins, and ETL-style datum manufacturing; schema as maps stays readable across languages without evaluation.

The closing third treats tests as programs built from data: generative Mastermind scoring, ASCII visual fixtures, time-ordered queue and failover interleavings, and storage failures validated via logs and metrics rather than heavy mocking. A large simulation harness drives timed actors on real infrastructure, with later validation against timestamped records. The takeaway is to favor data throughout, design abstractions deliberately, and invest upfront architecture so substantial systems stay understandable at scale.

talks.title: "Swearjure" by Gary Fredericks (2013)
talks.teaser: Shows how to write Clojure programs using only non-alphanumeric characters, and what that subset can and cannot express.
talks.summary:
Gary Fredericks presents Swearjure, an esoteric subset of Clojure whose programs contain no alphanumeric characters. The work is led by Tim McCormick and John Nicholas Laronge. He starts with what can be expressed: any positive integer, built by adding ones obtained from a multiplication call with no arguments; negative numbers and ratios through the negation and division functions; true and false through equality checks; and nil by looking up a missing key in an empty map. Floats remain out of reach.

Data structures are built mainly with the backtick reader, using unquote and unquote-splicing to cons onto lists, concatenate sequences, and make vectors. Functions can only be written with the reader literal, and it cannot be nested, so the talk shows workarounds such as wrapping a value in a vector and immediately calling it to return a data structure. Control flow relies on a function table, a map of functions passed as the first argument, which simulates if and recursion but consumes stack on every call.

On limits, he notes that Swearjure lacks Java interop, floats and higher-order features, so it is not Clojure complete and is not clearly Turing complete, though he believes the SKI calculus could be implemented. He concludes it is largely impractical yet surprisingly capable, and invites people to try it in production, report results, and help find ways to get changes into Clojure that would make it more powerful.

talks.title: "We Really Don't Know How to Compute!"
talks.teaser: Argues that programs must become easier to evolve, and demonstrates propagators, generic operators and automatic differentiation.
talks.summary:
He opens by arguing that computing is in real trouble. He notes a person spots an illusory figure within a few tens of neural steps, a process nobody knows how to program. He compares the human genome, roughly a gigabyte, to the size of a large operating system codebase, and notes that small edits turn it into a cow rather than a person. Hardware has become cheap while programmer time is the real cost, so he argues that evolvability matters more than correctness.

He first extends arithmetic at run time so addition works on functions, symbolic expressions and matrices. He builds a numerical integrator for stiff equations that generates code while running, and uses hyper-real numbers to get automatic differentiation and the chain rule. He then contrasts textbook circuit equations with how an experienced engineer reasons. In his propagator model, cells accumulate ever-better information about a value. A building-height estimate built from shadow, barometer and stopwatch measurements tightens as sources combine, and provenance tracking with truth maintenance isolates contradictions, while dependency-directed backtracking finds consistent subsets far faster than chronological search.

He closes by framing the core problem as evolvability rather than correctness: systems should handle uses their designers never intended. Generic extensions help but make proofs harder. He proposes rethinking machine architecture around redundancy and degeneracy, presented as directions to explore rather than solved answers.

talks.title: "Pushing the Limits of Web Browsers" by Lars Bak (2012)
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of "Pushing the Limits of Web Browsers" by Lars Bak (2012).

talks.title: "Computing Like the Brain" by Jeff Hawkins (2012)
talks.teaser: Explores how neocortex-style sparse codes and sequence memory power continuous learning on fast data streams.
talks.summary:
Jeff Hawkins describes a research program begun roughly thirty years ago to discover how the neocortex works and to build machines on the same information principles. The method starts with anatomy and physiology as constraints, adds theory and math, and implements models in software, with silicon envisioned later.

He presents the neocortex as a hierarchical predictive memory fed by millions of sparse sensory channels. Three ideas receive the most depth: sparse distributed representations with semantic overlap and robust partial matching; sequence memory built from cells that wire to neighbors active moments earlier, extended by columnar encodings so repeated symbols stay distinct; and online learning through rapid synapse formation and decay when patterns fail to recur. These mechanisms are tied to recent neuroscience on dendritic coincidence detection.

The Numenta Grok product streams structured records through encoders into SDRs, runs a cortical learning algorithm, and outputs predictions, probabilities, and anomalies. Examples include twenty-four-hour building energy forecasts, video transcoding server load, and wind-turbine oil-temperature pattern shifts that flagged events without threshold breaches. Hawkins closes by arguing that scalable intelligence depends on these representations, outlines open problems such as hierarchy and sensorimotor coupling, and discusses distributed models, fault-tolerant memory hardware, and applications beyond classic vision-and-language benchmarks. Audience questions cover expertise over time, community access during private beta, sparsity trade-offs, and nondeterminism in production deployments.

talks.title: Strange Loop Chat with Felienne Hermans about "The Programmer's Brain"
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Strange Loop Chat with Felienne Hermans about "The Programmer's Brain".

talks.title: "Babel: An Untyped, Stack-based HLL" by Clayton Bauman (2013)
talks.teaser: Walks through a stack-based, untyped language with built-in security primitives and a live demo of its interpreter.
talks.summary:
Clayton Bauman, the author of the Babel programming language, opens by arguing that device security depends on who controls the software a device runs. He ties the recent surveillance revelations to proprietary hardware, digital rights restrictions and government backdoors, and argues that the focus should shift toward the rights of device owners. Babel 1.0 is planned to use public key cryptography so the interpreter can check whether a piece of code is allowed to run locally. He is clear that this does not fix an insecure underlying platform.

He then introduces the language itself: a general-purpose, untyped, stack-based language in postfix order, with optional type tags. Data lives in leaf arrays, pointers in interior arrays, and tagged pointers carry a 128-bit hash. The virtual machine uses a data stack, an up stack and a managed return stack, along with a symbol table and a bootstrap written in Babel itself. The reference implementation is written in C, with a Perl front end that compiles S-expression source into bytecode.

The live demo covers hello world, arithmetic, iterating over lists and random numbers, hash table lookups, loops, and the difference between dupe and copy. He also shows unload and load to serialize a structure to a file and read it back, and reads environment variables through the symbol table. The talk ends with a program that loads and runs compiled Babel code from a file. He closes by noting that the language is still in development, with more crypto primitives, compression, web access and cross-platform builds planned.

talks.title: "Noether: Symmetry in Programming Language Design" by Daira Hopwood (2013)
talks.teaser: Explores how symmetry principles structure layered programming languages for security, robustness, and efficient concurrency.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with a software crisis framing: hardware and storage have grown by orders of magnitude since the 1970s, yet mainstream languages and tools have not kept up, leaving programs large, hard to verify, and economically costly to make correct, secure, and reliable. The speaker ties that gap to real-world harm, noting that agencies have successfully exploited flaws in widely deployed software because practical development rarely matches the rigor of niche high-assurance efforts.

The core proposal is to treat symmetry—invariance under meaningful program transformations—as a design discipline. Desirable language properties such as confluence, referential reasoning, and comment independence are symmetries; familiar features like side effects, shared state, failures, and concurrency often break them. The Noether design responds with stratified sublanguages ordered by decreasing symmetry, enforced through type inference, culminating in an object-capability security model, separated parallelism versus concurrency, pervasive transactional procedure calls with strong exception safety, and progressively richer layers from terminating pure functional cores through local mutable state, transactional failure handling, data-flow concurrency, and event-loop message passing, plus a distributed extension using a failure-recovery protocol.

Practitioners should take away a methodology: make symmetries explicit when adding expressive power, keep most code in high-symmetry inner layers, and use capability discipline plus transactions to limit exploit blast radius and inconsistent state after errors. Safe-language pitfalls in Haskell and OCaml illustrate how hidden unsafe primitives undermine advertised guarantees. Implementation remains early, with dense slides carrying formal and performance details skipped live.

talks.title: "Nimrod: A new approach to meta programming" by Andreas Rumpf (2013)
talks.teaser: Shows how Nim's macros, templates and term rewriting rules move work to compile time, using a hello world program as the example.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who designed the Nim language (called Nimrod in the talk), introduces it as a compiled language that generates C, JavaScript, C++ and Objective-C code and includes a real-time garbage collector. He explains how a hello world program works, including overloaded dollar conversions for custom types, and how a macro can derive a not-equals operator from a user's equals operator.

The core of the talk demonstrates macros on small examples. A tag macro generates HTML helper procedures, an immediate macro avoids type inference on undeclared names, and a once template runs a block exactly once using a hygienic guard. Lazy templates delay the evaluation of logging arguments, and an HTML domain-specific language is expanded into a procedure that the compiler evaluates at compile time into one string literal. Term rewriting macros then optimize a format operator by partially evaluating literal format strings, and a regex example hoists repeated pattern construction out of a loop.

The closing recap notes that compile-time evaluation, declarative and imperative AST macros, and term rewriting all help move work out of runtime. Term rewriting rules can be tricky and buggy, so they carry names that allow them to be disabled. Static file reading, external process execution, custom pragmas and quasi-quoting were mentioned but not demonstrated. The main takeaway is that macros let library authors optimize code without changing how it is written.

talks.title: "Dao Programming Language for Scripting and Computing" by Limin Fu (2013)
talks.teaser: Covers Dao's optional typing, syntax macros, concurrent tasklets and channels, LLVM JIT compilation, and Clan-based C++ library bindings.
talks.summary:
The presentation introduces Dao, a general-purpose language the author built to offer advanced features with a small runtime, initially motivated by frustrations with Perl and a need for better bioinformatics scripting. Dao supports optional typing with inference and static checking, instruction and function specialization, and extension APIs that reduce boilerplate compared with wrapping C libraries in Lua or Python.

The middle of the talk walks through distinctive language mechanics: BNF-style syntax macros, Ruby-like code sections, decorators, mixins, decorator classes, and aspects. Concurrency spans async function calls and objects, typed channels resembling Go, and an mt module with parallel map and search helpers, all backed by a concurrent runtime with lightweight tasklets and futures. Benchmarks from the language shootout compare interpreted Dao, JIT-compiled Dao, Python, and C, noting strong speedups on numerical workloads but limited JIT coverage elsewhere.

The close covers an LLVM-based JIT loadable module, ClanDaL for generating C and C++ bindings from headers (including templates and hint macros), a Qt4-based Dao Studio IDE with console highlighting and debugging, and planned work on documentation, unit tests, and toolchain improvements. Practitioners hear how Dao targets numerical computation, embeddability, and multi-core use while remaining a hobby project with gaps in docs and binding maintenance.

talks.title: "Axiomatic Language" by Walter Wilson (2013)
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning "Axiomatic Language" by Walter Wilson (2013).

talks.title: "Qbrt Bytecode: Interface Between Code and Execution" by Matthew Graham (2013)
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for "Qbrt Bytecode: Interface Between Code and Execution" by Matthew Graham (2013).

talks.title: "The J Programming Language" by Tracy Harms (2013)
talks.teaser: Demonstrates how J expresses array image processing, verb trains, and numeronyms, and situates the language in the APL and Iverson lineage.
talks.summary:
The presentation introduces the J programming language as an array-oriented descendant of Kenneth Iverson’s APL, implemented notably by Roger Hui. Rather than abstract syntax alone, it opens with a concrete demo: load a grayscale image, build a reduced “prepared” array and a smoothed shadow estimate using non-overlapping averages and transposes, then subtract shadow from the original to remove a flaw—showing how J applies verbs across entire nouns without explicit loops.

From there the session explains J’s vocabulary: nouns as data, verbs as operations, and higher-order structure formed by adjacent verbs in trains, forks, and hooks. Averages appear as a three-verb fork; a leap-year predicate illustrates right-to-left parsing of verb trains; a numeronym builder for words like internationalization walks through tally, head, tail, join, and format step by step. The speaker stresses that names are for human readability while the underlying verb compositions are interchangeable.

The closing arc covers Iverson’s Harvard notation, IBM’s hand-drawn formal machine description, APL’s commercial path, and Iverson’s later redesign that became J, recently released under GPL. Practitioners curious about compressed, mathematical array style are pointed to jsoftware.com as the primary hub for documentation and community links.

talks.title: "Enso: Composing DSL Interpreters, Languages & Aspects" by William Cook (2013)
talks.teaser: Presents Enso, a system for writing executable models and interpreted DSLs that compose into full applications without glue code.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the observation that developers carry an implicit strategy for building software. That strategy shapes all the code they write, yet it is rarely written down, so changing it later is costly. William Cook proposes making the strategy explicit by describing an application as a model and running that model through strategies implemented as interpreters or meta-programs. He contrasts this with the common practice of using small domain-specific languages embedded in a larger program and joined by general-purpose glue code.

Cook walks through examples built in Enso. A data manager turns schema-style descriptions into objects with checked fields, and optional behaviours such as mutability rules, observation, security checks and persistence can be selected across all data. Grammars are bidirectional, can build graphs rather than only trees, and are interpreted directly without parser or code generation. Four self-describing root schemas anchor the system, and a stencil maps a schema onto an editable diagram that stays synchronised with the underlying model. He also described a heating-system case from a language workbench challenge, where a state-machine controller and an asynchronous simulator updated the models live.

Cook is candid that Enso is currently slow but usable, and that partial evaluation is the planned route to better performance. The takeaway is that developers should make their designs executable and programmable, so that changing a strategy changes the resulting system's behaviour.

talks.title: "zip Code: Unpacking Data Compression" by Scott Vokes (2013)
talks.teaser: Explains core lossless compression algorithms and how a compressor was built to fit tiny embedded devices.
talks.summary:
The talk explains why data compression matters beyond file archives, pointing to gzip on web traffic, zip and tarball packaging, and streaming audio and video. Compression is framed as detecting and removing duplication in data, with the shortest possible description of a pattern as the goal. The speaker focuses on lossless methods, while lossy codecs such as JPEG get a shorter look near the end.

The core algorithms are covered in rough order of complexity. Run-length coding replaces repeated symbols with counts, and delta coding stores small gaps between sorted numbers. Huffman coding assigns short bit patterns to frequent tokens based on their statistics. The LZ77 sliding window and LZ78 dictionary methods replace repeated sequences with back references, with LZSS and LZW as variants, and DEFLATE combines these ideas with Huffman coding. The Burrows-Wheeler transform reorders data so that similar characters group together, which is the basis of bzip2.

The main case study is Heat Shrink, an LZSS library written for microcontrollers with only a few kilobytes of RAM. Decompression needs under 50 bytes and compression about 100 bytes, and the library is built as a state machine so input and output can be processed incrementally without blocking real-time tasks. A bug in handling 12-bit offsets surfaced before release and was fixed by splitting one state. The practical takeaway is to benchmark on representative data and to structure formats so they compress well.

talks.title: "Fast and Dynamic" by Maxime Chevalier-Boisvert (2013)
talks.teaser: Traces how dynamic languages evolved from Lisp through modern JavaScript VMs and the optimizations that made them fast.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames dynamic languages as tools that align machine behavior with programmer intuition, then walks from early programming constraints through Lisp’s introduction of dynamic typing, late binding, eval, interactive development, and garbage collection. It explains why these conveniences historically hurt performance: stop-the-world collectors, dynamic operator dispatch, growable objects, and eval’s ability to invalidate static reasoning.

The middle surveys decades of responses, including tagged representations on small machines, Smalltalk on the Alto, Lisp-machine hardware, Scheme flow analysis, and Self’s profile-guided tricks such as type feedback, inline caches, and hidden classes for object layout. It connects those ideas to the modern JavaScript engine competition between Chrome’s baseline JIT plus optimizing compiler and Firefox’s parser, baseline JIT, and IonMonkey, including incremental typing that can recover from eval.

The speaker closes with work on the Higgs ECMAScript 5 VM and basic block versioning, which clones specialized loop versions instead of joining types at a single conservative fixed point, reporting modest code growth and fewer type tests. Brief future guesses cover richer CPUs, smarter compilers, languages designed for speed, and ideas borrowed from Lisp, Haskell, and live Smalltalk-style systems.

talks.title: "Visualization Driven Development" by Jason Gilman (2013)
talks.teaser: Shows developers how to build interactive visualizations of their code's algorithms to debug and understand them.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that developers mostly understand their code through unit tests, debuggers, REPLs and logs, and that each has gaps. Debuggers show one moment on one thread, logs grow huge without structure, and tests miss problems nobody predicted. The speaker proposes Visualization Driven Development, the practice of building interactive visualizations of an application's algorithms alongside traditional testing.

The method captures the data produced as code runs, such as the intermediate states of a quicksort, and sends it over a websocket to a browser visualization. A playback control lets viewers step forward and back through the captured execution. The speaker outlines a design process: identify the nouns in the code, choose a visual representation for each, then choose a layout. Quicksort is shown as an animated bar chart, and a plain HTML list is presented as a simpler alternative to D3 for drawing trees. The main case is a boolean query-simplification tree from a NASA earth science search application. An animated view exposed a missed recursion into OR clauses during AND simplification, which was fixed once it was visible. A performance problem in the same work was traced to oversized query trees and slow tree manipulation.

The takeaway is that building visualizations takes upfront effort, so they should be made reusable across components and applications. The speaker compares such tools to a woodworking jig that gives repeatable results, and suggests they reveal problems and speed-up opportunities that developers did not know to look for.

talks.title: "Graph Computing at Scale" by Matthias Broecheler (2013)
talks.teaser: Argues that graphs fit how people reason and complex systems, and presents Titan, a distributed graph database.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a personal story about wishing for a notebook that always falls open to the right page. Two audience quizzes make the point: one asks for the highest degree of the current US president's wife, which people answer quickly but a relational table handles awkwardly, and the other asks for the average term length of presidents since the 1980s, which is easy for a database but hard to answer from memory. The gap is presented as a mismatch between how data is stored and how humans think about it.

The middle section presents graphs as a better fit for associative thinking. The speaker walks through the first question as a Gremlin traversal that follows a president edge, a spouse edge and a degree edge without any joins. He then argues that many real problems are complex systems, drawing on network science: spin glass models from physics, power-law degree distributions that keep social and internet networks robust when nodes fail, emergence in biology and social media, and the 2009 financial crisis as an example of interdependencies nobody had mapped.

The final part introduces Titan, a distributed graph database built on Cassandra and HBase and part of the Aurelius graph cluster. He covers two engineering problems: partitioning vertices across machines, where label propagation is combined with hints from the data model, and vertex-centric indexes that order a vertex's edges by a criterion such as timestamp so queries read only what they need. Faunus runs batch analytics over the same data using Gremlin. Graphs should become a routine developer tool, and the projects are open source under Apache.

talks.title: "Erlang for Authoritative DNS" by Anthony Eden (2013)
talks.teaser: Surveys EarlDNS on Erlang, covering binary DNS parsing, OTP packet caching, and anycast-scale latency and throughput tuning.
talks.summary:
Anthony Eden describes why DNSimple moved past PowerDNS with Ruby and Lua backends that could not keep up with custom alias-record logic and throughput needs. He frames authoritative DNS versus resolvers, then argues that authoritative servers look simple until decades of protocol edge cases appear.

The talk centers on the open source EarlDNS effort and three Erlang strengths: binary bit syntax aligned with DNS packet layout, pattern matching over JSON zone data for record types, and an OTP generic-server packet cache with synchronous lookups and asynchronous sweeps. He contrasts beginner hurdles—immutable data, Erlang-only operations tooling—with production tuning: PowerDNS-derived tests, outside-in latency sampling, and hotspot profiling.

Performance work exposed a single-process UDP read bottleneck (pre–Linux 3.9), then poolboy handoffs at about four milliseconds versus a fixed worker queue using cast that reaches 35–60 microsecond 99th-percentile handoffs and roughly 17,000–25,000 requests per second per node across a 40-node anycast fleet. Zone data moved in-memory with a Go zone loader feeding JSON at startup; metrics use Folsom and Librato. Rollout paired a cautious unicast trial with anycast expansion while keeping PowerDNS on the legacy network.

talks.title: "Building optimising compiler for Dart" by Vyacheslav Egorov (2013)
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in "Building optimising compiler for Dart" by Vyacheslav Egorov (2013).

talks.title: "Simplifying Asynchronous Code With Scala Async" by Philipp Haller (2013)
talks.teaser: Shows how Scala Async lets futures be awaited in straight-line code, avoiding nested maps and for-comprehensions.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Scala Async, a macro library that brings the async and await style used in C# and F# to Scala. The speaker argues that futures and actors are useful but become hard to manage once asynchronous logic is chained with map, flatMap and nested for-comprehensions. The library lets code read in a direct style while the macro rewrites it into non-blocking suspension and resumption.

Two constructs carry the model: an async block returns a future, and await suspends the enclosing block until another future completes, without blocking a thread. A regex date-matching example shows the difference, where the direct version is much simpler than the nested for-comprehension version. The speaker notes restrictions: await must sit directly inside an async block and cannot appear inside closures or by-name arguments, so closure bodies are wrapped in their own async and combined with Future.sequence.

The generated code is a state machine class, which the speaker describes as simple to inspect. Other points were a sequential debug mode, an experimental extension for Reactive Extensions observables, and use with Play and Akka. The library works on Scala 2.10 and 2.11 and is open source. The speaker argues it should remain a macro, so it can ship separately from the compiler.

talks.title: "Software for Programming Cells" by Colin Gravill (2013)
talks.teaser: Shows how software engineering methods can design and simulate DNA circuits and cell behaviour before any lab work.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that software engineering practices, such as abstraction, formal methods and simulation, could help biologists design living systems more reliably. It starts with DNA as a programmable medium, explaining base pairing and strand displacement, where a short toehold lets one strand push another off a longer duplex. Those reactions can be composed into logic gates such as AND and OR.

The speaker demonstrates a design tool that takes named strand components and compiles a circuit into the full set of intermediate species. Deterministic and stochastic simulations then show whether a design should behave as intended before anything is built in a lab. A three-component oscillator is solved against a parts database, and a poor candidate is contrasted with a better one that oscillates despite noise. Other examples include an approximate majority circuit and a square root circuit, which a collaborator checked with an SMT solver.

The talk then moves up to cells, comparing their parallelism and energy efficiency with current computers. It notes that DNA reading and writing costs are falling faster than Moore's law, although writing DNA remains expensive. A synthetic biology company's antimalarial precursor is cited as an example of engineered cells in production, and a GPU-based simulation of biofilm colony growth closes the talk. The takeaway is that simulation-first design could make biological engineering more predictable, though simulation parameters are not yet accurate enough for precise predictions.

talks.title: "Real-World Datomic: An Experience Report" by Craig Andera (2013)
talks.teaser: Explains Datomic's storage model and indexes through a hotel event-counting system that met a tight latency target.
talks.summary:
Craig Andera, a consultant at Cognitect, describes a production system he helped build for a hotel search company and uses it to explain how Datomic stores and retrieves data. The client needed per-day counts of impressions, leads and bookings for each hotel, across roughly 250 million hotel events over a 30-day window, answered in real time against a 100 millisecond target.

He walks through Datomic's split between the application, the transactor and the storage service, with queries running inside the application process. Data is kept as entity, attribute, value and time facts, and reference attributes link events to hotels and to singleton event-type entities. Four indexes (EAVT, AEVT, AVET and VAET) hold sorted copies of these facts, stored as immutable tree segments. A straightforward Datalog query over all the data was too slow, because no query order narrowed the data enough to meet the target.

The team instead iterated over an index directly with seek-datums, starting from entity IDs generated per partition and date, and cached the daily summaries in the application process, rebuilt at startup. Andera stresses the costs: joins and data-as-query are lost, performance depends on what fits in memory, and this technique should not be the starting point. The practical lesson is to understand how data is ordered in the indexes before designing queries around it.

talks.title: "How does text become data?" by Catherine Havasi and Rob Speer (2013)
talks.teaser: A practical walkthrough covers tokenizing text, bag-of-words features, and open knowledge graphs for everyday NLP tasks.
talks.summary:
The presenters open by contrasting how humans skim ambiguous, multilingual text with what machines see without structure. They argue that language ambiguity should be embraced rather than over-engineered away, then outline common goals such as spam and sentiment classification, document similarity, and search.

Live Python examples move from Unicode handling and regex tokenization to NLTK sentence and word tokenization, WordNet lemmatization, word clouds, and n-grams. They build bag-of-words matrices, use statistical collocation tests for phrases like “vice president,” train a scikit-learn naive Bayes classifier on 2,000 movie reviews reaching about 80% accuracy, and inspect influential positive versus negative terms. TF–IDF normalization and latent semantic analysis on the same corpus surface similar disaster-movie reviews, illustrating limits of document-only word meaning.

WordNet hierarchies and ConceptNet’s millions of commonsense edges appear as broader background knowledge, queried via REST and embedding-style association lookups. The session closes with pointers to shared notebooks, ConceptNet, and outreach around their text-analytics work.

talks.title: "Philosophy of Scala macros" by Eugene Burmako (2013)
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for "Philosophy of Scala macros" by Eugene Burmako (2013).

talks.title: "Learnfun and Playfun: A Nintendo automation system" by Tom Murphy VII (2013)
talks.teaser: Shows how two programs learn winning criteria from NES memory and then play old games automatically.
talks.summary:
Tom Murphy VII presents Learnfun and Playfun, two programs that play old Nintendo Entertainment System games without being taught the rules. The goal is a general, deliberately absurd method rather than skilled play. The NES suits this because its tiny memory keeps game state, such as position, world, level and coin count, at fixed addresses that a program can read directly.

Learnfun watches a recording of a person playing and examines memory snapshot by snapshot. It searches for ordered combinations of memory locations that tend to increase as progress is made, then assigns weights to them. Playfun uses these weighted objectives to choose button presses. Brute force is hopeless given the size of the input space and the cost of emulating each step, so it generates random futures about five seconds long, tests short sets of next inputs by the best outcome they can reach, scores the futures, keeps the promising ones and mutates them. Its random inputs follow the speaker's own button habits, and the search is spread across several machines over a network connection.

The closing section covers both successful runs and comically failed ones, such as jumping into pits. The practical takeaway is that a program can derive a progress signal from raw memory alone, without knowing the game's rules. That approach depends on being able to emulate the system and save and reload its states, which limits how far it applies to most real-world targets.

talks.title: "Building a Multi-Master Distributed Redis in Erlang" by Chad DePue (2013)
talks.teaser: Explores an experimental Erlang Redis clone with disk-backed storage, protocol parsing, and multi-master replication using vector clocks.
talks.summary:
The speaker introduces Edis, an homage and experimental rewrite of Redis in Erlang, motivated by building very large, high-traffic consumer applications. He positions Redis as the familiar in-memory Swiss-army datastore while explaining why Edis defaults to disk through LevelDB, targets keys bigger than RAM, keeps Redis-style algorithmic costs where implemented, and openly admits the result is slower and not competitive with production Redis.

The core of the session is systems architecture in OTP: supervisor trees, many TCP listeners, client managers, and a finite-state machine that incrementally parses the line-oriented Redis wire protocol before dispatching work. Each logical database runs in its own gen_server process, so unrelated commands can proceed concurrently—a structural difference from Redis’s single hot loop. He traces a SET end to end, shows pluggable backends, and contrasts Redis master–slave RDB streaming with Edis plans for background replication. Multi-master behavior broadcasts writes with distributed casts, uses vector clocks to judge ancestry when nodes miss updates, and currently resolves conflicts by overwriting with the latest value while acknowledging CAP trade-offs and hard problems like atomic increments.

Practitioners should treat Edis as a clean reference implementation and research sandbox—some teams even strip it into a smart Redis proxy—rather than a drop-in substitute. The close includes a live two-node demo, runtime process inspection, and candid Q&A on Lua scripting gaps, per-database semantics, and why naive client round-robin is risky under partition.

talks.title: "Functional Vectors, Maps, and Sets in Julia" by Zach Allaun (2013)
talks.teaser: The presentation builds persistent vectors, hash maps, and sets in Julia using bitmap tries, generic dispatch, and structural sharing.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by positioning Julia as a dynamic, fast language where generic functions dispatch on runtime types, then contrasts Julia’s ordinary mutable vectors, dicts, and sets with the behavior functional programming expects: updates should return new values while older versions remain usable.

The core of the session is a high-level tour of persistent structures rooted in Phil Bagwell’s array-map trie ideas and their use in Clojure and Scala. A bitmap vector trie routes indices by successive bit slices; indexing and associative update copy only the path to the changed leaf, sharing the rest. Push handling covers full leaves and nodes, and a tail buffer optimization limits trie updates during common append-heavy workloads, with performance discussed relative to mutable arrays and node sizes such as 32.

The same trie pattern extends to a sparse bitmap hash map that resolves collisions by sub-tries and uses population counts to index compact slots without resize-heavy empty buckets; persistent sets follow by storing keys in that map. The talk closes with complexity and practicality notes, pointers to RRB trees for faster concatenation, and an in-progress Julia package for readers who want full code.

talks.title: "Bust the Android Fragmentation Myth" by Chiu-Ki Chan (2013)
