talks.title: "Xiki: GUI and Text Interfaces are Converging" by Craig Muth (2013)
talks.teaser: Shows how a plain-text outline language can render one set of nested menus as web, command-line, desktop, and voice interfaces.
talks.summary:
Craig Muth presents Xiki, a lightweight user interface language built around nested menus. He argues that a simple UI should need little more than an indented outline in one plain-text file, and he shows the same outline rendered as a mobile menu, a web page, a command-line menu, a desktop window, and a voice prompt. The talk starts with a flight-booking example that grows from a few items into a menu with headings, inline Ruby code, and URL-style paths.

The middle of the talk focuses on developer uses. A trailing slash makes a line behave like a directory, and plain-text records can be edited inline and saved back to a SQL table. A text editor plugin runs a line when it is double-clicked and places the output beneath it. Further examples include shell commands, directory trees, code search, Rails console access, Bootstrap and DOM editing, and note-taking with memorization mode. A Rails plugin lets end users add menus to an app by visiting URLs that do not yet exist.

In closing, Craig compares GUI and text tooling. He notes that end-user software has largely moved to graphical interfaces while developer tools remain text-based, and he predicts that voice interfaces will make textual conversation with users more important. He invites developers to try Xiki, to support the project, and to pair with him on its development.

talks.title: "Creative Machines" by Joseph Wilk (2013)
talks.teaser: Examines machine creativity through painting systems, generative music, and recombination models, and what human judgment still adds.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by asking whether machines can be creative and splits the idea into psychological versus historical novelty. It frames human creativity as working inside rules, then combining ideas, exploring permutations, or changing the rules themselves, and argues that machines excel at search but struggle to recognize value.

The middle surveys concrete projects: chaotic neural-net movement, Harold Cohen’s AARON painter with simplified world models, and a personal path through Overtone and Clojure—from cosines and cellular automata through Markov chains on Bach, EEG loops with a child, and David Cope–style interval matching, beat shuffling, web-gathered MIDI, and learning systems such as Graduas. The speaker repeatedly notes human curation, small fixes, and selection as the gap between output and something judged good.

It closes with Ada Lovelace’s limits on originality, rebuts the vacuum metaphor, and argues machines can produce surprising blends without consciousness. The takeaway is that machine output reflects encodings and influences, while human creativity shows up in designing those systems and choosing what counts as art or music.

talks.title: "Category Theory: An Abstraction for Anything" by Alissa Pajer (2013)
talks.teaser: Git commit graphs, Scala functors, and currying illustrate initial objects, natural transformations, and contravariance.
talks.summary:
The presentation introduces category theory through familiar software artifacts, beginning with Git commit history modeled as a directed acyclic graph. Commits become objects, reachability along parent links becomes morphisms, and composition follows ancestry through merge commits. Initial and terminal objects are defined in that setting, with an example showing that some DAGs have neither.

The discussion moves to categories whose objects are whole graphs and whose arrows are structure-preserving homomorphisms, then to functors—including forgetting edge structure into sets—and to Scala type constructors. Option and List appear as endofunctors on types; a polymorphic mapping from Option to List illustrates a natural transformation when the associated diagrams commute. Currying is developed as a second natural transformation after Hom functors send morphism families into sets and reverse direction contravariantly in the first argument, with type signatures used to justify the flip.

Listeners can frame Git trees with categorical language, see why commuting diagrams matter for polymorphic helpers, and treat currying as naturality so evaluation order does not change outcomes. The close mentions adjoint functors and isomorphism between curried and uncurried forms, then opens the floor for questions.

talks.title: "Continuations on the Web and in your OS" by Jay McCarthy (2013)
talks.teaser: Explains delimited continuations, then shows how they drive web servers, threading and a tiny operating system.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by defining a continuation as the rest of a computation after a given point, and argues that the definition alone says little about why continuations matter. Using Racket, the speaker shows how a continuation can be captured as a function and how delimited continuations, bounded by a prompt, limit how far the captured future reaches. A small arithmetic example shows how resuming a captured continuation can change a program's result.

The middle applies this to the web. Because HTTP is stateless, a conventional application must split its control flow into separate URLs by hand. The Racket web server instead captures a continuation, stores it in a dispatch table and gives the client a URL that resumes it, with prompts ensuring each continuation returns only to its own servlet. Further examples include reusable web components that capture their caller's context, and event-driven servers where blocking calls are hidden behind an event loop, much as green threads do.

The final part builds a cooperative threading system in about a dozen lines, then a small operating system in roughly fifty lines, where system calls are implemented as aborts to a kernel prompt that guards a shared resource. In closing, the speaker answers questions on session state, on serializing continuations, and on the trade-off between compiler-generated and hand-written asynchrony. The takeaway is that knowing what delimited continuations do can suggest new designs for servers, concurrency and resource protection.

talks.title: "A Relational Exploration of the Chomsky Hierarchy" by Daniel Friedman and William Byrd (2013)
talks.teaser: Shows how relational programming with miniKanren can run automata, quines and combinator logic in both directions.
talks.summary:
Friedman and Byrd open with a review of miniKanren, a relational language embedded in Scheme. They walk through run, fresh, equality, disequality, and the type constraints symbolo and numbero, then absento, which forbids one term from appearing anywhere inside another. They explain how eigen variables stand in for arbitrary values that can be stored or compared but not inspected, and how query variables are reported back as answers.

The middle of the talk moves to finite automata. Using a nondeterministic automaton from Sipser's textbook, they encode it directly as mutually recursive relations instead of converting it to a deterministic machine, whose state count can grow sharply. The same definition can accept strings or, run in reverse, generate accepted strings. A test checks the nondeterministic version against a deterministic one by confirming that generated answers match. They then extend the approach to a pushdown automaton by representing its stack as a list. Quines are shown next, followed by a short demonstration that generates many "I love you" programs.

The final section covers combinatory logic, with the S, K, I and W combinators and their reduction rules, plus a relational reducer for combinator terms. A search for a Y combinator is slow, so the speakers supply a hint about a self-applying form, which produces a fixed-point combinator. Because Scheme is call-by-value, they replace it with the Z combinator and compute factorial, returning 120. The takeaway is that a relational definition can run in both directions, so one program can both check and produce the objects it describes.

talks.title: "How Developers can treat Ovarian Cancer" by Mridula Jayaraman (2013)
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning "How Developers can treat Ovarian Cancer" by Mridula Jayaraman (2013).

talks.title: "CQRS with Erlang" by Bryan Hunter (2013)
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding "CQRS with Erlang" by Bryan Hunter (2013).

talks.title: "Add ALL the things: abstract algebra meets analytics" by Avi Bryant (2013)
talks.teaser: Shows how monoids from abstract algebra let analytics systems roll up counts, maxes, averages and estimates across many machines.
talks.summary:
Avi Bryant opens with a statsd-style metrics pipeline in which a stream of payment amounts is folded into a running total. Addition works well here for three reasons: a single value is enough to hold, partial totals from separate time buckets or machines can be combined in any order or grouping, and only small results need to cross the network. He shows that taking a maximum has the same properties, which leads to the idea of a commutative monoid: a set, an associative and commutative operation, and an identity element.

He then fits several other aggregations into this shape. Top-k lists merge by combining two lists and keeping the largest entries. Averages carry a running sum and count and divide only when the result is presented. Histograms are element-wise sums of bucketed vectors. For unique counts, each item is hashed to a point between zero and one and the minimum of many hashes is kept, giving a HyperLogLog-style estimate in bounded space. For frequency, he uses a count-min sketch, a matrix of counters with one hash function per row, where a query takes the minimum across the rows. He notes that a plain min is not a clean fit because zero is not its identity.

He distinguishes monoids from groups, which also have inverses. Sums and counts can absorb a refund by adding a negative value, but unique counts cannot be rolled back. The structures also compose, such as a count-min sketch whose cells hold HyperLogLog counters. For practitioners, he points to Twitter's Algebra library in Scala as the main open-source reference, along with a blog that explains and simulates these probabilistic methods.

talks.title: "Make Your Mobile Apps Accessible to All" by Heath Borders (2013)
talks.teaser: Shows how to make iOS and Android apps usable with screen readers, and how to build an Android accessibility service.
talks.summary:
Heath Borders, a mobile technical lead, covers two topics: accessibility for iOS and Android apps, and building third-party accessibility services on Android. He frames the problem: many apps leave screen reader users without usable context, such as unlabeled image buttons, or table and collection cells that cannot be reached. On iOS, he explains how UIKit provides accessibility defaults for controls and how to override labels, hints and traits.

He demonstrates a custom view split into four rectangles, each exposed as a separate accessibility element, and explains when to post layout-change and screen-change notifications so VoiceOver rereads the updated screen. He also covers VoiceOver itself, the Accessibility Inspector used in the simulator, and the content size categories introduced in iOS 7. On Android, he covers content descriptions, focus order, testing with TalkBack on a device, and keeping touch targets at 48dp.

The final section shows an Android accessibility service that receives screen events, walks the node tree and performs actions for the user. As a demo he augments a conference guide app so that tapping a rating element speaks its value, which the default behavior did not provide. He closes with advice to test with real assistive tools and to structure service logic as a state machine, because screen content can change at any time.

talks.title: "Concurrency and Parallel Computing in JavaScript" by Stephan Herhut (2013)
talks.teaser: Explains JavaScript concurrency, promises, web workers, SIMD, and parallel array programming in browsers.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by separating concurrency from parallel computing: one actor interleaving tasks versus many workers acting at once. Web developers already live in the concurrent world because the browser runs a single-threaded event queue where handlers run to completion, which simplifies reasoning about global state but introduces non-deterministic ordering and subtle pitfalls such as registering an image onload handler after assigning a cacheable URL.

The middle section walks through promises as a way to model asynchronous pipelines in data, propagate failures like exceptions, and escape nested callbacks. Long-running main-thread scripts block the UI; web workers add separate JavaScript engines and message queues for finer scheduling without shared memory. The talk then shifts to hardware parallelism—multi-core CPUs, SIMD-style vector operations, and GPUs—and how web workers can map to true parallelism when the OS schedules workers on different cores.

The closing material covers a SIMD-in-JavaScript proposal with vector types and intrinsics, then Parallel JavaScript (River Trail): par-suffixed array primitives, temporal immutability during elemental functions, commutative reductions, and a typed-object grayscale example. Practitioners should treat event semantics, promises, and workers as baseline tools, and evaluate SIMD and parallel array APIs when compute-heavy work should scale with modern devices.

talks.title: "Programming a 144-computer chip to minimize power"
talks.teaser: Shows how a 144-processor chip is programmed in Forth to cut energy use per instruction.
talks.summary:
Chuck Moore introduces the Forth language and GreenArrays' 144-computer chip, a small die in which each computer talks to its neighbors. He argues that energy per operation should matter more than speed or size when writing software, since future devices such as wearables and sensors will have little power and memory. Each node has 64 words of RAM, two stacks and four ports to adjacent nodes, and its instruction set is small enough that source code maps almost directly onto machine code.

He then walks through example code. Communication between neighbors is a blocking handshake, so a node waiting for data draws almost no power. One demonstration drives an external ceramic oscillator from a single pin, waking the node only on signal edges and letting the oscillation ring down between pulses. Other examples show how preloaded stack values replace literal fetches, how circular stacks let a neighbor supply data endlessly, and why a repeated single instruction in a loop costs less energy than alternating between two.

He closes with practical guidance. Measure power with a meter on the supply, keep stacks and loops free of random data because switching bits costs energy, and prefer jumps within the same memory page. The most important step is reducing the number of instructions executed, which usually means choosing a better algorithm. Placing active nodes near the I/O pins and minimizing the hops that messages take between nodes also reduces waste.

talks.title: "Raft - The Understandable Distributed Protocol" by Ben Johnson (2013)
talks.teaser: Walks through the Raft consensus protocol, covering leader election, log replication and network partitions.
talks.summary:
The talk explains distributed consensus, the problem of getting a group of nodes to agree on a single value or system state. Typical uses include replicated databases, leader election and distributed locks. After a brief outline of Paxos and its many roles, the speaker introduces Raft as an easier-to-understand alternative built around three roles: leader, follower and candidate.

Leader election is walked through step by step. Followers that stop hearing from a leader wait a randomized timeout, become candidates in a new term and win with a majority of votes. Split votes can stall an election until a later term resolves it. Once elected, the leader replicates log entries to followers and commits an entry when a majority has stored it, with heartbeats carrying the commit status.

Network partitions are the hard case. A cut-off leader can accept writes that never reach a majority, while the other side elects a new leader and commits its own values. When the partition heals, the stale leader steps down and rolls back its uncommitted entries. The talk closes with unbounded log growth and slow recovery, and three snapshot strategies from the accompanying paper. The main takeaway is that a majority must stay reachable and that one leader per term keeps state consistent.

talks.title: "Dissecting Clojure Reducers" by Renzo Borgatti (2013)
talks.teaser: A live rebuild of Clojure reducers explores fork-join parallelism, protocol extension, and composable map-reduce transforms.
talks.summary:
The session assumes familiarity with Clojure and sets out to understand the reducers library by reimplementing its ideas from scratch. Earlier parallelism in Clojure—pmap, deprecated parallel reduce around the JDK fork-join framework, and experimental pv-map—is contrasted with reducers as a more composable way to combine collection transforms with efficient parallel reduction in one pass rather than parallelizing a map and then reducing separately.

Most of the delivery is live coding toward a parallel reduce that splits collections, dispatches work with fork join, and generalizes beyond simple plus and increment. The path runs through wrapping operations in functions, extending Clojure protocols on collections, and adding a call-parallel layer so refined reducer collections behave correctly. Debugging mispaired arguments and parentheses interrupts the demo, but the narrative continues by wrapping the API in fold to align argument order with ordinary reduce, and by sketching how filtering and composition fit the same pattern.

The speaker relates the exercise to the real reducers sources, then shows pwc, a parallel Unix wc-style word counter built on reducers (available via Homebrew tap and GitHub). It matches sequential wc but remains slower, partly due to regex word splitting and frequency counting; GitHub and an SD Journal article are offered for follow-up.

talks.title: "Scala vs Idris: Dependent types, now and in the future" by Miles Sabin and Edwin Brady (2013)
talks.teaser: Contrasts Idris and Scala as practical paths toward dependent types for compile-time correctness checks.
talks.summary:
The session opens with everyday software failures and the Mars Climate Orbiter loss, framing mismatched units as the kind of error a richer type system could rule out at compile time. Edwin Brady outlines Idris as a general-purpose language built around full dependent types: Peano naturals, length-indexed vectors, append and zipWith whose types enforce length relationships, and a variadic adder that computes function types from runtime inputs, with a live REPL demo. Types are first-class and share the same language as values, which simplifies expressive generic programming compared with splitting value and type languages.

Miles Sabin responds on Scala’s side, encoding similar vector operations with type-level naturals and path-dependent types so length mismatches become compile errors, including safe head on non-empty lists. He walks through concatenation and implicit resolution mirroring Idris case analysis, then Edwin demonstrates Idris’s effects DSL for file I/O state machines that reject programs leaving files open. Sabin shows a partial Scala port of that effects model and composed labeled state for tree walks, but concludes heavy annotations and inference limits make the full translation impractical.

Practitioners hear that dependent typing already catches real protocol and resource-ordering bugs in Idris today, while Scala via libraries such as Shapeless offers a noisier but usable playground. Both speakers argue statically typed mainstream development is trending toward greater type-level expressiveness, with Idris as a research-friendly reference and Scala as a bridge for experimenting now.

talks.title: "Sync is the Future of Mobile Data" by Chris Anderson (2013)
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of "Sync is the Future of Mobile Data" by Chris Anderson (2013).

talks.title: "The JavaScript Interpreter, Interpreted" by Martha Girdler (2013)
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding "The JavaScript Interpreter, Interpreted" by Martha Girdler (2013).
talks.summary:
### Overview
In "The JavaScript Interpreter, Interpreted," Martha Girdler, a software engineer at Uber, breaks down the internal mechanics of how ECMAScript specifications dictate JavaScript code execution. Rather than diving into low-level compiler construction or bytecode emission, Girdler examines how JavaScript engines manage language complexity through execution contexts, the variable object lifecycle, scoping rules, and context binding.

### Key Topics
- **Compilation vs. Interpretation**: While JavaScript source code is traditionally parsed into an abstract syntax tree (AST), bytecode, and interpreted into machine code, modern engines like V8 optimize execution by translating directly into machine code.
- **Function Lifecycle and Execution Phases**: Because functions are first-class objects in JavaScript, comprehending function creation versus execution is fundamental. Function creation sets up scope and context before code execution actually runs.
- **Execution Contexts & The Call Stack**: JavaScript operates in a single-threaded runtime where execution contexts are queued in a call stack. The three main context types are Global, Function, and Eval (with Eval noted as dangerous and excluded from common practice). Contexts are pushed when functions are called and popped upon completion.
- **Variable Objects and Hoisting**: During the creation phase of an execution context, an internal variable object is populated with argument parameters, function declarations (pointers stored immediately), and variable declarations (initialized as `undefined`). Hoisting explains why referencing variables prior to their declaration returns `undefined` rather than throwing a `ReferenceError`.
- **Scope Chain vs. Block Scoping**: JavaScript relies on function-level and global-level scoping rather than block-level scoping. Identifiers resolve sequentially upwards through parent variable objects to the global object.
- **Context Binding (`this`)**: Unlike identifiers resolved through lexical scope, `this` is a keyword referencing the object to which the function is applied during invocation (e.g., top-level functions defaulting to the global `window` object, method calls binding to the receiving object, and constructors pointing to the newly generated instance).
- **Closures**: Closures form naturally when a function retains access to the variable object and scope chain present at its creation, allowing internal data encapsulation.

### Technical Details
Girdler demonstrates the distinction between identifier resolution and keyword binding using code examples featuring custom objects (`bee` and `puppycat`). She highlights that assigning a method defined on one object to a property on another rebinds `this` to whichever object currently invokes the method. Additionally, she presents a "Find the Kitten" example illustrating how a closure encapsulates private state within an outer function scope while returning an interface method capable of operating on that hidden variable.

### Takeaways
Developers can demystify JavaScript's counterintuitive quirks by analyzing ECMAScript internal behaviors. Recognizing the two-stage lifecycle—creation (where hoisting, variable objects, and scope chains are established) and execution (where assignments take place and `this` is evaluated)—provides a predictable mental model for debugging hoisting, variable resolution, and context bugs.

talks.title: "Web Apps in Clojure and ClojureScript with Pedestal" by Brenton Ashworth (2013)
talks.teaser: Explains how the Pedestal ClojureScript library structures large interactive browser apps with messages, data flow and web workers.
talks.summary:
Brenton Ashworth argues that interactive applications, which need a continuous two-way flow of information, move coordination work into the browser. These long-running apps grow large, so they need real engineering structure to stay responsive. He presents Pedestal, a client-side ClojureScript library, as a functional alternative to libraries that rely on mutation and object-oriented patterns.

To ground the discussion, he describes a sales funnel visualization built for a client. Events arrived from collectors and a queue, were processed by aggregators into Datomic, and an analyzer sent browser updates about twice a second. Drawing was handled by JavaScript widgets built on Raphael and Highcharts, which held no application state. Pedestal managed the state and logic. A live demo compared two runs of the same code: one stalled while processing updates on the main thread, while the other ran the application logic in a web worker and stayed smooth.

The talk explains the core ideas: separating rendering, services and application logic, passing messages over queues rather than making direct calls, and keeping state in a tree with path-based change reporting. Data flow recomputes functions only when their inputs change, which makes dependencies explicit and logic easy to test. The speaker closed with planned changes, including core.async channels, separate inform and transform messages, and fixed-point data flow. The main takeaway is to keep application logic pure and isolated from rendering and back-end communication.

talks.title: "High Availability at Braintree" by Paul Gross (2013)
talks.teaser: A payment gateway engineer outlines Postgres migration tactics, traffic-pausing proxies, and ISP-aware routing to protect merchant uptime.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with Braintree’s role as a behind-the-scenes payment gateway and why outages hurt merchants and partners. At roughly $10 billion in annual processing, the speaker frames downtime in dollars per minute and contrasts popular “five nines” rhetoric with how hard that target is to measure across many dependencies.

Planned maintenance centers on shrinking deploy windows. The team moved from MySQL to PostgreSQL for fast DDL, concurrent indexes, and transactional migrations, then split Rails work into pre- and post-deploy steps, rolling code server-by-server with feature switches. Where schema renames or database failovers cannot run live, a custom Python proxy queues requests in Redis while Ruby dispatchers pause—letting maintenance finish as slow successes instead of hard failures, bounded by client library timeouts.

Unplanned failure adds home-grown Linux Virtual Server load balancing with Big Brother and Litmus Paper health checks, Pacemaker for stateful failover, BGP for inbound ISP redundancy with manual overrides, and Mallory processor proxies for outbound paths with strict TLS verification. The close covers operator mistakes through automation, environment guards, read-only investigation paths, Nagios and PagerDuty alerting, and live multi-app log tails so incidents are caught early.

talks.title: "Spanner - Google's Distributed Database" by Sebastian Kanthak (2013)
talks.teaser: Explains how Google's Spanner achieves global strong consistency using Paxos, TrueTime, and GPS-backed atomic clocks.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with the popular question of whether Spanner really relies on GPS and atomic clocks, then sketches how the system grew from Bigtable and Megastore. It highlights a familiar row-column model, synchronous replication so reads anywhere see recent writes, and distributed transactions across arbitrary rows. The architecture segments a large key space into tablets replicated with Paxos, managed by span servers and zone masters within and across data centers.

The core technical thread is why commit timestamps must respect real-world ordering when applications span regions. An advertising example shows a click in Europe that causally follows ad creation in the United States; local wall clocks can reorder those events. Logical clocks on every message proved impractical at Google's scale. Spanner instead exposes uncertainty intervals via a TrueTime API, waits until chosen commit times are safely in the past, and uses multi-version concurrency for lock-free snapshots and long scans.

GPS receivers and atomic clocks in each data center bound clock drift, with sawtooth uncertainty growth between syncs. Practitioners should treat strong database semantics as the default, push two-phase commit and similar complexity into the platform, and quantify timing uncertainty rather than hiding it.

talks.title: "Why Ruby Isn't Slow" by Alex Gaynor (2013)
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for "Why Ruby Isn't Slow" by Alex Gaynor (2013).

talks.title: "Getting Pushy: Pushing Data From Server to Browser" by David Pollak (2013)
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of "Getting Pushy: Pushing Data From Server to Browser" by David Pollak (2013).

talks.title: "Native Speed on the Web: JavaScript and asm.js" by Alon Zakai (2013)
talks.teaser: Shows how JavaScript can approach native speed in browsers using asm.js, typed arrays, and proposed SIMD and threading features.
talks.summary:
Alon Zakai presents evidence that native applications can run on the web at near-native speeds through JavaScript and asm.js. He demonstrates the Epic Citadel demo—the Unreal Engine 3 compiled from approximately one million lines of C++ to JavaScript—running in browsers at 58–60 frames per second without plugins. Over six months, the same demo improved from 20-second startup and 40 fps to 10-second startup and 60 fps, driven by browser optimization.

The talk introduces asm.js, a formally defined subset of JavaScript designed for optimization. Key features include typed arrays for data representation, bitwise operations (e.g., x|0) to enforce 32-bit integer types, and closure captures to provide static guarantees that variables never change. These patterns emerged naturally across multiple C++ to JavaScript compilers (Emscripten, Mandreel) before being standardized.

Benchmark results show asm.js code running 0.5–2× slower than native C++ equivalents. Box2D physics engine comparisons reveal asm.js outperforming standard JavaScript across Firefox, Chrome, and Internet Explorer 10. Firefox and Chrome achieve speeds comparable to Java, while Safari shows weaker typed array optimization and Internet Explorer is improving.

Three principal challenges remain to achieve full native speed: (1) 32-bit floating point support—JavaScript uses 64-bit doubles, with potential 10–20% speedup from 32-bit floats; ES6's proposed Math.fround enables fragile optimizations. (2) SIMD (Single Instruction Multiple Data)—a specification proposal (by John McCutchen, Google) for float32x4 and vector types could deliver 300% speedups for parallel operations; collaboration involves Google, Mozilla, Intel, and TC39. (3) Threads—Web Workers exist but prohibit shared memory to prevent data races; enabling multi-threaded access requires careful standardization.

Demonstrations include the JavaScript MESS project (emulating retro CPUs), a Bullet physics simulation with 500 cubes at 50–60 fps, and Banana Bread (Sauerbraten engine port) running alongside an embedded Doom game in a web worker—both at 60 fps on average hardware. The Doom integration required less than 100 lines of code, highlighting web platform benefits beyond performance.

talks.title: "How to Teach Your Kid to Code with Hopskotch" by Samantha John (2013)
talks.teaser: Explains how a visual, drag-and-drop programming app helps kids learn ideas, tools, algorithms and code.
talks.summary:
Samantha John, co-founder of Hopscotch, opened by arguing that programming is becoming a basic literacy, much as reading and writing did. She cited a projection of 1.4 million computing jobs by 2020 against roughly 400,000 computer science students, and warned that this gap leaves few people able to run the technology around us. Her goal was to show how adults can start teaching kids to code, and she noted that building something people actually use is often the spark that keeps learners going.

She organized learning around four steps: coming up with an idea, choosing the right tools, designing an algorithm, and writing code. Beginners usually need sample projects or prompts before their own ideas become workable, so she suggested having kids invent a game and play-test it. Tool choice is best practiced by matching options to a problem. For algorithms, she pointed to Logo-style turtle drawing and a game where kids must spell out every step of making a sandwich for a parent. For code, she argued that typing is a major barrier, so Hopscotch uses colorful drag-and-drop blocks that avoid the usual error messages.

She closed with ideas for teaching beyond the iPad, such as board games, the CS Unplugged curriculum and community coder dojos, and then answered audience questions about typed versus visual languages and group teaching.

talks.title: "Java Puzzlers, Strange Loop Edition" by Bob Lee and Josh Bloch (2013)
talks.teaser: Java puzzlers with voting expose Hashtable traps, proxy serialization bugs, enum init cycles, and literal pitfalls with practical morals.
talks.summary:
The session revives the classic puzzler format: short programs whose output surprises even experienced developers, with live audience voting before each reveal. The first puzzle builds a string-to-index map and counts matches, but prints zero because Hashtable’s contains method searches values, not keys; the fix is to declare Map and use containsKey instead of the legacy Hashtable API.

Later puzzles go deeper into the platform. A serialization proxy implemented as a non-static inner class creates a circular reference that deserializes with a ClassCastException weeks after data seemed safe; making the proxy a static nested class and testing round-trips avoids silent data loss. Enums Man and Woman with cross-references trigger class-initialization cycles that leave final fields null and cause NullPointerException until dependencies are broken manually or lazily. Short literal puzzles show silent narrowing casts and signed hex literals, while a varargs max function prints 4.9×10⁻³²⁴ because Double.MIN_VALUE is the smallest positive magnitude, not negative infinity.

The closing checklist urges interface-typed collections, varargs patterns that require at least one argument, static serialization proxies, simple class initialization, caution with short and byte, consistent API naming, and static analysis or IDE assistance to catch traps before production.

talks.title: "Patterns for Scalable Web Services in Go" by Richard Crowley (2013)
talks.teaser: Walks through building scalable Go web services: handlers, goroutines, channels, graceful restarts, testing and observability.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how to structure web services written in Go, starting from a minimal hello-world server and rebuilding it piece by piece. The speaker explains Go's handler and interface model, returning errors instead of throwing exceptions, and structs that hold only data. An echo server shows one goroutine per connection, with the runtime limiting how many threads actually run, which is why that pattern scales in practice.

The middle section covers channels and their trade-offs. Buffered and unbuffered channels give back pressure, but tightly coupling goroutines inside one process can block scaling out, and queues must be drained carefully to avoid data loss. A simple shutdown that closes the listener and waits a minute is compared with a fork-and-inherit approach that allows zero-downtime restarts. The speaker then shows a routing and JSON layer built on the standard library, with reflection used to check signatures at startup, and conditional request handling.

For production, the speaker recommends testing with fake requests and response recorders, vendoring dependencies at the point they pass continuous integration, terminating TLS in the Go process, and reducing heap allocations. Logs, aggregated metrics and profiling round out the advice. The takeaway is to keep handlers simple, use concurrency primitives deliberately for ordinary request workloads, treat errors as expected outcomes, and measure everything.

talks.title: "Thinking DSLs for Massive Visualization" by Leo Meyerovich (2013)
talks.teaser: Shows how program synthesis can generate regular expressions, SQL and parallel visualization code from examples and partial programs.
talks.summary:
The talk makes the case for program synthesis, where the tool searches for a program that matches input-output examples, instead of programmers hand-writing dense symbolic code. Leo Meyerovich starts with regular expressions built by demonstration on file listings, then adds a partial program as a hint to guide the search. He describes his first prototype, which simply enumerated candidate expressions, and a later version built on the Rosette framework, which encodes the search as SMT constraints solved by Z3.

He then applies the same idea to SQL, synthesizing a set-difference query that lists students who had not signed up for meetings, using positive and negative examples. Trends in supercomputer speed and SAT solver capacity are used to argue that search-based synthesis will scale to larger programs. The second half covers a browser-style visualization engine that filters and lays out about 100,000 data points in real time. Its layout language is compiled to parallel JavaScript and GPU code, with layout modeled as tree traversals. Traversal schedules can be given as synthesis input, so a change that introduces a dependency breaking parallelism is rejected.

The takeaway for practitioners is to keep the examples and schedules next to the code so maintainers can see the intent, and to build synthesis primitives into domain-specific languages so the compiler does the heavy search work.

talks.title: "Dart For the Language Enthusiast" by Bob Nystrom (2013)
talks.teaser: Explores Dart's design via Java, JavaScript, and Clojure comparisons, stressing simpler semantics, familiar syntax, and rich libraries.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens with a compressed tour of Dart syntax: first-class functions, classes with explicit fields, mixins, and optional types. Instead of a conventional language tutorial, the session frames Dart as a client-side web language nearing 1.0, compiling to JavaScript while offering a native VM for development.

The core argument unfolds through two design strategies seen in Java and applied to Dart. First, productivity can rise when a language removes decisions and pitfalls found in predecessors—contrasting Java’s access modifiers and overload rules with Dart’s simpler privacy, single-dispatch methods, unified getters and setters, and stricter behavior around coercion, scope, hoisting, and `this`. Second, familiar C-family syntax lowers adoption cost while semantics stay uniform, as with sugar that desugars to method calls. A parallel thread compares C’s types (motivated by code generation, not proof) with Dart’s optional, simple-but-not-fully-sound annotations aimed at tooling rather than speed.

The closing sections borrow from Clojure: lazy iterables with map and filter on DOM queries, plus asynchronous streams wired to DOM events. The takeaway for practitioners is Dart as a web language that blends OO and functional styles with a deliberately approachable type story and integrated collection APIs.

talks.title: "Generation Minecraft - Kids Building Software" by Seth Schroeder (2013)
talks.teaser: Shows how Minecraft multiplayer worlds and daily creative time nurture children's building skills beyond typical classroom drills.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with a parent framing creativity as the core skill children need in a world where more people can implement other people's ideas online. The speaker contrasts how adults actually use computers with how schools emphasize standardized tests, typing, and memorization, arguing that those habits discourage exploration and original work. A companion website and mind map carry the outline so attendees can revisit the material later.

The middle section brings two children on stage to tour their Minecraft worlds, including castles, community maps, server social dynamics, griefing incidents, and tax collection on a home server. A teenage son demonstrates redstone logic gates, command blocks, tower-defense minigames, and a capture-the-flag map built in vanilla Minecraft, while noting that some communities extend the game with Java plugins. The speaker ties these hobbies to Papert's Mindstorms, optional coding paths such as Scratch and Lisp, and learning driven by YouTube rather than forced programming lessons.

The closing advice urges parents not to rely on schools or competitive games alone. The family practice of thirty minutes of daily creative time, plus optional summer Khan Academy, is offered as a repeatable way to let each child follow their own interests. A brief Q&A covers screen-time boundaries, how redstone skill grew through practice and videos, and letting children pull adults toward what excites them.

talks.title: "Servo: Designing and Implementing a Parallel Browser" by Jack Moffitt (2013)
talks.teaser: Explores how Servo's experimental Rust browser engine runs script, layout and iframes in parallel.
talks.summary:
Jack Moffitt of Mozilla Research presents Servo, an experimental browser engine written from scratch in Rust. He argues that mainstream browsers carry path-dependent design choices from about fifteen years ago, such as script blocking the HTML parser and a serial loop between script and layout. The aim is to find which ideas work, and to build a browser that is safer and easier to change than multi-million-line codebases.

The core experiments are running script and layout concurrently, using a copy-on-write DOM where layout reads a stable snapshot while script edits a separate copy, and parallelising layout passes over a separate flow tree. Rust's type system restricts each traversal to children, which prevents data races at compile time. Iframes run in their own tasks, so cross-origin frames, and same-origin frames marked sandboxed, can work in parallel. In a live demo, an animation and the browser UI kept running during a long matrix multiplication inside an iframe, while the same test froze the UI in a Gecko-based browser. Servo also isolates crashes, so a failing iframe shows an error instead of taking down the page. Partial layout lets a script read an element's position early, with the answer sent by message while layout continues.

At the time of the talk Servo passed the Acid1 test, had GPU rendering and compositing, basic DOM APIs and a quadtree tile manager, and still lacked incremental layout and benchmarks. Moffitt says Rust itself is part of the experiment, and that the team will change Rust if its abstractions fall short. He closes by inviting contributors, pointing to easy issues on GitHub.

talks.title: "Go Circuit: Distributing the Go Language and Runtime" by Petar Maymounkov (2013)
talks.teaser: Presents Go Circuit, a framework that ships distributed cloud applications as Go source with a thin, standardized ops interface.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with friction between development and operations when companies run large distributed cloud applications. Modular pieces such as databases or UIs ship more easily than full stacks, while teams repeatedly rebuild monitoring pipelines and pay ongoing manual ops cost. Two structural gaps block packaging complex solutions like desktop software: no standard way for applications to start remote jobs, and no uniform way to negotiate elastic hardware. Documentation-driven deployment through tools such as Puppet keeps ops deeply involved in every product’s quirks.

The proposed answer is Circuit, a Go-only effort meant to run beside existing systems without backward compatibility. Applications ship as Go source so tooling can inspect and instrument them. Circuit offers a minimalist single-system image at the language layer: it does not hide cluster failures but exposes clean semantics for concurrency, spawning, and networking. Ops teams implement small drivers for connectivity, process start, and hardware requests once; developers compile applications into executables that encode infrastructure behavior. The design parallels Linux, Plan 9, and Erlang, but embeds runtime support in the binary instead of a separate OTP-style install.

The architecture section explains Circuit as an imported package, remote goroutines that look local, and translation from high-level code to simple network and spawn operations. A forthcoming legacy-Linux wrapper via instrumented containers is mentioned briefly. Programming walkthrough slides are skipped at the end; the practical hook is a spawn call plus Go reflection so existing code can distribute with little new API surface.

talks.title: "Finding a Way Out" by Chris Granger (2013)
talks.teaser: Aurora treats programs as observable data pipelines, cutting indirectness and incidental setup so builders focus on transformations.
talks.summary:
The presenter retraces a decade of attempts to improve programming, from large PHP sites and web frameworks through Visual Studio tooling and Microsoft user studies observed behind a one-way mirror. Those studies convinced him that slow feedback and mentally simulating execution matter more than typing speed or editor mechanics. Work on Light Table sharpened live connection to running code, yet immediate feedback still left programming feeling broken.

After asking hundreds of practitioners two questions—what programming is and what is wrong with it—he distilled recurring complaints into three pillars: programs are hard to observe, work is indirect translation into symbols, and incidental complexity buries the actual problem. He argues decades of local fixes stack like teacups without changing the foundation, and proposes programming as nothing but data transformation.

The closing demos walk through an environment where immutable data stays visible at every step, transformers handle effects like UI and state, and pipelines cover counters, grouped usage analytics, and a todo MVC-style interface. He positions Aurora as a medium for thought rather than an efficiency tool, aiming to remove setup and time-management noise so people spend cognitive effort on the problem itself.

talks.title: "Daimio: A Language for Sharing" by Dann Toliver (2013)
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of "Daimio: A Language for Sharing" by Dann Toliver (2013).

talks.title: "Gershwin: Stack-based, Concatenative Clojure" by Daniel Gregoire (2013)
talks.teaser: Presents Gershwin, a stack-based extension of Clojure, and how its words and quotations change how code is written.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at the Emerging Languages Camp, the speaker introduces Gershwin, an additive, experimental extension to Clojure that introduces a stack-based, concatenative programming model inspired by languages like Forth and Factor. The project was conceived to scratch two main exploration itches: investigating the concatenative paradigm and achieving a deeper understanding of Clojure's compiler internals. By building directly on top of Clojure, Gershwin enables developers to utilize point-free, data-flow-centric programming while retaining full access to Clojure’s hosted runtime, immutable collections, and concurrency constructs.

### Key Topics
- **Concatenative & Stack-Based Paradigm**: Programs operate on an implicit data stack without explicit invocation syntax, parentheses, or formal argument parameters. Execution flows from data directly into operations.
- **Vocabulary and Syntax of Gershwin**: Functions are referred to as 'words' defined using Forth-style colons (`:`). Anonymous functions are represented as 'quotations' with custom reader macro syntax. Parentheses are preserved exclusively to fall back to standard Clojure expressions.
- **Factoring and Mental Model**: Rather than traditional variable-based abstractions, concatenative programming relies on vigorous factoring—breaking out arbitrary sequences of data and operations into newly named words. When stack shuffling becomes noisy, higher-order data-flow combinators help manage the flow.
- **Data-Flow Combinators**: Borrowing directly from Factor, Gershwin avoids excessive low-level stack manipulation (such as `swap`, `dup`, `drop`, `nip`, `pick`, `over`) through combinators categorized into preserving (`dip`, `keep`), cleave (`cleave`, `tri`), spread (`spread`), and apply combinators.
- **Clojure as an Extension Base**: Comparing language structure to human linguistic mastery (phonetics, vocabulary, discourse), Clojure provides sound micro-level guarantees around identity, state, values, and time, making it an ideal bedrock for high-level language experiments.

### Technical Details
- **Compiler Modifications**: Gershwin compiles unmodified Clojure code and introduces additive changes to `LispReader`. It adds reader macros for quotations and Gershwin var resolution, extends the parser for `:` word definitions, and expands the pushback reader buffer to differentiate between keyword syntax and word definitions. At the compiler level, forms are translated into standard Clojure function invocations that either push values to the stack or execute words against it.
- **Stack Implementation**: The stack implements Clojure's `IPersistentStack` interface backed under the hood by Clojure vectors. It is stored as a dynamic var in `gershwin.core`, allowing isolated stacks per thread to prevent race conditions during parallel processing operations (like `pmap`).
- **Execution & Conditionals**: While many expressions read in reverse postfix compared to standard Clojure, conditionals such as `if` accept a boolean condition and two quotations (then/else branches) to delay evaluation until invoked.

### Takeaways
Concatenative programming acts essentially like Clojure’s thread-macro (`->`) built natively into the core syntax, excelling in data-transformation pipelines, shell scripting pipelines, and UI composition. Rather than replacing Clojure, Gershwin demonstrates how hosted Lisps can serve as flexible, reliable platforms for exploring alternative programming paradigms without sacrificing access to existing ecosystem libraries and runtime semantics.

talks.title: "JavaScript ... for Science!" by Angelina Fabbro and Bill Mills (2013)
talks.teaser: Developers see how scientific code debt grows and how modern web interfaces can simplify nuclear experiment control.
talks.summary:
The speakers argue that detector scale at facilities like CERN has outpaced software engineering habits in the natural sciences. They describe years on ATLAS without code reviews, legacy table-dump control systems such as MIDAS, and recurring anti-patterns in production physics code: deep nesting, copy-paste blocks, and JavaScript emitted from giant C strings.

Bill Mills walks through a Griffin experiment web application at TRIUMF that replaces opaque parameter tables with real-time skeuomorphic detector views, throughput monitors, and a graphical experimental cycle instead of hand-built hex instruction patterns. Angelina Fabbro notes tradeoffs such as canvas-heavy UI born from time pressure, and cites Space Apps experience where industry developers avoided science events despite having relevant skills.

They close with cultural barriers—fear of third-party libraries, black-box code behind papers—and a graded path for programmers: encourage open source, offer reviews, send small pull requests, and advise on data-scale infrastructure. Scientists are urged to accept help, iterate rather than one-shot scripts, and try test-driven development. They announce interdisciplinaryprogramming.com as a 2014 matchmaking effort linking labs and computing talent.

talks.title: "Partitions for Everyone!" by Kyle Kingsbury (2013)
talks.teaser: Shows how network partitions break popular distributed databases and which consistency guarantees actually hold when the network fails.
talks.summary:
Kyle Kingsbury opens by arguing that network partitions are unavoidable, because an asynchronous network can delay, drop, or reorder messages and a node cannot tell a slow peer from a dead one. He points to operational data from Microsoft and Google and to post-mortems from several companies, including a GitHub incident where a split brain exposed private repository information. To study these failures he presents Jepson, a harness that runs a cluster, injects partitions, and compares client-recorded results with the final database state.

Kingsbury applies this method to several systems. ZooKeeper fails cleanly: writes stop during the partition, and no acknowledged write is lost. NuoDB keeps acknowledged writes but blocks for long periods, sometimes well after the partition ends. Kafka's shrinking in-sync replica set can promote a stale leader, which loses acknowledged writes, so he recommends majority quorums. Riak and Cassandra rely on last-write-wins, which silently discards concurrent updates, and Cassandra's lightweight transactions lost data and deadlocked under his tests despite marketing claims.

His takeaways are to decide which liveness and safety guarantees a system really needs, to rely on logical clocks rather than wall time, and to avoid trusting vendor consistency claims. He recommends writing a test program that injects failures with tools such as iptables, skews clocks, and measures actual behaviour against the model you assumed.

talks.title: "Clojure core.async" by Rich Hickey (2013)

talks.title: "Exercises in Style" by Crista Lopes (2013)
talks.teaser: Nine term-frequency implementations show how constraints define programming styles beyond syntax and indentation.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames programming style as distinct ways of expressing computational tasks, arguing that introductory courses emphasize languages while leaving little room to teach different problem-solving mindsets. Art-school teaching of painting styles through explicit constraints motivates the approach, and literary precedents such as Raymond Queneau’s Exercises in Style—retelling one trivial anecdote in many formal variants—become the model for pedagogy.

The core demo keeps one problem fixed: given a text file, output the twenty-five most frequent words in descending order after handling stop words. Nine numbered solutions illustrate contrasting constraints, from a single page of nested loops without abstractions, through five dense Python lines with hidden inefficiency and file-handle pitfalls, procedural steps with shared mutable state, pure function pipelines without persistent state, continuation-style extra function parameters, and noun-oriented managers with inheritance hooks, up to map partitions and reduce for parallel counting across two hundred chunks. Audience members are asked to propose technical names because prior expert crowds disputed the speaker’s informal labels.

The talk closes with a planned book of roughly thirty-three styles for upper undergraduates and early graduates, plus GitHub examples once naming stabilizes, aimed at bookstore release in spring 2014. Practitioners gain a vocabulary for reading unfamiliar code and choosing representations deliberately rather than defaulting to whichever language syntax they learned first.

talks.title: "BODOL, or How to Accidentally Build Your Own Language" by Bodil Stokke (2013)
talks.teaser: A developer-oriented session walks through parsing, runtime primitives, monadic evaluation, and core.logic pattern matching for a toy Lisp.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with motivation drawn from Clojure, Haskell, and Shen: a desire for a Lisp with immutability, pattern matching, and a serious type system. The speaker describes building BODOL in roughly a weekend in Clojure, then spending months on types, and notes attention from Hacker News over Unicode in the syntax.

The middle is a hands-on pipeline for bootstrapping a language: Instaparse grammar rules for a small Lisp, mapping parse trees onto runtime values (numbers, strings, booleans, symbols, cons cells), and evaluation modeled with monads so environments update without mutation. Lexical scoping is explained by binding scope when lambdas are created, not when they are called. Pattern matching is prototyped with core.logic unification, and a short demo infers that a successor function takes and returns numbers.

The close skips a full Hindley–Milner implementation for time and pivots to naming a new language—famous names, “Script” suffixes, letter increments, ponies—before pointing listeners at slide and project repositories. The practical takeaway is that parsers and runtimes come together quickly; type systems and polish take far longer.

talks.title: "Functional Reactive Programming in Elm" by Evan Czaplicki (2013)
talks.teaser: Elm’s graphics layers lead into signals, lift, and foldp, culminating in a concise live-coded Mario demo with hot swapping.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with a motivating question: how to build graphics in a purely functional, composable way without mutable objects. Evan Czaplicki traces how Elm split the problem into text and links, rectangular layout, and freeform graphics, demoing elements, flow, collage, forms, and transforms before noting that static pictures alone cannot make a real GUI.

The middle introduces functional reactive programming through the 1997 functional reactive animation paper and Elm’s signal model. Live coding walks through mouse position with lift, keyboard history with foldp, and reusing the same collage code for interaction. The talk then structures a Mario-style program into model, update, and display: physics from time deltas, walking and jumping from keyboard input, gravity, ground collision, sprites for stand, walk, and jump, and extending the model when facing direction matters.

The close summarizes Elm’s concurrent FRP foundation, markdown and extensible records, PLDI-related work, and full-time development at Prezi toward practical HTML and JavaScript embedding, debugging, hot swapping with preserved state, and a small MVC-style todo demo. Practitioners see how FRP avoids callback-style rewrites when adding interactivity and how declarative structure scales from layout primitives to a complete game loop in roughly forty lines.

talks.title: "Taking PHP Seriously" by Keith Adams (2013)
talks.teaser: Makes the case that PHP's workflow, state and concurrency choices hold lessons, and shows the Hack type system.
talks.summary:
Keith Adams, an engineer at Facebook who helped build the HHVM engine, argues that PHP deserves serious consideration despite its reputation. He frames the talk as an experience report from years of running millions of lines of PHP at Facebook, and says the aim is to point out lessons that apply to other systems, not to claim PHP is loved or always the right choice.

He walks through the criticisms that circulate online, including division by zero returning false, arithmetic on strings silently truncating, inconsistent argument orders in the standard library, confusing value and reference semantics, and reference counting leaking into memory management and taking a large share of the JIT's output. He then argues that three design areas matter more to productivity than these quirks: programmer workflow, where saving a file and reloading the page is the whole loop; state, where each web request starts from an empty heap so faults stay contained; and concurrency, which is shared-nothing and built on task-style subrequests.

The closing section covers Hack, a gradual, opt-in type system for PHP that runs as a separate checker alongside the unmodified runtime and reports errors as a short story. Adams walks through its inference, nullable types and generics, compares it with TypeScript, and ends by suggesting that how a language fits its surrounding workflow can matter more than the features people debate.

talks.title: "The Trouble With Types" by Martin Odersky (2013)
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning "The Trouble With Types" by Martin Odersky (2013).

talks.title: "Making Software Development Make Sense to Everyone" by Jen Myers (2013)
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in "Making Software Development Make Sense to Everyone" by Jen Myers (2013).
talks.summary:
### Overview
In her keynote address, Jen Myers examines how the tech industry can make software development accessible and comprehensible to people from diverse backgrounds. Drawing on her experience as a designer, developer, and educator at Dev Bootcamp and Girl Develop It, Myers argues that broadening participation in technology requires treating culture and education as interfaces. Rather than attempting to rewrite an overwhelming cultural system all at once, technologists can create welcoming, supportive interfaces that lower barriers to entry, challenge harmful stereotypes, and elevate new learners.

### Key Topics
- **Demographic Disparities and Research**: Myers highlights findings from a September 2013 U.S. Census report indicating that women's participation in computing occupations has declined since 1990, young women's entry into STEM fields is slowing, and Black and Hispanic individuals remain severely underrepresented. She reviews psychological studies showing how subtle gendered language in job descriptions, stereotype threat, and societal expectations depress female test performance in math and physics, whereas self-affirmation or anonymous testing closes performance gaps.
- **The "Interface" Metaphor**: Comparing the complex culture of software development to a tangled, legacy codebase, Myers notes that developers do not need to overhaul an entire system overnight. Instead, creating targeted, user-centered entry points—such as accessible workshops—helps newcomers engage constructively with the system.
- **Personal Experience and "Unlocking the Clubhouse"**: Myers shares her background as a self-taught web designer from rural Ohio who felt isolated as the sole woman in her university computer science cohort. A pivotal conversation at a Carnegie Mellon youth camp and reading the study *Unlocking the Clubhouse* revealed that feelings of imposter syndrome and exclusion were widely shared by women across different skill levels, driven by systemic cultural factors rather than inherent lack of aptitude.
- **Grassroots Education Models**: Myers recounts founding the Columbus, Ohio chapter of Girl Develop It in 2011 and her work at Dev Bootcamp Chicago. She notes that women show immense interest in coding when provided with safe spaces that explicitly welcome questions and eliminate the fear of looking inexperienced.
- **Visibility, Role Models, and Inspiration**: Myers references historical examples—such as astronaut Sally Ride, science communicator Neil deGrasse Tyson, and actress Nichelle Nichols (whose role as Lieutenant Uhura on *Star Trek* prompted her to recruit women and minorities for NASA)—to demonstrate the necessity of visible role models. She contrasts these inspiring figures with prevailing anti-social developer stereotypes (such as the depiction of Mark Zuckerberg in *The Social Network*), arguing for public passion and "romance" in tech education over exclusionary elitism.

### Technical Details & Audience Q&A
- **Dev Bootcamp vs. Girl Develop It**: During the Q&A, Myers clarifies the operational differences between intensive nine-week immersive programs like Dev Bootcamp (which prepares beginners for software developer careers) and community-driven evening workshops like Girl Develop It. She reports increasing female representation in recent Dev Bootcamp cohorts and high retention and referral rates when educational environments prioritize psychological safety.
- **Actionable Allyship**: Addressing an audience member asking how men can effectively assist without oversimplifying complex problems, Myers recommends listening, providing practical mentorship (such as guiding beginners through their first open-source pull requests or reviewing conference talk abstracts), and supporting existing grassroots efforts where help is requested.

### Takeaways
The lack of diversity in software development does not stem from an absence of interest or ability, but from cultural barriers and psychological stereotypes. Addressing these challenges requires creating encouraging, accessible learning environments, cultivating visible and diverse role models, and actively mentoring newcomers rather than gatekeeping technical knowledge.

talks.title: "What Is a Strange Loop and What is it Like To Be One?" by Douglas Hofstadter (2013)
talks.teaser: Explores what a strange loop means, how perception simplifies the world, and why the self may be an illusion.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the speaker reflecting on a conference named after a phrase he coined decades ago, then turns to what gives rise to the self and consciousness. He places living things and machines on a scale of respect, asking why a mosquito draws less concern than a dog, and adds thermostats, flush toilets and plants to the comparison. He argues that perception is a heavy act of reduction: a crowd of over a thousand people collapses into the single word "audience."

Simple creatures respond without concepts, much like a knee reflex, and concepts emerge gradually as nervous systems grow more complex. Human self-image is built from feedback from others, mirrors and experience. He recalls hitting what he calls a ceiling of abstraction during graduate mathematics, which forced him to leave the field. Using a story about France claiming it decided to invade Russia, he argues that people attribute causes to an imagined "I," while real causation happens at lower physical levels. A snack-buying stop at a gas station illustrates competing desires rather than free will.

He distinguishes the strange loop from video feedback, where a camera pointed at its own monitor creates nested images but involves no real perception or simplification. He concludes that the self is a useful abbreviation, closer to a rainbow or mirage than a solid object, and that the story we tell about ourselves is far less complete than the processes beneath it.

talks.title: Strange Loop Chat with Ambrose Bonnaire-Sergeant
talks.teaser: Revisits gradual typing in Clojure and explores using spec-based generative tests to check static-style function types.
talks.summary:
This Strange Loop chat is a catch-up between host Mario Aquino and Ambrose Bonnaire-Sergeant, a past speaker who gave two Strange Loop talks on typed Clojure in 2014 and 2015. They recall how the gradual typing work from that period ran into implementation problems on the JVM, where Clojure's close mapping to Java made wrapping values for runtime checks clash with final classes.

The conversation then turns to clojure.spec, the library Rich Hickey designed for describing and checking data and functions at runtime without wrapping values, partly for performance reasons. Ambrose explains that spec does no static checking, and describes an experiment that enumerates useful subtypes of a function type, such as the identity function, and checks them with generative testing. He also describes an extension that lets static-style types be written as specs, and says it is a large experiment rather than something he expects anyone to use in production.

The chat closes on what Ambrose calls the annotation burden: writing precise types for every helper function across a codebase is a huge task, and the shared-annotation model seen in the TypeScript community has not taken hold in typed Clojure. A practitioner should take away that how far static checking should reach across untyped boundaries remains an open question.

talks.title: "Humanity 2.0" by Matt Taylor
talks.teaser: A walk from cosmic scale through genes, memes, and stored knowledge leads to brain interfaces and machines built to grasp exponential data.
talks.summary:
The presenter opens by stating the session is not a product or software pitch, then uses a peppercorn-sized Earth to convey how vast distances are between planets, nearby stars, and the galactic center, including what long-exposure deep-field imaging revealed in an apparently empty patch of sky. He pairs that macro view with how much empty space exists inside atoms and briefly notes bustling activity inside living cells.

On a timeline of roughly three and a half billion years, he describes early Earth conditions, the Miller–Urey style spark experiment forming organic building blocks, and the long odds then vast time needed for a self-copying molecule. From there he follows replicators, mutation, competition, membranes, and “survival machines” in the Richard Dawkins sense, through multicellular life and a logarithmic chart that shows biological change slowing while brains and technology accelerate. Brains store flexible lifetime learning; memes spread ideas across societies; technology lets information live outside biology, from carved stone to networks.

Closing sections argue humanity must cope with exploding data through tactics such as smoother brain–device interfaces (including examples like restored hearing) and new computational systems that can understand encoded world-knowledge. He lists environmental, resource, population, and motivation challenges, urges attendees to pursue hard frontiers and decide whether their work helps humanity as a whole, and thanks several scientists who shaped the talk’s ideas.

talks.title: "Privacy Governance & Explainability in ML/AI" by Jared Maslin
talks.teaser: Frames privacy as a full data lifecycle concern and surveys methods for finding and reducing privacy and bias risk in ML systems.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a short history of data privacy, starting from GDPR and moving through US state laws, data residency rules and sector regulations such as HIPAA and PCI. The speaker argues that privacy covers the whole data lifecycle, from collection to deletion, and not only security. Trust, transparency and privacy by design are presented as ways to keep consumer data an asset rather than a liability, with privacy built into processes from the start instead of added after a breach or audit.

The middle section turns to machine learning, where explaining how a model reached a decision is hard and bias can enter through domain knowledge, the training data, or how outputs are later used. Risk in data is examined through k-anonymity, l-diversity and closeness, each presented with its known weaknesses. Model-level techniques include adversarial training, which penalises reliance on a sensitive attribute, a variational autoencoder approach that surfaces latent attributes the model leans on, and differential privacy, which adds controlled noise to query answers. For documentation, model cards and a multi-dimensional privacy analytic are described as ways to record intended use, metrics, and potential harms.

The closing argument is that these checks should run as a repeatable part of agile work, such as during story grooming or retrospectives. Developers, engineers and data scientists are presented as the people best placed to supply the design context that lawyers, privacy offices and auditors need to assess risk.

talks.title: "Empowering people to build a digital bank" by Eric Yoshimura and Riad Vargas
talks.teaser: Nubank's platform team explains scaling Clojure microservices on Kubernetes with sharding, shared libraries, and blameless incident culture.
talks.summary:
The session opens with Nubank as a Brazil-based technology company offering credit cards, rewards, fee-free accounts, and personal loans to more than thirteen million customers, with engineering growth from ten people on eight microservices to over three hundred engineers on three hundred services. The speakers frame healthy scaling through horizontal platform teams that supply Kubernetes, Kafka, and shared tooling, versus vertical product teams, plus knowledge sharing via tech forums, RFCs, engineering mobility, and a homogeneous Clojure codebase with shared libraries and ADRs.

They trace platform evolution from early DevOps heroics to a 2017 platform team and a 2018 shift from EC2 to Kubernetes. Platform responsibilities include infrastructure-as-a-service, declarative EDN-driven pipelines, default observability alerts, and rolling out Prometheus, Grafana, and Thanos via a shared metrics library. Incident handling uses a Slack outage channel with severity levels, technical and communication leads, blameless postmortems stored in a central repository, and monthly company-wide reviews.

Sharding combines bulkheads with database partitioning across many parallel stacks, a global routing shard, contained blast radius, horizontal scale, and canary deploys, alongside operational cost, a global shard bottleneck, and no customer shard migration. nu-cli and the Nimbus Clojure tool reduce toil across twelve Kubernetes clusters. The close stresses culture over tooling: psychological safety, standards that make the right path easy, learning from failure, and hiring.

talks.title: "Pattern Matching @ Scale Using Finite State Machine" by Ajit Koti and Rashmi Shamprasad
talks.teaser: Attendees learn how Conduit uses regex-like paths and finite state machines on Spark to trace flows across terabyte-scale event logs.
talks.summary:
Product and data teams at Netflix need to understand how visitors move through flows such as signup or playback, but real journeys span forks, loops, and abandoned paths across heterogeneous, terabyte-scale event logs. Wildcard SQL, window functions, and graph models break down or demand heavy specialist tooling when paths grow complex and many non-engineers need repeatable answers.

The speakers introduce Conduit, which treats milestone sequences like regular expressions over named events: timestamps, logical event names, and entity identifiers feed a flow analyzer on Apache Spark. A live notebook demo shows simple homepage-to-signup counts, wildcard middle steps, grouped loops with quantifiers, incomplete-flow funnel stats, and per-user flow identifiers with sequence ordering. Rashmi Shamprasad outlines API and configuration surfaces aimed at analysts and product roles.

Ajit Koti explains the implementation: Scala partial combinators parse path expressions into abstract syntax trees, lower them to finite state machines in the Thompson non-backtracking style, and evaluate streams per partition via Spark mapPartitions, including upfront event filtering when expressions allow. Practitioners gain a pattern for declarative, distributed path analytics without adopting a separate graph stack, plus caching strategies to rerun multiple expressions efficiently.

talks.title: "¡Escuincla babosa! A Python Deep Learning Telenovela" by Lorena Mesa
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning "¡Escuincla babosa! A Python Deep Learning Telenovela" by Lorena Mesa.

talks.title: "CSS Algorithms" by Lara Schenck
talks.teaser: Presents CSS as a declarative programming language and shows how documented styling algorithms improve large design-system codebases.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by asking whether CSS counts as a programming language, citing informal Twitter polls that drew roughly 129 votes in an early round and about 5,300 in a later one. It frames CSS among imperative and declarative paradigms as a domain-specific declarative language for styling, then contrasts ad hoc stylesheet growth—described as a test-driven-style loop where design mockups keep “failing”—with disciplined engineering habits.

Several lenses are walked through in turn: Turing completeness argued for the combination of CSS, HTML, and human input, including cellular automaton rule 110; the real maintenance cost when product changes stack modifiers on a “square” layout until the CSS feels fragile; and algorithms in the Corbin sense, with declarative flexbox and grid treated as outputs whose browser implementations hide imperative work. The speaker defines a CSS algorithm as a well-defined declaration or set of declarations with a specific styling effect, citing patterns such as clearfix, the lobotomized-owl spacing selector, viewport-based fluid type, and grid layouts.

Production use comes from a Larva design system at Penske Media Corporation: shared NPM packages, an inverted-triangle CSS layout, and a dedicated algorithms folder where each pattern lives in its own stylesheet with minimal markup documentation—reportedly reused fifteen times, mostly by others. The close ties personal narrative (art-school background, unfamiliarity with FizzBuzz-style interviews, self-directed computer science study) to industry habits that treat HTML and CSS as non-engineering work, and invites the audience to rank languages in an ongoing survey.

talks.title: "A better story for Kubernetes secrets" by Seth Vargo
talks.teaser: Explains why default Kubernetes secrets sit in plain text in etcd and how envelope encryption with an external KMS fixes it.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by defining an application or machine secret, such as an API key, credential or password used at build or run time. It explains why secrets attract attackers: they guard valuable things, leak through public repositories and exposed storage buckets, and often carry overly broad permissions. Of four protections, auditing, encryption, rotation and isolation, the talk focuses on encryption, especially application-layer encryption that keeps a secret encrypted whenever it leaves the process holding it.

The middle section examines Kubernetes defaults. A secret created with the standard command is only base64 encoded in etcd, so anyone who reaches the etcd data, a backup or the node's file system can read it. A live demo shows this. Envelope encryption is then explained: each piece of data gets its own data encryption key, wrapped by a centrally managed key encryption key. Kubernetes 1.7 added this with a local key file, but that file sits beside the encrypted data, so a VM attacker still gets everything. Version 1.10 moved key handling to an external plugin, such as a cloud key management service or Vault. Demos show switching to a KMS provider and rotating keys, though the switch briefly disrupted the API server.

The closing advice is to layer encryption, keep file-system encryption, rotate credentials often, use envelope encryption, and protect Kubernetes secrets with an external KMS, while denying etcd nodes the permission to decrypt.
