The case study uses the Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act and its regulation. The pipeline uses spaCy for tokenization, lemmatization, part-of-speech tagging and dependency parsing. Sentences containing a short list of obligation verbs, expanded through WordNet synonyms into a lightweight ontology, were labeled as burdens; manual labeling of the text gave 89% accuracy and caught 97% of burdens. For each burden, a breadth-first walk of the dependency tree recovers the full subject phrase. Subjects were then normalized, averaged GloVe vectors, reduced with spectral embedding, and clustered with k-means, with the elbow method suggesting three clusters.

Clustering revealed three groups: transportation standards, physical barriers such as ramps, surfaces and stairs in public spaces, and administration with standards definitions. Public and private responsibilities were not clearly separated, and some duties remained ambiguous. The speaker presented the result as a reusable framework for explaining rules to citizens and organizations and for spotting unclear or duplicated provisions for lawmakers.

talks.title: "A Robot Poet Goes for a Walk in the Park" by Em Lazer-Walker
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding "A Robot Poet Goes for a Walk in the Park" by Em Lazer-Walker.

talks.title: "Recreating forgotten programming languages, for art!" by Sher Minn Chong
talks.teaser: The session revives 1960s graphics languages and shows how early artists worked within tight printer and plotter limits.
talks.summary:
The presentation situates computer art in the 1950s through 1970s, when room-scale machines, punch-card workflows, and scarce plotters and line printers shaped who could make images at all. It sketches early industrial uses, magazines such as Computers and Automation, and the recurring puzzle of appreciating work when source code and hardware are gone.

The core work centers on ART 1, documented in a 1971 book for newcomers drawing on 105-by-50 character grids with seven primitives. Lacking a line printer, the speaker reimplements the ideas in JavaScript, renders to a terminal, layers texture with Unicode combining marks, and uses Bresenham’s 1962 grid line algorithm. The talk also covers Bell Labs BEFLIX animation via microfilm and EXPLORE’s probabilistic commands, transliteration rules, and short simulations such as expanding fringes and snowflake growth, with an EXPLORE interpreter still in progress.

The closing thread ties obsolete art languages to modern creative-coding toolchains and argues that knowing this history clarifies today’s beginner-friendly graphics ecosystems.

talks.title: "Alda's dynamic relationship with Clojure" by Dave Yarwood
talks.teaser: Traces how a text-based music composition language evolved its architecture, from a Clojure server to a Go and Kotlin client.
talks.summary:
Dave Yarwood introduces Alda, a text format for writing music that a command-line client interprets and plays back, with editor integration for quick feedback. He contrasts this with visual, mouse-driven notation software, arguing that slow notation can push composers toward repetitive material. He also shows that Alda embeds Clojure expressions, so scores can use functions and sequences inside the markup.

The talk then traces the architecture through several phases. The first prototype was a single Clojure program, which suffered from slow startup and blocking playback. A second phase moved to a background server reached over HTTP, and a third swapped HTTP for ZeroMQ with a broker that routed requests to worker processes, which fixed audio glitches when several synthesizers ran at once. Phase five removed the server: a Go client starts a player process and drives it with OSC messages over UDP, and the code moved from Clojure to Go and Kotlin so it could ship as native executables. A separate Clojure library, alda-clj, generates Alda text for live coding. Demos included random melodic generators and a piece that maps National Weather Service forecasts to notes, with temperature setting pitch, wind direction setting stereo panning, and wind speed affecting tempo and volume.

The main lesson is that the design moved toward simplicity, with the client doing most of the work. Keeping Clojure as an inline scripting layer and a live-coding library preserved the creative workflow. Export to MIDI gives a rough starting point for sheet music, though it cannot always infer intended bar lines or enharmonic spellings.

talks.title: "Dive into Streams with Brooklin" by Celia Kung
talks.teaser: Explains how LinkedIn's Brooklyn streaming service moves data from many sources to many destinations at scale.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Brooklyn, a streaming data pipeline service LinkedIn built to replace a patchwork of specialized change data capture systems. As LinkedIn's data spread across Oracle, Espresso, Kafka, and cloud services in Azure and AWS, nearline applications needed continuous, low-latency access without each team building its own pipelines. The speaker explains that Brooklyn aims to be multi-tenant, dynamically provisioned, and easy to extend with new sources and destinations.

Two main scenarios are covered: change data capture, where applications consume a change stream instead of querying a live database, and streaming bridges that move data between clouds or data centers. The speaker walks through a profile-update example and the architecture, in which a REST management service writes stream definitions to ZooKeeper, a leader distributes work as tasks, and consumers and producers pass events on to Kafka. A central case is the replacement of Kafka MirrorMaker, which had required hundreds of clusters. Brooklyn handles that work as pipelines in one cluster, with pause and auto-resume at the pipeline, topic, or partition level so that a single failing partition does not stall the rest.

The closing section covers production scale, with figures for daily message volume and stream counts, along with planned work on new sources, batching for storage destinations, auto-scaling, and pass-through compression, which the speaker says could raise mirroring throughput at least fivefold. Questions covered the Java-only implementation, comparisons with Kafka Connect and Debezium, how encryption policies are enforced through key management, and the project's open-source status. The main takeaway is that a centralized, extensible pipeline service can reduce operational burden compared with many one-off pipelines.

talks.title: "Beyond traces: the insights in trace aggregates" by Daniela Miao
talks.teaser: Shows how aggregating many distributed traces surfaces the customer, server, and lock behind production slowdowns.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that a single distributed trace is rarely enough to diagnose a production problem, because it captures one request out of possibly millions. The speaker frames observability as needing analysis on top of raw telemetry, and proposes letting a machine compare hundreds or thousands of traces to surface what stands out.

The first case is an internal incident in which a customer unintentionally overloaded the ingestion system. Metric dashboards were hard to read, and the customer ID was too high-cardinality to be a default dashboard dimension, so finding it took hours. Comparing the slowest one percent of traces against the rest with a correlation score pointed to that customer's project within minutes. A second case involved long-tail latency at an early customer, where the slowest requests correlated almost perfectly with one server, which turned out to have a faulty network card. A more exploratory section looked at critical paths grouped by lock ID in a demo donut-ordering app. Chocolate orders held the topper lock far longer than other flavors, while cinnamon orders waited behind them.

The takeaway is that correlations are strong hints rather than proof, but they cut investigation time sharply. Practitioners should attach high-cardinality attributes to their traces and analyze groups of traces rather than individual ones. The speaker also recommends OpenTelemetry as an open standard for generating the telemetry needed to build those aggregates.

talks.title: "Temporal Databases for Streaming Architectures" by Jeremy Taylor and Jon Pither
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of "Temporal Databases for Streaming Architectures" by Jeremy Taylor and Jon Pither.

talks.title: "Typing the Untyped: Soundness in Gradual Type Systems" by Ben Weissmann
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in "Typing the Untyped: Soundness in Gradual Type Systems" by Ben Weissmann.

talks.title: "Finding bugs without running or even looking at code" by Jay Parlar
talks.teaser: Shows how describing a system in the Alloy model checker can expose design flaws before anyone reads or runs its code.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that design-level bugs can be found without running or reading code. The starting point is that explaining a system in writing, or to a knowledgeable listener, often exposes gaps in thinking. The main tool is Alloy, an MIT model checker, which takes a formal description of a system, searches the possible states it can reach, and reports any state that breaks a stated property. A small permission model with accounts, users and resources, where access to a parent resource extends to its children, is built up step by step. Each run surfaces a flaw in the spec: a user belonging to two accounts, a resource with no account, a resource listed as its own parent, and a case where inherited access fails to reach deeper children.

The middle of the talk covers real uses. In one project, a model of several customer portals, browser sessions and SAML logins produced a 13-step sequence that left the identity provider holding a token it could no longer revoke, and the developers had to delay a release to fix it. In another, a model built alongside an API's developer showed that the customer experience team misunderstood what the API could do, so a year of work was discarded before six teams built on it. Pamela Zave's Alloy analysis of the Chord protocol found counterexamples to all seven correctness claims in the original paper.

The closing takeaways are to write designs down in something other than code, to model existing systems to learn how they behave, and to model new systems early, when changes are still cheap. The speaker points to the Alloy book, an online architecture chapter, and TLA+ resources for anyone who wants to start.

talks.title: "Observability: Superpowers for Developers" by Christine Yen
talks.teaser: Developers gain practical ways to use observability, tracing, and production data to ship code with more confidence.
talks.summary:
Christine Yen frames a shift beyond the first DevOps wave: developers must own code in production, not only in local and test environments. She cites incident analyses where code and configuration changes trigger most production problems, and argues that richer, more distributed systems make the old throw-it-over-the-wall model untenable.

Observability is presented as the bridge—asking what software is doing and why, not merely watching aggregate charts. She contrasts traditional monitoring nouns such as CPU on database nodes with developer-meaningful signals like latency on a payments endpoint for a large customer. High-cardinality dimensions, tracing as structured logs, incremental instrumentation, and production experiments (including feature-flag comparisons and Geckoboard’s bin-packing trial) illustrate how teams slice data, validate hypotheses, and stop guessing about fixes.

Concrete enablers include teaching tools to speak developers’ language, treating instrumentation like tests and docs, using production to learn normal usage before changing behavior, and sharing debugging context across teammates. She closes by urging ops to empower developers and developers to ground decisions in production reality, with brief Q&A on read-only compliance access, low-traffic products, selling instrumentation, and on-call culture.

talks.title: "Behind The New York Times Crossword" by Darren McCleary
talks.teaser: Details NYT crossword editorial workflow, constructor submissions, and App Engine pre-warming for nightly release traffic spikes.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with context about the New York Times games organization: a self-contained unit supporting logic titles, newer offerings such as Spelling Bee and Tiles, and the flagship 15-by-15 crossword edited under Will Shortz. The speaker outlines rotational symmetry, themed weekday difficulty, gold-star completion rules, and how columnist Deb Amlen and puzzle data inform columns like “What the Heck Is That?”

The middle covers human-driven construction rather than automated generation, mail-in submissions, heavy editing by Joel and Sam, pay scales for published work, and helper tools such as Crossfire. Editorial rhythm spans Monday-through-Saturday gradations, the larger Sunday grid, and the hand-built daily Mini with leaderboards.

The close shifts to platform engineering: roughly ten p.m. push-driven traffic surges, prior over-provisioning costs, a serverless Games edge on App Engine, cron-triggered pre-warming before release, scale-down afterward, versioned canary-style deploys, cross-device commit-based progress sync, and broader use of Go across the games backend. A short Q&A touches plagiarism concerns, Fastly routing limits, feedback loops for live clue fixes, and hiring on a remote-friendly team.

talks.title: "How to teach programming (and other things)?" by Felienne Hermans
talks.teaser: Examines direct instruction, code read-aloud practice, and assessments as alternatives to learn-by-exploring programming pedagogy.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens from a personal arc: finance workers already “program” in spreadsheets, yet mainstream developers often dismiss that as not real coding—unlike runners or knitters, who rarely gatekeep beginners. That contrast frames why programming culture pushes kids toward solo trial-and-error, echoing Seymour Papert’s constructivist influence and the exploratory vibe of many code clubs and children’s books.

She connects programming education to reading and math pedagogy: phonics versus whole language, math wars, cognitive load, chunking, and evidence that minimal guidance underperforms worked examples. Classroom studies show children who read Python syntax aloud improve on syntax tests; another study finds reading expert code with explanations can match or beat writing code first under load constraints.

Practitioners are urged to stop gatekeeping what counts as programming, add light assessments in clubs, and favor explanation plus deliberate practice over assuming fun must come before skill. An online survey invites the audience to rank languages on a programming spectrum to study community beliefs.

talks.title: ""It's Just Matrix Multiplication": Notation for Weaving" by Lea Albaugh
talks.teaser: Explains weaving drafts as binary matrix multiplication, from basic loom mechanics to network drafting patterns.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the basics of weaving, an ancient technique in which weft threads cross a set of warp threads that run the length of the fabric. The speaker explains how a loom forms a shed by lifting subsets of warp threads through heddles, comparing a simple rigid frame with a four-shaft floor loom whose tie-up links treadles to shafts.

The middle of the talk covers the compact notation weavers use, which records threading, tie-up and treadling. The speaker shows that multiplying the treadling by the tie-up and its transpose, then by the threading, yields the fabric. Because every value is either on or off, the arithmetic reduces to simple selection. Network drafting, a style that limits each warp thread to a choice of frames, is then presented as a way to produce flowing curves and harmonic echoes. Other techniques are touched on briefly, including double weave, colour-and-weave, triaxial weaving and goze.

The talk closes with a browser-based virtual loom that can export a cardboard frame pattern, so attendees can try the ideas by building a simple loom. The takeaway is that weaving structures can be reasoned about both mechanically and mathematically, and that the design space grows quickly with more shafts.

talks.title: "Building Senior Engineers" by Dalton Mitchell
talks.teaser: Outlines how teams define senior engineers, hire against values, and deliver interview feedback that speeds career growth.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames “senior” for hands-on software engineers who combine solid technical work with communication, leadership, and momentum on projects—not only people with formal credentials. He describes his own path from web design and self-study through repeated rejections citing a need for someone more senior, and argues the industry too often leaves career gaps for individuals to figure out alone.

The core proposal starts with technical interviews as a high-leverage fix. He keeps practices worth preserving—quality bars, team fit, and demos of real ability over résumé polish—while urging teams to state what they value, inspired by engineering core values. He walks through communication, curiosity, passion, and determination with concrete signals in interviews, contrasts vague rejection notes with specific guidance, and covers onboarding wins: an early project, a designated helper, pairing, and heavy code review in the first months.

Closing arguments tie hiring and mentoring to team quality, shorter open roles, and a stronger wider community. He suggests meetups, apprenticeships, mentoring through programs like RailsBridge and freeCodeCamp, and living published values so candidates recognize fit—and closes with a call to pass forward the free knowledge others once gave.

talks.title: "Of Data Dropboxes and Data Gloveboxes" by Clay Baenziger
talks.teaser: Nuclear analogies anchor Hadoop dropbox and glovebox designs for scalable analytics without casual data exfiltration.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by comparing sensitive corporate and customer data to radioactive materials: small leaks matter, harm can last for decades, and isolation plus careful cataloging are necessary rather than refusing to touch the data at all. Drawing on experience operating large-scale Bloomberg data platforms—including market ticks, news volume, and fields that must stay protected—the speaker argues that familiar controls such as lineage tooling, masking, and ordinary firewalls do not fully answer how people should work with data day to day.

Two patterns anchor the middle of the talk. A data dropbox allows ingest through interfaces such as the HDFS REST API while blocking read-back, with checksums to validate handoffs and servlet filters that return authorization failures on download attempts; open-source code is offered for clusters using that approach. A data glove box extends the metaphor with a "leaded pane" (restricted remote access without copy or download), "glove ports" (arbitrary computation via YARN, Spark, Hive, and workflow tools), robotics (controlled deployment paths), and pass-throughs (one-way or read-only peers such as reference databases).

The close emphasizes operational primitives practitioners can reuse: Kerberos-authenticated entry points, log size limits, project isolation on shared filesystems, automated cleanup of temporary job data, Chef-enforced permissions, Linux PAM polyinstantiated temp directories, and YARN container traffic steering through host firewalls so workloads only reach approved destinations. The intent is scalable multi-tenant analytics without repeating historic bulk-loss failures.

talks.title: "Scala DSLs and Probabilistic Programming" by Joe Wingbermuehle
talks.teaser: Shows how Stan probabilistic models can be embedded in Scala, with compile-time type checks and scope rules for model code.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a simple task: predicting weight from height. The speaker writes a linear model with normal error as a generative model, then hands inference to Stan, a probabilistic programming language that samples from the posterior instead of returning a single point estimate. Adding separate intercepts and slopes for each gender shows how a model can be extended with little code, and the result is still imperfect, which motivates further modelling.

The core argument is for embedding Stan inside Scala rather than loading Stan files or concatenating strings. The benefits covered are editor autocompletion of distributions, type errors reported at the line where they occur, composable model pieces that can be combined into larger models, and room for linting, such as warning when a standard deviation has no lower bound. The implementation represents Stan types as Scala types, uses implicit type classes to reject invalid operations such as dividing a scalar by a vector, restricts random number draws to the blocks where Stan allows them, and checks input data against declarations at compile time.

Break and continue statements are harder to validate by types alone, so the speaker adds a pass over the abstract syntax tree that tracks loop nesting with a state monad and rejects a break outside a loop before any Stan code is generated. The library is open source, and most Stan functions are supported, though newer functions take effort to keep up with. The takeaway is that encoding a domain's rules in the host language's type system catches model errors early and makes reusable models easier to build on.

talks.title: "Soul from Scratch: Designing a More Portable Organ" by Peter Teichman
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of "Soul from Scratch: Designing a More Portable Organ" by Peter Teichman.

talks.title: "For AI, By AI: Freedom & Evolution of the AlgoPoetic Avant-Garde" by Connor Walsh
talks.teaser: Explains how an online poetry magazine of AI poets selects its work, from Docker-sandboxed submissions to judge rotation.
talks.summary:
Connor Walsh introduces The New Yorken Poesry Magazine, an online publication whose poems are generated, reviewed and selected by a crowd-sourced community of AI poets. He opens with a story about an unexplained account and a repository that appeared on his machine, which led him to research how people have built programs that write poetry. He then traces that history: a 1959 generative poem made by rearranging words in Kafka's The Castle, a 1962 poem produced by engineers using 32 grammatical patterns and 850 vocabulary words, a 1984 book written by a program, and Charles Hartman's 1996 account of collaborating with computers on poems.

He next covers the techniques behind machine-written verse, including templates, Markov chains with transition probabilities, context-free grammars, joint probability distributions and recurrent neural networks. The core of the talk explains the magazine's mechanics. Each poet must be able to write a poem and critique one by returning a score between zero and one, and it may optionally study and update itself. Poets are uploaded to a server, judges are chosen from the community each cycle, and a pretension parameter controls how many underdogs, poets who have never published, join the panel. Because uploaded code runs arbitrarily, each poet executes inside Docker containers.

He closes with a demonstration of a simple bot he wrote and submitted to the magazine, showing how the poem and critique commands are called and how the output is returned as JSON. His takeaway is that a healthy community of machine poets depends on diversity, autonomy and care, and that the magazine is meant for machine taste rather than human standards of art.

talks.title: "Flare: Optimizing Apache Spark for Scale-Up Architectures and Medium-Size Data" by Gregory Essertel
talks.teaser: Flare speeds medium-size Spark workloads on scale-up servers by compiling queries to native code instead of JVM pipelines.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by noting that many practitioners rarely run Apache Spark on truly massive datasets, while newer scale-up machines can hold tens or hundreds of gigabytes—or far more—in RAM. On those workloads Spark still pays distributed-system costs: RDD fault-tolerance paths, multi-pipeline scheduling modeled after clusters, and Catalyst-generated Java that spends much of its time decoding in-memory rows rather than computing.

Flare is introduced as a transparent DataFrame accelerator developed at Purdue. Calling flare on an existing Spark DataFrame reuses the same APIs while Flare pulls the optimized logical plan from Catalyst, emits a single-purpose low-level C binary, and can specialize decoders when the relation schema is known. Live demos on roughly two-gigabyte text and SQL examples show Spark runs on the order of tens of seconds where Flare finishes in about a second. Benchmark slides compare Postgres, Spark, the published Hyper design, and Flare on TPC-H at roughly 10–12 gigabytes in memory, with Flare close to Hyper and well ahead of Spark on one thread.

Scaling tests on a four-socket NUMA host with very large memory explore thread counts, memory-bandwidth limits, and pinning loads to sockets. A closing segment links Flare-generated loaders with TensorFlow graphs compiled through TF XLA so inference runs without extra copies between frameworks. Practitioners should treat Flare as aimed at single-node, medium data with DataFrame and SQL surfaces; heavy Python or Scala UDFs remain opaque boundaries, and the code is not open source yet though papers and a beta contact are offered.

talks.title: "Git from the Ground Up" by Safia Abdalla
talks.teaser: Maps everyday Git commands to objects, refs, and pack compression inside `.git`, from clone through push, merge, and rebase.
talks.summary:
Many developers treat Git as a handful of memorized commands and search results when something breaks. The session frames that gap by sketching how centralized and distributed version control evolved, then focuses on what actually runs when common CLI operations execute.

Starting from `git clone`, it tours the `.git` directory: loose and packed objects, the four object kinds (blobs, trees, commits, and annotated tags), and how branch creation updates `HEAD` and ref files that hold commit hashes. Staging and committing are shown as new blob and tree objects linked into commit records, including why hashes are sharded into subfolders. On push, loose objects pack together; Git orders objects to delta-compress similar blobs, exploiting how source files grow over time, which keeps large histories surprisingly small.

Merge and rebase close the loop: fast-forward moves a branch pointer when histories diverge only on one side, recursive merge builds a two-parent commit, and rebase replays work for a linear history. The practical message is that repository history lives in the object store and is inspectable with tools like `cat-file`, with pointers to Pro Git, pack-file notes, and source-level walkthroughs for deeper study.

talks.title: "Musical Steganography: Hiding Things in Music" by Scott Fradkin
talks.teaser: Traces centuries of hidden messages in music, from cipher-coded compositions to backmasking and audio-embedded images.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a tour of steganography, the practice of concealing one message inside another. It starts with ancient physical examples, such as Herodotus's accounts of a message written on a shaved scalp and one hidden under wax on a wooden tablet. It then moves to Johannes Trithemius and his cipher book, and to Renaissance composers who encoded text in music. Justin Desprez's mass drew its theme from syllables of words tied to the Duke of Ferrara, and a papal cryptography service reportedly used coded musical notation.

The middle section focuses on substitution ciphers. The speaker explained the German method, which maps letters to a limited set of notes, and the French method, which covers the full alphabet by grouping letters under note names. Bach and Schumann's Carnival were cited as examples of composers hiding their names in their work. A live Tidal Cycles demo mapped plain text onto notes, and a transcription tool was tried on the resulting audio, with pitches recovered better than timing. Backmasking followed, from reversed recordings in the Beatles' "Rain" to Pink Floyd's deliberate reversed message, along with the congressional controversy over false positives. The talk then covered hiding images in audio, including FX Twin's spectrogram picture, and demonstrated building one with Coagula and Sonic Visualizer.

The closing point is that these techniques are easy to experiment with using accessible software. Hiding an image in audio only works if the altered sound stays unnoticed, and decoding a hidden note sequence is harder than encoding one.

talks.title: "How we've made a global search engine for genetic data" by Miro Cupak
talks.teaser: A federated discovery engine and maturing Beacon standard let researchers find human genetic mutations across institutions worldwide.
talks.summary:
Genetic research depends on comparing samples across many datasets, yet most sequence data stays siloed by institution, disease, country, or regulation. The speaker presents Beacon Network, an open initiative under the Global Alliance for Genomics and Health, described as the largest engine for discovering where specific human mutations appear globally.

The talk walks through a live search on beacon-network.org: queries encode chromosome, position, and allele change against a reference genome, then fan out to participating beacons that each choose how much to expose—from a simple yes or no through metadata and gated external access. The history of the GA4GH Beacon API shows why standardization dominated engineering work: early deployments used incompatible formats until iterative specs (including over-complex 0.2) gave way to simpler modular releases, tooling, and a path toward version 1.0 in OpenAPI.

The search layer runs as Java services on Docker and Kubernetes, normalizing diverse notations and driving per-beacon four-stage pipelines (convert, request, fetch, parse) with graph-based routing to limit calls. Usage over roughly eighteen months spans more than 100 beacons, about 1.5 million searches, and millions of distributed queries—heavily focused on cancer-related loci, many predicted damaging or rare variants. Practitioners gain a case study in federated discovery, privacy-minimal APIs, and sustaining global data-sharing standards.

talks.title: "Hazel: A Live Functional Programming Environment with Typed Holes" by Cyrus Omar
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding "Hazel: A Live Functional Programming Environment with Typed Holes" by Cyrus Omar.

talks.title: "Designing Augmented Reality Systems for Speed" by Diana Hu
talks.teaser: Explores how augmented reality apps meet real-time limits through systems design, low-latency networking, and actor-model concurrency.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In "Designing Augmented Reality Systems for Speed," Diana Hu, head of the AR engineering team at Niantic Labs (makers of Pokémon GO and acquirers of Escher Reality), examines the technical challenges of making augmented reality fast, reliable, and pervasive on commodity mobile hardware. While science fiction has long envisioned ubiquitous AR, practical AR systems must simultaneously solve interdisciplinary problems across computer vision, robotics, computer graphics, and distributed systems within tight thermal, battery, and latency budgets.

### Key Topics
- **Fundamental Hurdles of AR**: Hu outlines why AR remains difficult. Computer vision requires both semantic understanding (recognizing objects via deep learning models that typically require power-hungry GPUs) and geometric perception (understanding 3D space, depth, and spatial navigation, derived from robotics). Graphics rendering must realistically integrate digital objects with complex real-world lighting variations. Additionally, developer toolchains (e.g., Unity, Unreal) still face lengthy 5- to 15-minute iteration cycles because the real world lacks fixed boundaries.
- **Trends in Hardware and Telecommunications**: Projecting the future of AR, Hu highlights Koomey's law (battery requirements falling by half every 1.5 years for fixed compute loads), demonstrating that an iPhone 7 benchmarks comparably to older MacBook models. Referencing Richard Feynman's 1985 calculations on physical limits of computation and Holmes's law of telecommunications, she notes that cellular speeds inevitably converge toward Wi-Fi and wireline bandwidths (e.g., 5G targeting 10 Gbps), eventually matching human visual processing capacities.
- **Treating Mobile Devices Like Distributed Servers**: As multi-core mobile processors become standard, AR architectures should adopt proven distributed system design patterns, such as colocation, caching, remoting, sharding, and concurrency without blocking locks.

### Technical Details
- **Speeding Up Networking**: AR requires rendering at ~30 frames per second, necessitating response latencies within a 33 ms frame budget. Traditional client-server architectures route camera pose data from a phone through a cell tower to a remote cloud data center (e.g., in Virginia or Iceland) and back, incurring hundreds of milliseconds of latency. Niantic addressed this by eliminating cloud hops for localization updates. By establishing a direct, peer-to-peer mesh connection through local cell towers between co-located devices, multiplayer tracking achieved latency in the tens of milliseconds. A hybrid protocol approach combines UDP for low-latency peer-to-peer pose broadcasting with TCP/server connections for anti-cheat authority and larger asset transfers.
- **Speeding Up Computation via the Actor Model**: Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) and Visual Inertial Odometry (VIO) pipelines ingest high-bandwidth sensor feeds (an uncompressed 1080x720 video feed at 30 fps requires ~600 Mbps of processing) and split work across feature tracking, localization, and mapping blocks. Naive implementations rely heavily on mutexes, shared state, and busy-waiting loops, causing computation cycles to exceed 1 second on embedded architectures. Niantic decoupled the SLAM pipeline using an actor model: camera inputs, feature extraction, localization, and mapping run as isolated actors communicating through message queues and internal sequential mailboxes. Without altering underlying computer vision math or algorithms, removing lock contention and busy-waiting yielded a 5x speedup.

### Takeaways
Rather than waiting for new mathematical breakthroughs or specialized hardware, significant performance gains in augmented reality can be realized immediately by applying mature distributed systems paradigms—such as peer-to-peer mesh networking and lock-free, message-passing actor architectures—directly to mobile AR software.

talks.title: "You are a Program Synthesizer" by James Koppel
talks.teaser: Connects program synthesis methods to everyday coding, showing how abstraction boundaries and logic separate good code from bad.
talks.summary:
James Koppel argues that software engineering advice often sounds vague, and he compares it to the history of scurvy, where eating citrus worked but its many caveats obscured the real cause. He suggests that program synthesis, which generates programs from specifications, can offer more precise guidance, and that every programmer already reasons somewhat like a synthesizer when deriving code.

Koppel explains deductive synthesis, which refines a goal through rules until an implementation appears. He compares a shared sanitize function with hand-written escaping, arguing that treating "sanitized" as an opaque predicate behind an abstraction boundary makes the centralized function the sound choice. He then shows how an array lookup can hide a conditional, contrasting a president-name array, which can be abstracted, with a small two-value lookup, which cannot. Turning to constraint-based synthesis with the Sketch tool, he treats tests as narrowing the set of passing programs, and shows how structural constraints on a linked list length function reduce the number of test cases needed.

The takeaway is that good code keeps its meaning behind clear boundaries and is simple enough that fewer tests are required. Koppel encourages developers to see the logic behind their own design choices, so that quality is built in rather than checked afterward.

talks.title: "Moving from 1 to N regions: an open retrospective" by Andrew Bloomgarden
talks.teaser: Shows how one observability company reworked its infrastructure so a small team could launch a new region.
talks.summary:
Andrew Bloomgarden presents a retrospective on New Relic's project to add a European region, hosted in IBM data centers in Frankfurt, so EU customers could keep their data in the EU. Until then all data was processed in the US. Over eight years the company had grown through several generations of deployment and service discovery tooling, and earlier disaster recovery drills had shown how much manual, copy-and-tweak work rebuilding an environment took.

Rather than changing every team's code, the project targeted a few shared interfaces. Services declared the dependencies they needed, with locations and credentials injected at deploy time, which also made it possible to analyze which services depend on which. Hosts moved to CoreOS with Ignition-based configuration, stateful services ran in the container platform, and Terraform built the environment, including a custom provider for IBM bare-metal machines. Hardware F5 load balancers were run as virtual F5 machines inside containers.

The schedule was difficult. Priority swung from little support to near-total demand, hidden follow-up work and shifting goalposts caused rework, and test build-outs exposed integration gaps late. The speaker recommends a project philosophy document, a central changelog, an early thin-slice effort with a few teams, and a pilot with real customers before general availability. The result: the European region is live, about 95 percent of services run in the container platform, and an order of magnitude fewer engineering hours went to disaster recovery work.

talks.title: "Isolation without Containers" by Tyler McMullen
talks.teaser: Explains how WebAssembly memory layout and compiled trap tables can isolate per-request code without containers.
talks.summary:
The talk treats isolation as the ability to run code without it unexpectedly affecting other running code. It borrows the stages of fault detection, isolation and recovery from control engineering, and argues that isolation mostly depends on control flow integrity and memory safety. The set of places a fault can reach is the fault domain, and the goal is to keep that set known and limited. Operating system processes get this through virtual memory and kernel boundaries, but loading shared libraries into a process is fast and provides no real boundary between them.

The case study is a content delivery network that needs to isolate every individual request. The speaker cites seven million requests per second overall, tens of thousands of requests per second on each server, and request lifetimes usually well under five milliseconds, which is too quick for spinning up processes or containers. WebAssembly is presented as a way to constrain the fault domain: its linear memory has no holes, grows in one direction, and uses 32-bit pointers, and code cannot address its own instructions, so control flow is constrained too. Large guard regions let the generated code skip most bounds checks, and trap tables record which faults are expected so that unexpected ones can be treated as fatal.

To run WebAssembly at speed, the team is building an ahead-of-time compiler and runtime, based on the Cranelift project, that turns WebAssembly modules into native shared objects. The calling convention passes a VM context pointer so that all memory access goes through one known base. The speaker said the work was not yet fully open source. The main takeaway is to reason about isolation in terms of control flow and memory, not only process or container boundaries.

talks.title: "Software Performance: A Shape Not a Number" by Kay Ousterhout
talks.teaser: Argues that high-fidelity latency histograms and tracing beat single metrics when explaining distributed system performance.
talks.summary:
Kay Ousterhout opens by contrasting how performance thinking evolved from flat averages on monoliths to tail-sensitive percentiles as apps called more dependencies, then to multimodal latency shapes in microservice estates where one summary number misleads. She shows internal histograms with distinct fast and slow clusters, joy plots over time, and why combinatorial service behavior makes many time series impractical.

For measurement she stresses statistical precision, cardinality for dimensions such as machine or customer, resisting harmful sampling, freshness near tens of seconds for incidents, and horizons of days or weeks. On diagnosis she walks through a slow page load where median stayed fine while the 99th percentile hit 17.7 seconds, rules out errors using history, uses distributed tracing and critical path to find listing—not reading—as the bottleneck, then hand-correlates slow modes to a large customer whose heavy reads exposed deserialization and CPU contention.

She closes with an observability scorecard: capture rich symptom data, then reduce search space via historical context, value context, critical path, correlation, contention, and error provenance. Practitioners should treat “network blip” excuses as missing tooling, not magic.

talks.title: "The Search for a New Visual Search, Beyond Language" by Bryan Minor
talks.teaser: A stock imagery platform explains how deep learning powers similar-image search, safe-content filters, and spatial keyword queries at scale.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with Shutterstock’s core challenge: helping diverse users discover the right photos, video, and music from enormous contributor archives where weak keyword tags and ambiguous language leave most assets unseen. Bryan Minor frames ingestion versus exploration, showing how noisy contributor tags fail simple relevance tests and how scale, GPU compute, and landmark vision models shifted industry practice toward deep learning.

The middle walks through production architecture on containerized cloud services, A/B testing that sometimes rejects new rankers, multilingual keyword confusion, and time-seasonality pitfalls. Product examples include safe-search image classifiers that outperform tags, similar-image vectors, click-normalized tag suggestions mined from behavior, and live multimodal search that pairs language with image embeddings—including spatial constraints such as wine left and cheese right—via CNNs, text models, pooling, dimensionality reduction, and inverted multi-index retrieval.

Closing lessons stress trial-and-error modeling choices, heavy production split testing, cold-start ranking for new assets, duplicate detection, geo-aware results, and looming synthetic and AR imagery. Practitioners should treat search as measurable discovery engineering: normalize position bias, validate in real traffic, and combine vision, language, and salience rather than relying on contributor metadata alone.

talks.title: "Freeing the software that runs our elections" by Roan Kattouw
talks.teaser: Outlines why election systems need software, why openness matters, and how San Francisco is building a reusable open-source stack.
talks.summary:
Elections in places like San Francisco generate enormous ballot complexity: dozens of contests per voter, heavy vote-by-mail volume, and rank-choice rules that demand computerized tabulation and fast scanning. The speaker walks through paper-based and scanner-based flows, contrasts them with direct-recording electronic machines that lack meaningful audit trails, and stresses paper ballots plus statistical and manual audits so results can be checked independently.

Proprietary Dominion-style deployments illustrate vendor lock-in, high licensing costs, and secret code neither the public nor the city fully controls. The talk surveys other efforts—New Hampshire’s accessible Prime3 setup, Colorado’s open risk-limiting audit tooling, and stalled or partially “open” projects in Texas and Los Angeles—to show how hard full-stack open election software is to deliver.

The San Francisco initiative aims for GPLv3-or-equivalent code developed in the open, commodity hardware, modular procurement, and an incremental first phase focused on central vote-by-mail scanning. A technical advisory committee publishes recommendations on GitHub; roughly 1.7 million dollars over two years funds planning and hiring a project manager, with calls for local advocacy and contributions elsewhere.

talks.title: "The bots that help run Wikipedia" by Niharika Kohli
talks.teaser: Surveys the bots that maintain Wikipedia and its sister projects, then walks through building a simple housekeeping bot.
talks.summary:
Niharika Kohli explains that Wikipedia's ecosystem spans sister projects such as Wiktionary, Wikimedia Commons and Wikidata, each run by its own community. The talk separates approved bots, which hold an account and can be blocked if they misbehave, from unauthorized ones mostly used for vandalism. It then surveys what approved bots do: maintaining articles by converting links to HTTPS and replacing dead references with archived copies, welcoming newcomers, signing comments and archiving old discussion threads, checking copyright, and fighting vandalism.

The vandalism history starts with the 2006 Squidward attacks, which blanked articles across English Wikipedia and led to a simple rule-based anti-vandal bot. Its successor, ClueBot NG, uses a neural network trained on past edit history and takes false-positive reports through a web interface. A second case covered bots that reverted each other in cycles. The talk also described the Cebuano Wikipedia, where a bot generating articles from government data left the large majority of that edition machine-written, drowning out local content and shifting editor effort toward cleanup.

For anyone wanting to write a bot, the talk points to community request pages for ideas, open-source frameworks mostly in Python and PHP, lab wikis for testing, and community approval before deployment on Wikimedia's cloud hosting. Its main lesson is that bots can save volunteers real time, but they need oversight and a clearly limited scope.

talks.title: "Algorithms for DNA Data Storage" by Ruthie Nachmany
talks.teaser: Traces how digital data came to be encoded in DNA, from early experiments to modern error-correcting and random-access methods.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the growing gap between the data being produced and the capacity of current storage media. It cites limits on hard disk density, the degradation of magnetic tape, and the archival needs of large scientific and genomic projects. DNA is presented as a dense, durable medium, but the speaker also covers its drawbacks: high synthesis and sequencing costs, slow reads and writes, and strands that mutate or drop out.

The middle of the talk walks through the field's milestones in order. Early work in 2001 mapped letters to nucleotide combinations, and 2009 brought Huffman coding for compression. Later efforts added error correction, including a 2012 block-based scheme and a 2013 study that stored overlapping chunks, followed by Reed-Solomon codes in 2015. Random access, first proposed in 2015 and demonstrated at larger scale in 2018, allowed specific files to be retrieved without sequencing everything. The 2017 DNA Fountain method used fountain codes to approach the theoretical capacity of DNA. Other threads included error correction tailored to cheaper nanopore sequencers, CRISPR-based recording of edits in living bacteria, and image search over photos stored in DNA.

The closing section covers efforts to lower costs, such as prefabricated DNA fragments that are assembled rather than synthesized base by base. It also surveys emerging uses, including cold storage of cryptocurrency keys, DNA computing, and hybrid electronic-molecular devices. The main takeaway is that progress will depend on combining coding theory, information theory, molecular biology and engineering.

talks.title: "Type-Driven Program Synthesis" by Nadia Polikarpova
talks.teaser: Refinement types and SMT synthesis turn specs into verified code; Lifty enforces flows and ReSyn blocks timing leaks.
talks.summary:
The speaker argues that the next step in programming-language automation is writing specifications instead of low-level implementations, with synthesizers generating efficient code that meets those specs. She walks through inserting into a sorted list: plain types are too weak and yield trivial programs, while refinement types encode predicates such as sortedness and element membership. Synquid searches a vast space of partial programs but prunes candidates early via bidirectional refinement type checking backed by SMT, illustrated on list insert and on negation normal form for propositional formulas, where the tool recovers boolean-algebra laws without the programmer spelling them out.

She cautions that full applications like entire products remain out of reach, and points to cross-cutting concerns—security and resource policies—as places synthesis can integrate orthogonal requirements separately. Lifty lets developers write functional code as if data were public while annotating sensitive sources; the compiler synthesizes policy checks and offers guarantees against information leaks, motivated by real recommendation leaks from private social graphs. ReSyn extends the idea to resource annotations so a length-comparison spec can be hardened against timing attacks when one list is secret, generating code that does not stop early on the shorter input.

Practitioners should see specifications as composable layers the compiler can merge, reducing manual policy sprinkling and side-channel mistakes, while Synquid remains available online for experimenting with type-driven synthesis today.

talks.title: "Understanding TypeScript's Structural Type System" by Drew Colthorp
talks.teaser: Explores structural typing, unions, and type-level programming to encode domain rules and catch bugs before code runs.
talks.summary:
The session frames TypeScript as a gradual static layer over JavaScript whose value lies entirely at compile time and in the editor: turning design invariants into constraints the checker can enforce before anything executes. The speaker contrasts nominal and structural typing, explaining that compatibility depends on shape rather than declared names, and uses intersections and unions together with control-flow narrowing to approximate sum types and exhaustive handling familiar from languages like F#.

Discriminated unions with literal tags illustrate how invalid states can be made unrepresentable, with examples ranging from translation keys to permission tokens for sensitive operations. The middle of the talk walks through generics as type-level functions and demystifies built-in utilities such as Partial via mapped types, keyof, and indexed access—treating the type checker as a terminating, substitution-driven language for deriving types from types.

The close emphasizes that these advanced features are optional day-to-day but pay off for teams pursuing type-first workflows. Audience questions cover simulating nominal types with branding, pain points around third-party typings, testing types with tooling like dtslint, intersecting conflicting property types, and generic higher-order functions.

talks.title: "A Funny Thing Happened On The Way To Reimplementing AlphaGo" by Xuanyi Chew
talks.teaser: Follows a small team rebuilding AlphaGo in Go, from neural network basics to the training and cost problems they hit.
talks.summary:
The talk walks through reimplementing AlphaGo and AlphaZero in the Go language, aimed at listeners with no neural network background. It starts by treating a neural network as a mathematical expression, covering expression graphs, backpropagation and gradient descent, convolutions and residual layers. The speaker then explains how the policy and value outputs narrow the search in Monte Carlo tree search, and how AlphaZero learns by playing against itself.

The middle section covers practical difficulties. Writing and tuning Monte Carlo tree search took several attempts, Go's rules proved intricate, and training needed heavy compute. A cloud cost estimate was off by two magnitudes, which ended the plan to train at full scale. The team then tried other approaches: synthetic gradients for distributed updates, which were not useful, and particle swarm optimization, which worked but was slower than gradient descent. They also used transfer learning and multi-task training across tic-tac-toe, Connect Four and Go. One tic-tac-toe run got stuck in an endless loop of passes, which the speaker linked to the halting problem.

The closing argument is that small teams can run useful experiments on unusual ideas, and that diverse implementations in different languages strengthen shared understanding. The speaker also argues that large-scale training remains concentrated in the hands of big companies, which he sees as a concern.

talks.title: "A Little Taste of Dependent Types" by David Christiansen
talks.teaser: Gives a gentle live tour of dependent types in the small language Pi, from natural numbers to proofs about evenness.
talks.summary:
The talk traces dependent type theory back to an early twentieth-century debate over what mathematics is. It contrasts Hilbert's view of mathematics as rule-governed symbol play with Brouwer's intuitionism, where mathematical objects live in mental constructions. Martin-Löf's intuitionistic type theory, developed from the 1970s, and the calculus of constructions later shaped proof assistants and languages such as Agda and Idris. The speaker's book, The Little Typer, co-written with a colleague, uses a deliberately small language called Pi that does not automate away the difficult steps, so readers can see how the system works.

The live demo walks through Pi one step at a time. Numbers, atoms and pairs are checked against their types, and type errors appear when a value does not match its description. Two values that compute to the same result are recognised as the same, even inside a function. Because recursion is not allowed in Pi, addition and doubling are built from eliminators that expose a value's structure. Types then double as propositions: a pair is evidence for "and", a function is evidence for "implies", and a dependent pair captures "there exists". The speaker proves that zero is even and that every natural number is either even or odd, and the resulting program returns a number's parity along with its half.

The main takeaway is intuition rather than mastery. A single program can be both a computation and a machine-checked proof, and the talk points listeners to the book and to library copies for further study.

talks.title: "Vellvm - Verifying the LLVM" by Steve Zdancewic
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for "Vellvm - Verifying the LLVM" by Steve Zdancewic.

talks.title: "Scalable Anomaly Detection (with Zero Machine Learning)" by Arthur Gonigberg
talks.teaser: Shows how Netflix built a real-time anomaly detector for gateway traffic using median estimation and no machine learning.
talks.summary:
Arthur Gonigberg of Netflix's cloud gateway team explains that the gateway routes traffic to a fast-growing set of backend services. Static percentage thresholds were set high to limit false positives, reached operators slowly from a company-wide time series database, and paged the gateway team even when a downstream service was at fault.

The team built Raju, a real-time anomaly detector that runs on Mantis event streams and keeps adaptive thresholds for each gateway cluster and origin pair. Its core is a median estimator that moves by one unit per event, so it stays stable when error counts jump from zero to thousands during an outage. Recovery is checked by comparing recent data against the pre-alert range with a Hoeffding bound. Anomalies are gathered into a window of about three minutes, then tagged by handwritten rules for impact and for whether to alert or page. In one incident, the resulting timeline pointed to the API service rather than the gateway. The same approach was extended to API's Hystrix commands, to start-play drops, to deployment events, and to emails sent directly to origin owners.

Machine learning was rejected because outages are rare, varied, and drift over time. The tradeoffs include manual rule creation, per-service tuning, and a need for deep operational knowledge. The speaker reported that weekly pages fell from about ten to about one. The takeaway is that simple statistics on well-sliced, real-time data can cut response time and alert noise.

talks.title: "The Magical Rebalance Protocol of Apache Kafka" by Gwen Shapira
talks.teaser: Walks through how Kafka's consumer group protocol assigns partitions and rebalances, and how other services reuse it.
talks.summary:
Kafka consumer groups need a way to hand out topic partitions to members as they join, leave, or crash, and the talk explains how Kafka's group protocol handles this without ZooKeeper. Each group is routed to a single coordinator, found by hashing the group ID onto the internal offsets topic. Members join, the first to join becomes the leader, and the group agrees on an assignment strategy. The speaker explains why partition assignment was moved to the clients rather than the brokers: brokers know nothing the clients do not, and getting broker and application teams to coordinate upgrades is hard.

The middle of the talk walks through the join and sync phases, heartbeats, and rebalancing, where members stop consuming, stop committing offsets, and rejoin. It shows how a group can move from round-robin to a sticky assignor during a rolling upgrade, because members rank their supported strategies and the coordinator picks the one most members prefer. Three other uses of the same protocol follow. Kafka Connect spreads connector tasks across workers, Kafka Streams uses a custom assignor that keeps tasks with their existing local state, and Schema Registry elects a leader by sorting eligible host identities and picking the first.

The closing section notes that the abstract coordinator is not a formal public API, so developers who build on it are asked to get in touch so it can be stabilised. Planned improvements include generation IDs for fencing and incremental rebalancing. For practitioners, the takeaway is that custom partition or leader logic can often be added by writing an assignor rather than a new protocol.

talks.title: "FaCT: A New Language for Constant-Time Programming" by Sunjay Cauligi
talks.teaser: A domain-specific language compiles readable crypto routines into constant-time assembly for embedding in C, Python, and Haskell projects.
talks.summary:
General-purpose languages and compilers ignore data sensitivity, so production cryptographic code is often hand-written in a restricted C style without ordinary control flow. The presenter illustrates timing leaks with PKCS#7 padding removal: early returns enable padding-oracle attacks, loop bounds leak message size, and even guarded branches can change micro-architectural timing until the logic is rewritten with opaque bit manipulations that are hard to read and maintain. Real libraries such as OpenSSL faced repeated timing fixes, follow-on attacks like Lucky 13, and later non-timing padding bugs buried in the same low-level code.

FaCT is presented as an embeddable domain-specific language for timing-secure functions rather than a full replacement for C. Developers mark values as secret or public; the type system blocks direct and control-flow leakage, disallows risky patterns such as secret-indexed memory access and secret-dependent division, and applies automatic constant-time lowering (including conditional selection and early-return lowering) while checking transformed programs with constraint solving to avoid new memory safety faults. Generated headers and object files integrate with C foreign-function interfaces, with Python and Haskell embeddings shown; constant-time properties are checked with an external verifier after compilation.

Reported OpenSSL and libsodium ports stay close to or above existing C throughput, and a classroom user study found clearer comprehension and fewer leakage mistakes when students wrote FaCT versus manual constant-time C. Planned work includes richer crypto primitives, additional CPU backends, WebAssembly constant-time alignment, and verifying the compiler’s transformations themselves.

talks.title: "Building Financial Systems on Eventually Consistent DBs" by Rahul Pilani
talks.teaser: Shows how Netflix billing moved from MySQL to eventually consistent Cassandra while keeping financial writes correct.
talks.summary:
In 2017, Netflix's subscription billing and financial reporting ran on a single-master MySQL database that could barely handle daily transaction volume as membership kept growing. Billing had to stay fault tolerant, since a failed charge could stop a member from streaming. Read replicas and standby promotions still risked stale reads and lengthy rebuilds, so the team looked at Cassandra.

Cassandra offered horizontal scale, multi-master writes and fault tolerance, but it has no multi-row transactions, no relational schema and weak support for aggregate queries. The team used lightweight compare-and-set operations instead. Updates relied on optimistic locking with a version column, and inserts used keys derived from the payload with UUID v5 so that duplicate queue deliveries were rejected. They chose local quorum for latency, accepting that concurrent cross-region writes to the same key could clobber each other, so processing was kept in the region where a write originated. Invoices were stored as a flattened top-level row with child relations serialized as JSON, and writes were copied to Kafka and compared nightly against a snapshot to catch inconsistencies.

The migration started in January 2017, reached limited production in October 2017, and by July 2018 nearly all traffic ran on Cassandra. The system processed 2 times the volume in about half the time and became available in all regions. The main takeaway is to design explicitly around the trade-offs of an eventually consistent database, retry failed compare-and-set writes from the start, and build monitoring to find the remaining problems.

talks.title: "Understanding Microservices with Distributed Tracing" by Lita Cho
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding "Understanding Microservices with Distributed Tracing" by Lita Cho.

talks.title: "PANOPTES: Open Source Exoplanet Discovery" by Jen Tong
talks.teaser: Explains how consumer cameras and open-source software form a robotic telescope network searching for exoplanets.
talks.summary:
PANOPTES is an open source astronomy project that uses low-cost robotic telescopes to hunt for planets around other stars. The talk starts with why exoplanet research long depended on expensive observatories and missions, then compares detection methods: direct imaging, which struggles against starlight glare, Doppler spectroscopy, which tracks tiny wobbles in a star's light, and transit photometry, which measures the small dip in brightness when a planet crosses its star.

The hardware is built from off-the-shelf parts: a consumer SLR camera, inexpensive 85 millimeter lenses, a commercial equatorial mount and a small Intel computer. The baseline unit was designed to be assembled with hand tools and simple soldering so a high school team could build one, and it has operated without a protective dome through harsh weather in Hawaii. Three units were online in Australia, Hawaii and Massachusetts, with more under construction. Each night a unit works through a list of target stars, taking between 10 and 300 exposures, with exposure length set by local light pollution. Software identifies stars in each frame, and the team compensates for the color filter on the camera sensor by matching stars whose brightness variations are identical.

Calibrated measurements produce light curves. One from a unit in the Los Angeles basin matched the expected transit of a known planet, a dip of about 1.3 percent, to within 1/10 of a percent of expectation. The talk closed with next steps: more schools building units, a cloud data pipeline, better scheduling software and a search interface for the shared images. The speaker argued that a network of units can fill gaps left by large surveys such as LSST.

talks.title: "The Glitching Hour" by Amy Wibowo
talks.teaser: Explains how JPEG compression works and how corrupting its data on purpose produces glitch art effects.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Amy Wibowo (known online as sailor HG) explores digital aesthetics, focusing on how image compression mechanisms can be understood and manipulated to create artistic "glitch" effects. Paralleling how digital filters recreate analog camera imperfections like light leaks and film grain, she examines how digital compression artifacts and file corruption can produce nostalgic visual aesthetics.

### Key Topics
- **Digital Image Fundamentals and Bitmap Glitching**: A basic digital image consists of color samples (pixels) arranged in rows and columns, typically represented as red, green, and blue (RGB) values or hue, saturation, and value. Straightforward uncompressed formats like BMP precede sequential pixel data with headers (width, height, color space). In raw pixel data, glitches can be achieved directly by sorting pixel rows/columns, shifting spatial sections, or shifting individual color channels.
- **Lossless vs. Lossy Compression**: Compression reduces storage space while preserving discernible meaning. Lossless compression removes redundancies (such as counting consecutive identical characters) and allows exact reconstruction. Lossy compression discards details that are hard to notice (analogous to stripping vowels and punctuation from text).
- **JPEG Color Channel Separation**: JPEG reduces file size by dividing image details into varying layers. Splitting RGB into luminance, blue-green, and red-green channels takes advantage of human visual perception, which is much less sensitive to color shifts than brightness. Because luminance contains the primary detail, color channels can be stored at half resolution with minimal perceptible degradation.
- **Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT) & Quantization**: Using an analogy of separating a string quartet recording into frequency tracks (violins, viola, cello) via Fourier analysis, the speaker explains how images behave like 2D waveforms. A Discrete Cosine Transform decomposes 8x8 pixel blocks into 64 2D basis functions. High-frequency coefficients (representing fine details) typically contribute less and are zeroed out or reduced by dividing by a quantization matrix determined by the JPEG quality setting.

### Technical Details
- **JPEG Artifacting**: Setting the JPEG quality setting very low discards high-frequency detail aggressively. Because each 8x8 block is transformed independently, block boundaries misalign and become visibly prominent, while sharp edges approximated by cosine sums exhibit halos or oscillations.
- **Targeted Byte Corruption**: Glitching compressed JPEGs without rendering the file unreadable requires avoiding image headers and metadata. Modifying only the compressed image stream—found after the `FF DA` section marker—ensures file decoders still parse the image.
- **Renderer Differences and Error Propagation**: Replacing a random byte in the compressed payload produces vastly different outcomes depending on how specific image decoders handle invalid data:
  - In Safari, corruption errors often terminate after a single row.
  - In Chrome, errors propagate across the rest of the image because the baseline (0,0) DC component of an 8x8 block is encoded differentially from previous blocks.
  - Byte corruption can alter location values, displacing blocks, or hit separate color channels to cause sweeping hue shifts.
  - Decoders like macOS preview render exposed basis function patterns differently.

### Takeaways
Understanding the mathematical foundations of JPEG compression—from color space subsampling and 8x8 DCT quantization to differential block encoding and file markers (`FF DA`)—allows creators to intentionally induce precise aesthetic glitches. Blending intentional quantization artifacting with targeted compressed-byte corruption enables complex artistic effects across web and desktop decoders.

talks.title: "Building a Canary Testing Framework" by Iheanyi Ekechukwu
talks.teaser: Walks through building a Go-based canary daemon that runs scripted tests against production systems on a schedule.
talks.summary:
Canaries are tests that run continuously against production to catch failures before users notice them. The speaker separates them from canary deployments and from ordinary integration tests, which often stop at the database layer. Drawing on networking work at DigitalOcean, the speaker describes canaries that create droplets, connect over SSH and verify traffic between them, and one canary that exposed a firewall race condition locking users out after a rule was applied right after creation.

The framework is built around a Go daemon that schedules each test on its own goroutine, runs it inside an embedded JavaScript virtual machine, and saves results to a key-value store. The stated requirements include concurrent and repeated runs, per-test timeouts, Prometheus metrics for running, passed and failed tests, and a GraphQL API for viewing results. The talk walks through loading configuration files, adding helper functions for reading secrets, making HTTP requests and emitting structured logs, then shows how the scheduler applies deadlines and records metrics.

A live demo runs a simple HTTP test and a deliberately failing one, with the results queried over GraphQL. The main takeaways are to give each product its own canary so results stay separate, and to use a loosely typed scripting language so checks are quick to write and change.

talks.title: "A Box of Chaos: The Generative Artist's Toolkit" by Benjamin Kovach
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for "A Box of Chaos: The Generative Artist's Toolkit" by Benjamin Kovach.

talks.title: "Mapping Imaginary Cities" by Mouse Reeve
talks.teaser: Explores how real and fictional maps encode agendas, then builds procedural terrain, neighborhoods, and road networks in JavaScript.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with cartography as embedded narrative: commercial navigation maps, alternative atlases of wildlife and pollution, John Snow’s cholera dots, trap towns, censored military features, and fictional maps whose form shapes how readers imagine worlds. The speaker frames every map as a partial model shaped by creators, in-world cartographers, inhabitants, and audiences.

The core project is a procedural tourist-style city. Terrain comes from simplex noise with tunable amplitude, frequency, and octaves, then coastlines via midpoint displacement, rivers that seek local lows, population density multiplied into neighborhood seeds, Voronoi cells, and heuristic parks and beaches. Roads grow recursively from a city center, favoring flat paths, snapping endpoints to avoid dead ends, sometimes bridging water where density is high, with perturbation controlling grid-like versus winding street character.

Outputs include generated neighborhood names, points of interest, and pamphlet-style context such as a seven-day weather forecast. Implementation uses JavaScript and p5.js, with code on GitHub. Questions touch inspirations from Solnit and Mieville, seeded randomness, neighborhood-specific road styles, and deliberate scope limits versus full simulation or planet-scale generation.

talks.title: "Leverage vs. Autonomy in a Large Software System" by Jake Donham
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of "Leverage vs. Autonomy in a Large Software System" by Jake Donham.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Jake Donham discusses how large engineering organizations balance leverage and autonomy when designing software architecture, drawing heavily on his experiences at Twitter. By applying organizational management principles—specifically Andy Grove’s concepts of functional versus mission-oriented teams and Conway's Law—Donham examines how software architecture affects developer productivity and efficiency. He traces Twitter’s evolution from an early Ruby monolith to a sprawling microservices ecosystem, and ultimately to Strato, a centralized platform designed to offer high operational leverage without stripping developer autonomy.

### Key Topics
- **Organizational Principles and Conway's Law**: Applying Andy Grove's team archetypes (functional teams offering leverage and economies of scale vs. mission-oriented teams optimizing for speed and autonomy) to system design. The talk references Conway’s Law (systems mirror communication structures) and Copeland's Law (mismatches between organization structure and software architecture cause operational friction).
- **Autonomy vs. Leverage Trade-offs**: Centralized systems maximize leverage and consistency but introduce single points of failure, monoculture risks, gatekeeping, and arcane knowledge. Decentralized architectures enhance local autonomy and decouple deployments, but lead to duplicated work, poor leverage, gratuitous variation, and severe difficulty in managing cross-cutting concerns.
- **Twitter’s Architectural Evolution**: The historical shift from a massive monolithic Ruby on Rails application (fraught with deploy queues, lack of modularity, and cross-cutting bugs) to an expansive microservices architecture (which improved autonomy but resulted in high per-service overhead, orphaned services, and fragmented cross-cutting libraries).
- **Architectural Sweet Spots**: Examples where centralization yielded massive leverage without sacrificing meaningful autonomy, notably Aurora/Mesos for cloud compute scheduling and Finagle for RPC communication, load balancing, failure detection, and service discovery.

### Technical Details
- **Compute and RPC Infrastructure**: Moving from manual host allocation and ad hoc deploy scripts to Aurora/Mesos provided automated scheduling, standardized configuration, and higher utilization on the JVM. Replacing raw Apache Thrift clients with Finagle delivered transparent RPC multiplexing, failure detection, distributed tracing, and futures-based asynchronous handling.
- **Microservices Challenges at Twitter**: Decomposing systems purely by domain nouns (e.g., users, tweets) led to awkward cross-cutting feature libraries embedded in client services, creating distributed deploy dependencies, ownership vacuums, and ad hoc internal platforms.
- **Strato Platform Architecture**: Strato addresses these issues by acting as a centrally operated monolithic platform hosting microservices defined as lightweight configurations. It isolates system concerns (timeouts, retries, RPC infrastructure) from business logic, and decouples platform code deployments from fast, frequent configuration deployments.
- **StratoQL DSL**: Strato services execute logic using StratoQL, a domain-specific, structurally typed language inspired by Scala's core (records, variants, pattern matching) and Facebook's Haxl. Key features include:
  - Direct native support for Apache Thrift data types without code generation.
  - Language restrictions to prevent infinite loops, unbounded memory usage, and heavyweight compute.
  - Built-in transparent concurrency and automatic request batching for asynchronous downstream RPC queries.
  - Runtime first-class types enabling automatic serialization and high-level interfaces, such as a centralized GraphQL layer for mobile clients.

### Takeaways
- Extreme decentralization generates hidden costs: duplicated infrastructure setup, orphaned services, and barriers to applying cross-cutting policies.
- Architectural "sweet spots" exist where generic capabilities with standardized interfaces (like compute scheduling or RPC transports) can be centralized without restricting product velocity.
- Domain-specific languages and purpose-built microservice platforms like Strato demonstrate that thoughtfully constraining developer runtimes can provide massive systemic leverage while preserving autonomous feature delivery.

talks.title: "Categories for the Working Hacker" by Philip Wadler
talks.teaser: Shows how products, sums and exponentials from category theory map onto records, variant types and functions in code.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the Curry-Howard correspondence, which links logical proofs with types in programming. The speaker argues that category theory forms a third member of this correspondence, so the same structures describe logic, lambda calculus and categories. He introduces the basic vocabulary of objects, arrows, identities and composition, and illustrates it with monoids, which are structures with an identity and an associative operation.

The middle section covers the core data structures. A product corresponds to conjunction and to records or pairs, and the number of values in a product is the product of the sizes of its parts. The speaker shows the idea in Java and then in a shorter Haskell version. A sum corresponds to disjunction and to tagged unions, such as an error message or a number, consumed with a case expression. An exponential is a function type, and counting its values gives the exponent. Flipping the arrows swaps products and sums, a duality that gives the same ideas in reverse.

The closing section connects these structures to blockchain languages, including Simplicity and Michelson, and to Plutus, which is built on System F omega. The talk ends by deriving an exponential law that matches an identity from high school algebra. The speaker encourages listeners to learn category theory first and to treat painful Java-style code as a sign that a cleaner abstraction exists.

talks.title: "All the Languages Together" by Amal Ahmed
talks.teaser: Advocates linking types and preserving compilers so mixed-language code can catch boundary violations before link time.
talks.summary:
Amal Ahmed argues that polyglot systems are routine—Rust for performance beside OCaml, or DSLs for protocols—but today's world forces coarse fixes: generic FFIs, microservices, or debugging ownership breaks only after link and run. She walks through small OCaml–Rust examples where returning a vector to Rust while still mutating it in OCaml breaks Rust's ownership rules, and similar refactoring pitfalls when impure callbacks enter code assumed pure.
