- Technologists possess outsized leverage through software and security expertise, which can be applied to defend civil liberties and at-risk communities.
- A robust ecosystem of grants (OTF, Open Knowledge) and fellowships (Mozilla, TechCongress, Ford Foundation) exists to financially support technical contributors outside Big Tech.
- Direct involvement does not require quitting a job immediately; engineers can contribute via conferences, open-source bug fixes, UX design improvements for privacy tools, and employer-sponsored volunteer programs.

talks.title: "Zuul's Journey to Non-Blocking" by Arthur Gonigberg
talks.teaser: Explains how Netflix moved its Zuul edge gateway to non-blocking Netty and RxJava, and when that move pays off.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Arthur Gonigberg presents Netflix's architectural migration of its edge proxy service, Zuul, from a blocking Java servlet model to a non-blocking, asynchronous architecture. Zuul operates as the front door to Netflix on AWS, managing tens of billions of requests per day and handling critical functions including routing, security (DDoS mitigation and blocking fraudulent traffic), monitoring, and resiliency. While initial micro-benchmarks showed dramatic throughput increases (up to 73,000 requests per second), real-world production performance between Zuul 1 and Zuul 2 showed only a modest 10% to 20% throughput gain. The talk explores how Netflix executed the rewrite, the severe engineering and operational pitfalls encountered, and the distinct resiliency and architectural benefits achieved.

### Key Topics
- **Zuul 1 Architecture & Limitations**: Zuul 1 ran on Tomcat with standard Java servlets using one thread per request. Latency spikes at origins or connection spikes caused rapid thread pool exhaustion and severe cascading failures during traffic surges.
- **Building Blocks of Non-Blocking Systems**: The shift required non-blocking I/O primitives (e.g., epoll on Linux, kqueue on BSD), an asynchronous programming paradigm (RxJava), and an event loop framework (Netty).
- **Incremental Migration via Zuul 1.5**: To safely replace the engine while serving massive production traffic, Netflix first adopted Tomcat's APR connector to decouple connections from requests, then converted the filter chain to return observables (`applyAsync`), allowing filter execution in both Tomcat and Netty.
- **Zuul 2 Architecture**: Netty server fronting incoming requests, Netty client managing outbound proxying, and an RxJava filter chain stitched in between on single-threaded event loops.

### Technical Details & Operational Pitfalls
- **Blocking Shared Libraries**: Shared platform libraries often made blocking calls (such as `Thread.sleep`), which paused Netty event loop threads and stalled hundreds of concurrent requests. Netflix used `reactive-audit` to detect blocking calls at runtime.
- **ThreadLocal State Corruption & The 'Geo Shuffle'**: Netty event loop threads multiplex many requests. Shared libraries relying on `ThreadLocal` storage leaked state between requests. A severe production bug dubbed the 'Geo Shuffle' occurred when geo-lookup IP data was stored in thread locals, causing San Francisco users to be assigned geo-data for Siberia, Brazil, or South Africa and routed to remote CDNs. The fix required explicitly copying and setting channel state onto thread locals upon entering Netty channel pipelines or RxJava threads.
- **Direct Memory Leaks**: Netty utilizes off-heap direct memory via JNI and epoll. Incomplete request lifecycles caused gradual direct memory leaks that silently brought server traffic to zero RPS without throwing traditional heap errors.
- **Debugging & The Request Passport**: Standard thread dumps and stack traces were ineffective in async code. Netflix truncated repetitive RxJava stack traces, disabled trace generation in high-CPU critical paths, and implemented the 'Request Passport' (inspired by Zach Hellman) to record timestamped channel state transitions to debug complex timing issues and ELB timeouts.

### Takeaways & Guidance
- **Workload Profiles Matter**: Zuul is fundamentally CPU-bound due to authentication, encryption, decryption, and hashing. Non-blocking models do not reduce core CPU processing requirements; hence, CPU-bound workloads see minimal throughput improvements (10–20%). In contrast, I/O-bound services, large file streams, chat systems, or push notification architectures benefit heavily.
- **Resiliency Benefits**: Zuul 2 excelled during 'retry storms' (when failing clients rapidly retry, outstripping auto-scaling capacity). Instead of aggressively throttling legitimate traffic, Zuul 2 handled significantly higher RPS at max CPU and safely dropped retries when origin error thresholds were breached.
- **Expanded Capabilities**: Zuul 2 comfortably handles tens of thousands of concurrent connections per instance, enabling WebSocket support for push notifications and removing the need for strict timeouts and Hystrix circuit breakers.

talks.title: "Keeping Time in Real Systems" by Kavya Joshi
talks.teaser: Traces clock drift, NTP, and leap seconds through Spanner TrueTime and Riak vector clocks in distributed stores.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues that a distributed store’s consistency model is really a contract about which event timelines are valid, and that contract depends on how the system keeps time. It starts with everyday wall clocks: kernel-maintained counters tied to drifting hardware, NTP’s slow public-Internet sync and disruptive clock steps, and Unix time’s assumption of fixed-length UTC days—problematic when leap seconds make civil time non-monotonic. A two-node write example shows how unsynchronized timestamps can label a newer value with an older time and leave the database unreconcilable.

The middle contrasts two production designs. Google Spanner targets external consistency across partitions, illustrated with savings and checking transactions that must never appear out of client commit order globally. Its TrueTime API returns an interval guaranteed to contain “now,” and commits wait a full uncertainty window so later transactions receive higher timestamps despite clock error; Google binds that window to about seven milliseconds, far tighter than typical NTP. Riak instead favors availability and eventual consistency, using vector clocks carried with reads and writes to separate causal updates from concurrent conflicts when replicas converge.

The close stresses tradeoffs among consistency, availability, and latency, notes that consensus can align replica timelines but was skipped for brevity, and briefly points to hybrid logical clocks in CockroachDB as a bridge between physical and logical time—helping practitioners match timekeeping machinery to the guarantees they actually need.

talks.title: "Redux: Architecting and scaling a new web app at The NY Times" by Juan Carlos Montemayor Elosua
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding "Redux: Architecting and scaling a new web app at The NY Times" by Juan Carlos Montemayor Elosua.

talks.title: "Observability for Emerging Infra: What Got You Here Won't Get You There" by Charity Majors
talks.teaser: Explains why lamp-stack monitoring fails on microservices and what observability practices replace dashboards and metrics.
talks.summary:
The speaker contrasts traditional monitoring, rooted in host-centric LAMP assumptions and known-unknown alerts, with observability suited to highly distributed, containerized platforms. She argues complexity has outpaced dashboards and coarse metrics: user reports often contradict green health checks, and rare intersections of conditions dominate incident time at scale, as she experienced at Parse and later at Facebook.

The middle of the talk maps practical building blocks. Instrumentation should yield rich, structured events with high cardinality, not tag-limited metrics alone; sampling keeps volume manageable while preserving tails that matter. Events support iterative questioning instead of dashboard hopping after past failures. She critiques write-time aggregation that discards context and advocates locating individual requests, using production-oriented rollout patterns such as canaries and feature flags rather than over-relying on staging.

Practitioners should treat operability as a core engineering skill: watch normal behavior, keep paging minimal around latency, errors, and saturation, and invest in tooling that answers arbitrary questions quickly. What worked for simpler stacks will not carry teams through platform-era unknown unknowns.

talks.title: "Alice's Adventures in Artificial Intelligence-land" by Coraline Ada Ehmke
talks.teaser: Traces a personal chatbot project from early text-based game experiments through its Ruby design, language processing and live demo.
talks.summary:
Coraline Ada Ehmke traces the history of Alice, a chatbot she has built and extended since the mid-1990s. The story starts with text-based social environments, where her first bot, Budge, answered questions about a virtual museum of Egyptian artifacts, and Ghouls, which listened to conversations and replayed phrases that drew responses. Alice later moved into a private IRC channel and then a Slack community of about seventy members.

The middle of the talk walks through the architecture. Alice is a Ruby application with a single Sinatra route, MongoDB storage and a newer Neo4j graph database. Each message passes through a listener, a processor, a commander and a mediator. Commands are matched either by a simple parser or by a natural language step backed by Google's NLP API. Context objects let Alice follow the topic or user under discussion, and she gathers facts from Wikipedia and web search, ranking them by a declarative index. The live demo covered a text dungeon with generated rooms, items, a map, brewed beverages and a grue that devours players, along with questions answered from context.

The closing section looks at planned work: parsing stored facts to answer questions, generating sentences from parts of speech with Markov chains, and a separate project, Sophia, that models concepts such as temperature using ranked expressions with synonyms and antonyms. The takeaway is that a playful side project can teach practical NLP ideas, and that play supports learning.

talks.title: "Wait, it does ??tahW: How supporting Right-to-Left can expose your bad UX" by Moriel Schottlender
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for "Wait, it does ??tahW: How supporting Right-to-Left can expose your bad UX" by Moriel Schottlender.

talks.title: "Kotlin: Uncovered" by Victoria Gonda
talks.teaser: Shows how Kotlin features such as data classes and null safety look once compiled Kotlin bytecode is decompiled back to Java.
talks.summary:
The speaker introduces Kotlin as a statically typed language for the JVM that interoperates with Java. Because Kotlin compiles to bytecode, that output can be decompiled back into Java to reveal what the compiler generates. Starting with a simple user class, the decompiled code shows a final class, private fields, null checks on constructor parameters and generated accessors.

Data classes add componentN functions, copy, toString, equals and hashCode, along with synthetic methods for default parameter values. For null safety, calling a method on an unchecked nullable value does not compile, the safe-call operator becomes a null-guarded ternary, and the double-bang operator becomes an explicit check that throws a null pointer exception. The Elvis operator becomes a conditional return. Delegation is illustrated with a copy-printer example from a blog post, where the generated class forwards calls to delegate objects. Extension functions compile to static methods in a utility class, and lambdas passed to inline functions are placed at the call site, while a non-inline lambda becomes its own class.

The talk ends by showing how to open the Kotlin bytecode view and decompile code in IntelliJ or Android Studio, and how to convert Java files to Kotlin while reviewing double-bang operators. The speaker argues that reading the generated code clarifies what language features cost, and that working in Kotlin has made them more attentive to nulls.

talks.title: "Datafun: a functional query language" by Michael Arntzenius
talks.teaser: Explains how set comprehensions and fixed points let a functional language express recursive queries like Datalog.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Datafun, an early-stage functional query language that is presented as an exploration rather than a finished system. The core idea is to treat tables as sets of tuples and to add set comprehensions to a pure, total functional language, so queries read much like list comprehensions. Sets become ordinary values that can be passed to functions or nested inside other data, and types choose between set, bag and list semantics.

The middle of the talk covers recursion. Relational algebra cannot express questions such as whether one person is an ancestor of another at any depth, while Datalog answers this with two rules. The speaker shows how repeatedly applying rules until nothing changes corresponds to finding a fixed point, which Datafun expresses directly. Purity and totality are needed because loop reordering, a standard database optimization, is unsafe when side effects or non-termination are possible.

The final part discusses incremental computation, where changes to inputs update outputs without full recomputation. Drawing on research into differentiating higher-order programs, each type gets a change type and each function gets a derivative, which the speaker hopes will speed up fixed-point evaluation. This work was recent and had no working implementation yet, so no performance results were given. The takeaway is that set comprehensions, fixed points and incremental computation together cover much of what databases do, though the approach remains unproven at scale.

talks.title: "Automating Cloud Security and Incident Response (DevSecOps)" by Jearvon Dharrie
talks.teaser: Shows how infrastructure as code and serverless remediation can replace ticket-based gatekeeping for AWS security controls.
talks.summary:
The talk follows a developer on a team that moved its back-office systems from a managed data center to AWS. Early on, security restricted account rights and required a ticket for every port or role, which slowed delivery and often missed needed ports. The talk frames this as a story about moving the team toward shared responsibility for security.

The approach has three parts. First, infrastructure is defined in Terraform, so networks, users, and password and MFA policies become reusable modules with code review, version history, and consistent baselines across accounts. Second, the team gains visibility through CloudTrail, VPC flow logs, and bastion logs shipped to Elasticsearch and Kibana, with dashboards for API calls and rejected traffic, plus AWS Config rules that flag public S3 buckets. Third, guardrails respond automatically: a Lambda function triggered by CloudWatch events turns CloudTrail logging back on, records who made the change, and sends a notification, while a tainted EC2 instance is moved into a quarantine security group. Cloud Custodian policies check for required tags.

The speaker concludes the effort was worth it, since the team now controls its accounts and works more closely with security. The main takeaway is that automation is a requirement, and any service with an API can be handled the same way. Future plans include benchmark checks, more Cloud Custodian rules, and Netflix security tools.

talks.title: "Why We Built Our Own Distributed Column Store" by Sam Stokes
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding "Why We Built Our Own Distributed Column Store" by Sam Stokes.

talks.title: "Tackling Concurrency Bugs with TLA+" by Hillel Wayne
talks.teaser: Demonstrates how TLA+ model checking exposes race conditions in a banking transfer design before any code is written.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that concurrency bugs resist the usual tools. Unit tests multiply combinatorially when timing-dependent systems interact, and type systems or pure functions cannot stop outside services from crashing mid-operation. A simple bank transfer with an overdraft rule shows the problem: two concurrent transfers can overdraft an account, and a crash between steps can duplicate money.

The speaker models the transfer in TLA+, a formal specification language, and checks an invariant that no account goes negative. The model checker, TLC, explores every interleaving of the steps. Adding a second concurrent transfer produces a counterexample trace showing how one transfer's balance check passes before the other's subtraction lands. Running the steps inside a single database transaction fixes the violation, and the fix is confirmed before any code is written. Three workplace cases follow: an app installer where the model caught an overlapping-worker bug, a zero-downtime deployment spec used as compact design documentation for another team, and a message-processing change that broke earlier invariants and exposed a gap in the team's understanding, leading them to relax older requirements.

The takeaway is that a specification validates a design rather than the code, so implementations still need careful checking, but design flaws can surface early. The talk closes with resources for learning TLA+ and PlusCal, from an introductory tutorial to Lamport's canonical book and a text on the temporal logic underneath.

talks.title: "GPGPU Programming with Metal" by Janie Clayton
talks.teaser: Explains how general-purpose GPU work runs through Apple's Metal framework on iPhone, from thread groups to shading functions.
talks.summary:
Janie Clayton opens with a short history of GPUs, from the fixed-function chips of the late 1990s to programmable pipelines and OpenGL ES on mobile devices. She explains that GPUs were used almost only for graphics until researchers began using them to train neural networks. Metal, introduced in 2014, was the first framework that let iPhone code run general-purpose work on the GPU.

The middle of the talk covers how work reaches the GPU. Data is encoded into Metal resource types and sent through command encoders and buffers, then organized into threads and thread groups sized to each device's limits. Kernel functions written in Metal Shading Language, which is based on C++14, perform the computation. Metal Performance Shaders provide prebuilt image-processing and neural network operations that Apple has tuned for each GPU, so developers do not have to write common operations such as a Gaussian blur themselves.

She uses a relocation-to-San-Francisco decision as a plain-language model of neural networks, showing how weights and biases shape the outcome, and notes that training happens on much larger systems than a phone while phones can run trained models. Her takeaways are that phones can keep sensitive data on the device, which matters for privacy, and that moving work to the GPU pays off mainly when data sets are large.

talks.title: "Level Up Your Concurrency Skills With Rust" by David Sullins
talks.teaser: Shows how Rust's ownership and borrowing rules prevent data races, using a game engine bug as the starting example.
talks.summary:
The speaker, a game developer who works on graphics engine technology in C++, argues that concurrency is hard because threads can interleave in different orders, so tests rarely catch timing bugs. As an example, they describe a game engine optimization in which a rendering thread and a physics thread shared a GPU vertex buffer and skipped a temporary copy by relying on careful timing. Late in development this produced blank screens caused by a data race, and the team removed the optimization to ship on schedule.

Next comes a primer on data races: two or more threads accessing shared state, with at least one write and no synchronization or atomic access. The talk then walks through Rust's model. Variables are immutable by default, each value has one owner that frees it when that owner goes out of scope, moves transfer ownership, and clones copy data. Borrows are checked at compile time, so a value cannot be written while it is being read. Compiler error messages illustrate each case.

The takeaway is that clear thinking about ownership, resources and lifetimes helps in any language, even if Rust is not used daily. Rust's compile-time checks remove a whole class of errors, including data races, which the speaker describes as the most common problem in game development. They do not eliminate every concurrency bug, however.

talks.title: "Bootstrapping the Web with Scala Native" by Richard Whaling
talks.teaser: Walks through building a small HTTP server in Scala Native, from forked sockets to FastCGI and libuv.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Richard Whaling explores low-level systems and server programming using Scala Native, an ahead-of-time (AOT) LLVM-backed compiler plugin for Scala that produces compact native binaries without the JVM runtime. Whaling addresses the architectural challenges of bootstrapping web and network services in an emerging language lacking massive ecosystem frameworks like Netty or Akka HTTP. The presentation demonstrates iterative approaches to building high-performance web applications, starting from basic Berkeley socket programming and classic Common Gateway Interface (CGI), moving to multiplexed protocols via FastCGI, and concluding with multiplexed asynchronous I/O using libuv.

### Key Topics
- **Scala Native Fundamentals & C Interop**: How Scala Native compiles Scala directly to native executables (typically 5–10 MB), providing C interoperability constructs including C struct tuples, raw pointer arithmetic, `stackalloc`, dynamic linking stubs via `@extern`, and memory management with `malloc` and `free` alongside a built-in garbage collector.
- **Network Server Architecture**: The mechanics of UNIX socket programming (`socket`, `bind`, `listen`, `accept`, `read`, `write`), operating system TCP connection backlogs, and traditional process-per-connection concurrency using the `fork` system call, alongside the operational pitfalls of zombie processes, porting challenges, and testing complexity.
- **Separation of Infrastructure and Application Logic**: Offloading complex HTTP parsing and connection handling to battle-tested proxies and web servers (such as Apache, NGINX, Envoy, or custom Go proxies) instead of embedding massive HTTP frameworks inside newly developed applications.
- **Multiplexed Protocols vs. Multiplexed I/O**: Strategies to avoid process-creation overhead via FastCGI binary framing and persistent connections over a single socket, compared to event-driven, non-blocking I/O multiplexing across multiple sockets.

### Technical Details
- **CGI Baseline**: Whaling implements a minimal CGI web handler in Scala Native running under Apache. Because Scala Native compiles down to a small native binary, the CGI app achieved a mean response time of 40 ms under light load and peaked around 400 requests per second (outperforming Python CGI at 136 ms, though trailing a trivial Node.js Express setup running at ~7 ms and ~2,000 req/sec).
- **FastCGI Implementation**: To avoid spawning processes on every request, Whaling implemented FastCGI parsing in Scala Native using unsafe pointer indexing, bitwise operations (`& 0xFF` to handle Java signed bytes), and manual 8-byte frame header extraction. Because open-source NGINX does not easily constrain connections to a single backend socket without NGINX Plus, he built an 80-line Go proxy to route traffic over a single persistent socket using blocking I/O, achieving 4 ms mean response times under light load and peaking near 1,500 req/sec.
- **Direct Multiplexed I/O with libuv**: Whaling linked Scala Native directly to `libuv` (`@link("uv")`), the C event loop library behind Node.js that runs on OS-specific primitives like Linux `epoll`. Utilizing Scala Native's C function pointer callbacks, he configured non-blocking socket handling over UNIX domain sockets. Under a Gatling benchmark simulating 500 users and 25,000 requests, this architecture achieved 4,166 requests per second, a 56 ms median response time, and an error rate far below 1%.

### Takeaways
- Scala Native provides viable C interoperability for low-level systems programming, allowing developers to safely leverage existing C libraries like `libuv` when standard JVM-based networking libraries are unavailable.
- Offloading HTTP protocol parsing to proxies and communicating via lightweight multiplexed protocols like FastCGI allows applications in emerging runtimes to achieve solid performance without maintaining complex HTTP RFC parsers.
- Combining non-blocking multiplexed event loops with compact native binaries yields throughput and latency competitive with or exceeding established frameworks like Node.js.

talks.title: "Policy as Code with Sentinel Language" by Armon Dadgar
talks.teaser: Explains how policy as code guards automated infrastructure changes, and the design choices behind HashiCorp's Sentinel language.
talks.summary:
The speaker begins with infrastructure as code, contrasting hand-built data centers managed through consoles and tickets with codified, API-driven provisioning. That leverage has a downside: a typo can request 5,000 VMs with no human asking whether it makes sense. Policy as code is offered as a way to define the sandbox automated changes must stay within, enforced by a separate codified rule set that security and compliance teams maintain.

Example policies cover instance counts and types, allowed regions per environment, billing tags, approved images, and deployment windows. The talk then covers the design goals of Sentinel, HashiCorp's policy language: readable by non-programmers, easy to embed in Go tools, and sandboxed. These goals led to dynamic typing, English operators, first-class rules evaluated lazily and memoized, and an undefined value that propagates errors so higher-level logic often absorbs them. Enforcement levels range from advisory warnings to soft mandatory rules that can be overridden and hard mandatory rules that cannot.

The surrounding tooling includes a simulator with apply, docs, and test commands, so policies can be checked in CI like software. An import SDK uses plugins to query external systems for decisions. The closing argument is that preventing violations at change time is simpler for compliance than detecting and remediating them afterward, and that codifying each lesson scales better than relying on memory.

talks.title: "Universal Reason" by Jacob Bass
talks.teaser: Shows how ReasonML adds compile-time safety to Express backends and React front ends while compiling to JavaScript.
talks.summary:
Jacob Bass opens with the difficulty of writing correct software in dynamically typed languages such as JavaScript and Ruby, where runtime checks and comments replace formal guarantees. He introduces ReasonML as a approachable syntax and toolchain over OCaml, emphasizing compilation to JavaScript so web developers can adopt stronger typing without abandoning the browser ecosystem.

The middle of the talk walks through concrete patterns: type-safe Express middleware that must always respond via an abstract done type, pattern matching on options instead of nullable pitfalls, ReasonReact components with inferred types instead of runtime prop types, and reducer-style state without a separate Redux layer. He cites Messenger.com-scale front-end adoption, fast BuckleScript builds, and very low bug counts discovered at compile time rather than in production.

He closes with phantom and opaque types that force validation before persistence—save accepts only validated person records—and with modules, mixins, and module functors as abstraction tools. The takeaway for practitioners is that much branching and plumbing coverage can move from tests and discipline into the type checker, shrinking cognitive load while refactoring remains safe.

talks.title: "The Holy Grail of Systems Analysis: from What to Where to Why" by Daniel Spoonhower
talks.teaser: Explains how distributed tracing can reveal which shared resources cause latency across microservice requests, using a demo.
talks.summary:
Monitoring tools are struggling as systems move to microservices. A single request now crosses many independently deployed services, and metrics with tags can show that something is slow but rarely explain why. Dashboards mostly reveal correlation, high-cardinality tags become expensive to collect and manage, and every new service tempts teams to add more metrics that quickly go stale. Distributed tracing answers where the latency sits by following a request across process boundaries. The speaker argues that sampling should happen after data leaves the process, since logging every transaction at scale is not practical.

The talk then turns to why latency happens. The central claim is that most latency comes from contention for shared resources such as locks, queues, databases or network links, rather than from one slow span alone. In a toy donut-ordering system, each important resource was given an identifier, spans that waited on it were tagged, and the call graphs of every other request contending for the same resource were aggregated. Audience members took part by placing orders, restocking ingredients and cleaning the fryer. In each round the aggregated view pointed to the responsible activity: sprinkles orders dominated the fryer lock in one case, and a restocking process loaded the toppings resource in another. A single misbehaving user could also be identified this way, even when overall percentile metrics looked normal.

The takeaway is to treat latency in distributed systems as a contention problem and to build tooling that analyzes concurrent transactions in real time, without deciding every tag in advance. The demonstration software was a rough prototype, but the speaker notes that the underlying data already exists in typical tracing setups. The instrumentation shown relied on the OpenTracing standard for exporting trace data from applications.

talks.title: "Tuning Elasticsearch for English-Language Precision" by Erin McKean
talks.teaser: Shows how to tune Elasticsearch analyzers so dictionary lookups balance precision and recall for odd English words.
talks.summary:
Erin McKean, who has spent about 25 years working on dictionaries, explains why English-language search is hard to get right when the goal is matching the word a user typed. Many lookups involve unusual forms: capitalized words typed in lowercase, hyphenated compounds, abbreviations, inflected verbs and accented letters. She frames the search box as a place where users want definitions, usage examples, spelling or pronunciation, so results should favor precision first and then widen toward recall.

The middle of the talk looks at how Elasticsearch handles text. An inverted index maps each unique token to the documents that contain it, so the mapping decides what counts as a word. She compares the standard analyzer, which mostly splits text and lowercases it, with a custom dictionary analyzer built from a whitespace tokenizer, HTML stripping, quote normalization, regular-expression punctuation filters and shingles. A stemmer-based analyzer handles possessives and verb inflections, and multi-field mappings index one string several ways. Keyword fields give exact matches, boosting fields changes ranking, and the explain parameter exposes the scoring math behind a result.

The closing advice is that tuning is a set of trade-offs. Know what users look for, pre-process data where you control it, check search logs, and accept that no analyzer will fit every case. She points to resources on Elasticsearch, relevance scoring and Unicode text segmentation, along with linguistics research on how modern search engines strip out the features linguists care about.

talks.title: "Riot Messaging Service - Message Players Like a Pro" by Michal Ptaszek
talks.teaser: Shows how Riot Games built its messaging service to push real-time notifications to millions of League of Legends players.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Riot Messaging Service (RMS), a back-end service that delivers fire-and-forget notifications and small payloads from internal services to connected League of Legends clients. The speaker explains why it replaced an older setup using persistent RTMP connections inside a monolith, which had security problems and could only hold about 30,000 players per server. Clients authenticate with a signed token, open a WebSocket, and receive notifications that publishers send over REST with a routing resource, a variant for deduplication, and a list of player IDs.

The system is split into two independently deployed tiers. Edge servers hold player connections, capped at about 350,000 per box, while the routing tier keeps a global table mapping player IDs to edge nodes. The stack is written in Erlang, packaged in Docker on AWS, and managed with Terraform. One outage dropped around 500 thousand connections that reconnected at once and overwhelmed a classic load balancer, which was removed in favour of service discovery. Other points covered health checks every 30 seconds, centralized monitoring, git-driven dynamic configuration, and Jepsen testing of network partitions.

A later spike doubled concurrent connections after a client patch, and the team absorbed it by scaling because earlier load testing had covered roughly ten times normal capacity. The roadmap adds topic-based routing and persistence for offline players. The main takeaways are to plan for failure, test distributed behaviour with fault injection, avoid overloading shared components during reconnect storms, and keep operational dashboards simple.

talks.title: "How to Play with Deep Space Data" by Lisa Ballard
talks.teaser: Surveys NASA search portals, JSON APIs, and Python scraping paths for reusing planetary probe archives in personal web and maker projects.
talks.summary:
Finding usable data from robotic planetary missions is awkward because each spacecraft carries multiple specialized instruments, and separate teams publish releases across many sites. The speaker outlines three practical lanes for hobbyists and developers: mission search portals, documented HTTP APIs, and targeted scraping when no formal API exists.

The core walkthrough centers on OPUS, the outer planets unified search tool tied to NASA’s Planetary Data System rings node. Live demos narrow millions of Cassini, Voyager, Galileo, and New Horizons observations by planet, moon, and instrument, then browse time-ordered thumbnails, animate Io volcano frames, and export collections. Related coverage includes composing color images from filter-separated frames, OPUS’s mirror JSON API, NASA’s open data catalog, Twitter bots built on those feeds, and community projects such as Spaceprob.es that track active probes.

For builders without a published API, the talk recounts reading Deep Space Network status XML via browser devtools, normalizing it in Python, and scheduling updates for live distance sorting. A Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter HiRISE scrape fed through WordPress XML-RPC illustrates a hackathon-friendly pattern. Closing pointers highlight rapidly released image blogs, Planetary Society processing guides, and NASA Datanauts as onboarding into the wider data landscape.

talks.title: "How to *be* a Compiler" by Mariko Kosaka
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding "How to *be* a Compiler" by Mariko Kosaka.
talks.summary:
Overview

Mariko Kosaka, a JavaScript developer at Google's web developer relations team, presents an unconventional introduction to compiler design through the lens of knitting. Rather than discussing recursion, visitor patterns, or traditional tools like Lex and Yacc, she demystifies compilers by drawing parallels between knitting patterns and code, making the topic accessible to those intimidated by compiler theory.

Key Topics

Knitting as Programming
Kosaka establishes that knitting patterns are fundamentally code: both use step-by-step instructions with atomic operations (knit and purl stitches). She demonstrates how to represent knitting logic in JavaScript, manipulating arrays to model stitches. This requires understanding dynamic array resizing—a key insight into why JavaScript is well-suited for knitting visualization compared to languages like C++.

The Path to Creating a Compiler
Kosaka's journey began with hobbyist projects (stitch counters, color helpers, image processing for knitwear) and evolved through her experience at School for Poetic Computation and work at Scripto (a TV production text editor). Frustrated by using tools like PEG.js without understanding their internals, she became determined to build a compiler from scratch. She was inspired by John Maeda's "Design by Numbers," a minimalist programming language designed to teach artists the fundamentals of programming.

Compiler Architecture: Four Key Steps
Kosaka walks through the actual mechanics of building a compiler that converts Design by Numbers syntax to SVG output:

1. Tokenization (Lexical Analysis): Breaking source code into classified tokens (words vs. numbers).
2. Parsing: Creating an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)—a map of code structure showing relationships between tokens.
3. Transformation: Converting the AST from source domain (DBN) to target domain (SVG).
4. Code Generation: Outputting executable code (SVG elements).

She demonstrates these steps using Design by Numbers examples (e.g., "paper 100 pen 0 line 0 0 100 50") and reveals that audiences who mentally "compile" these examples perform all four steps in their minds.

Technical Implementation
Kosaka built her compiler, named "SVG by Numbers" (sbN), using PEG.js. She also created "64 Stitches," an earlier DSL for knitting patterns with minimal syntax. An interactive online demo at github/kosamari/sbN shows step-by-step tokenization, parsing, AST transformation, and code generation.

The Compiler Perspective on Design
A central insight: the compiler doesn't care what the code looks like—it only reads and transforms it. The output (e.g., an SVG line) is independent of the syntax that produced it, making the compiler a universal translator between domains.

Takeaways

Starting Small Is Acceptable: Begin with simple, familiar operations. A tokenizer doesn't need to understand the entire pipeline; it can focus narrowly on dividing and classifying input.

Be a Good Parser (Helpful Communicator): When writing error messages or helping others, avoid saying "that's wrong." Instead, provide pointers (e.g., "try looking up this keyword"). Elm's compiler exemplifies this approach with human-focused error messages.

Context Is Everything: Compilers must transform information from source to target domains. Similarly, software teams benefit from members who understand context-switching—e.g., adapting products for different markets or cultures.

Internationalization in Programming: Kosaka emphasizes that programming itself is English-centric (function, if, while are English keywords). Making programming accessible in other languages—through translation tools or emoji-based languages—addresses an equity issue. She encourages developers to translate resources and build compilers for their native languages.

Learn by Building: The author encourages all developers to build a compiler, citing concrete lessons learned about modularity, communication, and context-awareness. Possible projects range from JavaScript-to-other-language translators to esoteric languages like Piet (color-based code).

talks.title: "Adventures in the vBuffer" by Sarah Groff Hennigh-Palermo
talks.teaser: A narrative walkthrough shows how virtual DOM diffing ideas apply to WebGL buffers, profiling, and immutability tradeoffs.
talks.summary:
The session frames a long quest to draw large-scale generative art with modern JavaScript and WebGL without drowning in procedural GL state. Early scenes explain virtual DOM diffing—trees, patches, thunks, and reference checks—and why that machinery targets the DOM, not the GPU. The middle follows building a vBuffer renderer that diffs a declarative tree of draw calls, bindings, and uniforms, then animating thousands of cubes until Chrome’s performance tools expose bottlenecks.

A mistaken reliance on shared object references breaks updates until explicit copying runs through reconciliation. Stripping lodash deep equality helps, yet scaling toward ten thousand objects still spends time on matrix generation and per-attribute checks. Experiments with Immutable.js and ClojureScript persistent structures trade clarity for heavy minor garbage collection, while a side trip notes Safari’s concurrent Riptide collector as a different runtime constraint.

Closing lessons stress matching paradigms to update rates: virtual trees suit moderate counts, but per-frame mutation may win at extreme scale; where copy versus reference membranes sit in an API shapes what optimizations remain; every approach hits a ceiling; and rough, unintended visuals can still be worthwhile artistic material.

talks.title: "Artificial Intelligence for Victims of Domestic Violence" by Brian Davis
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for "Artificial Intelligence for Victims of Domestic Violence" by Brian Davis.

talks.title: "Step by Step - Algorithms that teach you math!" by Evy Kassirer
talks.teaser: Explores how an open-source algebra solver produces intuitive step-by-step explanations for learners.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by contrasting how people read math—grouping symbols, order of operations, and ambiguous notation like fractions—with what typical computer algebra systems optimize for: a correct final answer, often after rewriting the input into an internal form that no longer matches what the student typed.

The speaker walks through Math Steps, built during work on the Socratic homework app: ASCII math is parsed into a tree (via Math.js), then iterated simplification rules match subtrees and emit teachable steps. Design choices include flattening associative chains of addition, mixing pre-order and post-order rule application for pedagogy, ordering rules to avoid confusing parses like nested fractions, grouping multi-step procedures such as adding fractions into collapsible substeps, and exposing implicit steps such as treating x as x¹ when combining exponents.

Limitations are stressed—no learner model, fixed answer formats, tension with school mnemonics like FOIL, homework cheating, and missing problem context—and future ideas include linking to Khan Academy resources, peer discussion, adaptive detail, richer metadata beyond the expression string, domain constraints when dividing by variables, and optional learner guessing before revealing the next step. The project is open source in JavaScript with tests that encode expected step sequences.

talks.title: "Lazy Defenses: Using Scaled TTLs to Keep Your Cache Correct" by Bonnie Eisenman
talks.teaser: Shows how scaling cache TTLs by repeated-read confidence cut inconsistent cached user data at Twitter scale.
talks.summary:
The talk traces how a simple read-through cache with one TTL evolves for the user data service at Twitter. Its problems include guaranteed misses on expiry, latency paid by end users, and irregular backend load. Soft and hard TTLs smooth that load, while a short in-process cache absorbs hot keys after a celebrity-driven spike overwhelmed a memcache cluster. Serving stale data during backend trouble, known as dark moding, also prevents retry storms.

A case study followed a transient not-found result for a popular account that stayed cached for twelve hours, so the account appeared to vanish. Cross-data-center races were a root cause of such bad values. The remedy is scaled TTLs: a new value starts at two minutes and its lifetime climbs through 30 minutes, six hours, 12 hours and 24 hours while consecutive reads agree, resetting when a value changes. Across the fleet this cut cross-data-center inconsistencies by up to 30%, most on frequently written fields.

Gotchas include ramping the change gradually, since a fresh deployment would drop every TTL to two minutes, and pairing it with automated back-off so shorter TTLs do not add load during failures. The team also wrapped the logic in a Scala library, letting service owners query repositories without handling caching themselves. The takeaway is to measure whether these problems occur and tune TTLs to each field's business needs.

talks.title: "Key to the City: Writing Code to Induce Social Change" by Jurnell Cockhren
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of "Key to the City: Writing Code to Induce Social Change" by Jurnell Cockhren.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at Strange Loop, civic hacker and infrastructure engineer Jurnell Cockhren explores how technologists can address social inequality through civic hacking, mathematical modeling, and collaborative open-source practices. Cockhren frames societal inequality not merely as a non-technical problem, but as a system bug characterized by divergent user experiences—where a system "works on my machine" for one group while remaining fundamentally broken for another, with little to no effort to reconcile the difference. Cockhren argues that by treating the government and societal systems as upgradable, citizens can contribute technical and non-technical efforts to patch these systemic bugs.

### Key Topics
- **Civic Hacking and Upgrading Systems**: Viewing government and societal structures as upgradable systems where civic engagement acts as a patch to fix bugs and protect citizens.
- **Inequality as a Hard Decision Problem**: Defining inequality as a decision problem blocked by decision-makers' emotions, unconscious bias, and an overwhelming lack of direction.
- **Computational Complexity (NP Framework)**: Formulating the hypothesis that instances of inequality fall within the set of NP problems, where proposed solutions can be verified deterministically in reasonable time by oppressed populations using modern technology.
- **Mathematical Modeling**: Mapping the Geographic Coordinate System to the complex plane via the Riemann sphere to define closed municipal boundaries and model localized instances of inequality.
- **Open Source Collaboration Model**: Drawing parallels to open-source software development, where distributed individuals contribute at varying levels of effort (writing core code, building charts, documenting, or reporting bugs) to achieve cumulative social change.

### Technical Details
Cockhren introduces a formal approach to model social disparities:
- **Decision Verification**: Framing the objective around verifying whether a disparity has been minimized (a "yes" answer verified in reasonable time, drawing on NP complexity concepts).
- **Coordinate Mapping**: Using the Riemann sphere to map geographic coordinates (latitude and longitude) to the complex plane. This mapping ensures density, meaning that between any two geographic locations on Earth, a complex number exists.
- **Closed Paths and Boundary Definition**: Utilizing closed paths on the complex plane to represent geographic and municipal boundaries (such as Davidson County/Nashville). Within any given closed boundary, distinct sets of inequality instances exist (e.g., income disparity, police treatment, digital access).
- **Axiom of Choice**: Invoking the axiom of choice to select instances of inequality from bounded sets in any order via a choosing function, starting with income disparity.
- **Data and Verification**: Demonstrating that verifying income disparity can be deterministic and computable in reasonable time (in P) by crowdsourcing data from the population and having at least one person build a visualization (e.g., using D3). For issues like policing or digital infrastructure (such as Google Fiber deployments and utility pole policies), crowdsourced location and open government data guide where non-technical efforts should be targeted.

### Takeaways
- Societal and government systems contain bugs that require civic engagement, code, and policy to patch.
- Modern technology and crowdsourced data enable communities to verify whether proposed solutions actually reduce inequality in reasonable time.
- Not all contributions require writing core technical code; similar to open-source software, meaningful impact arises from an aggregate of diverse efforts, from data submission to direct community advocacy.
- Technical framing, mathematical boundaries, and deterministic testing can help break down daunting, large-scale societal challenges into addressable components.

talks.title: "Scaling with Apache Spark (or a lesson in unintended consequences)" by Holden Karau
talks.teaser: Explains Apache Spark's lazy evaluation, partitioning and data frame design, and the trade-offs that caused performance problems.
talks.summary:
The talk explains why Apache Spark works the way it does, focusing on design decisions that backfired. It introduces the core abstractions, resilient distributed datasets and data frames, and describes Spark's laziness: transformations are recorded and only executed when an action such as saving output forces the work. This lets the optimizer combine steps into stages and lets Spark recompute lost partitions instead of writing intermediate results to disk, but errors surface late and stack traces are hard to read.

The middle of the talk covers partitioning. Spark's deterministic partitioner means key skew can overload a single node. A zip code example shows group by key failing on a heavily populated key, while reduce by key pre-aggregates on each partition and succeeds. Sorting by key hits similar limits, and salting keys to split them adds cleanup work later. Arbitrary Python or Scala functions are opaque to the optimizer, so data frame expressions allow filter pushdown to the data source, though that benefit depends on the source. Iterative machine learning also performs poorly on data frames.

The closing section looks at Python and other language bindings, where inter-process communication is costly, and at Apache Arrow as a possible interchange format for future work. The speakers suggest that changes to core design go through the project's proposal process, or that people build new systems that avoid these mistakes. The practical takeaways are to prefer reduce by key over group by key, watch for skewed keys, and tune the many configuration defaults for real workloads.

talks.title: "Scaling Validation and Quality of Streaming Data Products at Twitter" by Kelly Kaoudis
talks.teaser: Quality engineering practices for validating Twitter streaming data products through staging, system tests, and load tooling.
talks.summary:
The speaker describes how Twitter’s data products organization grew from a small ingestion pipeline into dozens of microservices streaming social data to paying customers. A dedicated quality engineering function runs adversarial checks, then turns them into deploy guardrails so passive streaming clients still receive complete, correct events without disturbing production traffic.

Staging mirrors production with controlled fake clients and soak periods before release. A long walkthrough of PowerTrack—filtering the full firehose with custom rules—shows how the team chased fidelity across API versions, capacity at high tweet rates, and subtle bugs such as emoji rule handling across data centers. Structured problem decomposition, tighter collaboration with feature teams, and principles borrowed from modern feature-testing guidance replaced a bottlenecked “testing as a service” model.

Later work addressed org-wide load: replaying real pub/sub traffic into staging with configurable duplication, rather than synthetic stress patterns that mis-model production. System tests became blocking deploy steps for owned services while simpler tools let engineers compose their own load profiles. The closing message balances shipping speed against contractual data quality and encourages periodic process resets as architecture and headcount scale.

talks.title: "The Performance Engineer's Guide To Java HotSpot" by Monica Beckwith
talks.teaser: Maps HotSpot's execution engine and runtime to footprint, throughput, and latency, with practical tuning guidance across Java releases.
talks.summary:
Monica Beckwith, a long-time JVM performance engineer, frames tuning as knowing what inside the virtual machine actually matters. She walks through HotSpot as application, JVM, and hardware layers, then splits the internals into runtime helpers—garbage collection, JIT compilation, class loading, and threading—and the execution path from interpreted bytecode to native code.

The core organizing idea is a performance trifecta: responsiveness (latency), memory footprint, and throughput. She ties responsiveness to thread-local allocation buffers, concurrent GC work, AOT compilation in Java 9, lock lightweighting, biasing, coarsening, escape-analysis lock elimination, and Java 9 quick-enter paths for contended monitors. Footprint coverage emphasizes compaction, compressed oops and class pointers (including practical heap size limits), string deduplication and Java 9 string density, code-cache deoptimization, and inlining. Throughput sections compare generational collectors—Parallel GC, deprecated CMS, and G1—with NUMA-aware Eden allocation, parallel GC worker threads, and G1’s regional incremental compaction.

Practitioners leave with a mental model for which JVM knobs and release-level features align with their latency, memory, or throughput goals, and when to experiment with options such as compressed oops alignment or G1 string optimizations.

talks.title: "The Security of Classic Game Consoles" by Kevin Shekleton
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for "The Security of Classic Game Consoles" by Kevin Shekleton.

talks.title: "How to Hack a Painting" by Tyler Hobbs
talks.teaser: Shows how a generative artist models watercolor paint in code using recursive polygon deformation and Gaussian randomness.
talks.summary:
Tyler Hobbs, a full-time generative artist with a computer science background, explains how he writes programs that produce artwork instead of using image editors. He begins with studies of natural subjects such as dry grass and a wooden fence, and concludes that the physical world mixes structured rules with randomness, which computers can model well by sampling from chosen probability distributions. He then picks a watercolor sketch as his target.

He builds the watercolor model in Processing through a Clojure wrapper. Each edge of a starting polygon is pushed outward using a split point, a bend angle and a magnitude drawn from Gaussian distributions, and the step is applied recursively with magnitudes scaled to edge length so detail appears at smaller scales. Soft blended edges come from stacking about fifty low-opacity layers, each starting from a partly deformed base shape. Per-edge variance levels imitate wet and dry paper, giving sharp edges in some places and gradual transitions in others, while a graded base produces a denser center.

He shows finished pieces built on this model, some with texture masks and painting all shapes layer by layer to blend colors better. He notes that his work depends on carefully constrained randomness and that he saves each piece by its random seed. Questions covered render times, from a tenth of a second to about a minute, and whether he studied fluid dynamics or pen and ink. The takeaway is that a simple, fully understood model can become a reusable medium for an artist.

talks.title: "Building switches like servers: the strange world of overlapping networking" by Sonja Keserovic
talks.teaser: Explains how Facebook built its own data center switches and ran them with server-style software and fleet upgrade practices.
talks.summary:
The talk covers how Facebook's data center network is layered, from top-of-rack switches up through fabric, spine and edge switches, with redundancy at every layer except the rack level. The speaker explains that the network was historically assembled from vendor equipment with different management interfaces, and that vendor-bundled software updates arrived slowly. An IPv6 migration stretched over years, and upgrading the top-of-rack switches meant draining traffic from racks one at a time across every data center.

To address this, the team began designing its own switch hardware and software, keeping the two separate so each could change on its own, and making the hardware modular. The switches were built to resemble servers, with more memory and stronger CPUs, and they run the same server software image used across the fleet. The forwarding agent that programs the Broadcom chip and the BGP process both run as Thrift services. Packet switching is still done in hardware, since CPU forwarding would be far too slow. Shared logging and metrics daemons also run on the switches. The team deployed top-of-rack switches first, then fabric switches, and rolls out agent updates every few weeks using canary testing. A fast restart preserves forwarding state, so traffic is not interrupted.

The speaker closes with lessons learned. Faster iteration and deeper visibility into hardware and software state made better automation possible, but network, software and production engineers had to share operational responsibility. Teams that own shared daemons now need to understand topology, such as never canarying on all four fabric switches at once. Future directions include automated remediation and Open R, a routing protocol being tested as an alternative to BGP, with designs shared through the Open Compute Project.

talks.title: "Particle physics, 10,000 times faster" by Jim Pivarski
talks.teaser: Explains how nested particle physics data can be queried as columnar arrays, far faster than the current C++ framework.
talks.summary:
Jim Pivarski starts with the scale of particle physics data. He argues that its real difficulty is not raw size but the deeply nested, cross-linked structure of collision events. Analysts today usually write custom C++ programs that run over lists of files, and selecting the subsets they need can take weeks or months. Relational tables fit this shape poorly, because searching sublists and pairing particles would require awkward explodes and joins.

He first tried a declarative query language with functional syntax, but found that the larger gain came from how the data is laid out. In a simple benchmark, a loop filling a histogram over a flat array reached 250 MHz, against 0.018 for the existing framework in the same units. He traced much of that gap to the framework being built to extract subsets for local work, not to scan petabytes. He described storing nested lists as flat arrays with offset arrays, the same layout Apache Arrow uses, and rewriting object-style code into array lookups compiled with Numba. A mass calculation over pairs ran in the tens of megahertz in Python, compared with just over one megahertz for the C++ code, with trigonometric functions as the main cost.

He then outlined a minimal set of types the transformation must handle: primitives, arbitrary-length lists, unions and records. He also showed how derived columns, such as candidate particles, could be added without copying the original data. He closed by inviting feedback and collaboration on the code transformation project.

talks.title: "The Lux Programming Language" by Eduardo Julian
talks.teaser: Describes Lux, a practical Lisp with static types, JVM and JS targets, first-class modules, and compiler hooks extensible like macros.
talks.summary:
The presentation introduces Lux, a purely functional language in the Lisp tradition that borrows semantics from Haskell, grammatical structure from Clojure, and polymorphism from ML. It is meant for everyday programming rather than research alone. As of the version discussed, Lux runs on the JVM and Android, with a JavaScript backend nearing release so front-end and back-end code can share libraries in one language.

The middle of the talk walks through distinctive mechanics: modules as first-class values, several concurrency styles (promises, transactional memory, actors, with more planned), macros that read real compiler state, monadic macro parsing, and types treated as data so developers can compute and pattern-match on types at compile time. The speaker also outlines polytypic programming to generate serializers and similar code from type structure, plus a long-term goal of portable libraries and programs without rewriting for each host.

The close centers on making Lux “redefinable”: users would add new expression forms, custom lowering to JVM bytecodes or JavaScript, extra compiler passes, or swap analysis layers—for example lazy evaluation or alternate type disciplines—while keeping the surface language. Platform-specific optimizations and even hosting other languages atop the same pipeline are presented as upcoming goals, with an initial wave tied to the 0.6 release. The speaker points listeners to the Lux book, repository, and Gitter room for deeper study.

talks.title: "Code Generating a Safer Web with Rocket" by Sergio Benitez
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning "Code Generating a Safer Web with Rocket" by Sergio Benitez.

talks.title: "Onyx-Native, Information Flow Models and Scientific computing" by George Kierstein
talks.teaser: Explains how declarative Onyx workflows wrap legacy Fortran and bash scientific pipelines without invasive rewrites.
talks.summary:
George Kierstein describes rehabilitating long-lived scientific computing pipelines, drawing on work at the National Centers for Environmental Information. He contrasts industry software culture with research environments where code grows organically over years, roles stay divided, and documentation often lives only in people’s heads.

The centerpiece is the ASA climate ingest system: roughly fifteen years in production on retired AIX hardware, polyglot stacks, modem-fed instruments, and thousands of lines of bash wiring a three-phase ingest, manual QC, and publish workflow. Rather than a full rewrite, the team modeled the system as nested workflows using information-flow ideas—data and declarative structure at every level—and adopted Onyx. Because Onyx was Clojure-centric and the site would not add Clojure, they built Onyx Java, JNI bridges, and native bootstrapping for C, C++, and Fortran so existing programs could run as isolated tasks with logging and other modern affordances.

Delivery finished far sooner than multi-year expectations, the jar-based deployment convinced conservative operators, and a coworker later extended the approach with a domain DSL. Practitioners hear when non-invasive re-architecture fits legacy science code: stable file formats, small chained programs, and human-paced change cycles.

talks.title: "Incident insights from NASA, NTSB, and the CDC" by Emil Stolarsky
talks.teaser: Cross-disciplinary incident practices from aerospace, transport, and public health inform proactive software reliability.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the April 2014 9-1-1 routing outage that blocked thousands of emergency calls, using that failure—and Ontario’s reliance on nuclear power—to argue that software’s scale removes the old luxury of learning only after disasters. Tombstone mentality in aviation and Three Mile Island illustrate reactive cultures; leverage in tech demands borrowing lessons before catastrophes multiply across continents.

Emil Stolarsky maps emergency management’s four cycles onto databases and on-call work, then pulls concrete tools from other fields: aerospace part lifecycles and fault trees for probabilistic failure reasoning; Laguna Fire and the incident command system (later NIMS) for structured leadership, including adoption by Facebook and Shopify; B-17 checklists as thought automation during response; and United Flight 173, which led NASA and airlines to crew resource management for speaking up under stress.

Recovery covers bias in “human error” RCA, NASA’s causal factor trees instead of linear five-whys, and the Aviation Safety Reporting System as anonymous near-miss sharing. Walmart and Waffle House hurricane preparedness—including FEMA’s Waffle House Index—close the call to be so prepared that others treat your uptime as a regional health signal.

talks.title: "Predictive Load-Balancing: Unfair but Faster & more Robust" by Steve Gury
talks.teaser: Explores client-side predictive load balancing that uses latency estimates to cut tail latencies and handle slow or outlier servers.
talks.summary:
The presentation begins with a simple question: when many interchangeable backends answer requests, which one should a client choose, and does that choice change tail latency? Animated demos compare random, round-robin, and least-loaded policies using per-server queues and p99 plots. Even when each server receives roughly equal traffic over time, bursty selection can stack work on a few hosts and inflate outliers—behavior that worsens when capacity is scaled out without rethinking the algorithm.

The middle section catalogs practical pains: persistently slow nodes under blind rotation, thundering herds after incidents, brief JVM pauses that queue large backlogs, and weakened per-server views when thousands of clients each maintain isolated counters. The proposed predictive approach weights servers by estimated load in latency units, using a streaming median of recent successful responses, warmup and decay for newcomers, success-rate penalties, and limited connection subsets to keep measurements fresh. Instantaneous offered load revises predictions while requests are still in flight, aiming to detect slowdowns sooner than waiting for completion.

Closing demos pit the method against random and least-loaded under heterogeneous pools and many clients, then shift to Netflix edge lessons: cautious rollout warming, canary comparisons distorted by uneven traffic splits, hosts that answered errors quickly with cached defaults, and autoscaler metrics that hide uneven utilization. The design is presented as experimental with narrow production use; operators should validate whether latency remains a meaningful signal for their workloads.

talks.title: "Empowering the next billion with OSTree, Flatpak, NDN, and the cloud" by Srdjan Grubor
talks.teaser: Shows how OSTree, Flatpak and named data networking can cut bandwidth use for people on slow or metered connections.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the access gap: roughly half the world's population has no internet connection, many users pay for metered data, and web pages keep growing heavier, so every megabyte matters. The speaker, who works on Endless, a GNOME-based Linux distribution, argues that developers should reduce transfer volumes, keep data close to users, and support offline use.

The first technology covered is OSTree, which treats a whole operating system filesystem like a git repository. Each boot checks out a signed commit, updates apply atomically, and hard links avoid duplicate files, so rollbacks are simple. Flatpak builds on it to package desktop apps with a shared runtime and sandboxed permissions. A live demo built a GEdit Flatpak from a short manifest, and because apps sit on a shared platform, a runtime security fix reaches every app built on it. Flathub was presented as a central app store.

The final part covers Named Data Networking, which requests content by name instead of by host address, caches data at intermediate nodes, and signs each piece of content. The speaker described it as a research project still in early phases, with IPFS as a related effort, and noted a testbed spanning the globe. The takeaway is to use existing bandwidth more efficiently so people with poor connectivity can reach online knowledge.

talks.title: "Towards new deep learning abstractions on top of exist frameworks" by Tristan Webb
talks.teaser: Introduces Nervana Graph, an open-source intermediate representation that connects deep learning frameworks to many hardware backends.
talks.summary:
Deep learning frameworks such as TensorFlow, MXNet and Caffe each need their own backend work to run on every new accelerator, which multiplies engineering effort and tends to lock users into one ecosystem. Tristan Webb, from Intel's Nervana group, presents Nervana Graph as a shared answer to that problem: an intermediate representation of the computational graph that many frameworks can target and many hardware backends can execute.

The talk walks through the design. The graph is a dataflow structure with a balanced set of core operations covering tensor math such as convolutions and matrix multiplies, element-wise kernels, reductions, and tensor reshaping and broadcasting. Front-end connectors bring in models from existing frameworks, including TensorFlow's XLA path and MXNet, while transformers lower the graph to CPUs, GPUs and Intel's Crest deep learning chips. Named tensor axes let the compiler check dimensions statically before anything runs. Webb contrasts the approach with ONNX, which at the time focused on inference without an optimizing compiler, and explains why general compilers such as LLVM lack tensor-level abstractions for steps like horizontal fusion and storage planning.

The talk closes with the project's status and roadmap. The code is on GitHub, and the intended users are framework authors, hardware and system software teams, and anyone deploying models trained elsewhere. Planned work includes control flow for recurrent networks, a C++ API, fuller TensorFlow XLA and MXNet integration, multi-device and multi-node training, and deployment features such as weight quantization and pruning.

talks.title: "Stop Rate Limiting! Capacity Management Done Right" by Jon Moore
talks.teaser: Explains why rate limiting fails under overload and how concurrency control with adaptive capacity protects shared services.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the common API gateway habit of rate limiting each client to a fixed number of requests per second. The speaker argues this breaks down in two cases: when the origin service is overloaded, and when quotas are strict enough to reject requests the origin could have served. In a live demo, a single origin with seven worker threads and a one-second average response time was hit with steady load. When its latency doubled, requests queued up without bound behind it and nearly all of them timed out, even though the origin kept finishing work.

Using Little's Law (concurrent requests equal arrival rate times response time), the speaker makes the case for limiting concurrent requests instead of request rate. Under normal conditions the two behave the same for clients, but under overload a concurrency limit pushes back on clients, which lets the origin recover. He also shows that throughput is not the same as capacity: raising the worker count from seven to fourteen let the same load succeed. To find an unknown capacity without being told it, he borrows the additive-increase, multiplicative-decrease approach from TCP congestion avoidance. The proxy grows its target connection count slowly, backs off to a fraction of it on timeouts, and settled near nine concurrent requests in the run shown.

For multiple clients, the speaker replaces fixed quotas with configured percentages of the adaptive capacity estimate, so clients can borrow unused capacity. In a demo with a 25 percent and a 75 percent client, the aggressive client was allowed roughly 22 concurrent connections while the other stayed within its share. Several proxy instances reached a fair split without central coordination. The takeaways are to apply Little's Law to each subsystem, limit concurrency rather than rate, and adapt to what the origin can actually handle.

talks.title: "Designing 1000 genomes in a single bound: The Codon DSL" by Aaron Kimball, Theron Rabe
talks.teaser: Explains how the Codon domain-specific language turns microbiology experiment designs into large genome search spaces.
talks.summary:
The company works in industrial fermentation, engineering microbes that convert sugar into chemicals. Because controlling an organism means searching an enormous space of possible DNA changes, it pairs robotic manufacturing and testing with search methods that scan genomes for promising edits. The speakers describe the software needed to let scientists define those very large search spaces at once, rather than one hypothesis at a time as typical design tools allow.

The solution has three parts: a core data model of DNA components and specifications, Codon, a Scala-based language that maps biologist vocabulary onto that model, and Helix, which rewrites specification trees into factory instructions. A promoter-swapping example shows a short script expanding three promoters across two genes into a full combinatorial set of designs.

The lessons learned are candid. Allowing user code demanded a sandboxed, statically typed, transactional runtime. Flattening the tree into a list at the code boundary limited which functions could exist. Cookbooks and CSV tooling helped less technical staff, but power users eventually built a fragile chain of Python, CSV and DSL steps. The advice is to prototype such a language as a library in a general-purpose language first, and to separate safety concerns from functionality.

talks.title: ""Flutter: How we're building a UI framework for tomorrow at Google" by Eric Seidel
talks.teaser: Explains how Flutter's layered framework, hot reload and composition model deliver fast, customizable and consistent mobile UIs.
talks.summary:
Eric Seidel, who helped found the Flutter team at Google, presents Flutter as a mobile UI framework built for fast development, flexible design and faithful rendering on iOS and Android. He opens with a demo of one app that runs on both platforms and adapts its scrolling, titles and navigation to each one. He then frames the project around three goals: a fluid developer experience, flexibility for designers, and output that matches what developers built.

The middle of the talk covers the technical choices behind those goals. Hot reload applies code changes to a running app in place, so developers stay on the screen they are working on. The team first built on JavaScript, then switched to Dart, which compiles ahead of time to native ARM code, shakes out unused code, uses generational garbage collection and offers optional strong typing. The framework is organized in layers, from a runtime API and rendering layer up through a React-inspired widget layer to Material and Cupertino style layers. Rendering separates layout from painting, uses simple min and max constraints, and invalidates subtrees rather than dirty rectangles. Composition over inheritance is shown live, as Seidel builds a custom floating action button from small widgets while the app keeps its state.

The final part explains fidelity. The team reused graphics and text components from Chrome and Android, including the GPU backends of Skia, so the same stack runs across platforms, and it tuned feel details such as scroll physics and touch targets to match each platform. He closes by noting the alpha release, the growing set of apps and packages, and the open-source community, inviting developers to contribute.

talks.title: "Origami Software from Scratch" by Robby Kraft
talks.teaser: Builds origami tools from planar graphs through flat-fold simulation, axiom explorers, and browser-based crease-pattern utilities.
talks.summary:
The presenter describes learning classical origami design after years of folding, including long failed attempts at a dog design, a self-designed crane that goes three-dimensional early, and a flat-foldable sea turtle whose shell mapping came from custom code. Motivated by how Robert Lang’s TreeMaker enabled algorithmic animal design, the talk surveys Reference Finder for axiom-based construction points, Oripa for drawing and simulating crease patterns, and Origamizer for mesh-to-crease workflows used on a simplified Stanford Bunny.

Starting from Lang’s planar-graph view of crease patterns, the speaker built TypeScript structures for graphs and planar graphs, fighting floating-point cases such as near-parallel intersections and collinear edge handling, plus clockwise angle measurement between rays. Interactive localhost pages doubled as documentation and regression checks for fragmenting edges, face walking, and node cleanup. The core flat-fold simulation picks a fixed face, stores per-face reflection matrices along an adjacency tree, multiplies transforms to leaves, and validates every vertex with Kawasaki’s theorem so shared edges realign after folding.

Demos include a crease-pattern validator with live adjustment, an axiom-driven crease explorer, a reference finder that honors lines already committed to a design, and real-time Voronoi output exportable to creasing hardware. The library targets the web via JavaScript, a Paper.js wrapper styled like creative-coding sketches, creases that record generating axioms and parents, and ideas for auto-generated folding diagrams and future machine learning on crease datasets.

talks.title: "Practical Applications of the Dickerson Pyramid" by Nat Welch

talks.title: "Biomaterials as UI" by Ruthie Nachmany

talks.title: "Dependent Types in Haskell" by Stephanie Weirich

talks.title: "Geo-Replicated Transactions in 1.5RTT" by Robert Escriva
talks.teaser: Presents a masterless geo-replication design that commits serializable transactions in about 1.5 wide-area round trips.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames geo-distributed fault tolerance around wide-area latency dominating local optimization when data centers span coasts. It contrasts primary-backup replication, eventual consistency, Spanner-style TrueTime, and one-shot transactions with the tradeoffs each imposes on availability, read freshness, and commit cost.

The core system, Casas, targets serializable transactions without a single primary, using a commit manager that replays transaction logs across full replicas and decides commit or abort when a quorum of sites can proceed. The commit path ships the log, replays locally, broadcasts per-site outcomes, then reaches agreement in three message delays—one and a half round trips—via generalized Paxos on incomparable commit/abort commands. Deadlock-induced aborts add totally ordered retractions so every site tallies consistently; the speaker notes implementation work to make learning fast enough for real time.

Benchmarks on AWS with artificial 200 ms RTT compare one, three, and five data center TPCC and stock-level workloads. Practitioners are urged to specify fault-tolerance and availability requirements first, because demanding always-on quorum behavior shapes whether simpler but less available designs are acceptable.

talks.title: "Angelina Ballerina Learns About Memory Allocation" by Allison McMillan
talks.teaser: Explains Ruby memory allocation and garbage collection through a Heroku web server memory case and the GC tools used to diagnose it.
talks.summary:
