The speaker explains the three notions of time (event time, ingestion time and processing time), windowing types such as tumbling, hopping, sliding and session windows, triggers, and watermarks for handling late data, using a click-counting example.

The middle of the talk compares three engines. Samza checkpoints Kafka offsets and local state to changelog topics, but lacks built-in event time and watermarks, and recovering large state is slow. Spark Streaming uses micro-batching on RDDs, so window sizes must match the batch interval, and back pressure support was incomplete, which led one team to run a monitoring job that killed lagging jobs. Flink processes true streams, uses barrier-based checkpoints that do not block processing, and offers savepoints that let teams run canary or A/B tests of new jobs against existing state.

The speaker then describes Netflix's pipeline, built from a managed Kafka messaging service, a stream processing service with per-stream dashboards and lag alerts, and automated cluster failover that is exercised regularly. For one use case, moving from Samza to Flink reportedly cut cost by about 17 percent and improved CPU and network utilization. The takeaway is to choose an engine by latency, cost and accuracy needs, and to measure results on your own workload, since the figures may not carry over.

talks.title: "Exotic Functional Data Structures: Hitchhiker Trees" by David Greenberg
talks.teaser: Explains hitchhiker trees, immutable storage structures built on fractal trees, with fast inserts and free snapshots.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with what makes a data structure functional: it is immutable, so an update produces a new version while the old one stays intact. David Greenberg shows how copying and sharing pointers keep those updates cheap, first in linked lists and then in binary search trees, where only the path from the changed node back to the root must be rebuilt. That keeps the cost of an update logarithmic, the same order as a mutable tree.

From there the talk turns to storage. Wide B-tree nodes read more useful data per disk access, which the speaker presents as a constant-factor speedup, and B+ trees keep values only in the leaves. Fractal trees add a small buffer to each index node so that inserts collect there and are pushed down in batches. Reads account for pending operations along the path, and scans only project the operations that fall within the requested range.

The hitchhiker tree combines these ideas with path copying, so the structure stays immutable while keeping the faster inserts, and snapshots come at no extra cost. Using a seven-insert example, Greenberg compares I/O counts across the B+ tree, fractal tree and hitchhiker tree, and notes that when to flush is a tunable trade-off between latency and I/O. The talk closes with datacrypt, a pluggable open-source implementation, and an outboard API that keeps application state in Redis off the heap, so a restarted process can reconnect to its data quickly.

talks.title: "GraphQL: Designing a Data Language" by Lee Byron
talks.teaser: Traces how Facebook's GraphQL grew from an iOS Newsfeed fix into an open specification, and the design lessons behind it.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces GraphQL, a query language for web APIs that Facebook built as an alternative to REST. The speaker explains the problem behind it: the iOS Newsfeed team struggled to retrieve interrelated data over slow mobile networks, and REST endpoints led to subtle bugs when clients guessed the shape of the response. Example queries show nested selections, pagination arguments and fetching related data in one round trip. The type system lets a server validate a query before running it and powers introspection-based tools such as an in-browser IDE.

The history section traces the project from a prototype built in about three days, through a first version developed alongside the Newsfeed team within weeks, to a rollout across Facebook's products. After a 2015 public talk drew strong interest, the team redesigned the syntax and semantics, then released a specification and a JavaScript reference implementation. The speaker covers the nullable-by-default type design, which confines a failed field to its own subtree, and notes that the data schema had not seen a breaking change in four years.

The closing lessons are to start from one important problem, design around the needs of the first client, and resist speculative features with the YAGNI principle. The speaker also recommends having an editor who challenges the designer, and waiting before open sourcing an idea that still needs room to evolve. He ends with work in progress on subscriptions and live queries, which are being tested before they are offered as general features.

talks.title: "The Future of the Mobile Web" by Paul Kinlan
talks.teaser: Traces how software distribution moved from punch cards to URLs, and where the mobile web platform is heading next.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a timeline of how software got distributed, from punch cards and floppy discs through CDs to the web, where a single URL gave access to an application without installation. The speaker argues that distribution has steadily become easier, and that sites designed for desktop screens and native app stores have left mobile users with heavy install steps and slow loads.

Performance is the central concern. The speaker cites data on users abandoning slow pages, cellular-only households in the US, and mobile-first growth in India, where data is costly and devices are constrained. Messaging apps and content platforms such as AMP and Instant Articles compete by offering fast experiences inside their own walls. In response, browser vendors are closing the gap with native by adding permission-gated APIs for camera, geolocation, Bluetooth, USB, sharing and payments, and by pursuing consistent cross-browser behaviour.

The talk then turns to progressive web apps, where features such as home-screen installation and push notifications become available as a user's engagement grows. Service workers act as a client-side proxy that controls offline behaviour and caching. The speaker closes by looking at headless browsers used for testing and auditing, and at lightweight web experiences on watches and beacons. The takeaway is to focus on fast loading, reliability and user engagement.

talks.title: "Humanities x Technology" by Ashley Nelson-Hornstein
talks.teaser: Argues that good technology comes from pairing engineering with the humanities, using ads, games, and social platforms as examples.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens with a confession: despite building gaming PCs as a teen, they no longer know the specs of their own Apple devices. They blame Apple's advertising, which sells experiences rather than technical merit. A well-known teen-montage ad is contrasted with a confusing Android spot to show why experience-first marketing lands. The core argument is that products should start from the user experience and let technology follow, an idea the speaker ties to Steve Jobs and the humanities.

Historical and modern examples follow. Edwin Land's SX-70 camera hid its complexity behind a simple interface, and the game Never Alone was built with Alaska Native storytellers and elders to share Inupiaq culture. Depression Quest and That Dragon, Cancer use interactive design to convey illness and caregiving from the inside. The talk then examines Twitter's slow response to harassment of Leslie Jones and Microsoft's Tay chatbot, which took on abusive behavior within hours, contrasted with a Chinese chatbot team that emphasized empathy. The speaker urges teams to examine their blind spots.

The closing section covers gadget reviews that focus on how a product feels, Pixar's central atrium designed to spark encounters between disciplines, and the speaker's own start in programming. The takeaway is that programming should feel approachable to people who do not see themselves as math or science people, and that product teams need diverse perspectives to build responsibly.

talks.title: "A Frontend Server, Front to Back" by Zach Tellman
talks.teaser: A gateway design for monolith decomposition prioritizes transparency, stability, speed, and careful extensibility at the traffic edge.
talks.summary:
Zach Tellman describes Fitbit’s path from a long-lived Java monolith toward modularity, starting with a dedicated front-end server that sits upstream of other tiers. That component routes requests, validates and authenticates them, and sheds or prioritizes load when backends struggle. He argues the role is a small but powerful fulcrum: changes there ripple through the whole system.

The implementation uses an async Netty server shaped by extreme-case thinking rather than average daily traffic. An informal request state machine—documented as a diagram and mirrored in code via a “passport” that stamps states and timestamps—separates business logic from metrics so intervals stay trustworthy. Callback-style code is kept deliberately flat instead of hidden behind promise libraries, because granular failure modes matter. A pumpkin-carving metaphor motivates load balancing: round robin spreads volume evenly and worsens slow nodes, while least-inflight routes around backlog; combining inflight counts with an exponentially weighted failure average avoids steering everything at nodes that fast-fail. After switching from HAProxy round robin, p99.9 latency during deploys reportedly fell from about nine seconds to about 1.5 seconds, with far fewer long timeouts.

Practitioners should rank goals explicitly, design for edge behavior, and watch a small set of metrics—in this case p99.9 overhead near four tenths of a millisecond, plus traffic volume and error rate. Q&A covers passport-driven testing, why a custom gateway beat generic proxies for Fitbit-specific validation, Zookeeper server sets for discovery, and a painful off-heap memory incident traced to a misleading JMX metric.

talks.title: "End-to-end encryption: Behind the scenes" by Martin Kleppmann, Diana Vasile
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding "End-to-end encryption: Behind the scenes" by Martin Kleppmann, Diana Vasile.

talks.title: "Caching at Netflix: The Hidden Microservice" by Scott Mansfield
talks.teaser: Explains how Netflix runs its EVCache distributed caching layer on AWS, including a disk-backed L2 server.
talks.summary:
The talk covers the caching layer Netflix calls the hidden microservice, known internally as EVCache (ephemeral volatile cache). It is a distributed, sharded and replicated key-value store built on memcached and tuned for AWS, where instances and zones fail often. The speaker walks through how clients connect directly to every server in a cluster across availability zones, how reads fall back to other nodes, and how writes go to every copy. Common use cases are shown: cache-aside reads in front of a slower service, transient session data, and offline pre-compute pipelines that write personalized homepage data for online services to read.

The middle of the talk covers cross-region replication driven by a Kafka mutation stream, and cache warming when a cluster is resized. The main focus is Moneta, a newer server that moves cold data from RAM to SSD. It pairs a proxy called Ren with an L1 memcached process and an L2 store called nemonic, which maps memcached operations onto RocksDB using FIFO compaction. The speaker reports production averages of roughly 230 microseconds for gets and 367 microseconds for sets on the server side, and about 70 percent cost savings on one cluster with a small hot set and a large cold set.

The takeaway is that tiered storage with a clear split between hot and cold data can cut cost substantially while keeping latency low. Several components are open source, including the Java client, the REST API and Ren. The question period touched on the choice of RocksDB, the use of Go and the rollout timeline.

talks.title: "Systems programming as a swiss army knife" by Julia Evans
talks.teaser: A walkthrough uses Linux strace, perf, and packet tools to solve three everyday performance and configuration mysteries.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues that most bugs become tractable once you can see what a program actually does at the operating system boundary, regardless of language. Instead of relying mainly on reading source and adding prints, it treats tools such as strace, opensnoop, dstat, perf, tcpdump, and Wireshark as a shared kit for conversing with the kernel and the network.

Three invented mysteries drive the demos. A missing config case uses strace to list which files a shell actually opens, separating bashrc from bash_profile without reading docs. Slow programs are classified with time: one waits on the network and its kernel stack shows TCP receive work; one burns CPU and needs a Python profiler for fourteen million additions; one writes hundreds of megabytes to disk and perf top points at ecryptfs encryption on an encrypted home directory. A local site that speaks English in Chrome but French under curl is explained by comparing HTTP requests and the Accept-Language header with ngrep.

Later sections contrast sampling versus tracing profilers, show perf stat for L1 cache load misses, introduce flame graphs from perf record, and describe capturing filtered traffic to pcap for calm offline analysis. The closing point is that learning these OS interfaces turns ordinary developers into wizards who can fix unfamiliar stacks, including an anecdote where strace on Erlang exposed a lock problem.

talks.title: "Expressing complex data aggregations with Histogrammar" by Jim Pivarski
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in "Expressing complex data aggregations with Histogrammar" by Jim Pivarski.

talks.title: "Knowing What You See - Let's Talk About Front-end Consistency" by Yifan Wu
talks.teaser: Explores why interactive data visualizations show inconsistent results and reframes the front end as a database problem.
talks.summary:
Interactive visualizations over large datasets often mix old and new data on screen, because several backend requests return at different times. The talk names the recurring anomalies: reordering, where a map arrives after the pins it should sit under; varying delays with no feedback about pending work; mistaken correspondences, where some charts refresh and others never do; unclear selection, when live updates land during a user's brush; and overwritten marks, when delayed results draw over earlier ones. It then reviews common fixes, namely blocking the whole interface, showing spinners, and labeling values. Each trades interactivity, comprehension, or ease of programming against consistency.

The central argument is that the front end increasingly resembles a database. Mouse events become streams, each user interaction becomes a transaction that reads the underlying data and writes to the interface, and a conflict occurs when two interactions write the same pixels or when data changes during another interaction's read. Framing conflicts this way gives a systematic method for detecting them, including the read-write conflicts caused by human reaction time.

For prevention, the talk borrows from database systems. Declarative interaction constraints can enforce that pins render only after maps, merging can replace outright rejection of overlapping updates, and multiversion snapshots let reads proceed without blocking. The presenter closes with an API under development: a shim layer where developers supply interactions and request handlers, and the layer detects conflicts so they can be prevented or communicated to the user.

talks.title: "Building Secure Systems in Haskell" by Deian Stefan
talks.teaser: Shows how Haskell's information flow control can enforce data policies so web app bugs cannot leak sensitive data.
talks.summary:
Large-scale privacy breaches often trace back to developers scattering access checks through application code, where one missed check can expose data. An early Facebook bug let any user delete other people's photo albums because a single check was absent. In a blogging app, a password-hash leak was patched by adding checks in about eight places, and a draft-leak flaw was handled the same way.

The approach keeps security policy separate from functionality, attaching it to the data model as a function from each record to a read and write label. LIO, an information flow control language embedded in Haskell, enforces these labels at runtime through a labeled IO monad that tracks what a computation has read and blocks writes that could leak data. Hails, a Haskell web framework built on LIO, extends the model-view-controller pattern so that views and controllers need not be trusted. In a demo, a blog with a permissive policy showed drafts to anonymous visitors; after the policy was corrected, private posts returned not found. A GitHub-style platform needed about 250 lines of policy code amid roughly 200,000 lines of application code.

The trusted code shrinks to policy specifications and the roughly 8,000 lines of runtime, so bugs in ordinary features stop being security holes. The main catch is setting labels correctly, since a permissive policy still creates a vulnerability.

talks.title: "Diocletian, Constantine, Bedouin Sayings, and Network Defense" by Adam Wick
talks.teaser: Uses Roman frontier strategy to argue for early intrusion detection, layered defenses and cooperation among network defenders.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with the familiar picture of a network protected by a single firewall at its edge and argues that this chokepoint thinking misses how porous networks really are. The speaker describes an IT engagement where administrators undercounted their nodes by about a factor of three, and a subnet scan that found Telnet open on 25 of 80 hosts, including door locks nobody remembered. He also points to devices with separate 3G connections that bypass the firewall entirely, and says cloud environments have the same problem because they depend on many layers and providers getting everything right.

The middle of the talk uses Roman history as an analogy. Early Rome kept a few legions at its borders and campaigned outward, but after the crisis of the third century it lost the money, manpower, training and technology that made that approach work. Diocletian and Constantine responded with walled cities, small border guards that raise the alarm, and a mobile army held back to reinforce them. Mapped to networks, the border guard becomes intrusion detection, layered protections across subnets and hosts become defense in depth, and a fast-moving IT team becomes the reserve force. The speaker cites a 2013 study with a median time of 229 days between an intruder's foothold and detection, improved to 205 days in 2014, to show why early detection matters.

The closing section urges defenders to share information about attacks with peers, since attacks often cluster by industry, and to press managed-service providers on which detection systems they run and how they respond. In questions, he recommends encrypting traffic even between internal hosts and treating internal subnets as if they were internet-facing. The main takeaways are to assume a long border and a limited budget, detect intrusions early, spread protections across the whole network, and cooperate with others.

talks.title: "Debugging Diversity" by Anjuan Simmons
talks.teaser: Uses Star Trek, open-source history and debugging analogies to argue for inclusion and privilege-sharing in software teams.
talks.summary:
Simmons opens with the story of Leonard Nimoy using his influence to secure equal pay for Nichelle Nichols on Star Trek, and uses it as a model for how people with privilege can correct inequities in tech. He separates diversity, which is about who gets invited, from inclusion, which is about whether people feel welcome once they arrive. He draws on Eric S. Raymond's The Cathedral and the Bazaar to argue that open, widely contributed development produces better outcomes, and that excluding people wastes the talent that could solve problems.

The middle of the talk applies four debugging ideas to the industry. Expected behavior means noticing when people without male privilege are denied the usual benefit of the doubt, such as a startup founder being asked whose girlfriend she is at a happy hour. Tracing means spotting subtle microaggressions, such as a Black engineer being quizzed about her home life and pressed into beer outings she did not enjoy. Refactoring means replacing the "airport test" for hiring with role-based questions about past results. Sample code means lending privilege, such as co-presenting a conference panel with a designer colleague or bringing colleagues into conversations they are otherwise left out of.

The closing section covers awareness, action and allyship. Simmons recommends listening before offering help, accepting that allies remain imperfect and must keep examining their own biases, and treating the work as a marathon rather than a sprint. He argues that inclusive teams are more innovative and that the effort benefits everyone in the industry.

talks.title: "Project Jigsaw in JDK 9: Modularity Comes To Java" by Simon Ritter
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in "Project Jigsaw in JDK 9: Modularity Comes To Java" by Simon Ritter.

talks.title: "Exploring Conversational Interfaces with Amazon Alexa and Go" by Mike Flynn
talks.teaser: Shows how to build simple conversational voice apps for Amazon Alexa in Go, with design tips and a helper library.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at conversational interfaces, where people speak plain language to a device instead of issuing commands. It argues that voice platforms such as Amazon Alexa took off around 2016 because natural language services became cheap, large vendors competed for the space, and users found novelty in them. Early real usage included music, timers, ordering rides and food, and family or group games played on a shared device. The speaker surveys example skills, from trivia and car tools to joke and quote apps, and notes that single-task designs work best.

Design advice comes next. Vary the responses so the app does not always say okay, avoid promising more than the app can do, and add features gradually because users cannot see an update menu. Prompt clearly when input is needed and keep the session open, limit each request to one thing, and accept polite phrasing so it does not break the speech model. The talk then walks through the Alexa flow: the device sends a request to a skill, the platform matches intents and sample utterances set up in a developer dashboard, and the app returns a spoken response.

For implementation, the speaker presents a Go helper library that handles the request signature and timestamp checks, so the developer writes only handlers for launch, intents and session end. A short example reports a status page result aloud. Testing uses development mode on a linked device or a web simulator. The closing advice is to keep apps and speech models simple, use a library rather than re-implement verification, and avoid building quote apps. Audience questions covered monetization limits, data retention, and accent support.

talks.title: "Point-Free or Die: Tacit Programming in Haskell and Beyond" by Amar Shah
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for "Point-Free or Die: Tacit Programming in Haskell and Beyond" by Amar Shah.

talks.title: "Fold, paper, scissors - an exploration of origami's fold and cut problem" by Amy Wibowo
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for "Fold, paper, scissors - an exploration of origami's fold and cut problem" by Amy Wibowo.

talks.title: "An Interactive Web Visualization for Watershed Topology" by Mark Phillips
talks.teaser: Shows how public watershed data and graph traversal reveal where rainfall drains and which areas feed any given point.
talks.summary:
Mark Phillips presents an interactive web map that answers two questions about rainfall: for any point on the ground, where does the water flow downstream, and which area feeds into it upstream. He opens with a live demo of the United States, where hovering highlights the downstream path in blue and the upstream catchment in red. Examples include the Continental Divides, the Mississippi basin draining to New Orleans, Chicago's canal link to the Illinois River, and the Great Basin, which has no outlet to any ocean.

The method starts with a terrain grid in which each point drains to its lowest neighbor, forming a directed acyclic graph. A full national grid would have over a trillion nodes, so he switches to the USGS Watershed Boundary Dataset, about 100,000 polygons linked by downstream relationships. The six-gigabyte dataset is simplified and converted to TopoJSON so shared borders are stored once. SVG rendering stalled with tens of thousands of polygons, so he moved to canvas and merged the interior edges of upstream regions, reducing drawing cost. A mobile version fetches only the geometry of a tapped watershed.

He stresses that the watersheds are built from long-running manual surveys rather than computed by a model, and that live river gauge data is a separate source. Audience questions raised flood insurance and water rights as possible applications. The practical lesson is that a well-structured public dataset, graph traversal and careful rendering can turn large geospatial data into a responsive browser tool.

talks.title: "Modelica: Component Oriented Modeling of Physical Systems" by Michael Tiller
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in "Modelica: Component Oriented Modeling of Physical Systems" by Michael Tiller.
talks.summary:
This talk introduces Modelica, a declarative component-oriented modeling language for simulating complex physical systems. Tiller opens with historical context about computation's role in engineering, using ENIAC and artillery trajectory calculations as examples of why simulation matters. The core problem addressed is handling hybrid nonlinear simultaneous differential-algebraic equations (DAEs) in an accessible way. Traditional imperative approaches require tedious, error-prone manual discretization and equation manipulation; Modelica instead allows engineers to declare physical behavior using equations, deferring complex transformations to the compiler.

Key technical concepts include connectors (abstracted interaction points between components with flow attributes), inheritance (shared model definitions to reduce duplication), and hierarchical composition (systems built from nested sub-components spanning multiple engineering domains). The industrial robot example demonstrates scalability: a demo model contains 4,000 variables, 1,342 parameters, and approximately 500 components integrating electrical, mechanical, and control systems simultaneously.

Compiler optimizations are substantial. Equation sorting transforms dense O(n²) matrix operations into lower-triangular O(n) structures through dependency analysis. The Pantelides algorithm handles index reduction for differential-algebraic equations. Additional optimizations include state selection, tearing for nonlinear systems, and constraint handling for closed-loop mechanical systems. For the 4,000-variable problem, complexity reduces from n²·³⁷³ to linear n, a significant computational gain.

Practical ecosystem contributions include the Functional Mock-up Interface (FMI) standard for cross-tool model exchange, npm-based scientific model packaging (demonstrated with artillery trajectory simulation), and educational resources including an interactive web tour and a crowdfunded open textbook with embedded interactive simulations. The Q&A addresses solver limitations (particularly variable-index problems in impacts and separations), inter-tool component integration via FMI, and parameter sensitivity analysis approaches.

talks.title: "PureScript & Pux -- a safer, more expressive way to React" by Michael Trotter
talks.teaser: Surveys PureScript's typed effects and Pux on React, with demos of exhaustiveness checking and embedding components in JavaScript apps.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by positioning PureScript as a typed, purely functional language that compiles to CommonJS JavaScript, contrasting it with Elm, TypeScript, and Haskell on bundle size, flexibility, and type-system power. Citing Robin Milner, it argues for types that help programmers reason rather than merely describe machine representation, and explains purity as controlling side effects through an effect type that tracks DOM, network, time, and randomness in signatures.

The middle section walks through language mechanics with concrete examples: folds over numbers and ints via type classes, record and newtype modeling (including validated email), algebraic data types that force exhaustive case handling, and async effects. It then introduces Pux as a lightweight Elm-inspired layer on React—actions, state, update, and view—and shows wrapping React libraries like Spectacle through the foreign function interface, plus a rock-paper-scissors game where the compiler rejects incomplete pattern matches when game choices expand.

Practitioners should take away a migration pattern: build self-contained PureScript modules (for example autocomplete or analytics clients), export them as ordinary React components via helpers such as toReact, and lean on small bundles with dead-code elimination. The speaker points to introductory resources, community channels, starter tooling with hot reload, and answers questions on incremental file-by-file adoption versus isolated modules and compiler bundling options.

talks.title: "If Gaudí Had a Cluster" by Max Grigorev, Jen Carlile
talks.teaser: Traces Antoni Gaudí's modelling methods, then shows a cloud-backed visual programming language built for architects and engineers.
talks.summary:
The talk asks how Antoni Gaudí's architectural practice might have changed with modern computing power. Speakers Max Grigorev and Jen Carlile, from a startup building a web platform for architecture and engineering, begin with Gaudí's coppersmith background, his decades on the Sagrada Família, and his hanging-chain models that revealed catenary curves. They then survey physical and digital modelling, from mid-century terminal models to Frank Gehry's digitising arm.

Demos show a parameterised model of the church where tower count and floor dimensions change within seconds, ornamentation swapped between wheat, nautilus shells and grass, and a genetic algorithm evolving a thousand generations of fifty candidates in the browser against a golden-ratio fitness function. The team then explains its visual flow-based language, built around reusable blocks, parallel execution and responsiveness. A front-end lesson: Polymer's treating everything as an element bloated the DOM, so non-visual parts moved to plain JavaScript.

The back end is a distributed system in Go and C++ that compiles each program into a graph, schedules blocks onto worker pools running V8, and uses remote pointers so large values can sit on other machines or disk. Moving from JSON over HTTP to faster serialization and RPC gave significant gains. The talk ends by tying the work to urban growth, projecting 3.3 billion more city residents by 2050, and argues that optimisations once limited to the largest projects should reach everyone.

talks.title: "Is It A Bug Or Is It A Story?" by Nicola Hughes
talks.teaser: Walks through real journalism data cases to show when analysis results are a story and when they are a data bug.
talks.summary:
The speaker, an investigative data journalist who later became a developer, walks through real cases from her career. For each, she asks whether a result is a legitimate story to act on or a bug in how the data was collected or analysed. An opening example shows how small public fragments, joined together, can trace a network from an anonymous party scene to a named company owner.

Several cases show how data misleads. Leaked emails from a single mailbox produced a network that looked complete but was only partial. Subscriber logins hid female readers behind family accounts. A food aid analysis combining scraped procurement and shipping records held up because its totals landed within about 10 percent of the budget and the work could be reproduced in a virtual machine. Prescription data broken down to individual surgeries exposed a tiny population, so the results were re-aggregated to avoid identifying people. Census-based regression forecasts and running-time trend lines were bugs, since their outcomes depended on chosen start and end points. A random forest used for post-analysis of election results was a legitimate story.

The practical lessons are to check results against an independent metric, test whether someone else can reproduce them, avoid predictions from linear trends, and never deanonymise data. She also argues that non-specialists, such as business and QA staff, need enough understanding to spot where data is likely to break.

talks.title: "Designing Cypher - a Graph Query Language" by Tobias Lindaaker
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for "Designing Cypher - a Graph Query Language" by Tobias Lindaaker.

talks.title: "Reasoning about performance (in the context of search)" by Dan Luu
talks.teaser: Shows how back-of-envelope math, Bloom filters, and memory-access models size large-scale boolean search throughput.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames performance as more than raw speed, arguing that large services should justify optimization through operating cost and latency’s tie to revenue. He contrasts teams that design before coding with those that profile late, noting order-of-magnitude gaps when architecture cannot be reworked cheaply.

Using boolean AND search over growing corpora, he walks from grep-sized workloads through RAM bandwidth limits, indexing, and sharding across thousands of machines with replication and geographic latency. He introduces posting lists, then BitFunnel-style Bloom filters with parallel bitwise AND over document blocks, false-positive tradeoffs, early exit, and a memory-access cost model that yields expected queries per second for a Wikipedia-scale example.

He stresses index sharding by term cardinality so pathological documents do not poison the structure, mentions ranking and ingestion as separate performance drains, and cautions that average throughput is easy to estimate while loaded tail latency is not. Practitioners should treat simple arithmetic as a gate before multi-year builds, without assuming Bloom filters always beat classic inverted indexes.

talks.title: "Practical data synchronization with CRDTs" by Dmitry Ivanov
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of "Practical data synchronization with CRDTs" by Dmitry Ivanov.

talks.title: "Failing (and recovering) asynchronously: a saga" by Daniel Solano Gómez
talks.teaser: Explores the saga pattern for automatic rollback when multi-step async cloud operations fail.
talks.summary:
The speaker describes building microservices tooling that chains sequential AWS calls, using KMS key creation followed by alias creation as the running example. When the second step fails, the key can remain orphaned unless something explicitly deletes it; hand-written recovery with futures and flatMap works for two steps but becomes unwieldy as graphs grow.

The talk traces the saga idea from long-lived database transactions and compensating actions through its later use in service-oriented and microservice systems, citing industry examples while stressing a narrower goal: undo semantics for asynchronous local concurrency, not crash persistence or distributed two-phase commit. The core design pairs each forward operation with a rollback, threads successes and failures through a Try-like model, and uses stream primitives such as broadcast and zip so downstream failure triggers coordinated cleanup. Stacked stages cap the pipeline; the KMS scenario reappears as composable saga flows with matching deleters.

Practitioners are encouraged to treat sagas as reusable library material rather than one-off error handling. Futures-based variants are possible but awkward without an execution context; Akka Streams is presented as the working prototype, with parallel graphs and forward recovery left as future work before a public library release.

talks.title: "Distributed Commit Log: Application Techniques for Transaction Processing" by David McNeil
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding "Distributed Commit Log: Application Techniques for Transaction Processing" by David McNeil.

talks.title: "An Introduction to Combinator Compilers and Graph Reduction Machines" by David Graunke
talks.teaser: Explains how combinator compilers and graph reduction machines execute lazy functional programs by rewriting graphs in place.
talks.summary:
David Graunke introduces graph reduction machines, a virtual machine model for functional languages that runs a program by repeatedly rewriting a graph structure in place instead of stepping through a vector of instructions. He contrasts this with familiar bytecode virtual machines and explains that function application is essentially substitution, which the model makes concrete.

The talk then covers combinator compilation, which rewrites a program into a small set of primitive functions. Using the SKI basis, he shows that a doubling function, a flip function and Church's successor can each be expressed with only a few combinators and still reduce to the same results as the original lambda expressions. The rewrite rules are small enough to fit in a few lines, and because each rewrite touches only a local part of the graph, normal-order application keeps the runtime simple. He also covers extensions such as B, C and the Turner combinators, along with super combinators generated for a specific program.

Graunke describes Miranda as a popular 1980s functional language built on these ideas, and explains why graph reduction struggled on stock hardware because of memory bandwidth limits. He contrasts two responses: custom hardware such as the Reducer and Norma, and closure-based reduction, which GHC uses. The takeaway is that these techniques explain the origins of lazy functional languages and offer a useful lens on how they run today.

talks.title: "How to Get Started With Functional Programming" by Julia Gao
talks.teaser: Introduces functional programming ideas like immutability and pure functions for developers used to object-oriented code.
talks.summary:
This talk aims to help front-end developers, many of whom learned object-oriented habits first, begin applying functional programming ideas in JavaScript. The speaker argues that mutable data makes code hard to control, since shared values can change unexpectedly and cause bugs, and that it is unsafe when several threads touch the same data. Immutable data structures are presented as a workable alternative: unchanged parts are shared between versions and only the changed path is copied, which keeps copying cheap and removes the need for locks across threads.

The middle of the talk compares loops with recursion. A factorial function that mutates a running result inside a for loop is rewritten as a recursive function with a base case, so no variable changes. Pure functions, which return the same output for the same input without side effects, are linked to how arithmetic already behaves, and they are shown to make refactoring and onboarding easier. Composable functions are demonstrated by chaining built-in string methods, then a stateful example is reworked so the mutating step returns a new value instead of altering the original. A short section on types explains how a type checker can cut down the unit tests needed to check inputs.

The closing part surveys alternatives to plain JavaScript, including Immutable.js, ClojureScript, PureScript and F#, with notes on how each can be adopted gradually, for example by writing a single component in one language. The speaker concludes that immutable structures can be efficient and that functional thinking encourages developers to plan a solution before writing code.

talks.title: "Idealized Commit Logs: Code Simplification via Program Slicing" by Alan Shreve
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning "Idealized Commit Logs: Code Simplification via Program Slicing" by Alan Shreve.

talks.title: "Agility & Robustness: Clojure spec" by Stuart Halloway
talks.teaser: Shows how Clojure spec describes data and functions for validation, example generation and automated testing.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a tension Clojure developers feel. The language favors generic data structures such as maps, which keeps code small and composable, but real domains are full of specific things like addresses, order items and equipment models. Halloway argues that Clojure spec lets developers describe those specifics separately from their code as an opt-in layer, instead of encoding them in types throughout the system. He contrasts this with example-based tests, which are costly to maintain, and with static types, which mostly cover code and do not reach configuration files, wire formats or stored data.

The middle of the session builds up the vocabulary. Predicates act as specs, collections and maps can be described with composable forms, and named specs can be shared across namespaces. Regex-style operators describe ordering, so specs can cover language forms and function argument lists. Function specs add semantic checks relating arguments to return values. From these descriptions the talk demonstrates validation, explain output that points to the failing path in nested data, conform to show how a value matched, example generation, instrumentation during development, and generative checks that shrink failures to minimal cases.

The closing section notes that spec runs at runtime and can serve as assertions left in production code, and that it is dynamic and entirely optional. The practical takeaway is to adopt it incrementally and avoid over-specifying, since overly specific statements undermine the flexibility that makes code easy to change. Halloway said the library was then in alpha with production use already underway, and he expected a beta soon.

talks.title: "Storytelling with your data" by Aysegul Yonet
talks.teaser: Shows how to build data visualizations with Angular 2 and D3, from SVG scales to animated bar charts.
talks.summary:
## Overview
The speaker introduces themselves as 'Aisha' (noting potential transcription discrepancy with title), a Senior Software Engineer at Autodesk A360 Cloud Platform and Google Developer Expert in Angular. This was their first Strange Loop presentation. Beyond their primary role, they educate through Girl Develop It, Black Girls Code, AnyCanons (teaching human trafficking survivors to code), and mentoring programs including Last Mile at San Quentin prison. The core topic: how to help users understand complex data through visualization and storytelling.

## The Problem: Data Without Context
Autodesk's 3D viewer is powerful but reveals a critical gap: providing access to complex models and robust tools is insufficient if users don't understand what they're seeing. Complex 3D models (more intricate than the Golden Gate Bridge) leave users confused about how to interact with or interpret the data. The Autodesk Forge platform offers open APIs that developers have used creatively—one example displays building sensor data (heat and gas inefficiencies) overlaid as green dots on 3D models; another created an animated Ikea furniture assembly guide. These demonstrated that visualizations need narrative context to be useful.

## Angular 2: Modern Architecture for Data Apps
Angular 2 had just released (beta completion the week of the conference). Key improvements include: modular code organization making applications easier to understand; performance improvements; eliminating the need to ship the compiler to clients (60% reduction in shipped Angular code). Angular CLI provides scaffolding and project management. NG modules organize components, services, and functionality into reusable units. Angular's animation system allows defining reusable triggers for state transitions and keyframe animations. The speaker emphasized treating parent-level "smart components" as data handlers while keeping child components application-agnostic—preventing tight coupling between backend data structure and component implementation.

## D3.js: Flexible Data Visualization
D3.js (Data Driven Documents) underwent major changes in version 4. Key features: modular architecture allowing developers to load only needed parts; new merge function for managing enter/exit patterns with dynamic datasets (crucial for real-time data); scales for mapping data ranges to display dimensions; transitions and the enter/append/exit/remove pattern for data binding. TypeScript integration is valuable because D3 is "very picky"—missing or incorrectly-typed data points cause silent visualization failures. RxJS (originally Microsoft, now Netflix-maintained) enables observables instead of promises for more efficient asynchronous operations.

## Angular + D3 Pattern
Wrapping D3 functions into reusable Angular components allows parameterized visualizations (bar charts, scatter plots) that can be reused across applications. Angular's component structure and change detection mesh seamlessly with D3's data-driven approach. A practical example: a bar chart component sets up SVG, populates data, and draws axes—repeating these operations whenever data changes. This combination avoids code repetition while building sophisticated visualization libraries.

## Case Study: Syrian Refugee Data
The speaker demonstrated storytelling with multiple perspectives on the same dataset: refugee count by country, GDP comparison (showing wealthy nations aren't accepting proportionally), country area, population impact, and GDP per capita. Each visualization revealed different aspects; together they provided genuine insight. The principle: complex visualizations shouldn't attempt showing everything simultaneously—multiple focused views help audiences understand data meaning.

## Takeaways
Use appropriate tools: D3 for truly complex custom visualizations, simpler libraries for straightforward needs. Angular 2's maturity, tooling (CLI, Chrome DevTools, open source charts), and component architecture excel for data-driven applications. TypeScript prevents type errors before visualization failures. The fundamental message: storytelling matters. Raw data access and complex tools mean nothing without helping users perceive and understand information.

talks.title: "Government Hacking and Human Rights: The Why and the How" by Amie Stepanovich
talks.teaser: Surveys government hacking from FBI cases to modern network techniques and human-rights safeguards advocates demand.
talks.summary:
The presentation traces law-enforcement hacking from the Nicodemo Scarfo trial, where FBI keylogging yielded encrypted evidence, through modern network investigative techniques. It describes sparse public records on early FBI use, Wired FOIA disclosures, and Judge Steven Smith’s 2013 refusal to authorize a remote search when the target computer’s location was unknown—a decision grounded in Rule 41 jurisdiction limits and Fourth Amendment particularity.

The talk explains procedural amendments that let magistrates authorize searches when a machine’s location is unknown, the stretching of the Electronic Communications Privacy Act without new statutory hacking authority, and advocacy by Access Now, EFF, ACLU, and EPIC. It surveys bulk and extraterritorial operations abroad, commercial spyware markets revealed in the Hacking Team breach, and Five Eyes programs, then classifies state activity as messaging control, causing damage, or surveillance.

Framing hacking as interference with due process, privacy, and expression, the speaker argues for a presumptive prohibition rebuttable only with strong safeguards aligned with the International Principles on the Application of Human Rights to Communications Surveillance. She outlines ten policy measures—clear public law, necessity and minimization, judicial review with technical expertise, limits on bulk hacking, transparency, bans on compelled vendor backdoors, and prompt vulnerability disclosure—and closes by stressing that dangerous cases do not justify sacrificing human rights.

talks.title: "Ceptre: A Language for Modeling Generative Interactive Systems" by Chris Martens
talks.teaser: Presents Ceptre, a linear logic language for writing playable game rules, with stages that handle turn-based interaction.
talks.summary:
Chris Martens introduces Ceptre, a programming language she built for her thesis to sketch games as formal rules, not as code tied to a particular renderer, input device or genre. She opens with a short card game played with volunteers from the audience, where each turn changes attack and health values, to show the kind of rule-driven system she wants to describe.

The language is grounded in linear logic. World facts are propositions, and a rule replaces its premises with its conclusions while leaving the rest of the state untouched. Running a program is treated as multiset rewriting. A stage mechanism, driven by a quiescence signal, lets the author make one phase interactive, such as a tournament where players act until nothing else can fire, before automatic steps run. She notes that negation and aggregation can be encoded using stages. She also describes checking program invariants, which reduces to Presburger arithmetic and is currently too expensive to be practical.

For the payoff, she describes several case studies: a narrative generator driven by social-interaction rules, a multi-agent social simulation, a roguelike, and a simplified Settlers of Catan. Fuzzing player input with lightweight strategies let her run 200 random trials on teams of 25, which showed that when teammate buffing was available from the start, the team that moved first gained a large advantage. She closes by arguing for minimal, logic-based intermediate languages and for future front ends that output to existing game formats.

talks.title: "A Live Programming Experience" by Sean McDirmid
talks.teaser: A live demo shows immediate feedback, value scrubbing, and time-travel debugging in a custom programming environment.
talks.summary:
The presenter contrasts everyday coding, where each edit and debug pass feels like shooting arrows at a target, with a programming style that offers immediate, continuous feedback—like aiming with a hose. He positions live programming as the next step in a long arc from punch cards toward richer interactivity, and names prior work on conversational programming, learnable programming, and scrubbing as influences.

Most of the session is an extended live build in a custom imperative language with React-like reactivity. Unknown slots called “holy terms” receive defaults so graphics appear as soon as choices are completed. The demo walks through drawing and scrubbing geometry, a bouncing ball with physics and screen clamping, scrubbing simulated time and loop indices to inspect individual objects, debugger-style probing tied to execution context, and dragging on-screen handles that rewrite parameters such as velocity. Later steps abstract balls and pill shapes, union shapes on the canvas, promote literals to arguments, and attach drawable velocity and force vectors—with a brief note that shared versus per-instance parameters change what edits affect.

The talk closes on implementation themes without deep technical slides: a virtual time machine for sampling recent frames, a type-inferred system that enables scrubbing widgets when types are known, and native code generation through a dynamic runtime. The speaker revisits whether such UIs scale beyond 2D sketches to hard domains like compilers, and frames the work as shaping requirements for future programming environments rather than a finished product pitch.

talks.title: "Apparatus: A Hybrid Graphics Editor / Programming Environment" by Toby Schachman
talks.teaser: Presents Apparatus, a graphics editor merged with dataflow programming, aimed at building interactive diagrams in minutes.
talks.summary:
Toby Schachman argues that interactive diagrams help people convey and test a mental model, but building them in code is slow and forces constant switching between symbolic and spatial thinking. Adapting a diagram found online also means untangling its source. He presents Apparatus, a direct manipulation graphics editor combined with a spreadsheet-style dataflow environment, where state is always visible and editing and running happen together.

He demonstrates the core features live. Attributes can reference one another across shapes, and dragging a shape runs a numerical minimization that adjusts the chosen variables to follow the mouse. Reused diagrams behave like copies that inherit later changes unless a value has been overwritten, which lets him build a slider and a color picker. Spreads give a value a range of values, producing bar charts, grids and curves plotted from many anchor points.

For examples, he shows a cycloid diagram and a bicycle model. The bike model poses a puzzle: when the pedal is pulled backward, does the bike move backward or forward? The answer depends on the gear ratio relative to the wheel and pedal radii, and a spread of six bikes lets the audience compare gear ratios at once. He closes by noting Apparatus is free, open source and on GitHub, and invites feedback and collaboration.

talks.title: "Eve" by Chris Granger
talks.teaser: Traces more than twenty prototypes of Eve, a language built to make programming accessible, and what user testing revealed.
talks.summary:
The talk is an experience report from a small startup building Eve, a programming environment meant to bring programming to a wider audience. The speaker walks through more than twenty versions built over roughly a year and a half. The first, Aurora, was a Clojure-style notebook platform shaped by the speaker's own taste for immutable data and functional programming. When it was tested with non-programmers at a research lab opening, the functional model did not work for them, and scope proved the hardest concept to get across.

That result led the team to drop scope, nested data structures and execution order, a model they compared to Excel and to relational databases. Drawing on Datalog research from Berkeley's Bloom project, they built a prototype where rules read like fill-in-the-blank statements, and a to-do app came out far smaller than usual. Even so, readers had to hold the whole system in their heads to understand any one rule, so it did not make programming easier. Later versions tried table-based views, drag-and-drop interface building, a Foursquare clone, and entity-relationship style query diagrams. In one small comparison, people understood a query shown as a diagram faster than the equivalent SQL.

The closing point is that the team has repeatedly thrown away their own work and kept testing assumptions with real people. The speaker argues that the design space for these tools is still largely unexplored and invites others to experiment with it.

talks.title: "Constraint Logic Propagation Conflict Spreadsheets" by William Taysom
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of "Constraint Logic Propagation Conflict Spreadsheets" by William Taysom.

talks.title: "The Gamma: Programming Tools for Data Journalism" by Tomas Petricek
talks.teaser: Shows how data-driven news articles can be written as programs, letting readers change indicators and inspect the source.
talks.summary:
Tomas Petricek opens with data journalism, where newspapers such as The Guardian and The Economist publish charts built from open government and World Bank data. He argues these articles are hard to check or reproduce, because readers rarely get the source code or the underlying data. A single chart comparing China and the US on total carbon emissions can also hide context, such as what changes when emissions are measured per capita.

He then demonstrates a prototype in which an article is a Markdown page of text plus F# code. A type provider for the World Bank gives the editor autocomplete over years, categories and indicators, pulled live from the data source. The article's interactive controls are generated by analysing the code's structure: when a field can be swapped for another of the same type, the page shows a dropdown, and choosing an option rewrites the source. Lists of countries get an editor in the same way. He also shows a generic type provider that infers types from a sample JSON response, and explains how the World Bank's three-dimensional data cube maps onto a programming environment.

He closes with future directions: linking text to its data sources in the spirit of literate programming, mapping messier government formats such as PDFs into type systems, and bringing reactive visualization ideas into these reports. The takeaway is that treating an article as a program can improve transparency and reproducibility, with journalists relying on programmers for the data-mapping layer.

talks.title: "An Overview of Probabilistic Programming" by Vikash K. Mansinghka
talks.teaser: BayesDB, Picture, and VentureScript demonstrate probabilistic programming for tabular data, generative vision, and modular inference.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames machine learning as a hard path for newcomers—sklearn-style decision charts that dead-end at “tough luck”—and for experts who ship opaque systems that accumulate technical debt. He argues probability and computer science are colliding uncomfortably because the real world cannot be reshaped to fit classical computing abstractions, and that probabilistic programming is the software layer meant to integrate rigorous uncertainty handling with usable engineering.

Most of the material walks through three MIT platforms. BayesDB pairs Bayesian query language primitives (infer, estimate, simulate) with a meta-modeling language so tabular data supports predictive fills, dependence questions, and synthetic checks without forcing false certainty. Examples touch malnutrition biomarker assessment, satellite anomaly exploration, and telco marketing proxies. Picture inverts graphics pipelines: generative 3D scenes, approximate renderers, and neural “squinting” comparators recover faces, bodies, and simple road scenes while surfacing when assumptions fail. A design map contrasts how most ML code hides math in dashed boxes versus making models, inference strategies, and estimation explicit.

VentureScript closes as a general-purpose attempt where models, declarations, and inference tactics share one probabilistic language, illustrated by higher-order Bayesian optimization akin to modular tree search. Practitioners should see domain DSLs as research tactics with deliberate syntax choices, expect perpetual residual uncertainty in automated modelers, and treat the field as early-stage language design—not only faster data science.

talks.title: "BayesDB: Query the Probable Implications of Data" by Richard Tibbetts
talks.teaser: Introduces a probabilistic query language that infers missing data, simulates populations and flags unlikely values.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces BayesDB, a system with a query language that asks what a dataset implies, not only which rows match. The speaker argues that people struggle to trust statistical conclusions, and that database research has added few new kinds of questions in decades. The language offers infer, which fills in missing values with a confidence, and simulate, which generates synthetic records from a modeled population.

Demonstrations use public satellite data. For a 500 kilogram satellite in geosynchronous orbit, simulation points to a likely communications satellite, probably from the United States, while a simple range search returns surprising results. Inferred orbit types come with confidence values, and an estimate query flags implausible period values, such as entries that look like a decimal error. Plain correlation recovers little about orbital mechanics, but composing a Kepler's laws model with the default model improves predictions of orbital parameters.

Models are learned as an ensemble of about 100 approximations, and agreement among them serves as a confidence measure. The main takeaways are to separate the question from the modeling choices, to check how confident results are, and to add domain knowledge where available. The software is open source under the Apache License and installable with pip, while machine-assisted modeling remains in alpha.

talks.title: "How NOT to Measure Latency" by Gil Tene
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of "How NOT to Measure Latency" by Gil Tene.

talks.title: "Feet in Both Worlds: From Objective-C to Swift" by Andy Matuschak
talks.teaser: Traces Swift's Objective-C heritage and shows adapter shims for bridging modern Swift types into legacy code.
talks.summary:
The talk traces Objective-C from its 1983 origins through NeXT's frameworks, Cocoa, and the NS-prefixed APIs that Swift still relies on. It argues that Swift's interoperability with this legacy gave new users a large library base from day one, but also imposes lasting costs: a sizeable mapping layer between the two languages, unusual keyword argument syntax, the dynamic keyword, and no cycle detection. These constraints also limit language design, since features that would suit Swift well are harder to introduce.

The second half is a field report from migrating a large app at Khan Academy, where the team ended up rewriting far more Objective-C into Swift than it had planned. The speaker found that idiomatic Swift types such as enums, structs, and generics are invisible to Objective-C, so writing Swift that feels like the standard library caused constant friction. To bridge the gap, the talk walks through adapter strategies: extensions that expose enums and structs through Objective-C-visible initializers and properties, boxing values inside an ID-typed storage field, and wrapping a generic table view data source in a non-generic class built from closures.

The closing takeaway is to isolate new code behind temporary shims so it stays clean and can be removed once the legacy Objective-C is gone. Teams maintaining mixed codebases get concrete patterns for doing that, while the speaker expects the deeper design costs to persist for years.

talks.title: "Relevance of ClojureScript" by Jearvon Dharrie
talks.teaser: Introduces ClojureScript through immutable data, core.async channels, React state undo, and live hot reloading demos.
talks.summary:
The speaker introduces ClojureScript, a compiler that turns Clojure code into JavaScript. He argues that JavaScript now works as a runtime that many languages target, and gives his reasons for choosing it: it is a Lisp, its design is clean, and it offers namespaces and macros. A hello-world build shows that compilation modes keep the output small. Basic syntax follows, covering prefix function calls, named and anonymous functions, JavaScript interop, local bindings and atoms for state.

The middle section focuses on asynchronous code and immutability. Nested callbacks are shown as hard to read, and core.async is presented as a way to write sequential logic with channels and go blocks, which the compiler turns into a state machine. Immutable values make equality checks reliable, even after a library call. A small React contact-list app built with a ClojureScript wrapper demonstrates undo by keeping earlier application states in a vector. A transducer example and a Node.js command-line tool that generates fake credit card numbers round out the examples.

The closing part covers the developer workflow. Source maps take browser errors back to the original ClojureScript lines, Figwheel reloads code and CSS as they change, and a REPL connected from an editor can run code inside the running page. JavaScript libraries are used through externs, and a community project ports popular ones. The speaker encourages developers to consider non-JavaScript tools when they fit the job.

talks.title: "Cognitive Bias: A reflection and path forward" by Bryan Liles
talks.teaser: Examines how personal biases shape tool choices and who gets into software, using anecdotes rather than technical content.
talks.summary:
This non-technical talk opens with the speaker explaining his choice of title and then reflecting on how personal bias shapes everyday decisions in software. He recalls learning Linux and FreeBSD in the 1990s and wondering why the community settled on one over the other, concluding that habits and early influences, not clear merit, kept people looking in the same direction. He extends the idea to programming languages and editors, arguing that preferences often come from the schools people attended, their mentors, and the peers around them.

The middle of the talk turns to diversity in tech. The speaker describes growing up as a Black developer without developers in his family, and he argues that appearance tells you nothing about who writes software. He sketches historical barriers such as housing covenants and unequal schooling as context for why some groups are underrepresented. He suggests that organisations should ask why people are missing rather than how to recruit more of them, and he urges developers to separate their identity from their code so criticism of work is not taken personally.

He closes by arguing that understanding builds trust, trust speeds teams up, and faster teams are more valuable. His takeaways are to question your assumptions, to recognise that being correct in one situation does not make you correct in another, and to value colleagues whose views and experiences differ from your own.

talks.title: "Using Race Conditions in Correct Concurrent Software" by Devon O'Dell
talks.teaser: Shows how lock-free compare-and-swap slab allocation, linearizability, and generation counters tame contention on cache nodes.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames a concrete CDN problem: many cache processes on a node cannot safely share data through private heaps, so the team built Microslab, a fixed-size slab allocator with cross-process shared state. The speaker walks from a single-process free list through allocation protocols, execution histories, sequential consistency, and linearizability, using spin locks as the first correct but contended implementation.

Benchmarks show lock-based paths collapse under thread contention and produce wild latency tails, while deliberate races in spin-lock tuning and progress guarantees (lock freedom) motivate a non-blocking design. The core implementation uses compare-and-swap on the slab stack, explains when those races remain safe, and fixes the ABA failure mode with a generation counter and wide compare-and-swap, including why generation must be read before the head pointer.

Final measurements contrast unpredictable lock latency with steady behavior from the lock-free allocator as contention rises. Practitioners gain a workflow for reasoning about correctness (protocols, linearization points) before chasing throughput, plus the caveat that cache coherence and memory ordering are out of scope. The allocator is open sourced under Apache 2.

talks.title: "How the web is democratizing science (join in!)" by Abigail Cabunoc Mayes
talks.teaser: Shows how open source volunteers can help scientists share data, write analysis tools, and make research freely accessible.
talks.summary:
Abigail Cabunoc Mayes, who works at Mozilla, invites developers to join open science projects. She starts by comparing two problems: video game graphics squeezed into limited memory and genome assembly, which both need algorithms that work within tight memory. Many researchers lack computing backgrounds, so people with programming skills can help.

The talk traces openness from the Royal Society's early journal, which encouraged sharing and credit, through Eric Raymond's essay on open development and the free software work that led to the Netscape browser and Mozilla. A fictional graduate student example shows the costs of closed research: duplicated sequencing spending, months spent rewriting code that a library already provided, high fees to make a paper open access, and findings unavailable to the community being studied. Real projects follow, including a worm biology data visualization, a hackathon where community members taught a student bioinformatics tools for bacterial and viral data, and a distributed astronomy analysis effort looking for volunteers.

In audience questions, she said researcher pushback often comes from fear of being scooped and the pressure for high-impact publications. She pointed to Mozilla Science Lab resources for finding projects and a badge effort that credits specific contributions to papers. Her takeaway is that people with coding skills can contribute meaningfully to open science, even when newcomers meet resistance.

talks.title: "Kolmogorov music" by Christopher Ford
talks.teaser: Shows how Kolmogorov complexity meets music through Clojure macros, live canons, and paradoxical lexicon pieces on copyright.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with a string of a billion repeated G characters to illustrate how a huge output can have a tiny specification. Kolmogorov complexity is framed as the length of the shortest program that produces a value, with randomness tied to strings that cannot be shortened. In Clojure, macros measure description length versus evaluated result length, linking the idea to compression and to whether data exposes internal structure.

Live coding turns melodies into data structures: Row, Row, Row Your Boat as a canon, Steve Reich’s Clapping Music with drifting rhythms, and comparisons inspired by David Meredith’s analysis-by-compression work. Borges’s Library of Babel and a lazy combinator over ASCII illustrate infinite catalogs from finite code. A Champernowne-derived “lexicon” composition uses skip-ahead playback to land near Blurred Lines, arguing tongue-in-cheek that one infinite piece could embed all past and future tunes. References include Contact’s pi speculation and UK rave legislation parodied on an Orbital release.

The close is a layered canon on G, B, and E as notes and ASCII, building listener “model formation” through gradual additions, distortion, and text-to-speech. The practical takeaway for programmers is to treat concise generative code as evidence of understood structure—and to exploit that expressiveness when representing or transforming music.

talks.title: "Aggregator: MapReduce in the type system" by Dan Frank
talks.teaser: Shows how the Aggregator type in Scala separates reduction logic from execution, using merchant fraud features as the running example.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the idea that many data analysis jobs take raw events, such as payment charges, and reduce them to statements about properties, like counts or distinct values. The speaker compares a SQL query, which states the desired result, with a MapReduce job, where the logic is split between map and reduce phases and the programmer must keep both in step. The alternative presented is Algebird's Aggregator trait, which describes a reduction with three types: an input type, an intermediate accumulator, and an output type.

Using a merchant example, the speaker shows how a distinct-card count is written as an aggregator. Compose-prepare adapts an existing aggregator to a different input type, such as charges instead of cards, and approximate data structures can replace an exact set with a fixed memory footprint. Aggregators can also be combined so that several features are computed in one pass, for example a ratio of international cards to all cards a merchant has used. The aggregator can be applied to a whole sequence at once or updated incrementally as data arrives.

To serve these features in near real time, the speaker describes running the same definition through Summingbird, with a streaming layer and a batch layer whose stored accumulators are merged at query time. The takeaway is that treating the accumulator as a first-class value lets a team define a computation once, reuse its parts, and choose the execution platform separately.

talks.title: "Non-Imperative Network Programming" by Mindy Preston
talks.teaser: Contrasts imperative Unix sockets with composable MirageOS module types for clearer, testable unikernel network stacks.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens by defining non-imperative network programming as interfaces that aim to be independent, stateless, and deterministic, while stressing that the talk will not deliver a fully working interface that meets every criterion. She scopes network programming to application code that sends and receives messages across lossy links, deliberately excluding distributed systems theory.

Traditional Unix networking centers on the sockets API: opaque file descriptors, side-effecting calls like connect, weak typing of connection state, and hundreds of implicit tunables exposed only through kernel parameters outside application code. Unikernels, especially MirageOS in OCaml, replace the monolithic OS boundary with a compiled image where transport, network, link, and virtual hardware layers are explicit libraries. Module types for IPv4, IPv6, IP, Ethernet, TCP, and FLOW make implementations swappable; creating a TCP connection yields a FLOW or an error rather than silently mutating hidden state. She walks through a trivial discard service, explicit stack functors, and sugar such as s.listen for binding ports.

Practitioners gain a design lens: explicit stacks improve determinism and independence for testing. Virtual network interfaces can simulate loss, mangling, or absurd latency; injectable clocks and random sources make time and stochastic behavior controllable. For unavoidable mutable state such as ARP caches, she points to Irmin-style persistent stores with type-aware merge rules, using ARP as an example where expiry dates simplify reconciliation.

talks.title: "CRDTs Illustrated" by Arnout Engelen
talks.teaser: Animated examples walk through operation-based and state-based CRDT rules for partition-tolerant replicated application state.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with why a single shared server breaks down when links fail, then motivates spreading replicas so work can continue during partitions. It revisits the tension between strong consistency and availability, introduces eventual consistency, and positions conflict-free replicated data types as a way to guarantee that replicas seeing the same updates end up identical.

Using paired-user scenarios, it builds operation-based CRDTs step by step: concurrent updates must commute, duplicate application must be harmless so at-least-once delivery suffices, and a source’s own messages must arrive in send order. A naive distributed set shows why ideal set semantics are unattainable; an add-wins style models real tradeoffs. State-based CRDTs shift burden to idempotent merges that are commutative and associative, illustrated with increment-only counters, positive–negative composition, and version vectors to allow decrements while preserving a forward partial order.

Live curls against an eventually consistent store show transparent counters, and a small synced to-do demo keeps two browser clients progressing after the server dies until reunion. The close stresses composing types, tombstones and state growth, choosing operation- versus state-based replication for connectivity patterns, and when strong consistency remains mandatory.

talks.title: "Side Effects are a Public API" by Christopher Armstrong
talks.teaser: Shows how to model side effects as testable values in Python and Haskell, so tests check effect order instead of mocks.
talks.summary:
Armstrong argues that implicit side effects such as console input and output, network calls and shared state are hard to test, and that mocking them in Python is messy. He proposes treating effects as first-class values: a function returns a description of the action it intends, and a separate performer carries it out. This separation of intent and performance lets application code stay pure while deployers choose how effects actually run.

He walks through his Python library, effect, which uses a generator-based do decorator, an effect object holding an intent and callbacks, a dispatcher that maps intents to performers, and a synchronous perform function that interprets them. Tests declare the expected sequence of effects with simulated results, so a change in order fails the test, and mismatches produce a readable log. He also covers a Twisted-based variant, parallel effects, and wrapping low-level HTTP writes in higher-level intents so tests stay at the right abstraction. For Haskell, he models the same idea with free monads and writes a custom interpreter for each test.

The main takeaway is to test side effects as carefully as return values, since their order matters, and to keep them at the edges of a program. He cautions that effects add complexity of their own and should not be used everywhere. He also notes limits: the approach is sequential, it effectively uses a single monad, and free monads can be slow in production, which can be avoided by swapping in direct IO.

talks.title: "Specter: overcome your fear of nested Clojure data" by Nathan Marz
talks.teaser: Shows how composable navigation paths in the Clojure library Specter simplify querying and updating nested data.
talks.summary:
Nathan Marz introduces Specter, a Clojure library for querying and transforming nested data such as maps that hold sequences of records. He starts with a world structure containing bank funds and a list of accounts, and shows a hand-written transfer function that needs careful navigation and manual rebuilding of each container. He then shows a Specter version that moves money from any number of givers to any number of receivers, with the structure described by paths passed in as arguments, so the function does not depend on one data layout.

He then walks through the mechanics. Select collects values and transform updates them, and navigators such as keywords, all, filter, subrange and selected compose into a single path. Each step creates a navigation context, the update is applied at the end, and the original structure is rebuilt on the way back while sequence types are preserved. Further examples cover incrementing the last odd number, reversing the even values inside a range, appending to every subsequence, and collecting a value from elsewhere in a map to use in an update. A conditional navigator and a walk-based approach are also mentioned.

For performance, he benchmarks a nested lookup, where precompiled paths come close to hand-written code, and a nested transform, which runs at over five times the speed of update-in. A recent release allows precompilation when paths depend on function parameters, and a filter-and-range example ran over twice as fast with it.
