He closes with a sketch of a graph extension for ancestry data. The takeaway is that composable navigation can replace verbose nested update code in Clojure.

talks.title: "Evidence-Oriented Programming" by Andreas Stefik
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning "Evidence-Oriented Programming" by Andreas Stefik.

talks.title: "Cleaning the Tar: Using React within the Firefox Developer Tools" by James Long
talks.teaser: A Firefox DevTools engineer describes migrating debugger UI from mutable Zul toward Redux, React, and replay-friendly immutable state.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames “tar” and incidental complexity in large UIs, using Firefox Developer Tools as a case where legacy Zul-based views, widespread DOM mutation, and state scattered across controllers make small fixes cascade into unrelated breakage. The speaker argues for a single immutable application-state object, pure render logic, and centralized updates through actions—patterns familiar from Elm and ClosureScript—rather than leaving state implicit in the DOM.

On the debugger panel, a Redux-style model already exposes the full UI as a JavaScript object, enables scrubbing through prior states, and yields record-and-replay with only a short history stack in userland. Action logging becomes a transactional trace of every change, including duplicate breakpoint events from async work, and serialized state plus actions can be restored outside the original instance—a path toward richer bug reports. Because React is not wired in yet, reducers temporarily emit events into the old mutation-based views, including painful “empty everything” and reload paths when navigating or jumping to arbitrary states.

Practitioners hear a staged migration: controllers become action creators, reducers own synchronous transitions, and async stays confined to action creators so UI code stays testable without promise-heavy coupling. Pure update functions ease unit testing compared with DOM-heavy “milky” tests on Mozilla’s try server; shallow React rendering is pitched as a faster next step. The talk closes with open work—React rollout, immutable libraries, hot reload, component-local state in the global atom, and query helpers decoupling views from state shape—and invites contributors once the codebase is less fragile.

talks.title: "When the OS gets in the way" by Mark Price
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for "When the OS gets in the way" by Mark Price.
talks.summary:
Mark Price from Elmax Exchange discusses optimizing the Linux operating system to minimize latency and jitter for ultra-low-latency applications, particularly relevant to high-frequency financial trading systems. The talk emphasizes that while Linux is an excellent general-purpose OS, specific tuning is necessary for sub-millisecond latency requirements.

The speaker defines system jitter as variations in response time and identifies that the underlying causes are the operating system's task scheduling decisions, CPU housekeeping tasks, and hardware interrupts. Most systems exhibit a "long tail" where worst-case latency significantly exceeds typical performance.

The technical foundation covers modern multi-socket, multi-core hardware: NUMA nodes with local RAM per socket, physical cores with shared L1/L2 caches, logical hyperthreads sharing physical core resources, and L3 caches spanning multiple cores. The completely fair scheduler (CFS) distributes CPU time fairly across all runnable tasks but lacks application-specific awareness.

The core solution involves CPU isolation and affinity techniques: using the isolcpus kernel parameter to reserve CPUs, creating separate CPU sets via cgroups to compartmentalize OS and application tasks, pinning latency-critical threads to specific cores using sched_setaffinity(), and restricting runtime threads using taskset. The speaker demonstrates that cpusets are superior to isolcpus alone because they maintain proper load-balancing within isolated domains.

Verification requires Linux tracing tools: lstopo for hardware topology discovery, perf for sampling scheduler events, and ftrace for function-level tracing. Through tracing, specific jitter sources are identified including cache_reap (slab allocator maintenance), vmstat_update (kernel statistics), kworker threads, hardware interrupts, and timer ticks (1000/second default).

Measurements of inter-thread latency on a 64-CPU system show tuned latency approximately 2x better than untuned on quiet systems. Under realistic workloads with deliberate thread contention every 30 milliseconds, untuned latency spikes above 800 microseconds while properly tuned systems remain consistently low.

The methodology emphasizes measurement discipline: end-to-end testing with production traffic replay, isolated one-change-at-a-time testing, and rigorous verification through tracing. Key principles include identifying latency-critical threads, reserving CPU resources, pinning threads to isolated cores, carefully handling interrupts, and continuously validating assumptions rather than relying on intuition.

talks.title: "Cursors Illustrated: Collaborative sketching" by Ryan Dy and Marlena Compton
talks.teaser: Explores React performance, immutability, and cursors through simple shapes and collaborative sketches for clearer web app data flow.
talks.summary:
The presenters open by treating sketching as a way to tame intimidating blank pages and dense technical ideas, using squares, circles, and triangles rather than polished art. They map a square to a pure function—a black box with inputs and outputs—and extend that picture to modern web apps that outgrow traditional page-turning models and MVC-style thinking. React enters as a view-layer framework where components behave like idempotent functions with props and state, JSX models layout, and the virtual DOM optimizes updates until highly interactive lists force the real issue: thousands of wasted renders when only one item changes.

The middle of the talk walks through JavaScript references versus deep comparison, mutable push versus immutable concat, and why reference equality enables fast change detection when data stays immutable. They illustrate one-way data flow with a todo app’s checkboxes—lifting state to a parent, passing props down, and sending intentions back up through callbacks. Cursors package that pairing of data and update logic: immutable push-style updates trigger callbacks that drive a single React render cycle per real change, making application history replayable and predictable.

They close by noting that immutability is not idiomatic JavaScript by default, yet matters for ambitious single-page experiences. The narrative they built live—code plus shared drawings—is offered as a method teammates can reuse when unpacking layered topics together.

talks.title: "How to run Neural Nets on GPUs' by Melanie Warrick
talks.teaser: Walks through why GPUs speed up neural network training and how to launch a small network on one in code.
talks.summary:
The talk explains neural networks at a high level and why training them is often the bottleneck. Each node applies weights and an activation function to its inputs, and supervised training adjusts those weights against known answers. Applications mentioned include speech assistants, self-driving cars, anomaly detection on equipment, and personalization in recommendations and ad placement.

GPUs suit this work because neural network calculations are many independent operations that can run in parallel. The speaker contrasted a 2012 Google experiment using about a thousand servers with 16 CPU cores each against later work that used three GPUs and far fewer resources. Practical challenges covered included moving data between CPU and GPU memory, memory limits often near four gigabytes, mini-batching, and branching code that slows parallel execution. Frameworks such as Caffe, Theano and DL4J can enable GPU use through configuration rather than hand-written CUDA code.

The live demo trained a small fully connected network on the MNIST handwritten digit dataset, with 784 inputs, a thousand hidden nodes and ten outputs, and reached 69% accuracy on about a thousand examples. For troubleshooting, the speaker suggested checking GPU status with nvidia-smi, restarting the CUDA driver when it stops being detected, shrinking the mini-batch when memory runs out, and limiting how often data syncs between CPU and GPU. The main takeaway is that training time is the hard part, and GPUs help most when the workload is parallel.

talks.title: "Performance Engineering At MasterCard" by Ted Boehm
talks.teaser: Details tiered architecture, per-tier stress tests, and capacity modeling for tens of thousands of fraud decisions per second.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens with how card theft shifted from SQL injection and database leaks toward memory scraping at point-of-sale devices, and why processors need global, real-time visibility. He describes work on Mastercard’s Safety Net platform, brought in to sustain fraud decisions as cards are swiped, with latency measured in tens of milliseconds and throughput in tens of thousands of transactions per second.

The core of the talk is three principles: tiers, tools, and “strategery.” A monolithic deployment created scaling and licensing pain; separating rules engines, databases, analytics, and management tiers made independent growth possible. On tools, he argues full production clones for performance labs are unrealistic, favors representative slices, and stresses per-tier stress testing until components break—uncovering limits like a rules engine versus a NoSQL ceiling, a vendor library defaulting to debug logging, and MQ receive paths pinned to one CPU. He covers metrics design, ongoing server monitoring to end blame games, Java garbage-collection pain (thousands of major collections daily), moves through CMS and then Azul Zing for flatter latency, and building production-aligned Excel models plus heat-map forecasts for executives.

Practitioners are urged to show problems graphically, propose concrete fixes before asking for budget, and follow up with measured results. Dashboards and Splunk helped keep leadership engaged; a dedicated performance team avoids being pulled entirely into feature delivery.

talks.title: "PTero: Architecture and Development" by Michael Kiwala and David Morton
talks.teaser: Explains how Tarot, a service-oriented workflow engine for genomics pipelines, is architected, developed and deployed.
talks.summary:
The talk traces how a genome research center at Washington University moved from its original genome modeling system to Tarot, a workflow orchestration engine. Early bioinformatics tools were fragile file-based programs, so the team wrapped them behind a uniform interface. A later engine, Flow, scaled well but was tied to Perl and an internal database, which limited outside adoption.

Tarot is built from three kinds of services: a Petri service that runs the nets, a workflow service that accepts submissions and manages task inputs and outputs, and job services that execute shell commands or dispatch work to an LSF cluster. All are Python services with JSON-based REST APIs and webhooks. Tasks describe goals, while methods describe how to reach them, and methods are tried in order until one succeeds. In a worked example, a set of per-sample variant files was reorganized into per-chromosome files, using a shortcut method to skip indexing that already existed and parallel execution across files.

The team develops under a 12-factor, stateless design, tracks issues across submodules with a Kanban-style view, and runs submodule tests on Travis CI. Jenkins handles LSF tests because that license is proprietary, and the system test doubles as a production monitor every fifteen minutes or so. Developers can run the whole stack in a Vagrant VM. The speakers note a new job service needs under 300 lines of Python, and they invite contributions.

talks.title: "Make the Back-End Team Jealous: Elm in Production" by Richard Feldman
talks.teaser: Shows how a web team moved part of a production front end from JavaScript to Elm and what it gained in bugs and refactoring.
talks.summary:
Richard Feldman describes how his company builds a grammar tool for teachers on Ruby on Rails, with React and Flux on the front end. He demonstrates an active and passive voice exercise whose interface took months to iterate on, because reorganizing the tangled component wiring was error-prone and broke the tests that covered the old design.

He then recounts rewriting his open-source side project, Dreamwriter, in Elm. He highlights Elm's virtual DOM, semantic versioning enforced by the package manager, and a time-travel debugger. Using a Maybe type, the compiler rejects a list lookup that could come back empty, and pure functions with tasks make side effects easy to trace. Refactors that compile usually work on the first run.

His team then tested Elm in one production Flux store, using ports to exchange data with the existing JavaScript. They reported fewer bugs, cheaper refactoring, better morale and hiring interest, and a newcomer who wrote production Elm within a couple of weeks through pair programming. The takeaway is to accept the setup risk and start with a small, isolated piece.

talks.title: "Pixie - A Lightweight Lisp with 'Magical' Powers" by Timothy Baldridge
talks.teaser: Presents Pixie, a small Lisp with a tracing JIT, lightweight threads, and direct C interop built on RPython.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Timothy Baldridge introduces Pixie, a lightweight, dynamically typed Lisp language built on top of the RPython toolchain. Initiated roughly a year prior to the talk, Pixie sits between alpha and beta stages. Designed to be small, fast, and feature-rich, Pixie features a ~2.5 MB gzipped download size, a 10 MB RAM footprint at REPL startup, and starts in approximately 175 milliseconds on a laptop. Baldridge outlines Pixie’s core strengths, specifically its tracing JIT compiler, lightweight green threading via stacklets and continuations, and automated foreign function interfacing (FFI) with C.

### Key Topics
- **Pixie Design & Syntax**: Pixie adopts Clojure-inspired syntax with S-expressions, immutable collections (such as persistent hashmaps), and REPL-driven development, while introducing distinct implementation choices such as passing variadic function arguments as arrays rather than linked lists.
- **RPython Architecture**: Pixie leverages the RPython translation toolchain (from PyPy), which translates statically inferred, restricted Python code into C, embeds a garbage collector, and automatically generates tracing JIT infrastructure from loop and optimization hints.
- **Tracing JIT Compilation**: Rather than optimizing entire methods or relying heavily on complex inlining heuristics, the tracing JIT records loop execution paths at runtime, unrolls polymorphic function dispatches, strips guards and unused branches, and flattens abstract functional code into concise CPU machine instructions.
- **Concurrency & Asynchronous I/O**: The runtime provides lightweight threads decoupled from operating system threads via stacklets and delimited continuations (`call-cc`). This mechanism integrates with Node.js's underlying `libuv` library and enables high-level abstractions like Communicating Sequential Processes (CSP).
- **Native C Interoperability (FFI)**: Pixie provides an automated FFI system named `ffi-infer`, which inspects C headers via C++ Boost type traits to extract types, struct layouts, constants, and function pointer signatures without requiring large dependencies like LibClang or handwritten parsers.

### Technical Details
- **Benchmark Performance**: In a Mandelbrot set benchmark, Pixie renders the algorithm in dynamic Lisp code in about 743 ms without type hints once the JIT warms up, competitive with static Java (600 ms) and LLVM bytecode (500 ms).
- **JIT Hints & Optimizations**: Functions like double-polymorphic dispatch (`-add`) can be annotated with `@elidable_promote`. This informs the JIT that repeated argument types will yield the same function lookup, effectively reducing polymorphic dispatch and overhead down to roughly four machine instructions.
- **Continuation Mechanics**: A delimited `call-cc` captures a continuation up to the lightweight thread's body rather than the full program continuation. This continuation handle can be passed into asynchronous C callbacks in `libuv` (such as sleeping or async I/O) to seamlessly pause and resume threads.
- **FFI Inference via Boost**: Pixie avoids parsing C code manually or bundling heavy compilers by writing small C++ files with Boost type-traits templates to deduce argument types, sizes, and offsets. The resulting compiled bytecode can be cached to disk for fast startup on production nodes.
- **Python Interop Experiment**: Baldridge demonstrates using Pixie's open-ended dot-operator dispatch (`.append`) and C FFI to wrap Python's C API, allowing Pixie code to instantiate and manipulate native Python lists.

### Takeaways
Pixie showcases how pairing modern language toolchains like RPython with functional Lisp semantics can yield a compact, high-performance runtime. By automatically inferring C bindings and compiling functional abstractions into optimized traces, Pixie offers high-performance dynamic scripting with minimal operational footprint. The project is open-source on GitHub for experimentation and development.

talks.title: "No, Really... Robots and JavaScript?!" by Raquel Vélez
talks.teaser: The session connects JavaScript and inexpensive microcontrollers so web developers can prototype robots without a robotics PhD.
talks.summary:
Industrial robotics often looks out of reach because sensor fusion, advanced degrees, and huge budgets dominate the story. The presenter reframes the problem for software people: Node’s asynchronous I/O matches the steady stream of sensor input and actuator output, and a small core plus npm packages such as Johnny-Five and robotics-oriented math libraries lowers the hardware barrier.

The middle of the talk walks through the Nodebots idea—robots programmed in JavaScript—with hello-world blink demos, sumo bots, off-the-shelf drones, and community projects like a Twitter-driven LED sash and a smooth hexapod built by combining browser animations with hardware. Honest downsides follow: deep dependency stacks can hide linear algebra and bugs, and the ecosystem still lacks mature patterns for errors, testing, and architecture.

Live demos cover forward and inverse kinematics on a serial manipulator, servo setup with Johnny-Five, and strobing an LED, along with how Firmata and serial packages bridge code to Arduino boards. Starter kits around one hundred dollars or less are suggested for safe experimentation. The closing message is that pairing JavaScript with cheap open boards is a playful on-ramp that can pull more people into engineering before they wrestle with syntax and theory.

talks.title: "The Programming Language Called Classical Chinese" by David Branner
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for "The Programming Language Called Classical Chinese" by David Branner.

talks.title: "Everything Old is New Again: Quoted Domain Specific Languages" by Philip Wadler
talks.teaser: Shows how to embed SQL in a functional host language by quoting queries and normalizing them into a single database query.
talks.summary:
The talk shows how to integrate a domain specific language, here SQL, into a functional host language without the usual mismatch between code and data. A naive version that loads whole tables as data and loops over them is shown to be slow and impractical at scale. The proposed fix treats queries as quoted terms, data structures that represent code, which a normalizer simplifies before translating them into one SQL query.

The middle works through examples: range queries parameterised over values, higher-order predicates reduced to flat SQL, and predicate trees built as data and then translated. The speaker contrasts closed quotations, which bind no free variables, with the open style common in embedded DSLs, and explains why standard F# forces the closed form. Gentzen's sub-formula property is presented as the reason normalization removes functions when tables and results hold only scalar records. A timing comparison suggests normalization adds little cost next to query runtime, while older F# query systems sometimes produced many queries.

The talk closes by noting the same technique was applied to Feldspar, a signal processing DSL integrated into Haskell, and that it works for both lazy and strict host languages. The main takeaway for designers is to choose normalization rules that fit the host language, with the main cost being the effort of writing the normalizer once. Audience questions covered sorting and grouping, recursion, and catching unsupported host functions before runtime.

talks.title: "Security for Humans: Privacy and Coercion Resistant Design" by Morgan Marquis-Boire
talks.teaser: Maps the attackers behind targeted surveillance and argues for designing systems that resist coercion.
talks.summary:
Morgan Marquis-Boire opens with a personal account of how the early internet looked like a liberating force, then explains that powerful institutions soon adopted the same tools. He presents a threat-modeling taxonomy of attackers, starting with a passive eavesdropper and an active man-in-the-middle operator, and then moves through state intelligence agencies, commercial surveillance vendors, cyber mercenaries, criminal groups and coercion through physical force. He ties each actor to cost, using the price of a network injector rack and the expense of human intelligence as examples.

He then walks through case work. Malware aimed at Syrian activists and journalists, spyware sold by FinFisher and Hacking Team used against activists in Bahrain, Morocco and the UAE, and a Hacking Team mobile implant that could place covert calls to record ambient audio are all covered. He also describes filtering and monitoring gear from Blue Coat found on networks in Syria, Iran and Sudan, and state-linked targeting of bloggers and journalists in Vietnam. Services, he notes, increasingly face legal demands for data or key material, and he cites Skype's redesign, Lavabit and BitLocker as examples.

He concludes that any popular service will eventually be pressured to weaken its security model, so systems should be designed with that pressure in mind rather than fixed after an audit. He argues that the security community has too often produced systems people do not use, and that the people who build systems need to take this on directly.

talks.title: "Architectural Patterns of Resilient Distributed Systems" by Ines Sombra
talks.teaser: Surveys resilience literature and industry case studies, then distills design and operations patterns for distributed systems.
talks.summary:
The talk asks why resilience matters in distributed systems: the ability to keep working or adapt when things go wrong. The speaker walks through three models from the literature. The first is the harvest and yield paper, which argues that yield, the fraction of answered queries, matters more than uptime and suggests strategies such as graceful degradation and composing systems from independent subsystems. The second is a healthcare-derived safety model, where an operating point drifts toward an accident boundary under efficiency pressure. The third ranks failures by probability and treats the unknown-unknowns area as growing with scale.

Industry examples follow. Netflix isolated API dependencies with per-dependency thread pools, aggressive timeouts, retries, and circuit breakers. Google's Chubby lock service paired a server with a client library and restricted the operations users could perform. The speaker's own company shows a purging system that evolved through three versions, and a failover design that moves MAC addresses between hosts when a node fails.

The closing section turns these ideas into design and operations questions: does the service favor harvest or yield, are redundancies and failure domains real, can operators control and be on call for it, and do alerts link to actions? Testing dependency failures, treating configuration as an interface, and accepting that resilience cannot be bolted on later are the main lessons.

talks.title: "Cache à la carte: a framework for in-memory caching" by Yao Yue
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning "Cache à la carte: a framework for in-memory caching" by Yao Yue.

talks.title: "Look ma, no OS! Unikernels and their applications" by Matt Bajor
talks.teaser: Surveys lean unikernels versus containers, efficiency and security tradeoffs, and library-OS projects practitioners can try.
talks.summary:
Modern microservice stacks pile orchestration, configuration management, and polyglot runtimes on top of Linux and hypervisors, creating layers that are hard to debug, patch, and reason about. The speaker contrasts necessary versus unnecessary complexity in typical container deployments, including duplicated isolation, oversized kernels, shared attack surfaces, and upgrade cadences that mix security and functionality fixes.

A unikernel is described as a specialized virtual machine bundling the application, configuration, language runtime, and minimal library operating system drivers for virtual hardware, deployed directly on a hypervisor with far fewer middle layers than Docker on Linux. Posix-compliant variants target unmodified applications with smaller footprints; forward-compatible, language-specific builds pursue maximum specialization. Benefits outlined include higher density, faster incident isolation to owned code, smaller images, hypervisor-level isolation, reduced homogeneity across deployments, and limited post-compromise tooling on the guest.

The talk surveys projects such as MirageOS, rump kernels, Runtime.js, LING, HalVM, OSv, Clive, and ClickOS, plus a self-service Vagrant repository with Mirage static-site, Jitsu on-demand deployment, LING, Runtime.js, and a multi-unikernel WordPress stack. Practitioners are encouraged to experiment where production use already exists, while accepting tradeoffs like weaker backward compatibility and hypervisor dependencies.

talks.title: "rustc in userland" by Richo Healey
talks.teaser: A walkthrough traces Rust compiler libraries and LLVM bindings through a naive Brainfuck pipeline to assembly and beyond.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens from a security researcher's angle on Rust, memory safety, and the appeal of controlling how code is translated and executed. It introduces bootstrapping ideas around Rust's object model, where compiler components ship as libraries with rich metadata, and notes the tradeoffs of nightly feature gates and unstable compiler internals.

The core demo path builds a deliberately naive Brainfuck toolchain: tokenizing and parsing into a structured program representation, interpreting it, then emitting x86 assembly with naive loop labeling before discussing peephole-style improvements. The speaker contrasts monolithic GCC with modular Clang and LLVM, explains intermediate representation as a portable codegen target, and walks through replacing hand-written assembly with Rust LLVM bindings and a later approach that pattern-matches a strict subset of Rust syntax into the same machinery.

Practitioners should expect frank limits—fragile assumptions, linker involvement, compile-time pain, and APIs that move quickly—including newer Rust intermediate representation work that landed shortly before the talk. The closing emphasis is that Rust exposes unusually usable compiler-facing building blocks for experimentation, with excellent diagnostics during iterative parser and codegen work, while warning against treating any of this as production-stable infrastructure.

talks.title: "Gamma: A simple model for WebGL" by Kovas Boguta
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning "Gamma: A simple model for WebGL" by Kovas Boguta.

talks.title: "HTTP/2 in Erlang" by Joe DeVivo
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in "HTTP/2 in Erlang" by Joe DeVivo.

talks.title: "GC Tuning Confessions Of A Performance Engineer" by Monica Beckwith
talks.teaser: Explains JVM garbage collector trade-offs, metrics pitfalls, and practical tuning guidance for HotSpot G1 and CMS.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames performance engineering as planning around non-functional requirements—throughput, latency percentiles, and worst-case pause times—before tuning. A four-system example shows how averages and 99th percentiles can look healthy while a single system hits roughly 20,699 seconds of pause time from full collections and evacuation failures, reinforcing the need for detailed GC logging in production.

The middle walks through HotSpot collectors and their trade-offs among throughput, latency, and footprint. Serial and parallel collectors, CMS concurrent marking with promotion and concurrent mode failures, and G1 region-based mixed collections are compared. G1 topics include incremental compaction, marking thresholds, evacuation failures, humongous objects, reserve percent, heap waste percent, and reading common log tags for Eden occupancy, parallel scaling, and reference processing.

Practitioners are urged to set realistic goals, avoid copying CMS flags onto G1, start with simple heap and pause-time settings, and adjust marking thresholds, concurrent threads, and mixed-collection ergonomics deliberately. Collector-specific guidance covers young-generation sizing, premature promotion, CMS fragmentation, and distributing G1 mixed work to limit full GC fallbacks.

talks.title: "big-bang: the world, universe, and network in the programming language" by Matthias Felleisen
talks.teaser: Demonstrates how Big Bang turns school math into animations, event-driven worlds, and networked student programs in Racket.
talks.summary:
Matthias Felleisen opens with a critique of traditional school arithmetic and describes a 1995 effort to combine mathematics with programming so learners work with images, scenes, and animations instead of only numeric drills. He walks through middle-school examples such as building trees from shapes, placing a horse buggy along a route over time, and using the animate construct to turn those ideas into motion drawn from familiar pre-algebra.

The core of the session is the big-bang language construct as a small functional model of input and output: state as ordinary values, handlers for clock ticks, keys, and mouse events, and a to-draw renderer, demonstrated first on simple counters and then on a string-based text editor with shift handling, deletion, and conditional logic. He extends the same picture to multiple communicating worlds and a central echo server that registers peers and broadcasts messages, including a live audience exercise typing speak commands toward a hosted address.

He closes by sketching a larger universe layer that nests networks of functional actors, publish-subscribe style coordination, and early prototypes such as chat and proxy servers built by collaborators including Tony garok Jones. The practical takeaway is a deliberately continuous curriculum from sixth grade through college, using explicit design discipline and tools that grow with the learner rather than treating programming as an end in itself.

talks.title: "A History of Programming Languages for 2 Voices" by David Nolen and Michael Bernstein
talks.teaser: A two-voice chronology juxtaposes landmark programming languages with period music to trace reinvention, access, and cultural diversity.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames itself as an idiosyncratic mixtape rather than a complete survey. It opens in the mid-1930s, linking Alonzo Church’s lambda calculus and early computability ideas with recorded music’s rise and experimental composers such as Olivier Messiaen and the musique concrète work of Pierre Henry and Pierre Schaeffer.

A “reinvention” segment covers the 1940s–1950s emergence of real programmable machines and higher-level languages, including Fortran, Lisp, and ALGOL 60, paired with bebop and hard bop examples from Thelonious Monk and Cecil Taylor. Later sections highlight BASIC as computing for broader audiences, Motown as popular craft, and 1960s shifts toward new semantics and paradigms—Landin’s language-design vision, Smalltalk, and Prolog—alongside psychedelic-era rock and Brazilian Tropicália.

The 1980s and 1990s pair “underground” languages such as Miranda and Erlang with independent and sample-driven music, then note how Ruby and peers spread via mailing lists rather than academic papers alone. The closing argument urges continued invention in programming languages, aspiring to the diversity and depth found in twentieth-century recorded music.

talks.title: "Distributed, Eventually Consistent Computations" by Christopher Meiklejohn
talks.teaser: Shows how convergent data structures and dataflow let distributed programs stay correct without heavy synchronization.
talks.summary:
Christopher Meiklejohn presents Lasp, a programming model for distributed computation that combines convergent data structures with a dataflow execution model. The problem he starts from is that synchronization is costly, and it becomes a real obstacle for low-power IoT devices with limited connectivity and for mobile games where players keep playing offline and their changes must later merge into shared leaderboards. Rather than building on strongly coordinated systems, the talk argues for starting with no synchronization at all and adding coordination only where a global invariant requires it.

The middle of the talk covers the building blocks. Replicas that receive identical updates in any sequence converge, which the speaker ties to monotonic functions, and conflict-free replicated data types provide that behaviour for each object. He walks through an add/remove set that keeps tombstones so concurrent operations resolve deterministically, then shows how Lasp composes such objects with map, filter, fold and product while keeping their metadata monotonic. Inflationary reads let a process resume from another replica without going backwards. A gossip-based runtime called selective hearing is presented as work in progress.

The worked example is an advertisement counter for a mobile game. Clients increment local counters while offline and periodically report to a data center, where a process waits for a threshold of 50,000 before removing ads from the set. Only the sync step needs coordination, and the dataflow graph can be placed on any machine. The closing points are that synchronization is expensive, that some properties such as global invariants and atomic visibility still need it, and that a 0.0.1 release of Lasp is available with a runnable demo program.

talks.title: "The art of service discovery at scale" by Nitesh Kant
talks.teaser: Explores how large data centers map microservices dynamically and why discovery controls visibility, not true availability.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens in a large data-center setting where hundreds of microservices and constantly shifting instances make static machine labels useless. Service discovery is framed as a live registry: instances announce startup and shutdown, while callers ask which endpoints exist and which ones seem reachable right now.

Heartbeats and shutdown signals cannot answer availability uniformly because network partitions make reachability a local judgment. The speaker argues that marking nodes unavailable is safer to trust than marking them up, which supports draining, debugging, and graceful isolation without pretending discovery proves liveness. Under partition pressure, choosing availability over strict consistency fits how callers already cope with failed calls, especially when long-lived verified connections reduce blind routing.

The later design direction favors coordination-free discovery nodes, stateful client-server streams, ordered updates, and temporary tolerance of conflicting copies until heartbeats and replication bound convergence. A production partition story shows aggressive eviction spreading stale absence signals, motivating self-preservation limits. Practitioners should treat discovery as visibility control, plan for its own outages during scale-up, and harden clients rather than expecting the registry to guarantee that every listed instance will answer.

talks.title: "Sweaters as a Service" by Amy Wibowo
talks.teaser: Follows a team of engineers who hack a 1980s knitting machine so it can knit custom images from a computer.
talks.summary:
Amy Wibowo's project began with a Kotaku article about a knitting peripheral Nintendo had considered for the Super Nintendo but never released. Wanting that device to exist, she tracked down a decades-old home knitting machine and set out to make it turn images from a computer into knitwear.

The work started as an internal hackathon project with a group of engineers who knew nothing about knitting. The team first had to learn the machine's built-in patterns, and when parts were missing they improvised a yarn spooler from paper cups. They found that animal-fiber yarns snagged less often. To send custom pictures, they emulated a floppy drive, built a USB-to-serial cable to match an unusual pinout, and converted images into 1-bit bitmaps using dithering. A small Ruby and Sinatra web app then let anyone upload a photo and see which buttons to press on the machine.

The talk closes with lessons about respect for craft, teamwork without ego, and the value of being a beginner again. Ideas for future work include a drawing interface, a robotic arm to automate the knitting, and replacing the machine's logic board with an Arduino.

talks.title: "Literate interactive coding: Devcards" by Bruce Hauman
talks.teaser: Shows how DevCards and Figwheel widen live feedback so ClojureScript UI work can exercise many component states at once.
talks.summary:
Bruce Hauman frames front-end work as fighting two frustrations: constant full browser reloads and relying on the main application as the only place to see behavior. He contrasts manual reload loops with hot code reloading via Figwheel, arguing that reloadable imperative code pays off quickly in a world of endless UI tweaks.

The core of the session introduces DevCards, a ClojureScript library built around a defcard macro that pairs literate markdown with live code examples in named visual namespaces. Through a Strange Loop todos demo, he renders values, React/Hiccup elements, and multiple todo states side by side, fixes styling and blank-item edge cases, and layers thin custom tooling such as raised tests, state atoms, time-travel undo, and even ad hoc graphs for a music generator.

He closes by contrasting feedback rate from hot reload with feedback bandwidth from developing outside the main app: less environmental coupling, room for playful experiments, and durable validation documents others can exercise. Practitioners take away a pattern for example-driven UI development rather than serial state clicking in one running application.

talks.title: "Beating Threads - live coding with real time" by Sam Aaron
talks.teaser: Sonic Pi virtual-time sleeps, named threads, scoped effects, and cue/sync get a technical tour for reliable live performance.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with why classroom-friendly live coding needs trivial entry points and timing that survives real performance conditions. Ordinary Ruby sleep and wall-clock drift break loops and concurrent parts on slower hardware, so execution time stacks unpredictably across threads.

The middle walks through Sonic Pi's replacements: virtual time as a per-thread clock, delta sleeps that realign to schedule, lookahead when messaging an external synth process, and timeout exceptions when a thread falls too far behind. In-thread concurrency, with-fx blocks that close over time and tidy effects, and live loops that pair named functions with named threads enable hot code changes without spawning duplicate voices. Cue and sync add cross-thread barriers; syncing also copies the cuing thread's logical time so restarted or fixed parts line up with ongoing loops.

Practitioners gain a concrete picture of how liveness, determinism, and coordination interact in a live system, including why formal timing proofs matter when audiences expect the beat to hold. The close encourages trying the built-in tutorial, examples, and on-stage error recovery via sync rather than stopping the whole set.

talks.title: "Probabilistic Programs Which Make (Common) Sense" by Zenna Tavares
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in "Probabilistic Programs Which Make (Common) Sense" by Zenna Tavares.

talks.title: "All In With Determinism for Performance and Testing in Distributed Systems" by John Hugg
talks.teaser: Shows how all-in determinism cuts replication latency while a nefarious self-check workload validates serializable ACID on VoltDB.
talks.summary:
The talk opens on replicated database designs—primary/replica changelogs, multi-writer conflict resolution—and argues that ordering deterministic operations on identical starting state yields matching replicas without last-write-wins merges. That active-active model centers on a logical log: the same ordered operations applied in parallel locally, replicable across clusters or replayed after failure.

The middle section maps non-determinism sources (randomness, wall clock, record order, external calls, bad memory, security libraries) and how VoltDB constrains SQL, hashes DML outcomes across replicas, and snapshots cluster-wide state. Deterministic logical logging is pitched as synchronous replication with modest added latency, compact network payloads, and overlap of persistence with execution—on the order of hundreds of thousands of asset transactions per second per node in cited deployments, with tradeoffs around mixed-version upgrades and divergent-replica shutdown.

The closing half targets verification: serializable isolation enforced by ordering, contrasted briefly with simulation-style approaches elsewhere. The TransactionID selfcheck 2 workload floods concurrent nasty transactions, extends schema and mayhem threads, runs across OS and fault injection, and uses committed-transaction checking for durability—extended by engineers when coordination or bulk ingestion changes.

talks.title: "Transactions: myths, surprises and opportunities" by Martin Kleppmann
talks.teaser: Traces database isolation levels from System R to microservices and shows where serializability and causality fit.
talks.summary:
The talk traces database transactions back to IBM's System R in the 1970s and questions how vague the ACID acronym really is. Each property is examined as it is used today. Durability has moved from archive tapes to fsync and replication. Consistency is a property of how an application uses the database, not of the database itself. Atomicity is better seen as abortability: whatever goes wrong, a failed transaction can be rolled back and retried.

The isolation section is the core. Examples show dirty reads and dirty writes under read committed, read skew in a bank transfer that makes money appear to vanish, and write skew in an on-call doctor scenario that breaks an invariant even under snapshot isolation. Many databases label snapshot isolation as repeatable read, and about half of a surveyed set do not offer serializability at all. Serializability can come from two-phase locking, from serial execution as in VoltDB, or from serializable snapshot isolation as in PostgreSQL.

Across microservices and stream processing, transactions usually stop at service boundaries, because atomic commit and total ordering need consensus, which is brittle across services. Teams fall back on compensating transactions, sagas and after-the-fact apologies. The talk proposes causality as a middle ground that can be tracked without global coordination, preserving the order of events such as unfriending before posting. The takeaway is to know which isolation guarantees your database actually provides.

talks.title: "Streams: The data structure we need" by Pam Selle
talks.teaser: Covers Unix pipes, push and pull streams, and JavaScript patterns from Node through RxJS and emerging browser APIs.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues that streams are an underappreciated abstract data structure worth learning end to end. It opens with Unix shell piping as everyday stream usage, then uses a simple cup-and-water analogy for source, transform, and sink. Streams are framed as delayed lists from SICP: list-like operations without holding everything in memory, modeling unbounded or unknown-length data, and avoiding mutable assignment in stream processing.

Push versus pull modes are contrasted with fire-hose versus bucket-from-the-lake metaphors, overload versus blocking tradeoffs, and mapping to callbacks versus iterators. In JavaScript the speaker walks through Node readable streams and piping for efficient servers, ES6 generators as pull streams with live demos, and libraries such as Bacon.js, Highland.js, and RxJS. Emerging pieces include browser streams with fetch, Object.observe, and proposed observables.

Practical demos tie the ideas together: an RSS aggregator built with Highland, a star visualization using fetch, Gulp’s stream-based builds, DOM mutation observers in a browser extension, and a small RxJS click demo. References point to node streams handbooks, Kyle Simpson’s generator router, Cycle.js, and rewriting RxJS. Practitioners should leave with a mental model for when to pipe, yield, or observe, and where standards were heading at the time of the talk.

talks.title: "Hopelessness and Confidence in Distributed Systems Design" by Camille Fournier
talks.teaser: Three real-world systems show how embracing tradeoffs replaces hope-and-fear cycles in distributed design.
talks.summary:
Distributed systems marketing promises hassle-free scaling and flawless synchronization, yet rigorous testing of popular stores often exposes lost data and fragile behavior. The presentation argues that hope and fear feed each other, and that engineers gain steadier judgment by accepting imperfection and treating every architectural choice as an explicit tradeoff between competing goals.

The central tension is scale versus failure tolerance: more components mean more independent and cascading failures, while stronger resilience adds coordination overhead that limits growth. Three production histories illustrate different balances. A bank risk-analysis cache moved from a single machine to a sharded, synchronous cluster that prioritized scale over availability, succeeding partly because exhaustive automated tests allowed a small team to refactor millions of lines while dozens of developers kept shipping. A global service-discovery layer used ZooKeeper with a smart client that wrote locally but read across regions, trading a single global consistency model for WAN bandwidth and latency. A microservices migration shifted complexity into service interconnections, highlighting human bottlenecks, the efficiency-versus-thoroughness tradeoff, and data designs that minimize coordination while accepting benign staleness.

The closing message is that no design stays optimal forever—hardware, organizations, and requirements change—so wrong choices are normal. Practitioners should identify worst cases that truly matter to the business, invest in tests and mindful client behavior, and replace paralysis with confident, informed tradeoffs rather than chasing perfect platforms.

talks.title: "Strange Loops: Capturing Knots With Powerful Notations" by Katherine Ye
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in "Strange Loops: Capturing Knots With Powerful Notations" by Katherine Ye.

talks.title: "Visualising program execution" by Jan Paul Posma
talks.teaser: Shows how recording full execution traces makes JavaScript program behaviour visible, from simple loops to a production web app.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that debugging JavaScript is largely guesswork: developers form a hypothesis, add logging, rerun the program and repeat. The speaker proposes recording a complete execution trace once, so every value and step can be inspected afterwards without reproducing the problem again and again. This approach is called omniscient debugging.

A short live-coding example shows how a source-to-source transform can rewrite a small loop so that each variable declaration and assignment logs its values to a global array, which then feeds a spark-line view. For larger, performance-heavy applications, the speaker describes an educational game editor for children that takes periodic snapshots and replays the program deterministically with full instrumentation only when it is paused. That replay technique is drawn from an existing WebKit research project called TimeLapse.

A demo on a company website shows a timeline of events laid out by time and call depth, with logged function arguments, search and collapsible branches. The speaker points out how a scroll-driven rendering pattern shows up clearly in the trace. The tool is described as experimental, built over roughly two months, and its effect on developer productivity is not yet measured. The takeaway is that a full trace, paired with the right visualisation, can make unexpected behaviour recognisable quickly.

talks.title: "Faster Objects and Arrays" by Gil Tene
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning "Faster Objects and Arrays" by Gil Tene.

talks.title: "Aurelia - the next generation JavaScript framework you will love" by Jakub Jedryszek
talks.teaser: Builds a small single-page app live in the Aurelia framework, using mostly plain JavaScript and convention-based binding.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Aurelia, an early-alpha JavaScript framework created by Rob Eisenberg after he left the Angular team over differing views on where the framework should go. The speaker, a Microsoft engineer working on a large single-page application, wanted to check the blog's Angular-versus-Aurelia claims himself. He starts from the project's navigation skeleton, installs its npm and jspm dependencies, and walks through the default setup, which transpiles ES2015 code with Babel and uses Gulp and BrowserSync for automation.

Working live, he builds a small app from scratch. He binds two text inputs to view-model properties, computes a full name with a getter, and styles the form with Bootstrap. A list supports adding, deleting and inline editing, with the binding handled by convention rather than framework-specific code, so the app ends up at about 28 lines of JavaScript. He then adds routing with configure router, a navigation menu and a second view. A live call to the GitHub API to list repositories returned an error during the demo, so he switched to a sample JSON endpoint and logged the response instead.

The main takeaway is that most of the code is plain JavaScript, though some framework behaviour happens behind the scenes and has to be learned. He cautions against production use while the framework is still alpha, although its star count and contributor base are already notable, and expects it to become a serious competitor to Angular 2 later. In the Q&A he said real performance numbers would have to come from large projects built with it.

talks.title: "Apache Kafka and the Next 700 Stream Processing Systems" by Jay Kreps
talks.teaser: Explains how Kafka's log abstraction and related building blocks combine to support large-scale stream processing.
talks.summary:
Kreps frames stream processing as a third paradigm alongside request-response services and batch jobs. In a stream processor the program decides when to emit outputs, which lets it trade latency against efficiency. He argues that the middle ground between millisecond request handling and hours-long batch runs has had little supporting infrastructure. He then lists the hard problems such a system must solve: partitioning and scaling, state and fault tolerance, reconciling streams with tables, handling time and late-arriving data, and reprocessing after code changes.

He then explains Kafka's core as a partitioned, replicated log that producers append to and consumers read from. Consumer groups divide partitions among processes and rebalance when members join or leave. Stateful processors back their local state up to changelog topics, and log compaction keeps only the latest value per key. In this model a batch job is just a reader that stops at the end of the log, so batch and streaming become the same pattern. Rewinding to offset zero lets a team reprocess history after changing logic. He also describes Kafka Streams as a library rather than a separate cluster.

He closes with a stream data platform pattern: capture changes from databases and applications into Kafka, run transformations in an asynchronous middle layer, and feed the results to analytics and to Hadoop or data warehouses. He cites LinkedIn's volume of about 1.1 trillion records per day as evidence of scale, and points to the open source project and design documents for further reading.

talks.title: "Typed Clojure: From Optional to Gradual Typing" by Ambrose Bonnaire-Sergeant
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in "Typed Clojure: From Optional to Gradual Typing" by Ambrose Bonnaire-Sergeant.

talks.title: "Immutable Data Science with Datomic, Spark and Kafka" by Konrad Scorciapino and Mauro Lopes
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in "Immutable Data Science with Datomic, Spark and Kafka" by Konrad Scorciapino and Mauro Lopes.

talks.title: "Building Scalable Stateful Services" by Caitie McCaffrey
talks.teaser: Explains how keeping state inside services enables data locality and stronger consistency, along with the routing trade-offs involved.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the stateless service model that has dominated for years, where a database holds the source of truth and each request fetches the data it needs. For chatty, session-based applications such as ride ordering, fitness tracking or games, the same data gets pulled across the network and thrown away again on every request, which adds latency and load on the database. The speaker argues for bringing state into the services themselves, so that a client's requests reach the machine already holding its data. This gives lower latency, the ability to keep answering when the database is down, and sticky connections that allow stronger consistency models while staying available.

The middle section covers how to build this. Persistent connections are the simplest route, but they need back pressure, since clusters can be overwhelmed when many long-lived sessions land on one server. Routing needs answers on cluster membership, which can be static, dynamic via gossip, or dynamic via consensus when strong agreement matters, and on work distribution, which can use random placement, consistent hashing or distributed hash tables. Real systems illustrate the options: Facebook's Scuba fans queries out across all machines and reports how much of the data answered, Uber's Ringpop uses gossip and consistent hashing to route dispatch sessions, and Microsoft's Orleans actor runtime, used for Halo 4 services, moves actors between machines to reach high CPU utilization.

The closing part lists pitfalls: unbounded in-memory structures, garbage collection costs for long-lived data, slow first connections that call for percentile-based measurement, crash recovery and deploys that must reload state. Facebook's fast restart approach, which copies memory to shared memory during deploys, is presented as one remedy. The main takeaway is to read the database literature, reuse proven protocols rather than inventing new ones, and make the assumptions behind stateful design explicit.

talks.title: "From Protesting to Programming: Becoming a Tech Activist" by Idalin "Abby" Bobé
talks.teaser: Links a path into technology with Ferguson-era activism, surveillance pitfalls, and hands-on training for community organizers.
talks.summary:
The speaker defines tech activism as the overlap between technologists and community organizers who share knowledge and build tools to protect oppressed people. Through a personal narrative—from a North Philadelphia upbringing, name and hiring bias, a crowd-funded first laptop, and work with groups such as Black Girls Code—they illustrate how access and representation shape who can enter the industry.

The talk centers on the Ferguson uprising after Michael Brown’s death: mapping St. Louis County’s fragmented municipalities and court-driven revenue policing, amplifying events through social media, and ThoughtWorks collaboration with Hands Up United on handsupunited.org, fundraising, and a police brutality reporting tool. They describe how phones, live streams, hashtags, and email were later turned against organizers through seizures, account suspensions, filtered hashtags, hacked donation sites, and surveillance ahead of the grand jury.

The speaker stayed in Ferguson to help launch the Roy Clay Sr. workshop—web development, graphic design, information security, and mobile skills tied to political awareness—with ThoughtWorks donating thirty laptops, twenty graduates receiving stipends and laptops, and projects such as sites for local businesses. They urge technologists to research repression, partner with groups like Hands Up United and Dream Defenders, host neighborhood tech nights, and build sustainable in-person programs rather than online-only curricula unreachable to half the world.

talks.title: "When "Worst" is Best (in Distributed Systems)" by Peter Bailis
talks.teaser: Maps how worst-case assumptions yield coordination-free designs improving scale, throughput, and latency.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a familiar tension: planning for extreme worst cases—from planet-scale load to space-hardened hardware or fully malicious developers—usually drags down average-case cost and performance. The speaker frames that tradeoff as a curve where handling more corner cases lowers everyday performance, then asks when deliberate worst-case thinking can bend the curve instead.

The core argument centers on distributed systems and networks. Delays, drops, and partition uncertainty push designers toward availability without coordination. Coordination-free execution can enable linear scale-out, much higher throughput on multi-item transactions (with large gains over lock-based coordination on EC2-style setups), and better use of multicore parallelism. The CAP theorem explains why strong consistency forces coordination, but the speaker argues many guarantees people rely on—including read committed—were historically implemented with locks that are costly across the network, and that alternatives such as multiversioning can preserve semantics with far better performance.

Beyond databases, the same mindset appears in replication and automated failover used for upgrades and slow nodes, in microservice tail latency amplified by large fan-out, in universal design benefiting all users, and in robust optimization preferring stable solutions over brittle peaks. Practitioners are encouraged to use extreme worst-case questions not as provisioning targets but as a way to map design space, set sensible boundaries, and challenge assumptions about what “normal” means.

talks.title: "How machine learning helps cancer research" by Evelina Gabasova

talks.title: LaunchCode CoderGirls
talks.teaser: A St. Louis all-women coding meetup shares weekly learning tracks, mentor-led projects, and job-placement outcomes.
talks.summary:
LaunchCode’s CoderGirls program in St. Louis is presented as a community extension of an organization that helps people enter tech jobs. Crystal Martin frames the group as a collective effort rather than a single organizer’s project: a Wednesday meetup focused on networking, learning, and bringing more women into the local tech scene.

Mentors outline parallel learning tracks. The web development group works through HTML, CSS, PHP, and JavaScript and describes building a dedicated CoderGirls site, including a mobile-responsive design from the start. The Java track addresses the gap between classroom basics and job readiness through small team projects, tooling such as version control and ticketing, and iterative scoping; examples include a roommate finance tracker and a recipe program, with several participants placed or near placement in jobs. A CS50 continuation group describes structuring work in roughly twelve-week quarters and demos an Asteroids-style game built in Ruby after Harvard’s introductory CS course.

The closing message emphasizes scale—on the order of thirty-five to forty attendees and fifteen to twenty professional mentors weekly—and invites local participation, mentoring, or remote advocacy via Slack, social channels, and meetups at the CIC on Duncan Avenue.

talks.title: "Safe and fast parsers with Nom and Rust" by Geoffroy Couprie
talks.teaser: Shows how the Nom parser combinator library in Rust makes binary and text format parsing safer and fast.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why parsers for media and network formats keep producing memory-safety bugs, and why hand-written code in C is a common source. Couprie links the problem to ambiguous specifications, context-sensitive binary formats, and length calculations that overflow. He uses examples from a VLC media player bug history and from TLS implementations whose state machines let certificate verification be bypassed.

He then presents Nom, a parser combinator library for Rust. Small functions are chained into grammars that read much like the format itself, and parsers return slices of the input rather than copies, which keeps them fast without a garbage collector. The library also covers streaming through an incomplete result, bit-level parsing, a hex-dump combinator for debugging, and error chains that can be matched against stable messages. In his benchmarks on an MP4 file and an HTTP parser, Nom ran at latency comparable to a hand-written C state machine.

The takeaway is that Rust's compiler removes whole classes of memory bugs, but hand-written length arithmetic and unsafe code still need care. The practical goal is to make the safe approach the easy one, using readable and testable combinators. Couprie notes that about 50 open-source projects already use Nom for text and binary formats.

talks.title: "Propositions as Types" by Philip Wadler
talks.teaser: The lecture connects formal proofs with typed programs, spanning decidability, natural deduction, and the Curry-Howard correspondence.
talks.summary:
Philip Wadler frames the talk with early twentieth-century computability: Hilbert’s decision problem, Gödel’s incompleteness result, and the near-simultaneous definitions of algorithm due to Church, Gödel, and Turing. He then introduces Gentzen’s natural deduction, paired introduction and elimination rules, proof normalization, and the subformula property, including a small example where an indirect proof simplifies to a direct one.

The middle develops Church’s simply typed lambda calculus alongside the same logical rules, showing that proof simplification matches program evaluation and that simply typed terms terminate without general recursion. Wadler states the Curry–Howard correspondence—propositions as types, proofs as programs—and notes rediscoveries by Howard, Milner, Reynolds, and others that underpin modern functional languages and proof assistants.

The ending turns philosophical: equivalent independent definitions suggest discovery rather than invention, lambda calculus might communicate with aliens more plausibly than C, yet it is not a truly universal language. Questions cover linear logic and session types, category theory, probabilistic analogues, research impact timelines, and informatics as a broader name for the field.

talks.title: "How to Have your Causality and Wall Clocks, Too" by Jon Moore
talks.teaser: Adds epic resets and flocking to hybrid logical clocks so rogue server time cannot drag cluster timestamps beyond real time.
talks.summary:
Jon Moore frames a common service-oriented pattern: a request fans out downstream, each hop emits logs, and centrally collected timestamps can contradict the true causal order when wall clocks drift. He reviews Lamport’s happens-before logical clocks, then hybrid logical clocks that pair a physical time component with a counter so ordering respects causality while staying closer to human time.

Production reality undermines that neat picture. NTP can stop synchronizing after skew, reboots, or firewall mistakes, and a single manual clock fix set years into the future can force every node to assign logical times beyond real time until that year arrives. His distributed monotonic clocks add an epic counter for operational reset, and a degraded mode where outliers advance only the counter when they detect they are too far ahead of the flock.

The coordination layer piggybacks on ordinary inter-service messages, using population-protocol style interactions and recursive independent-set grouping to estimate a median clock and propagate relative offsets. Simulations on random graphs report logarithmic convergence time at about ten messages per second per node. He closes with open work on payload size, joins and departures, richer topologies, and formal guarantees, plus Q&A on lagging clocks, complementing NTP, and clockless clients that trust counters alone.

talks.title: "Teaching Kids Programming at the IOT Farm" by Jessica Ellis and Jesse Phelps
talks.teaser: Shows how a Boys and Girls Club program teaches teens programming through gardening, IoT boards and Raspberry Pis.
talks.summary:
The speakers run a teen programming program at a Boys and Girls Club in San Diego, where it is paired with a healthy lifestyles program that already grows food and teaches cooking. Teens who attended 30 hours of Java over a summer all came back the next session, and the work is done in pairs and mobs. An earlier camp that combined programming with cooking drew mostly girls, and its teenage counselors were paid for their skills.

The first hands-on project was a soil moisture monitor on an Intel Edison, meant to water plants only when the soil needed it. The sensor code was simple, but setup and software installation were the real obstacles, so the speakers judged it a failed project and learned from it. A tweeting display then hit Twitter's rule against repeated messages, forcing students to add changing suffixes. The team switched to Electric Imp boards, which connect to Wi-Fi through a phone app and let 84 kids finish a first IoT project. Later projects included a Raspberry Pi proximity alarm written in Python.

A data unit used pesto made four ways, with students collecting taste-test results and organizing them into visualizations that a community judge reviewed. The speakers argue that students drop out of computing around middle school, and that tying code to gardening and cooking keeps them engaged. Their takeaways are to give kids quick payoffs, use group work so failure feels shared, and frame tasks around something kids already care about. They plan a pilot with a nearby middle school.

talks.title: "Unconventional Programming with Chemical Computing" by Carin Meier
talks.teaser: Shows how molecule-style reaction rules compute primes, maxima and a self-healing mail system without sequential ordering.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a personal anecdote about a bump on the head while mowing the lawn, which led the speaker to think of living things as systems that process information through chemical reactions. It then sets up a comparison: finding primes the conventional way, with a filter over candidate divisors, versus a reaction-based approach where integers act as molecules that react pairwise under simple rules. Repeated shuffling and reacting leads the population to a steady state that contains the primes, and the speaker explains that this approach, called gamma chemical programming, is hard to predict in how many cycles it needs.

The middle section covers demos and extensions. A maximum is found by molecules that coalesce into the largest value, and higher-order reactions turn functions into molecules that capture values and hatch back out. Reducing reactions shrink the solution set, and a dining philosophers setup is modelled with fork, thinking and eating molecules. A mail system uses membranes that separate molecules, server molecules that route messages, and a sentinel molecule that repairs crashed servers, so the system organizes and heals itself.

The main takeaway is that removing built-in sequencing from code makes concurrency easier to reason about, and that simple local behaviours can combine into robust systems. The speaker notes that this work is still mostly research and points to code examples published online.

talks.title: "I See What You Mean" by Peter Alvaro
talks.teaser: Traces how a small Datalog-based research language shaped ideas about writing correct, order-tolerant distributed programs.
talks.summary:
Peter Alvaro, a UC Santa Cruz computer science professor, tells the story of Dedalus, a small research language he and colleagues built at UC Berkeley. He argues that abstractions often hide details that matter, and that distributed systems are hard largely because messages get reordered, lost, or delayed, which makes ordinary imperative code difficult to reason about. He recounts his earlier work at a search company, where he found that SQL-style queries were easier to get right than the C code he wrote for infrastructure.

He then explains why Datalog appealed to him. A program's meaning can be taken as the smallest set of facts that makes its rules hold, and that meaning does not depend on execution order. Lineage of each derived fact also shows why an output exists and whether it survives the loss of some inputs. Dedalus extends Datalog with time, using deductive, inductive and asynchronous rules, so state becomes facts persisting from one moment to the next and nondeterminism is stated openly. He shows that negation and self-reference can produce several possible meanings, and that confluence, a single outcome regardless of ordering, is undecidable in general. Programs without negation are confluent, which gives a practical target.

He closes with the follow-on systems: Bloom, which reports where a program is nondeterministic, Blazes, which suggests where ordering protocols are needed, and lineage-driven fault injection, which tests whether outcomes have redundant support. His takeaway for language and library designers is to avoid rigid abstractions that conceal failure, and to favor semantics that stay honest about what cannot be controlled.

talks.title: "How to make error handling less error-prone" by Daira Hopwood
talks.teaser: Explains why common error-handling mechanisms fail and proposes rollback-based recovery as a more dependable alternative.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that common error handling mechanisms fail too often and do the wrong thing. Errors are defined broadly as any departure from a program's usual path, from language faults like division by zero to library or program-level bugs. Mechanisms examined include global error state like errno, return codes that are easy to ignore, and error values such as NaN that can silently hide problems. A certificate-checking bug in one TLS library came from an inconsistent return convention introduced during refactoring.

Signal handlers and per-object handlers are shown to give little context about where a failure happened, which makes them hard to use safely. Exceptions are presented as a major improvement, since propagation is the default and handlers run only on error. Their weakness is that they do not keep program state consistent when an operation fails midway. The talk reviews exception guarantees, from basic to strong to no-throw, and argues that they compose poorly in general-purpose code, so it proposes making the strong guarantee a structural property of synchronous code.

The closing section covers recovery blocks, a 1975 mechanism that rolls state back and tries alternative implementations until an acceptance test passes. The speaker values that the shared acceptance test explains intent without reading every alternative, and that a simpler fallback can serve as an executable specification. A downside is the loss of detail about the failure. The talk suggests rollback-based recovery is worth adopting, with a reminder to choose memory-safe languages first.

talks.title: "Elixir and the Internet of Things" by Doug Rohrer
talks.teaser: A walkthrough shows how Elixir and OTP replace a Ruby backend so mass Wi-Fi thermostat reconnects no longer stall the platform.
talks.summary:
A home automation vendor needed its cloud backend to grow from a few thousand installed Wi‑Fi thermostats to a six‑figure rollout. The legacy Ruby stack, built around EventMachine, could not absorb the spike when every device reconnected at once after outages or deploys. Load testing and fixes to the AMQP client still left the event loop starved; an actor-style Ruby alternative only reached target connection rates on JRuby at enormous memory cost.

The team prototyped a TCP and RabbitMQ message router in Elixir on the Erlang VM, choosing readable syntax while leaning on OTP supervisors, lightweight processes, and clustering. They implemented a large acceptor pool on one listen socket, tuned restart strategies, and marked connection processes as temporary so routine disconnects would not trip default supervisor restart limits and tear down the whole tree. Routing backend messages to the right socket used globally registered names keyed by connection identifiers rather than a single registry process that serialized every lookup.

Practitioners hear when to reach for existing libraries such as Ranch or Thousand Island instead of custom acceptor pools, how child restart specifications interact with max restart intensity, and when global naming, ETS, or sharded maps fit clustered IoT gateways.

talks.title: "FRP In Practice: Taking a look at Reactive[UI/Cocoa]" by Paul Betts
talks.teaser: Surveys how GitHub native clients use ReactiveUI and ReactiveCocoa to model UI, git, and network work as composable signals.
talks.summary:
The speaker argues that modern desktop and mobile apps are inherently asynchronous, so scattering event handlers and mutable flags becomes hard to keep correct when timing races update UI state. He traces GitHub’s Mac and Windows clients from imperative beginnings toward a model where UI events, git output lines, and network calls are all treated as signals, inspired by Microsoft’s Reactive Extensions but bridged into mutable Cocoa and .NET UI stacks.

The middle of the session walks through the sister libraries ReactiveUI and ReactiveCocoa: property watching, derived values such as color from RGB inputs, commands that run background work and re-enable controls, and observable collections that filter and sort from changing predicates. Examples pulled from GitHub for Windows include shortening commit SHAs, an undo popup whose dismissal blends timers and user activity, and scheduler-driven “time travel” tests that advance simulated clocks for relative timestamps and pomodoro-style delays.

He closes with production friction teams should expect: onboarding takes months, automatic UI-thread scheduling had to be removed for speed, long signal chains leak memory tied to heavy views, virtualized lists struggle with operator cost on scroll, and stacks become deep and anonymous under AOT. Better signal logging, ETW-style concurrency views, and graph tracers are presented as the path to make the style maintainable at scale.

talks.title: "Writing a game in Haskell" by Elise Huard
talks.teaser: Shows how a solo developer builds a 2D top-down game in Haskell, covering OpenGL, reactive game loops, sound and animation.
talks.summary:
Elise Huard, a consultant who works mostly in Haskell, describes making her first video game in the language as a solo project. She starts with the design choices that shape a game, including format, perspective and a concept about a small alien that resurrects extinct creatures. The technical start covers opening a window with OpenGL and GLFW, setting an orthogonal view, and running a loop that polls input, updates state and renders each frame, with a short pause to hold about 60 frames per second.

Next she shows how functional reactive programming with the Elerea library turns the loop into signals over time, with per-level generators so state is discarded when a level ends. Textures are mapped through texture coordinates, and a run of unsafe number conversions cost her weeks of debugging. Sound runs through OpenAL on a separate thread, and animation moves from hand-coded sine motion toward keyframes exported from Blender. Chipmunk physics through hipmunk was possible but fit poorly with the reactive design, and her game did not need it.

Her lessons include that Haskell's types and pattern matching suit state machines and that native bindings mostly worked. Laziness calls for strict data structures in games, and finding a usable set of libraries took a long time. Compiled rebuilds slow iteration, and distribution, porting and performance stay open questions. She argues the hardest part is making the game enjoyable, and she plans an ebook to ease newcomers past the setup.

talks.title: "Spreadsheets for developers" by Felienne Hermans
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning "Spreadsheets for developers" by Felienne Hermans.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Felienne Hermans, an assistant professor at Delft University of Technology, argues that spreadsheets should be understood and treated as actual source code rather than mere data. She demonstrates that spreadsheets are Turing complete, solve typical software calculation problems, and suffer from common software maintenance issues such as a lack of documentation and long lifespans with multiple maintainers. Hermans pitches spreadsheets as a live, pure functional programming language and advocates for bringing established software engineering practices into spreadsheet environments.

### Key Topics
- **Spreadsheets as Programming Languages:** Hermans provides three core arguments for treating spreadsheets as code: they are used to solve software problems (often chosen because traditional software projects take too long and cost too much), they are Turing complete (demonstrated by implementing a Turing machine entirely within spreadsheet formulas), and they suffer from classic software problems.
- **Advantages of the Spreadsheet Paradigm:** Spreadsheets offer live programming without explicit compilation steps, enforce pure functional semantics where formulas only produce outputs from cell inputs without side effects, and act as a ubiquitous computing interface used across many disciplines.
