- **Implementing Algorithms in Excel:** Hermans walks through implementing the selection sort algorithm in Excel using native functions (`MIN`, `MATCH`, `INDEX`, `OFFSET`) and conditional formatting as a visual debugger. She then refactors the implementation into readable, novel-like code using space-based intersection syntax, constants, and dynamic named ranges powered by `ROW` and `INDIRECT`.
- **Software Engineering Tools for Spreadsheets:** Based on her PhD dissertation and work at the Spreadsheet Lab, Hermans introduces two Excel plugins designed to assist end-user developers: Bumblebee (a formula refactoring tool) and Expector (a test suite generation and test coverage visualization tool).

### Technical Details
- **Turing Completeness and Sorting:** Hermans showcases a Turing machine where each row represents an iteration of the tape. For selection sort, she tracks minimum values and swaps using `MATCH` and `OFFSET`. She eliminates hardcoded cell coordinates by using dynamic named ranges that evaluate Excel formulas containing `INDIRECT` to reference preceding rows.
- **Bumblebee:** An Excel 2010 plugin that parses spreadsheet formulas and suggests automated rewrites, such as replacing `SUM(...) / COUNT(...)` with `AVERAGE(...)`. It also features a domain-specific rewrite language enabling power users to specify custom refactoring patterns across ranges, worksheets, or whole workbooks.
- **Expector:** An Excel plugin that inspects spreadsheets for informal ad-hoc assertions (e.g., `IF(SUM(...) <> 100, "error", "ok")`), parses passing and failing heuristic outputs (such as text keywords or smiley faces), converts them into formalized regression test suites, and calculates visual test coverage across dependent cells.

### Takeaways
Hermans concludes that spreadsheet creators are programmers who lack the tooling standard in modern software engineering (such as IDEs, linters, refactoring tools, and test suites). Applying software engineering principles and specialized tooling to spreadsheets improves code maintainability, correctness, and auditability in critical settings like finance.

talks.title: "Haste: Full-Stack Haskell for Non-PhD Candidates" by Erin Swenson-Healey and James Cooper
talks.teaser: Hands-on samples show web developers how Haste compiles Haskell to JavaScript for DOM work, storage, Ajax, canvas, and FFI.
talks.summary:
Two industry web developers frame Haskell as alluring for safety and types yet hard to approach without formal computer science training. They position Haste, Anton Eklund’s Haskell-to-JavaScript compiler and browser API library, as a practical on-ramp: install via Cabal, run haste boot, import the Haste standard library, and compile small programs that drive familiar browser behavior without diving into compiler theory or large-app architecture.

The core of the session is example-driven and deliberately imperative. After a minimal syntax refresher (functions, currying, map, lambdas) shown beside JavaScript equivalents, they walk through hello world, DOM manipulation and events on a cat image demo, local storage save/load, Ajax with pattern matching on responses, and HTML5 canvas animation. They cover bidirectional FFI—ccall with an external JavaScript file versus inline ffi strings—and exporting Haste functions into a global namespace for plain JavaScript callers. Debugging advice favors console logging over stepping through generated JavaScript; testing splits pure Haskell tested with GHC and hspec from browser-facing code, with a warning that arbitrary-precision integers in GHC tests may overflow in JavaScript. They close with hackage packaging via haste inst, a wish list (source maps, higher-level DOM APIs), and pointers to community projects.

Practitioners without a PhD should treat the talk as a confidence-building cookbook: lean on online courses such as CIS 194, copy the low-level API patterns first, backfill theory later, and keep imperative JavaScript mental models handy while learning.

talks.title: "Clojure in Unity 3D: Functional Video Game Development" by Ramsey Nasser and Tims Gardner
talks.teaser: Shows how Clojure runs inside the Unity engine, with live REPL scene editing and components written in Clojure.
talks.summary:
The speakers start from why game development is hard: inputs are unusual, state changes constantly, frame rates must stay high, and most tooling is C++. They wanted Clojure's dynamic, REPL-driven workflow and persistent data structures inside Unity, a widely used engine. Their first plan was to run the Clojure CLR port on Unity's Mono, but Unity ships an old Mono build, so they made a small set of focused edits to the Clojure CLR code and got it running inside the editor and in exported games.

They then demonstrate a REPL connected to the Unity scene graph, creating cubes, spheres and lights live. A hydration library converts Clojure maps into Unity game objects and components and back again. Its populator functions are generated by reflecting over roughly 81 component types at build time, so no reflection happens at runtime. The talk also covers a component macro that defines Unity components in Clojure. It needed a custom special form because Unity requires class-based inheritance, and Unity's message methods such as Awake, Start and Update are matched by name. Terrain and dungeon generators written by an outside developer illustrate what the approach makes possible.

The speakers stress that the code is pre-alpha and undocumented, and that it relies on workarounds such as commenting out reader-writer locks. A future Unity Mono upgrade may break it. They close with ideas that persistent data structures make practical: snapshotting and dehydrating a scene for debugging, constraint-based level generation, and speculative AI that tries actions on cloned world state before committing one.

talks.title: "Mesos: The Operating System for your Cluster" by David Greenberg
talks.teaser: Explains Mesos as a cluster operating system, covering its offer-based scheduling, existing frameworks and when to build your own.
talks.summary:
David Greenberg, an engineer at Two Sigma, opens with a familiar problem: people sharing one machine or one Hadoop cluster end up waiting on each other. He argues that Mesos acts as an operating system for a data center and maps Linux ideas onto it. Containers provide isolation, a fair scheduler divides capacity among applications, and launch and kill calls hide networking details. Docker serves as the package manager.

A distributed system on Mesos is called a framework, and its coordinator is called a scheduler. Greenberg then covers frameworks that need no code: Jenkins for elastic build capacity, Hadoop clusters that start in seconds, Marathon as a highly available init system, Chronos as distributed cron with job dependencies, Aurora for phased rollouts at Twitter, and Spark for in-memory analysis. Mesos sends resource offers instead of fixed task specifications, and it uses two-level scheduling, where Mesos allocates resources and each framework picks its own tasks.

For custom work, bindings exist for several languages, but most users only need existing frameworks. Two Sigma built its own because its workload has nearly a hundred users and a queue too long to clear in a day. In the Q&A, he described planned reverse offers for preemption and persistent offers for storage. The takeaway is to build a framework only when off-the-shelf options cannot meet your scheduling needs.

talks.title: "You can be a kernel hacker!" by Julia Evans
talks.teaser: Shows how learning Linux kernel basics, system calls and tools like strace can make everyday programming easier.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that Linux kernel programming is within reach for ordinary developers, and that understanding the operating system pays off even for those who never write kernel code. The speaker describes the kernel as the layer that handles hardware, networking, file systems and memory, and explains that programs ask it for work through system calls such as open and execve.

Much of the talk shows system calls being used to debug everyday software. With strace, the speaker looks at which files Chrome opens and how its sandbox processes are started, works out how an HDFS client talks to its server, and finds the shell command hidden behind a Ruby script at her job, all without reading the source. Perf is used to measure L1 cache misses, comparing a sequential array scan with a deliberately scattered access pattern. A deleted executable can also be recovered through /proc while a process still holds it open.

For getting started, the speaker suggests tracing a program and following a single system call such as chmod through the kernel source with a code search tool, reading Linux Weekly News, and building a small kernel module. Her demo module intercepts open and substitutes a different file for MP3s. She also describes writing a toy operating system and working through a series of graded kernel challenges. For a paid route, internships such as Google Summer of Code and the GNOME Outreach Program for Women accept kernel patches. The main takeaway is that the kernel is learnable and that knowing it makes you a better programmer.

talks.title: "Towards "annex", a Fact Based Dependency System" by Mark Hibberd
talks.teaser: See how time-aware facts and content-addressed artifacts shape annex’s approach to dependency management.
talks.summary: Mark Hibberd presents annex as a cross-language dependency manager built around a store of facts that can change over time. The talk explains how immutable world snapshots, precise queries, content-addressed artifacts, and integrations with existing tools support reproducible resolution while allowing new knowledge, such as test results or vulnerability reports, to affect later checks. Attendees learn how annex approaches source and binary substitution, distributed fact stores, trust, and dependency resolution, along with challenges still being worked through.

talks.title: "Shen: A Sufficiently Advanced Lisp" by Aditya Siram
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in "Shen: A Sufficiently Advanced Lisp" by Aditya Siram.

talks.title: "Ludicrous Speed: Designing For Performance on the JVM" by Cliff Moon
talks.teaser: Explains JVM memory layout, primitive-oriented libraries, and JIT-aware design for building fast large-scale analytics pipelines.
talks.summary:
The presentation reframes the familiar warning about premature optimization, arguing that modern hardware and mature VMs make thoughtful performance design part of maintainable engineering rather than an afterthought. Using mechanical sympathy as a frame, it walks through the memory latency hierarchy and locality of reference, then shows how the JVM splits work across stack, heap, and direct memory—and how boxed generics and pointer chasing often punish idiomatic Java collections.

The middle of the talk surveys practical escape hatches: HPPC for primitive-specialized maps and lists, the speaker’s FastTuple library for runtime schema generation and contiguous tuple storage, and live allocation comparisons against standard `java.util` structures and nested lists. Threading advice favors bounded thread pools fed by queues or disruptors over actor models on the JVM, with a nod to bytecode weaving costs. Benchmarking with JMH, JIT inlining limits, monomorphic versus polymorphic dispatch, escape analysis, and intrinsics such as `System.arraycopy` round out the tuning toolkit.

Demos quantify memory overhead for million-entry maps and tuple workloads; Q&A touches on measuring allocations with a Java agent, FastTuple’s lack of variable-length string support, and contention hidden behind UTF-8 string encoding. The takeaway is to design for caches and the compiler: prefer primitives where it matters, benchmark seriously, and structure code so HotSpot can inline hot paths.

talks.title: "etcd: distributed locking and service discovery" by Brandon Philips
talks.teaser: Walks through etcd's Raft design, HTTP API, cluster bootstrap, watches, TTL-based leader election, and production pitfalls.
talks.summary:
Brandon Philips introduces etcd, an open-source key-value store CoreOS built for highly available, sequentially consistent cluster configuration with an HTTP interface, watches, and runtime reconfiguration—gaps he saw in systems like Zookeeper when operating on elastic cloud infrastructure.

The talk walks through Raft leader/follower roles, bootstrapping five-node clusters via discovery.etcd.io, compare-and-swap semantics, revision-indexed reads versus wall-clock assumptions, optional linearizable reads, long-poll watches with truncated history, and fault tolerance under cloud latency. TTL keys synchronize deletion through the leader, enabling patterns used in Kubernetes and Fleet scheduling and in locksmith, a cross-cluster semaphore that throttles CoreOS reboots during rollouts.

He surveys ecosystem tools (Vulcan, confd, SkyDNS), outlines the standalone Go Raft library and Diego-style configuration changes, and closes with hard-won lessons: rolling CRCs on log files after bit flips and truncation, internally generated node UUIDs instead of hostnames, and tuning election timeouts for slow cloud fsync. Planned work includes MVCC, read-only proxy observers, and client abuse protection.

talks.title: "Time Series Data With Apache Cassandra" by Eric Evans
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning "Time Series Data With Apache Cassandra" by Eric Evans.

talks.title: "Jepsen II: Linearizable Boogaloo" by Kyle Kingsbury
talks.teaser: Explores how network partitions expose linearizability failures in RabbitMQ, etcd, Consul and Elasticsearch.
talks.summary:
This talk, the fourth in the Jepsen series, starts from the fact that distributed systems can delay, drop, duplicate or reorder messages, so a delayed reply looks the same as a lost one. It walks through consistency models, from linearizability to sequential consistency and serializability, and explains what the CAP theorem's consistency term specifically means. It then shows how Jepsen generates random operations while injecting faults, records the history, and checks it against a model with a linearizability checker, using state pruning and memoization to keep the search tractable.

Several case studies follow. RabbitMQ used as a lock service could grant the same lock twice during a partition, and its pause-minority mode still discarded a large share of acknowledged queue inserts. etcd returned stale values through its non-consistent reads, and Consul's fix for its leader issues was to shorten a timeout, with documentation updated to admit the lack of linearizability. Elasticsearch lost acknowledged writes under partitions, including cases where two primaries were accepted, and the speaker describes data loss seen in production after node reboots and shard rebalances.

The closing advice is practical. Ask how the system behaves under partitions, long garbage-collection pauses, and clock or timeout assumptions, and treat clients as part of the distributed system. Decide which data truly needs strong guarantees and which can be eventually consistent, then write fault-injection tests that check your system against its model, ideally as part of CI.

talks.title: "Dynamic programming at ease - with Grammars, Algebras, Products" by Stefanie Schirmer
talks.teaser: Explains algebraic dynamic programming, splitting candidates, scoring and choice into grammars, algebras and products.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces algebraic dynamic programming, an approach for writing dynamic programming solutions to combinatorial optimization problems without hand-building tables. The speaker starts with the classic four-step recipe, illustrated by a small money-changing counting example, and explains that recurrences become very hard to get right as tables grow to two or more dimensions.

The core idea is to treat candidate solutions as trees. Using a sequence alignment example, the speaker reverse engineers a final score of 42 back into the formula that produced it, showing a maximum choice pushed down through the tree. From this, the talk separates three parts: a tree grammar that generates candidates from the input, an evaluation algebra that scores candidates and makes choices, and an objective function. Swapping the algebra gives variants such as gap cost changes or local alignment. An RNA structure example prints a folding as dots and brackets using an algebra, while counting structures needs almost no extra code.

The speaker then covers products of algebras, which compute several analyses in one pass, such as the best score together with the best candidate, the number of co-optimal solutions, or results grouped by shape. Products also remove the need for a separate backtracking step and help check a grammar for ambiguity. Tools built this way cover RNA folding and alignment, along with matrix chain multiplication and satisfiability. The takeaway for a practitioner is that the creative modelling remains while the table bookkeeping is handled by a compiler, although the speaker notes that textbooks still use older recurrences and the method currently targets sequence-like data.

talks.title: "The Road to Akka Cluster, and Beyond" by Jonas Bonér
talks.teaser: Milestone consensus limits yield Akka Cluster gossip, convergence, quarantine, and split-brain handling.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by arguing that distributed computing is the default for modern applications, shaped by network latency, partial failure, and ambiguous node health. It compares lambda, von Neumann, and actor models for synchronization, distribution, and mobility, then walks through milestone results: FLP on consensus in asynchronous settings, CAP and its limits on linearizability, Lamport and vector clocks for causal time, and fault-detector tradeoffs including phi-accrual and SWIM-style quarantine and delegated probes.

The middle covers strong versus eventual consistency at a high level—Paxos, Raft, ZAB, and Dynamo-style epidemic gossip with consistent hashing—while noting sections skipped for time. The closing focus is Akka Cluster: actors and remoting, cluster membership rings, gossip with vector clocks, convergence and unreachable quarantine, leader-assisted coordination, randomized fault-detection probes, and split-brain responses via manual or automatic downing.

Practitioners should treat time, failure suspicion, and consistency as explicit design choices rather than hidden assumptions. The speaker points to aka.io, upcoming Akka HTTP and streams work, experimental data replication and Akka Raft modules, and a reference list for deeper reading on the papers cited.

talks.title: "Simulation Testing" by Michael Nygard
talks.teaser: Explores property-based simulation testing on live systems to expose failures that example-based suites often miss.
talks.summary:
Michael Nygard opens by sorting automated testing along example-based versus property-based approaches, white versus black box visibility, and why hand-picked unit examples often give thin coverage, brittle maintenance, and little assurance that correct parts compose into a correct system. He positions property-based testing as stating domain invariants and sampling inputs, then introduces simulation testing as that idea scaled to whole running systems: model behavior, generate a fixed action script up front, execute against the real target, capture outputs and internal state, and only afterward check global properties.

The middle walks through a multi-part pipeline—activity models such as weighted Markov user flows, generators that turn states into atomic actions, distributed runners, and validations expressed as queries over recorded results rather than per-step asserts. He illustrates the approach with the open source Simulant framework and Datomic-backed repeatability, including tricks to keep execution deterministic after generation-time randomness.

He closes with practical tradeoffs: model realism versus build time, run length versus insight, clock multipliers for load without outpacing the system, and lower long-term maintenance than shared scripted functional tests. A short Q&A covers exploring varied trajectories through state space, possible temporal validators, and running the same checks continuously in production-like environments.

talks.title: "Deterministic Memory Management for Managed Runtimes" by Aaron Bedra
talks.teaser: Shows why sensitive key material lingers in JVM heaps after encryption code runs, and what runtime fixes would be needed.
talks.summary:
Aaron Bedra opens by asking why critical crypto code such as TLS is not simply written in a managed language like Java, then narrows the talk to what happens to sensitive data inside the JVM runtime. He builds a small encryption service, first pointing out that his initial cipher choices and the missing message authentication step were flawed, and then exposes the code over HTTP as a soft HSM. The example encrypts and decrypts correctly in a basic sense, but the data is only safe at rest.

Using heap dumps and a simple query for byte arrays of the key's length and known byte values, he shows that the encryption key appears in many places in memory. Loading a key from a Java key store creates a secret key object holding a copy the developer cannot control, and clearing a local array with Arrays.fill is undone by the JIT optimizer when the array is never read again. Calling System.gc is only a suggestion and hurts performance. A JNI call to get a primitive array critical can force zeroing but adds overhead, and off-heap direct byte buffers help only partly, since wrapping them still creates heap objects and incoming data can spill.

He concludes that no current JVM approach is good enough and that key management remains unsolved. Possible fixes he raises include garbage collector regions for sensitive data, a language marker to request them, and libraries that accept buffers instead of copies, with Microsoft's SecureString offered as a precedent. He invites people to help prototype changes in OpenJDK and points to a repository of small examples for trying the heap behaviour themselves.

talks.title: "How types can turn a SQL interpreter into a SQL compiler" by Tiark Rompf
talks.teaser: Staging types specialize a Scala SQL interpreter into generated C that runs analytical queries far faster than interpretation.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by contrasting massive commercial and open-source database codebases with shifting bottlenecks as more data lives in memory, then motivates a minimal alternative: a SQL processor implemented in Scala in under roughly five hundred lines. Through live coding on workshop schedule data, the speaker evolves hand-written CSV parsing into relational algebra operators—scan, project, and filter—wired through a parser built with parser combinators and a tree-walking interpreter.

Performance on a multi-gigabyte Google Books n-gram file exposes interpreter overhead: tens of seconds versus MySQL load and query times on the same laptop. The core pivot applies partial evaluation and Futamura-style specialization via Lightweight Modular Staging: fields become staged representations while schemas and operator trees stay static, so each query yields specialized hash structures and tight loops. Generated C with memory-mapped input drops runtime to a few seconds, resembling the original low-level approach while retaining SQL ergonomics.

The talk closes with LegoBase, a larger in-memory engine compiling Oracle execution plans at runtime, TPC-H coverage in a few thousand lines, and benchmark comparisons showing large speedups over commercial and research systems. The takeaway for builders is that staged types let high-level query engines emit low-level, query-specific code without abandoning abstraction.

talks.title: "Cap'n Proto and Rust: Type Systems for Sharing" by David Renshaw
talks.teaser: Shows how Cap'n Proto schemas pair with Rust for zero-copy messages, safe lifetimes, and user-mediated app capabilities.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with Sandstorm, an open-source platform for installing sandboxed web apps on a personal server with minimal trust in each developer. Cap'n Proto is introduced as the mandatory communications layer that tracks authority flow and supports efficient, multi-language distributed computing, contrasted with XML, JSON, Protocol Buffers, and similar stacks.

The middle of the talk walks through a photo-album and image-analyzer example: schema definitions for images and detection results, generated Rust readers and builders, tagged unions for algebraic data, and pattern matching with forward-compatible handling of new variants. The speaker explains Cap'n Proto’s single in-memory and on-wire representation without separate encode/decode steps, then shows how Rust lifetimes statically prevent dangling pointers into message buffers—failures that have plagued C++ users—and how borrow rules block invalid returns.

The closing sections cover capability-based RPC: interfaces in schema, Rust tasks and channels implementing servers, unforgeable capability references, and a Sandstorm flow where apps publish services, the user approves connections via a power box, and only granted analyze calls cross sandbox boundaries. Implementations live in separate GitHub repositories, with brief Q&A on wrapping capabilities, endianness, message size, and optional fields.

talks.title: "Fast, secure, safe: the web that can still be" by Chris Morgan
talks.teaser: Shows how strongly typed languages like Rust can rule out web bugs such as header misuse and injection before code runs.
talks.summary:
Morgan argues that much of the modern web is built on dynamically typed languages that let bugs, slow responses and server sprawl pile up, and that stronger type systems can address all three. He frames the problem around tight deadlines and business pressure, then compares Ruby with Rust on startup time and request handling. In the Twitter case, a move from Ruby to Scala was expected to give about 10 times more throughput per server, and it reached about 50 times. He also cites server counts for sites on slower stacks and argues that longer compile times are often repaid by bugs caught earlier.

The middle of the talk turns to security and correctness. Using the DNT header, he shows that HTTP headers are usually handled as plain strings, and demonstrates a Rust library where each header maps to a typed value, so invalid input is rejected by the type system and two libraries can each read the same header as their own type. He then turns to templating and escaping, arguing that one escaping method cannot serve HTML, JavaScript and CSS, while typed templates and typed SQL parameters can rule out whole classes of injection at compile time.

He closes by suggesting developers experiment with Rust or another good type system, while admitting Rust is not yet production-ready for every case and that humans remain a weak link. In questions, he says a developer moving from Python can become fluent in Rust within months, and that parameterised queries prevent most SQL injection in PHP-style code unless queries are built from strings.

talks.title: "Taming the 9s" by Ariel Weisberg
talks.teaser: Shows how a database team cut worst-case latency by tuning Java garbage collection, moving data off heap, and hunting outliers.
talks.summary:
The talk examines long-tail latency, the rare slow outliers at high percentiles that averages and standard deviation tend to hide. It explains how a service level agreement should specify a percentile, a maximum, an arrival rate and a validity window, and why histograms give a fuller picture. The speaker then describes the constraints of VoltDB, an in-memory SQL database with a C++ storage engine and Java for procedures and coordination: Java garbage collection pauses, Linux noise and the hardware it runs on.

The middle covers the fixes. Young-generation collections were kept to single-digit milliseconds by shrinking the working set, and old-generation collections were avoided by moving data off heap into memory-mapped files and direct buffers, with a wrapper that catches double frees and use-after-free. Outliers were then hunted with canary timers, watchdog threads, rate-limited logging, a distributed heartbeat monitor and Java Flight Recorder. Performance runs were automated and charted against a 90-day history so regressions could be tied to code changes. Linux-level issues, such as blocking page-cache writes and transparent huge pages, were worked around or disabled.

The end result was that tail latency at the highest percentiles fell from several hundred milliseconds to under 80 milliseconds during a failed-node rebuild, and to about 25 milliseconds in regular one-hour runs. The speaker stresses that no single fix exists. Practitioners take away the value of measuring with histograms, instrumenting for outliers, and designing tasks so that large or deferred work does not stall responses.

talks.title: "Benchmarking: You're Doing It Wrong" by Aysylu Greenberg
talks.teaser: Covers common benchmarking mistakes involving caches, JVM warmup, coordinated omission, and weak statistics, with practical fixes.
talks.summary:
The speaker frames performance benchmarking as a way to hit latency goals and compare against industry practice, then walks through a flawed pattern: repeatedly hitting one image, starting the timer immediately, running three trials on a dev box, and reporting only the mean. That setup confuses cache hierarchy effects (application cache versus S3, L1/L2/L3 and TLB), JVM warmup and steady state, periodic noise such as garbage collection, and mismatched hardware between test and production, including power scaling.

The middle of the talk builds on machine behavior and statistics. Dataset size changes which cache level dominates latency; instruction-cache misses from large binaries can swamp unrelated tuning. Too few samples hide convergence; means mislead when distributions are skewed or multimodal, so medians, percentiles, and histograms matter. Outliers and coordinated omission show missing observations when clients back off during slow responses, which erodes SLA reasoning at scale. Workload mistakes include optimizing non-critical code, benchmarking thumbnails instead of production-sized assets, and ignoring memory pressure and cross-service interference.

The closing guidance stresses modeling real user actions and goals, using profiling, production instrumentation, aggregating logs, and distributed tracing, and treating microbenchmarks cautiously (clock resolution, dead-code elimination, growing work per iteration). The speaker cites Flume maintenance experience and real colleague incidents, and points to JVM microbenchmarking resources and a related talk on coordinated omission.

talks.title: "Coder Decoder: Functional Programmer Lingo Explained, with Pictures" by Katie Miller
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of "Coder Decoder: Functional Programmer Lingo Explained, with Pictures" by Katie Miller.

talks.title: "Turning the database inside out with Apache Samza" by Martin Kleppmann
talks.teaser: Argues that databases should be built around an append-only event log, with derived views rebuilt by stream processing.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with the stateless application tier, which pushes shared mutable state into the database. The speaker compares this with the actor and channel models that avoid shared-memory synchronisation inside a single process, and asks why the same idea is not applied system-wide. He then reviews four database features: replication through a change log, secondary indexes, application-level caching, and materialized views. Replication and secondary indexes are presented as well-handled derived data. Hand-managed caches are described as prone to invalidation and race problems, and materialized views as a sound idea that adds load to the database.

The core proposal is to make the replication log a first-class element. Writes are appended as immutable facts to a log such as Apache Kafka, and read-optimised views are built by consuming that log with a stream processor such as Apache Samza. Any view can be rebuilt by replaying history, which removes cache invalidation and cold-start concerns, while serial processing per partition avoids synchronisation races. The speaker argues this also helps analytics, point-in-time queries and recovery from human error, and that normalisation choices can be made per view.

The talk closes by extending the model to clients: changes flow through the views to devices via subscriptions such as WebSockets, instead of request/response REST calls, so user interfaces update as data changes. In the questions, the speaker discussed delivery errors and counting, read-your-writes consistency for asynchronous views, schema evolution with formats such as Avro, access control at subscription time, and key-based log compaction. The takeaway is to treat data as a stream of facts and derive other state from it.

talks.title: "Visualizing Persistent Data Structures" by Dann Toliver
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding "Visualizing Persistent Data Structures" by Dann Toliver.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Dann Toliver explores the complexity and nuances of data structures, focusing on distinguishing abstract data types from concrete implementations, understanding persistent data structures, and developing intuitive ways to inspect them. Toliver highlights that much of the difficulty surrounding data structures stems from accidental complexity and confusing terminology. To address this, he proposes framing data structures through relatable metaphors—such as collectible cards—and demonstrates a visual rendering technique in JavaScript that maps in-memory data states to color-coded pixels, enabling developers to reverse-engineer and observe data structure behaviors in real time.

### Key Topics
- **Abstract vs. Concrete Data Structures:** The distinction between an API or protocol (abstract, such as stacks, queues, and generic lists) and the underlying memory representation (concrete, such as linked lists or tries). Toliver notes that terms like 'array' can refer to both, and provides heuristics (e.g., adjectives, proper names, or acronyms like PATRICIA denoting concrete structures).
- **Ephemeral vs. Persistent Structures:** Ephemeral structures reflect only the current state, whereas persistent structures retain history. Toliver covers fully persistent structures (which allow branching and building off historical states) and confluently persistent structures (which allow merging branches, analogous to Git).
- **Structural Sharing via Trees and Tries:** Achieving persistence efficiently without copying entire datasets is made possible by organizing data into trees or tries. By copying only subpaths down to modified leaves and updating pointers back up, operations achieve logarithmic time and space overhead.
- **Data Structure Cards:** Inspired by early 20th-century baseball scorecards and trading cards, Toliver (with slide assistance from Henry Faber) presents data structure cards as a mental model to compare operational costs, tradeoffs, and composition rules (e.g., pairing stack and queue APIs with linked lists or batched queues).
- **Visualizing Internal State:** Using a custom JavaScript rendering pipeline that flattens objects, evaluates values, and colorizes them into pixels, Toliver demonstrates how runtime behavior and memory layouts can be visualized dynamically without inspecting the underlying source code directly.

### Technical Details
- **Batched Queues:** Implemented using two stacks (one for pushing, one for popping). When the pop stack empties, items are transferred and reversed from the push stack. While operating in amortized $O(1)$ time, it incurs periodic latency spikes that make it unsuitable for hard real-time systems.
- **Hash Array Mapped Tries (HAMT):** Uses sections of a hashed key (such as 5-bit chunks) to index into arrays of size 32, providing efficient branching down to the stored values.
- **Visual Analysis of Mori vs. Immutable.js:**
  - Toliver compares vector and map implementations from Facebook's Immutable.js and Mori (ClojureScript data structures brought to JavaScript).
  - The visualization renders values as colors (e.g., lower sequential numbers in red, higher in green) and structural steps/nesting depth as black dots or bands.
  - Immutable.js vectors display 32-element banding consistent with HAMTs and show accumulator tails that pop up levels when full.
  - Mori exhibits batched queue behaviors and distinctive pointer structures when popping, which may help optimize for expensive JavaScript array shifts and garbage collection overhead.
  - Map structures visualized with random versus sequential keys reveal distinct hashing characteristics and structural branching behaviors between the two libraries.

### Takeaways
Toliver concludes that developers do not need complex tools to gain deep insights into data structures. A simple visual pipeline—even in a few pages of JavaScript—can render dynamic memory states, uncovering internal mechanics, branching, and performance characteristics in running applications. He suggests future visualization extensions, including discrete Fourier transforms to observe update frequencies, taking into account data locality, and computing differential state displays.

talks.title: "All of this has happened before, and it will all happen again." by Mark Allen
talks.teaser: Early Fortran, Lisp, Algol, and COBOL design goals are traced through papers and books, with lessons that still apply today.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with Jean Sammet’s 1972 observation that programming was widely seen as an art rather than a science, and invites the audience to weigh that question while reviewing primary sources on the first wave of high-level languages. It sketches computing before 1954—octal coding, Grace Hopper’s A-0 compiler, and widespread doubt that automatic programming could yield efficient machine code—then walks through stated design goals and what actually shipped.

FORTRAN’s team aimed to eliminate tedious coding and cut debugging cost; delivery slipped from a six-month promise to a 1957 release, yet the compiler’s optimizations surprised practitioners even as early syntax checking and language features fell short. Lisp pursued symbolic reasoning, lists, recursion, and garbage collection born from list operations, with homoiconic programs emerging unexpectedly from Steve Russell’s eval work. Algol united European and ACM efforts toward mathematical readability and implementation-independent specification, contributing blocks, booleans, call-by-name, and Backus-Naur Form, while COBOL’s English-heavy, portable design arose under brutal timelines, manufacturer politics, and government pressure.

Closing points stress that languages did not fully solve programmer error, efficiency, or cognitive load; those tensions remain human as much as technical. The speaker urges readers to mine the bibliography—Dijkstra’s “Humble Programmer” among them—and to notice how decades-old motivations still mirror modern toolchain debates.

talks.title: "The Eight Fallacies of Distributed Computing" by Stephen Asbury
talks.teaser: Eight common beliefs about distributed systems get dissected via outages, latency, breaches, and deployment mistakes.
talks.summary:
Stephen Asbury revisits Peter Deutsch and James Gosling’s eight fallacies of distributed computing as deliberate wrong beliefs, meant to surface subconscious assumptions programmers bring to messaging, replication, and deployment. He walks fallacy by fallacy: backhoes and cut fiber undermine “the network is reliable,” millisecond trading links and the “500 mile email” tale illustrate that latency is never zero, and a Tibco primary-backup timeout story shows latency includes garbage collection on peers—not just wire delay.

He contrasts “bandwidth is infinite” with Hadoop’s move-the-computation-near-data pattern, then treats “the network is secure” with Heartbleed, large retailer breaches, and password-driven leaks. CAP partition tolerance, Fog Creek spanning-tree loops, brittle three-server deploy scripts, privileged administrators from Edward Snowden to Terry Childs, Netflix–ISP peering fees, and heterogeneous mobile clients each anchor later fallacies through pop-culture slides and audience prompts.

He closes by warning that CORBA, RMI, and other “hide the network” stacks bake the fallacies in, and that cheating with permissive timeouts masks real failures. Practitioners should trust physics, read documentation skeptically, and test on imperfect networks rather than assuming homogeneous, cost-free, admin-managed perfection.

talks.title: "Function Passing Style: Typed, Distributed Functional Programming" by Heather Miller
talks.teaser: Shows how sending serializable functions to stationary data can simplify distributed systems and fault recovery.
talks.summary:
The talk presents function passing, a model for distributed programming that the speaker describes as a dual to message passing with actors. Where actor systems keep behavior in one place and move data between them, this approach keeps immutable data in place inside containers and sends serializable functions to it. The speaker frames it as an early research experiment rather than a finished framework, built on earlier work in Scala on compile-time serialization and on spores.

Spores are functions whose environment must be declared explicitly in a header, so the compiler can check that everything captured is serializable and fixed when the spore is created. Each data container is reached through a reference offering two operations. Apply is lazy: it queues the function and returns a new reference representing the result on a remote machine. Send forces the queued chain to run and returns a future with the final value. A distributed list example walks through a map, another map and a reduce, showing that the chain of spores forms a lineage. Because that lineage can be serialized, stored and replayed, it can rebuild lost pieces after a failure, and adjacent operations can be composed to avoid extra passes over the data.

In the question period, the speaker compared the model with Spark, noting that Spark does far more but is loosely typed, and said side effects such as logging are not prevented. The practical takeaways are to keep the design stateless where possible, to make communication and latency explicit rather than hiding remote calls behind local ones, and to treat the lineage as the recovery mechanism. The speaker also invited feedback on use cases the model cannot handle.

talks.title: "The challenges and benefits of a functional reactive frontend" by Ian Davis
talks.teaser: A production walkthrough explains how ClojureScript, React, and Om simplify mutable-state pitfalls and large interactive UIs.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames front-end work through the distinction between easy and simple, then argues that JavaScript’s design favors accessibility over predictable structure. Mutable globals, hoisting, and untracked shared state make bugs hard to localize; linting helps only partway. The speaker positions ClojureScript as enforceable guard rails—lexical bindings, macros, lazy sequences, and schema-checked data extraction—while still calling ordinary JavaScript libraries when needed.

On the UI side, imperative DOM updates multiply work whenever application data changes, as illustrated with topic feeds where a single boolean toggle must appear consistently across the page. React is described as a referentially transparent map from data to virtual DOM, with minimal real DOM diffs; Om layers a single application state atom, cursors for localized updates, and reference-equality shortcuts via shouldComponentUpdate.

Drawing on Prismatic’s early production use of Om, the talk reports simpler architecture, strong expressiveness in few lines, a drop from roughly 26,000 to about 5,000 lines after migration, and two-to-four times faster To-do MVC benchmarks versus Backbone, alongside a steeper learning curve and thinner community support. Practitioners are urged to pilot React on a small surface before committing to a full rewrite.

talks.title: "EventRacer: Finding Concurrency Errors in Event-Driven Applications" by Pavol Bielik
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of "EventRacer: Finding Concurrency Errors in Event-Driven Applications" by Pavol Bielik.

talks.title: "Concurrency Options on the JVM" by Jessica Kerr
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for "Concurrency Options on the JVM" by Jessica Kerr.

talks.title: "PureScript (Maybe This Time We Get JavaScript Right)" by Bodil Stokke
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of "PureScript (Maybe This Time We Get JavaScript Right)" by Bodil Stokke.

talks.title: "Controlling Time and Space: understanding the many formulations of FRP" by Evan Czaplicki
talks.teaser: Maps the many formulations of functional reactive programming, from Elm's static signal graphs to arrowized and higher-order designs.
talks.summary:
Elm's designer untangles the many meanings of functional reactive programming. He starts with first-order FRP as used in Elm, where signals are wired straight to the outside world, such as mouse position and key presses, and are transformed, accumulated over time and merged into a graph. Static, always-running, synchronous graphs make architecture, hot swapping and time-travel debugging practical.

Later variants relax these constraints. Higher-order FRP lets the graph be reconfigured through a join operation, but switching to a signal that needs its full past can cause unbounded memory growth, so research restricts the types to rule that out. Asynchronous data flow, found in Reactive Extensions and Bacon.js, lets signals end and be flattened, trading away default synchrony and raising questions about hot and cold signals. Arrowized FRP, seen in Yampa, netwire and Elm's automaton library, uses automata detached from world inputs, which suits structuring code.

No variant wins outright, since each trades features against others. The closing advice is to judge them by the properties an application needs: synchrony by default, asynchrony for network or disk work, reconfigurable graphs, direct world inputs, debugging tools, and code that stays clear as it grows.

talks.title: "Building Real-time Systems with Open Source Technologies" by Gian Merlino and Fangjin Yang
talks.teaser: Walks through a real-time analytics stack built from Kafka, Storm, Hadoop and Druid for querying fresh event data.
talks.summary:
The speakers, both engineers at the ad-tech startup Metamarkets, describe building a real-time analytics stack for interactively exploring large volumes of time series event data. They explain why relational databases, precomputing key-value stores, and plain Hadoop MapReduce queries fell short for business intelligence style aggregation at scale. They then describe adopting Druid, an open source column store that rolls up data, splits it into immutable time-based segments, and answers queries quickly across many nodes.

The middle of the talk layers in streaming components. Events arrive through an HTTP API into Kafka, Storm cleans, transforms and joins them using windowed reductions, and real-time indexers feed Druid so queries reflect events within seconds. The speakers are candid about the trade-offs: late corrections are hard to apply, and short join windows leave a small share of records unmatched. To address this they add a Hadoop batch path that reprocesses older data, a lambda-style design, with the Druid broker merging results from all three layers.

The closing section lists the open source projects and connectors that glue the pieces together, and sums up the roles: Kafka for transport, Storm and Hadoop for preparation, Druid for serving. The takeaway for practitioners is that a fresh, queryable analytics pipeline can be assembled from existing open source parts. A Q&A covers Druid's pluggable deep storage, with S3 or HDFS as the usual choices, and its lack of precomputation, which it replaces with fast scanning and filtering.

talks.title: "Production Prolog" by Michael Hendricks
talks.teaser: Shares lessons from running Prolog in production, covering its debugger, useful libraries, and the trade-offs the team found.
talks.summary:
This talk is an experience report on using Prolog, a logic programming language, in production for about eighteen months at a shop that runs many languages. The speaker starts with the basics: the execution model rests on unification, backtracking and lazy search, code is stored as data in a database, and one predicate can often run in several directions, so a short relationship definition can answer many different questions.

The middle of the talk covers the tooling and libraries the team relies on. SWI-Prolog was chosen largely for its open-source development tools, especially a debugger that lets you edit code mid-run and retry a failed call from an earlier point. The speaker also points to Mercury's bisecting debugger as an idea that could be brought to Prolog. Other examples include a static checker that team libraries can extend, packs for function-style syntax and optional runtime type checks, constraint-based date and calendar logic, and concurrency wired up automatically from data flow. Saved states, which bundle a compiled program into one file for deployment, and a reversible bencode parser round out the examples.

The closing section lists the downsides: a small ecosystem with fewer tools such as static analysis, a learning curve for developers used to imperative code, failure messages that give little explanation, hard-to-debug macros, and performance costs that only occasionally surface. The takeaway is that the language rewards declarative thinking, but a team has to be willing to invest time before it pays off.

talks.title: "Retaking Rules for Developers" by Ryan Brush
talks.teaser: Developers learn to embed production-rule patterns in ordinary code via an open-source Clojure rules engine.
talks.summary:
Ryan Brush opens with the 1970s expert-systems movement: codifying domain knowledge as rules, Charles Forgy’s efficient production-network matching, and real wins such as NASA mission control—followed by hype, Lisp machines, and a second AI winter. He argues the recovery went wrong when vendors pitched rule engines to business users instead of engineers, yielding awkward workarounds such as Java buried in spreadsheets and little real simplification.

He reframes rules as a first-class control structure inside normal code: typed inputs, constraints, automatic wiring, unification across related facts, truth maintenance, and actions—mapping the classic working-memory match-act cycle onto functions developers already write. Using fabricated healthcare examples, he demonstrates Clara on Clojure: macro-defined rules, composable inferences, immutable sessions, performance comparable to Drools, explainability traces, and experimental graph visualizations that help users see why a conclusion fired.

Practitioners should treat rule authoring as development, favor libraries that live in the host language idioms, and use rule structure as data for tooling and shared understanding with domain experts—while avoiding the “floor plan versus blueprint” trap in deeply complex policy domains. The closing caveat: do not encode logic as Java in Excel.

talks.title: "Distributed SWI-Prolog Development" by Anne Ogborn
talks.teaser: Explains sandboxed Prolog pensions for federated queries across servers, with APIs, demos, and a growing ecosystem.
talks.summary:
Web systems today push developers through many proprietary endpoints, which makes federated reasoning across machines awkward and encourages huge families of similar AJAX APIs. The talk frames that pain and introduces recent SWI-Prolog work around Torbjörn Lager’s pensions library from the University of Gothenburg, where remote callers receive sandboxed Prolog interactors instead of grinding through each host’s custom feed.

The middle walks the architecture: applications expose pension VMs, foreign servers request an id and run nondeterministic queries, and nested pensions isolate per-user or per-character knowledge bases. The sandbox application strips unsafe predicates, analyzes code before execution, and allows explicitly blessed access to storage or databases. Prolog and JavaScript clients share a small event-loop API; a SWISH demo runs eight queens via create, ask, and next. Module import and multifile safe-primitive declarations show how operators publish APIs without handing out shell or halt.

Closing sections tie pension_rpc to federated RDF-style queries, mention Cleopatra as background reading, and survey a fast-moving ecosystem—WebSockets, hub.pl broadcasting, collaborative editors, chat, and teaching tools—with public demo hosts, version notes, and slide resources. Takeaways are where the tooling stands, how sandbox boundaries are enforced, and why the approach speeds iterative Prolog web development even as interfaces keep changing.

talks.title: "Analyzing Rap Lyrics Using Python" by Julie Lavoie
talks.teaser: Walks through scraping and word-counting rap lyrics in Python to probe whether they can measure sexism.
talks.summary:
Julie Lavoie, a programmer and hip-hop fan, starts from a question: could a program measure sexism in rap lyrics and rank artists against each other? She warns the audience up front about heavy profanity and violent content. A short history of East Coast, West Coast and Dirty South rap explains why different styles bring different subject matter, and why that matters for the data.

The lyrics came from a fan-annotated lyrics site covering about 2,700 songs by roughly 32 artists. Automated scraping failed because the pages load more songs only on scroll, so she saved the full song lists with a browser extension and parsed the saved HTML in Python. Counting one target word per song, averaged across each artist's catalogue, put most rappers at one to three uses per song, with a few at three or more. Raw counts proved too blunt: stop words, artist nicknames, guest verses and stemming errors with slang all skewed the results. Removing common words exposed each artist's distinctive vocabulary, such as the recurring themes of some East Coast artists compared with the political focus of socially conscious groups.

The closing section outlines next steps: looking at how often words tied to women appear near violent words within short windows of text, and asking whether lyrical sexism has changed over time or tracks with gangster or club-oriented rap. The practical takeaway is that a simple metric is a starting point, and that a good-enough scraper that finishes is often more useful than a perfect one.

talks.title: "Web Apps without Web Servers" by Richard Feldman
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning "Web Apps without Web Servers" by Richard Feldman.

talks.title: "Practical Fractals in Space" by Michelle Brush
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in "Practical Fractals in Space" by Michelle Brush.

talks.title: "Democratizing Hardware" by Chris Williams
talks.teaser: Argues that JavaScript and open hardware put robot building within reach of anyone, from kids to developers.
talks.summary:
Chris Williams argues that hardware stays out of reach for many software developers, who fear damaging components. He wants robotics to be as simple as building a web page. He makes the case for JavaScript, whose callback style suits single-threaded microcontrollers and whose serial-port libraries send commands to boards over USB. A live demo has a small humanoid robot named Hexy go to its zero position, get up and dance.

He traces the nodebots movement, which has grown into an international day of local build groups. Johnny-Five, a library that models a robot as a tree of parts, lets one program run on boards such as Arduino, Spark, BeagleBone and Imp by swapping only the lower layer. Examples included a $35 wooden robot built from laser-cut open designs and a $50 3D-printed quadcopter. A planned drone demo was dropped when its battery failed.

He links a shrinking pool of expert hardware knowledge, as experienced workers retire, to a need for open, accessible tools. His advice is to teach children and adults through makerspaces and Maker Faires, starting with Arduino because setup takes about a minute, compared with about 20 minutes for a Raspberry Pi. Choose boards by need, such as Wi-Fi, battery life or mesh networking. Build with a child, he urges.

talks.title: "Nashorn: implementing a dynamic language runtime on JVM in 2014" by Attila Szegedi
talks.teaser: Explains how Nashorn speeds up JavaScript on the JVM using optimistic typing and on-the-fly recompilation.
talks.summary:
Nashorn is the JavaScript runtime that ships with Java 8. It runs on the JVM and is developed in the open in the OpenJDK repository. The talk explains why a fast dynamic language runtime is hard to build and reports on the performance work done for later Java releases, with benchmark comparisons against the older Rhino engine and against V8. The speaker concedes that V8 is still faster in many cases, but says number-crunching performance had caught up considerably.

The middle of the talk covers the main optimizations. Nashorn compiles separate versions of a function for different parameter types. It uses optimistic typing, assuming values are integers and recompiling when that assumption fails, and it widens integer arithmetic to long when overflow occurs. To deoptimize running code without relying on VM-specific tricks, it throws an exception, catches it at the call site through an invokedynamic try-catch combinator, and resumes execution in a generated continuation method. Static type inference within a function, careful handling of local variables across try and catch blocks, and dead-code elimination reduce how often recompilation is needed.

The closing section looks at future plans. The team wants to extract these techniques into a reusable library, a kind of LLVM for dynamic languages on the JVM, with an intermediate code representation that sits between JavaScript and bytecode. The main takeaway is that the JVM's strict bytecode verification shapes how dynamic language engines must be designed.

talks.title: "Building Analog Displays for Your Data" by Larry Ogrodnek
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for "Building Analog Displays for Your Data" by Larry Ogrodnek.

talks.title: "Liberating the Smalltalk lurking in C and Unix" by Stephen Kell
talks.teaser: Shows how Unix debug metadata and liballocs can unite compiled C with dynamic introspection without conventional FFI.
talks.summary:
Stephen Kell contrasts the Unix style of compiling, linking, and editing programs from outside a running process with Smalltalk’s integrated, in-image programming. He argues both camps underestimate how much dynamism already exists in Unix: attaching debuggers through proc, dynamic linking, injecting changes into a live X11 clock, and reading relocation records in a hello-world binary illustrate infrastructure that evolved in the 1980s.

He criticizes foreign-function interfaces as brittle, repetitive, and poor at discovery, then reframes languages as views onto shared code and data rather than isolated worlds. The liballocs project wraps C compilation to preserve DWARF-like metadata efficiently and preloads a runtime that can describe arbitrary pointers, stack or heap allocations, and linked libraries. A hacked Node demo calls printf and explores newly loaded libzip without manual FFI bindings.

Future work includes emitting the same metadata from JavaScript engines so dynamic code is visible process-wide, and decomposing garbage collection into tracing, freeing, and moving across malocs, VM heaps, and hybrid regions. Q&A touches ownership metadata, comparison to COM/IDL, and cross-process introspection.

talks.title: "Art.js: Transfigure Data to Create 21st Century Art" by Sarah Groff Palermo
talks.teaser: Explores data art as a creative practice distinct from data visualization, with examples built in JavaScript and D3.
talks.summary:
Sarah Groff Palermo, a designer who taught herself to code, argues that data art differs from data visualization. Traditional visualization seeks comprehensive datasets to communicate what has been found, while data art works with small, fragmented, personal data to express an experience. She gives four reasons to make it: understanding oneself, understanding the systems people live within, broadening one's data skills, and because it is fun.

The examples fall into two groups. The literary approach treats data like a novel. First Chapters draws novel openings as connected sentence lengths, a taxi project replays one New York cab driver's shift, Quantified Breakup charts an artist's divorce through bubble and line charts, and the speaker's own timeline of neglect shows unread books decaying over time. The language-based group includes Patatap, a keyboard-driven sound animation, a patent generator that writes applications for classic literature, and Matthew Connelly's analysis of redaction patterns in government documents to suggest FOIA requests.

For process, she recommends sketching, gathering rough data even by hand, testing repeatedly, and sharing the work. Ideas can start from a personal interest, from a tool such as D3 layouts or the topo time library, or from translating an artwork into data. In the question period she suggested guiding viewers from a simple overview to an interactive sandbox, so artistic framing and statistical depth can coexist.

talks.title: "A core.async Debugging Toolkit" by David McNeil
talks.teaser: Shows how a stepping library makes core.async concurrency visible and repeatable, and catches a hidden deadlock.
talks.summary:
The talk presents a Clojure library that wraps core.async, the concurrency library, so code running inside a controlled step machine can be paused, inspected and replayed. Normally, threads and channels are hard to see into. The library lets a developer advance execution one core.async operation at a time or run until everything stops, and it records the state of threads and channels, including every item that has passed through a channel, so the run can be visualized.

Scheduling is the central idea. Rather than letting the runtime choose freely, the machine runs threads in series and makes each choice itself, using either a fixed scheduler or a pseudo-random one seeded for repeatable runs. Timeouts fire only when told to, and conditional breakpoints stop execution when a predicate over the machine state holds. A worked example had two workers that deadlock only when a third thread wins a race. Running a testcheck property over many seeds found a failing seed, which reproduced the deadlock on demand.

The speaker also described a production use: a team runs a thin, proof-of-concept slice of the library to model Amazon Simple Workflow executions, moving a running workflow between hosts by recreating its machine state. The approach gives up performance, since execution is serialized, but it offers control and determinism. Practitioners would take away that deterministic replay can turn hard-to-reproduce race conditions into repeatable tests.

talks.title: "Highly Concurrent Services with Finagle & Clojure" Sam Neubardt
talks.teaser: Shows how to build concurrent Finagle RPC services in Clojure without messy Scala interop.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Finagle, an open source Twitter library for highly concurrent RPC services on the JVM, built on Netty. Its core abstraction is the future, which can be pending, successful or failed, so a missing reply is not treated as an error. Services are modeled as functions from a request to a future response, letting clients and servers stay non-blocking, and the library supports several protocols including Thrift and HTTP.

Next, finagle-clojure acts as a translation layer so Clojure code can use the Scala API without explicit interop. The speaker uses javap to show how one Scala source file compiles into many JVM classes, which is why the wrapper hides those details. A demo builds a small Thrift service from a project template, with Scrooge generating the Java code. The client then chains map, flatMap, handle and rescue, gathers parallel requests with collect, sets per-request timeouts, and runs blocking calls such as a Cassandra driver on a future pool.

The closing section covers planned work: Zipkin tracing support, wrappers for more Finagle clients such as Redis and MySQL, helpers for writing asynchronous code on Netty, and better type checking. In questions, the speaker said the wrapper returns plain Finagle futures to stay compatible with other Finagle libraries, and that one production service had run since January. The takeaway is that Clojure developers can build RPC services while keeping blocking work off the Finagle runtime.

talks.title: "Vulpes: A functional approach to deep machine learning on the GPU" by Rob Lyndon
talks.teaser: An open-source F# stack trains deep belief networks on the GPU using typed parameters and composable kernel launch pipelines.
talks.summary:
The presentation introduces Vulpes, an open-source deep learning project written in F# for GPU-backed matrix work the speaker argues is impractical on a CPU alone. After situating modern recognition benchmarks from large image search through MNIST and ImageNet, the talk walks from perceptrons and XOR limits to backpropagation, then to Hinton-era deep belief nets, greedy layer-wise pre-training, and restricted Boltzmann machines with contrastive divergence-style updates, momentum, and readable parameter names instead of Greek symbols.

The middle connects those ideas to implementation: visible and hidden units as zero-to-one signal vectors, bias folded into weight matrices, and F# discriminated unions so learning rates and momentum are typed rather than raw integers. GPU programming is framed through AlloyCuba—quotations that compile CUDA kernels at runtime, strongly typed device pointers, and a CUDA monad that handles scatter, gather, and launch so successive kernels chain without repeated host-device copies. A live pass through the training loop shows forward and backward launches, positive and negative phases, and periodic gathers for progress reporting.

Practitioners leave with a conceptual map from classical nets to belief-net pre-training plus fine-tuning, and a concrete pattern for expressing belief-net iterations as composable GPU programs in a statically typed functional style. The speaker points to the public repository and discusses licensing for Cubase, operation graphs, and where to find foundational papers and talks.

talks.title: "DOMStep: Audio Synthesis, AI and a JavaScript Dance Party" by Jamison Dance
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding "DOMStep: Audio Synthesis, AI and a JavaScript Dance Party" by Jamison Dance.

talks.title: "Typed Clojure in Practice" by Ambrose Bonnaire Sergeant
talks.teaser: Shows converting Clojure to Typed Clojure, occurrence typing, HMaps, and CircleCI's production adoption story.
talks.summary:
The presenter opens with a hands-on bug hunt in untyped Clojure: a recursive summarize function overflows the stack when rest is used instead of next, and later throws null pointer exceptions on empty vectors until seq refines the control flow. Converting the same code to Typed Clojure shows how local type inference demands top-level annotations, surfaces function-application errors by comparing expected domains to actual arguments, and validates fixes before runtime.

After tracing Typed Clojure from an honors thesis and core.typed through a crowdfunded development year, the talk surveys IDE support in Cursive, cross-project annotation harvesting, and Vim hover typing. It then explains occurrence typing on conditionals, HMaps for keyword maps, multimethods over expression trees, variable-arity polymorphism for map-like functions, and Java interop where reference types are non-nullable unless explicitly unioned with nil.

A CircleCI case study describes roughly fifty thousand lines of Clojure with a substantial typed subset, unchecked annotations for unsupported idioms, and HMap-heavy APIs such as encrypt-key-pair that block leaking raw private keys. The roadmap covers ClojureScript checking, better gradual-typing error messages at typed–untyped boundaries, and library annotation efforts; Q&A notes that types are not fed back into the compiler and that schema bridging remains incomplete.

talks.title: "Write the Other Half of Your Program" by Jason Hemann and Daniel Friedman
talks.teaser: Shows how stylized Racket functions translate into miniKanren relations via live refactoring and a mostly automated transform tool.
talks.summary:
Two presenters outline a workflow for turning ordinary functional programs into miniKanren relations while keeping most of the authoring in familiar function form. They open with a hands-on introduction to miniKanren: syntactic unification, the run operator, fresh variables, conde for nondeterministic choice, and disequality constraints. A list append example illustrates how a two-argument function becomes a three-place relation that can concatenate lists, infer missing pieces, or verify structure from a single definition.

The middle of the session walks through manual "miniKanronization" of set utilities written in Racket style—custom membership as a predicate, cond reshaped into non-overlapping conde clauses, car and cdr broken into named variables, and recursive calls extended with output arguments. They stress properties that survive reordering of clauses and contrast pattern-matching helpers that either fall through or fail hard. When union is run relationally, duplicate elements appear in answers because inputs were described as sets without enforcing uniqueness in the function; they argue that fixing assertions on the functional side and re-running translation is easier than debugging the relation alone.

They finish with an automated transform-from-functions pipeline (chiefly editor operations plus a small amount of manual tuning), acknowledge proof-of-concept limits around nested recursive calls, and mention a compact microKanren core beneath the macro layer. The practical lesson is a round trip: write constrained functions, generate relations, test relational modes, then refine the function and regenerate.

talks.title: "Consistency without consensus in production systems" by Peter Bourgon
talks.teaser: Explores consensus-free consistency via CALM, ACID 2.0, and CRDTs, using SoundCloud's Roshi for high-volume time-series feeds.
talks.summary:
Distributed programs must cope with partitions, delays, duplicates, and unavailable endpoints—behavior that single-machine intuition does not prepare you for. The speaker traces idioms from RPC through CORBA to the CAP tradeoff, contrasting CP consensus stacks (Paxos, Raft, ZooKeeper) with AP data stores and the messy early era of ad hoc eventual consistency.

He introduces the CALM principle and ACID 2.0 (associative, commutative, idempotent, distributed) as a foundation for conflict-free replicated data types, walking through a G-set style play counter and read repair via union and symmetric difference. A DevOps-style argument follows: embrace network failure modes instead of hiding them, and reshape the problem when theory demands it.

At SoundCloud the team moved from fan-out-on-write toward fan-in-on-read streams, defining a Roshi set CRDT merged from add and remove sorted sets with timestamp scores. Redis shards sit behind pool, cluster, and farm layers with hybrid reads, targeted read repair, and a background walker that scans the keyspace in about eight hours. Operators gain deterministic merges under replay and duplication; clock trust and tombstoning on delete remain explicit limits.

talks.title: "Idris: Practical Dependent Types with Practical Examples" by Brian McKenna
talks.teaser: Shows how dependent types in Idris can prove algebraic laws, check inputs and bound computational cost at compile time.
talks.summary:
Brian McKenna opens with the seL4 kernel, a formally verified kernel running on a drone. He contrasts its workflow, with proofs in Isabelle, a high-level Haskell layer and hand-written C, with older attempts at extraction from Coq, where Peano numbers, unsafe coercions and a shell script patching generated output made the process fragile. Idris is presented as a dependently typed language that compiles to executables, and he shows idium, a window manager written in Idris with a small Objective-C layer for the macOS API.

The middle of the talk is live coding. He starts with a bitwise OR on a single bit type and proves it is associative, letting proof search fill in simple goals and using the tactic language to rewrite with the earlier result. He then extends the proof to bit strings. Next, he defines a binary character type indexed by its value, so a string only typechecks as binary digits when evidence for every character is supplied, and a bad literal fails to compile. The final example tracks computation cost in the type. A cost-indexed monad adds costs on bind, a recursive day-by-day computation is shown to have factorial cost, and a bounded Fin type prevents running it beyond six.

He closes by arguing that proofs can raise confidence in algorithms, types can encode input rules and resource limits, and examples can be checked by the compiler instead of by separate tests. He notes that the cost bind is asserted rather than verified, that Idris has known bugs, and that it should not yet be used in production.

talks.title: "Testing Distributed Systems w/ Deterministic Simulation" by Will Wilson
talks.teaser: Shows how deterministic simulation lets engineers reproduce and hunt rare distributed system bugs that random failures hide.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from why distributed systems are so hard to debug. Timing, packet loss and disk behavior are outside the programmer's control, so a failure may vanish on the next run and a fix cannot be verified. The speaker presents deterministic simulation as the answer: an entire cluster runs inside a single process, with networks and disks replaced by simulated versions whose randomness comes from a seeded generator, so every run can be repeated exactly.

He describes the pieces this requires. Code is written in Flow, a C++ extension that lets developers write actor-style concurrency while running single-threaded. Simulated networks inject latency, dropped connections and read errors. Test files pair a workload, such as a ring-of-keys invariant that exposes atomicity or isolation failures, with faults like clogged connections, rolling reboots, configuration changes, simulated failing disks and swapped hardware. Techniques such as bugification, time acceleration and correlated failures modeled on heavy-tailed statistics help surface rare bugs faster than customers would. Some runs are executed twice to catch hidden nondeterminism, and millions of simulations run each night.

The talk ends with the limits. Debugging often falls back to print statements, the simulation is only as accurate as the team's understanding of operating systems and hardware, and third-party code such as ZooKeeper cannot be simulated. A physical test cluster of programmable power supplies complements the simulator and exposed bugs in outside software. The main takeaway is that determinism makes bugs reproducible and fixes verifiable, but it should be paired with real-world testing.

talks.title: "Type Systems - The Good, Bad and Ugly" by Paul Snively and Amanda Laucher
talks.teaser: Walks through what separates good type systems from bad ones, from Curry-Howard and dependent types to syntax and culture.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the shared goal of writing better software and argues that type systems vary widely in quality. The speakers frame a good type system as one that makes the desired path the effortless one, and that lets developers make illegal states unrepresentable. They note that even developers in dynamically typed languages reason about types in their heads, so the real question is how much of that reasoning a checker can take over.

The middle of the talk covers the features that separate strong systems from weak ones. Sum types with pattern matching, product types, parametric polymorphism, extensibility and type inference are discussed, along with the Curry-Howard correspondence, which treats a type as a theorem and a function as its proof. A dependent-type example on vector append shows code that fails to compile when sizes do not line up. Weak systems are illustrated with stringly typed code, false positives from structural typing, and type systems that mainly block correct programs and force casting. Syntax, tooling and community are presented as equally important to the type system itself.

The talk closes with an informal hierarchy of type systems, moving from basic correctness through expressivity to dependent types, and points to the Lambda Cube as a way to compare them. The takeaway for practitioners is to ask what is at stake when a program misbehaves and to pick type-system strength to match. The speakers also say that dependent-type languages are not yet production-ready, so the field still has considerable room to develop.

talks.title: "The Sociology of Programming Languages" by Leo Meyerovich
talks.teaser: Examines how programming languages spread and get adopted, using survey and repository data and diffusion-of-innovation theory.
talks.summary:
The talk treats programming languages as social systems rather than purely technical artifacts. The speaker argues that designers often optimize for speed, safety and expressiveness, while adoption depends on how easily people can try a language, see others using it and fit it into existing work. Drawing on an ecological model of adoption, languages spread through overlapping groups of users and grow niche by niche.

To test these ideas, the speaker's group analyzed a survey of about 13,000 people rating languages, a follow-up survey of roughly 15,600 developers about their real projects, a smaller online-course sample, and about a quarter million SourceForge projects. Languages clustered into niches: Java spread broadly, while Scheme appeared in narrower areas such as build tools. Usage formed a long tail, suggesting room for smaller languages to sustain communities. Respondents mostly chose languages for libraries and familiarity with their team or existing code rather than speed or safety. Most people knew about four languages well, mainstream languages took months to learn, and C and C++ took years.

The talk then draws on diffusion of innovation research, including a 1980s safe-sex campaign that enlisted visible opinion leaders and gave them observable markers. Trialability, observability, relative advantage and compatibility emerge as useful lenses for language design, with examples such as Stack Overflow's network effects.
